items.title: RustGIS
items.text:
A fast, free and open-source GIS written in Rust for mapping, analyzing and sharing geospatial data.

RustGIS runs natively on Windows, macOS and Linux, and in your web browser. Local files are processed on your machine; web data sources, AI providers and plugins can use the network. Map operations are commands you can script from the command line, Python or the AI Assistant.

Try it in your browser Download Get started Compare

RustGIS with the World Atlas sample in the Equal Earth projection.

items.title: Highlights
items.text:
• Your data, any source

    GeoJSON, Shapefile, GeoPackage, GeoParquet, GeoTIFF, LiDAR, Zarr and desktop File Geodatabases; live PostGIS, MySQL, MariaDB and SQL Server databases on the desktop; public data from STAC catalogs, Overture Maps and open-data portals. Save and browse reusable data connections; open supported QGIS projects. Data · Web Data · Formats

  • Cartography and 3D

    Graduated colours, curved line labels, stacked line symbols, publication layouts and map series; a 3D globe, projection presets and supported EPSG/ESRI systems, terrain and extrusions, and maps of the Moon, Mars and other worlds. Cartography · Maps · Layouts

  • Analysis

    SQL selection, overlay and proximity tools, guided workflows, ModelBuilder, imagery tools, spatial join, kriging, zonal statistics, data-cube time series and trends, and over 1,000 tools through the optional GeoLibre/Whitebox suite. Analysis

  • Editing

    Create features and edit their vertices with snapping and templates, keep attributes valid with domains, subtypes and rules, check topology, and undo project edits. Editing

  • AI Assistant

    Ask about your data or tell the map what to do. Choose a model provider or sign in with ChatGPT; approve file, network and plugin operations before they run. Project edits are undoable. AI Assistant

  • Scriptable and extensible

    rustgis-cli and the rustgis Python package run engine commands and render maps; MCP connects AI agents to headless sessions or the open app. The Script pane completes commands, parameters, layers and fields. Plugins add tools, commands and assistant skills, with sandboxed WebAssembly or desktop-only process runtimes. Command Line · Python · MCP · Plugins

items.title: A tour
items.text: Symbology and tables. Graduated colours, with the selection synced to the table. AI Assistant. Ask about your data or tell the map what to do. Analysis. A tool gallery, the Tools pane and 1,000+ GeoLibre tools. ModelBuilder. Chain tools on a node canvas and run them in one go. Rasters. GeoTIFF and COG, with stretch, RGB and shaded-relief styles. Globe and projections. A 3D globe, Equal Earth, Robinson and supported EPSG/ESRI systems. Terrain. Tilt the map and drape it over elevation. Other worlds. The Moon, Mars and nine more bodies, on their own basemaps. Extrusion. Stand features up by a field, lit and shaded. Web basemaps. XYZ, WMS and vector tiles, and MapLibre styles. Web Data. STAC, Overture Maps, NASA and open-data portals, where the map is. Time Slider. Step dated features and imagery through time. Layouts. Map frames, legends, scale bars, map series and PDF export. Plugins. Install tools, commands and assistant skills from plugins.rustgis.app. Dark mode and the View tab's effects, panes and linked views. Projects. Start blank, from the World Atlas sample, or open a project.

items.title: Acknowledgements
items.text:
RustGIS stands on the work of many projects and their authors. Thank you to all of them. If your work is missing here, please open an issue.

Disclaimer

RustGIS is primarily built with Claude Opus 5.5, an AI model by Anthropic, working under human direction and review. Its results are tested, but check them for your own use, and please report anything that looks wrong.

items.title: The GIS that came before
items.text: QGIS and ArcGIS Pro set the expectations of a desktop GIS that RustGIS is measured against, and GDAL those of reading geospatial formats. MapLibre defines the style specification RustGIS implements a subset of for vector tiles, and PROJ the coordinate operations it follows. Zarr defines the chunked-array format read by RustGIS's raster provider.

items.title: Geoprocessing
items.text:
The optional GeoLibre tool suite (geolibre-rust, built on whitebox-wasm) brings more than 1,000 raster, vector, LiDAR and hydrology tools, after John Lindsay's WhiteboxTools.

The suite runs separately from RustGIS: through an optional downloaded geolibre program on the desktop and command line, or a WebAssembly runner loaded on demand in the browser.

items.title: Data
items.text:
• Natural Earth (public domain) for the sample data.
  • The EPSG Geodetic Parameter Dataset of IOGP, PROJ's database and Esri's projection-engine-db-doc for coordinate systems.
  • OpenFreeMap, whose free vector tiles and styles (such as Liberty) draw RustGIS's vector basemaps.
  • OpenStreetMap and its contributors, Overture Maps and Protomaps for basemaps and open map data.
  • The scientific colour ramps of matplotlib (Viridis and family, Cividis), Google (Turbo), Fabio Crameri's Scientific colour maps and cmocean.

ATTRIBUTION.md lists every asset with its source and licence.

items.title: Rust crates
items.text:
RustGIS is written in Rust, built on these crates, among others:

Crate For egui and eframe, wgpu The interface, natively and in the browser, and the GPU map tiny-skia, lyon, ab_glyph, image, epaint_default_fonts CPU drawing, tessellation, text, images and fallback interface fonts geo, geozero, shapefile, a5 Geometry, formats and the A5 grid proj4rs, crs-definitions Coordinate systems tiff, laz GeoTIFF and LAZ Apache Parquet and Arrow, flatgeobuf, rusqlite (SQLite), calamine, csv, roxmltree GeoParquet (Arrow writes test fixtures), FlatGeobuf, GeoPackage, spreadsheets, CSV and XML postgres, mysql, tiberius, rustls PostgreSQL/PostGIS, MySQL/MariaDB, SQL Server and TLS miniz_oxide, brotli-decompressor, ruzstd, zstd, lz4_flex, weezl, zip Compression for rasters, Zarr chunks, map tiles, GeoParquet and plugin packages wasmi Sandboxed WebAssembly plugins ureq, serde HTTP and JSON PyO3, wasm-bindgen, rfd The Python package, the web app and file dialogs

The full dependency list is in Cargo.toml, the crate and application manifests, and Cargo.lock. Dependency licences and copyright notices are collected in THIRD-PARTY-LICENSES.txt, with a separate list for Python.

items.title: Architecture
items.text:
RustGIS is a layered Cargo workspace. Lower layers never depend on the UI, which keeps the engine scriptable and the front end swappable.

Layer Crate Job L0 rustgis-geom Coordinates, extents, Web Mercator, geodesic distance/area, scale L1 rustgis-data Features, typed attributes, vector and spreadsheet I/O, SQL where clauses, LiDAR, rasters and EPSG reprojection; indexed file and remote data providers; live PostGIS, MySQL/MariaDB and SQL Server providers on the desktop; optional GDAL and DuckDB programs (see Data formats) L2 rustgis-map, rustgis-analysis Layers, symbology, labeling, camera, basemaps and web tile layers; geoprocessing tools L2 rustgis-tiles Web map tiles: XYZ/TMS/WMS raster tiles, Mapbox Vector Tiles, PMTiles and MBTiles archives and a subset of MapLibre styles; a cache that fetches in the background (worker threads natively, the browser's fetch on the web) L3 rustgis-render tiny-skia renderer, label placement, font discovery, map and layout export, and UI-independent GPU scene preparation L3 rustgis-geolibre The GeoLibre tools as geoprocessing tools: run by the optional geolibre program natively, by geolibre-rust's WASI runner in the browser L3 rustgis-plugins Plugins: sandboxed WebAssembly modules, desktop process plugins and assistant skills packages; .rgplugin packages and the plugin registry L4 rustgis-engine Session, undo, command registry, projects, sample project L5 rustgis-assistant The AI Assistant: provider request/response formats, conversation loop, command tools, skills and agent integration; native HTTP transport and local agent/MCP connections, with browser I/O supplied by the web app L6 rustgis-ui-egui Ribbon, panes, map view, dialogs and the optional wgpu map backend apps rustgis, rustgis-cli, rustgis-web, rustgis-python Desktop app, command line, browser (WebAssembly), and the PyO3-backed rustgis Python package tooling xtask Workspace checks, third-party licence notices and web service-worker generation

items.title: Everything is a command
items.text:
Engine actions are CommandSpecs with an id, label, ribbon location, shortcut, parameter description, an enabled check and a run function. The ribbon, keyboard shortcuts, command search, CLI and Python dispatch engine commands through Session::run. UI-only commands (ui.*) live in crates/ui-egui/src/lib.rs; engine commands never open dialogs.

The UI exports big_split_menu for a large ribbon control with independent, accessible primary and alternatives buttons. Pass the primary command id and parameters separately from the menu closure; menu choices run their own commands and never replace the primary action. The primary's enabled state comes from its command, while menu_enabled controls the arrow independently. Use ui.push_id when placing repeated controls whose order can change. Keep whole-button dropdowns for choices without a clear everyday default.

For tab purposes, pane shortcuts and choosing controls, follow the ribbon guidelines.

Mutating commands snapshot the project for undo and restore it on an error or escaped panic. View-only commands do not take undo snapshots. Undo and rollback cover project state, not external effects such as files already written.

Plugin commands (plugin:<plugin>/<command>) dispatch through Session::run too; their project changes form one undo step. WebAssembly plugins reach the session through permission-checked requests. Process plugins use the same host protocol but are not sandboxed (see Plugins).

items.title: Never crash
items.text: Production code forbids unsafe Rust. Library crates deny Clippy's unwrap, expect, panic, unimplemented, todo and unreachable lints. Readers treat file contents and command parameters as hostile. Session::run and analysis::run catch escaped panics as a last resort. Hostile-parameter tests exercise engine commands and built-in geoprocessing tools; some file-writing and network commands are skipped.

items.title: Never silent
items.text: When a reader, writer, tool or command can't represent something, approximates it or drops it, it says so in a notice: what was lost, how much and where. Notices go through Session::notify, which the app shows, the CLI prints and Python returns from take_notices. Commands pass on the notes readers return, and geoprocessing tools report theirs in ToolResult::messages. A result that would be unusable is an error instead. Older code doesn't yet report every loss; each one found is treated as a bug.

items.title: Pure Rust
items.text: RustGIS's engine and apps are written in Rust and run without GDAL, PROJ or any other GIS library installed. GDAL, DuckDB and the geolibre program are optional extras: on the desktop, when they are installed, RustGIS calls them to read more formats, run DuckDB queries and run the GeoLibre tools. In the web app the GeoLibre tools run in the browser instead, through geolibre-rust's WASI runner. Some dependencies do compile C code into the build: the Zstandard decoder (zstd-sys, desktop and browser), SQLite (libsqlite3-sys through rusqlite, desktop), the TLS cryptography libraries (aws-lc-sys and ring, desktop) and GeographicLib's geodesic routines for the azimuthal equidistant projection (proj4rs-geodesic, desktop). Building them needs a C compiler; building the web app needs clang for Zstandard.

items.title: Secrets
items.text:
Services::secrets gives the desktop app its OS credential store: the login Keychain on macOS, Windows Credential Manager (persistence Local), and the Secret Service (GNOME Keyring, KWallet) over pure-Rust D-Bus on Linux and the BSDs. It is None in the browser, and the session's store is None on the command line and in Python unless --use-saved-secrets / use_saved_secrets asks for it. Only rustgis-keychain uses an OS API; other crates use only the rustgis_data::secrets trait. CLI and Python call rustgis_engine::prefs::opt_in once to read the desktop's preferences, load its saved connections without writing changes back, and install the lazy store. The generic rustgis_data::secrets::Reporting wrapper warns once on failure and stops retrying an unavailable backend. The preferences module also owns desktop writes, refuses to overwrite unreadable or malformed preferences, and returns read errors for callers to report without preference values. Assistant API keys additionally require the desktop's Remember preference and matching provider/address; an environment key wins. The CLI uses shared assistant preference names and only reads a saved API key for a prompt, never for account management or model listing.

  • Keys. The service is RustGIS. The account is owner/name with a lowercase owner (for example assistant/<provider> or connection/<id>); each feature defines its own. Values are opaque strings in Secret.
  • Errors, not fallbacks. A missing or locked store, or a refused prompt, returns a SecretError to show the user. Never write the secret anywhere else instead.
  • No leaks. Secret's Debug is redacted and it has no Display. Never log a secret, and never put one in command parameters, History, workspace recordings or assistant tool output.
  • Blocking. A call can wait on an OS prompt or D-Bus. Make it on a user action or a worker thread, never every frame, and keep the value in memory for the session. Don't access one account from two threads at once. Python releases the GIL for commands, rendering, data reads and lock waits. A process-wide native-operation gate preserves serialization across Python sessions because driver activations are process-global; a per-session mutex protects each session's state. Diagnostics are logged only after both locks are released. Non-throwing rustgis logging cannot replace an operation's result or original error. The Assistant queues legacy API-key migrations once at startup and serializes its keychain reads, writes and deletions on a worker. An existing keychain key takes precedence over a legacy preference. The preference is removed only after a successful read of that key or a successful migration write; new API keys are never written to desktop preferences.
  • S3 request snapshots. The registry lock protects selection of the exact live login and the requested bucket's explicit-grant status. Copy only that login and grant boolean, not the grant list; parse and validate addresses and prepare signatures outside the lock. Keychain calls and network I/O never run under the registry lock.
  • Earthdata Login token. rustgis_tiles::earthdata::set_secret_store gets Services::secrets from RustGisApp::with_services, and prefs::opt_in's store for the command line and Python. earthdata.login with remember keeps the token at earthdata/token, and without it (or when the store refuses it) deletes the remembered one; earthdata.logout always deletes it. The token is read back once per store given, on the first request to an Earthdata data host or when the NASA Earthaccess pane opens (on a worker), never over a token typed this session. An expired token is deleted, not sent, and the pane and the refusal message ask for a new one. The token and its store are process-global, like the session token before them.
  • ChatGPT sign-in. The desktop app gives its store to chatgpt::set_secret_store at start. The keychain keeps only each registration's refresh token, chatgpt/<client_id>/<subject>, with the rev its entry in chatgpt-auth.json names (any other is out of date and never used), without the access and id tokens, to stay within Windows Credential Manager's 2560 bytes of UTF-16 (a real refresh token's length is not verified yet). Access and id tokens stay with the process that got them; a process without one renews first. The keychain is read only to renew, sign out or remove, under the file's store-lock (and, to renew, the renewal-lock), so a rotating refresh token is never used twice. The entry's keychain flag is set before the first keychain write and cleared after a delete, so removal never strands an item. Tokens the keychain couldn't keep stay in memory for the session, with an empty rev; a new sign-in never replaces one the keychain holds. Tokens from an earlier version's file leave it only after the keychain has taken them. Config::from_env never reads the sign-in, and a configuration's key is a marker (chatgpt::SIGNED_IN), never a token: chatgpt::send authorizes each request. The Assistant reads the sign-in on a worker (startup, switching to the provider, after a failed request) bound to the selection that started it, and requests wait for it.
  • macOS. The system asks again for access when the app's code signature changes, which happens with unsigned or re-signed builds.
  • Tests. Use MemorySecrets, and MemorySecrets::failing(..) for error paths. The shared backend's smoke test is #[ignore]d: cargo test -p rustgis-keychain keychain_round_trip -- --ignored.

items.title: Quality gates
items.text:
cargo xtask ci        # fmt, clippy -D warnings, tests, layering check

cargo xtask layers checks that workspace dependencies point to lower layers and that crates below L6 do not directly depend on UI crates such as egui, eframe, rfd, wgpu or winit. The browser build is a separate CI gate:

cargo build --locked --target wasm32-unknown-unknown -p rustgis-web

Keep platform-specific I/O behind native target gates or the UI's Services callbacks. The web app supplies asynchronous file pickers, downloads, HTTP requests and the GeoLibre WASI runner. See Contributing for the remaining CI gates and developer tasks.

items.title: How to Cite
items.text:
If you use RustGIS in your research, teaching, software, or other work, please cite it. Citations help others find the project, recognize the contributors, and support the continued development of free and open-source geospatial software.

RustGIS is archived on Zenodo, which mints a Digital Object Identifier (DOI) for every release. The DOI above is the concept DOI: it always resolves to the latest version. To cite a specific version instead, open the Zenodo record and copy the DOI shown for that release.

items.title: Recommended citation
items.text: Wu, Q., Rincón Albarracín, J. G., Filho, E., Hofbauer, D., Fitzgerald, M., & Strebel, D. (2026). RustGIS: A fast, free and open-source GIS in pure Rust for mapping, analyzing and sharing geospatial data. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23633281

items.text:

items.title: Citation metadata file
items.text: The repository ships a CITATION.cff file, so you can also use GitHub's "Cite this repository" button (in the sidebar of the repository page) to copy a ready-made APA or BibTeX entry. Reference managers such as Zotero and tools like cffconvert read the same file.

items.title: Citing dependencies
items.text: RustGIS builds on many open-source projects. If your work relies heavily on a particular component, please consider citing it as well. See the Acknowledgements page for the full list of projects that make RustGIS possible.

items.title: Command Line
items.text:
rustgis-cli runs RustGIS engine commands headlessly, using the same ids as the app. Window and pane commands (ui.*) belong to the app and are not available in a private CLI session.

rustgis-cli commands                  # every command id with its parameters
rustgis-cli tools                     # geoprocessing tools
rustgis-cli info data.geojson         # project and layer summary as JSON
rustgis-cli render data.geojson map.png --basemap ocean --width 1600 --height 900
rustgis-cli render data.geojson map.png --tiles 'https://tile.openstreetmap.org/{z}/{x}/{y}.png'
rustgis-cli logo icon.png --size 256  # the app icon as a PNG
rustgis-cli plugins                   # installed plugins (also: browse, get, install, uninstall…)
rustgis-cli skills                    # the AI Assistant's skills (also: add, remove, enable, disable)

commands lists the engine commands and their JSON parameters; tools lists geoprocessing tools and their parameters. See Installation for the CLI packages, and The command line in Docker for its image.

items.title: Rendering
items.text:
render <data|project> <out.png> opens a data file or saved project and exports its map. It defaults to 1600 × 900 pixels at 96 DPI; --width, --height and --dpi change those. A data file is zoomed to its full extent; a project keeps its saved view. --tiles accepts an XYZ template, vector tiles or a MapLibre-style address.

--worldview auto|default|china chooses the disputed borders in the built-in countries and world outline, for render, run and the other subcommands. auto follows RUSTGIS_WORLDVIEW, else the system time zone and locale.

items.title: Chaining commands
items.text:
run starts with an empty project. --sample loads the World Atlas sample, --project <path> opens a project, and repeatable --data <path> adds files, in that order. Repeat --cmd to run commands in order; --save <path> saves the resulting project:

rustgis-cli run --sample \
  --cmd 'gp.run={"tool":"countPoints","params":{"polygons":"Countries","points":"Cities"}}' \
  --cmd 'layer.symbology={"layer":"Countries_Summarize","type":"graduated","field":"point_count"}' \
  --cmd 'bookmark.go={"name":"Europe"}' \
  --cmd 'share.exportMap={"path":"europe.png","dpi":192}' \
  --save atlas.rgis

Each non-null command result goes to standard output as JSON. --cmd 'id' runs a command with no parameters; otherwise use --cmd 'id={json params}'. What a command reports beside its result, which the app shows in its status bar, goes to standard error.

Pass --use-saved-secrets to load the desktop app's saved connections and let connection.login and project sources use their remembered database passwords and S3 keys. It also lets ask use the API key the app remembers, only for the same provider and address when the environment supplies no key, and the ChatGPT sign-in kept in the system keychain, and lets files on NASA's Earthdata data servers use the Earthdata Login token the app remembers (earthdata.login with "remember": true remembers one from here, too). Command parameters and environment variables take precedence over saved secrets. Connection changes aren't saved back to the desktop preferences. The flag applies to run, ask, mcp, render and info; for example, rustgis-cli run --use-saved-secrets --cmd connection.list. Without the flag, nothing reads the keychain or desktop preferences, including in CI. Reads are lazy: a command that doesn't need a secret neither touches the keychain nor emits a keychain warning. If the keychain is unavailable (a headless server or locked keyring, for example), the run continues without that saved secret and warns once on standard error. An unreadable or malformed preferences file produces a separate warning when opting in; missing preferences are normal. On macOS, Keychain may ask once per item whether rustgis-cli may read it; Always Allow stops that question for the executable and item.

Nothing waits on run the way a window does, so a long run takes the bounds the app's panes give it on a thread: a trend over a data cube (cube.trend) may compare up to 20 billion pairs, ten times what the Script pane allows, and a trend's or a summary's STAC search up to 10,000 items, where the app takes 2,000. A trend or a summary over time (cube.reduce) prints its progress to standard error (cube.trend: 42%; a line every tenth when standard error isn't a terminal). ask and mcp keep the Script pane's bounds, as an assistant or an MCP client waits on them, and so does Python. See Trend analysis.

Installed plugins load first (--no-plugins skips them), and --plugin <file or folder> (repeatable) loads one more for this run only. Their commands and tools have ids like plugin:vector-toolkit/hexagon-grid:

rustgis-cli run --sample --plugin vector-toolkit-0.1.0.rgplugin \
  --cmd 'gp.run={"tool":"plugin:vector-toolkit/hexagon-grid","params":{"input":"Countries","size":300}}' \
  --cmd 'share.exportMap={"path":"hexagons.png"}'

plugins install and plugins get also prepare a Python plugin's environment; plugins prepare <id> prepares it on demand, reusing it if it is already ready. --registry <URL> points plugins browse and plugins get at another registry.

Rasters work the same way:

rustgis-cli render dem.tif dem.png
rustgis-cli run --data dem.tif \
  --cmd 'raster.symbology={"type":"shadedRelief","ramp":"Terrain","zFactor":1.5}' \
  --cmd 'raster.info={}' \
  --cmd 'share.exportMap={"path":"relief.png","dpi":192}'
A map exported by rustgis-cli, with no window open.

items.title: Asking the AI assistant
items.text:
ask gives the AI Assistant one request. It loads data like run, then the model answers and acts on the project through commands; --save keeps the result:

export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=…            # or OPENAI_API_KEY, GEMINI_API_KEY, OPENROUTER_API_KEY, …
rustgis-cli ask --sample "Which 5 countries have the largest GDP?"
rustgis-cli ask --sample "Buffer the cities by 200 km and label them" --save buffered.rgis
rustgis-cli ask --data parcels.geojson --provider ollama --model qwen3:8b "Summarise the fields"
rustgis-cli ask --models --provider openai          # the provider's models
rustgis-cli ask --login                             # sign in with ChatGPT to use your ChatGPT plan
rustgis-cli ask --sample --provider chatgpt "Zoom to Tokyo"

The provider is --provider (anthropic, openai, chatgpt, gemini, openrouter, ollama, custom), else RUSTGIS_ASSISTANT_PROVIDER, else the first with a key in the environment, else the app's saved provider when --use-saved-secrets is set, else Ollama. ChatGPT sign-in is used only when that provider is selected. Account management and --models do not read saved API keys: model listing uses environment API keys (or the selected ChatGPT sign-in), whereas a prompt can use a remembered API key. --model (or RUSTGIS_ASSISTANT_MODEL) and --base-url override the defaults. The answer goes to standard output and each command the assistant ran to standard error. Commands that read or write files or use the network are declined unless you pass --yes; plugin commands, scripts, tasks, models and replacing the project are always declined here. --trace log.txt appends each request and response body (never the headers, which carry the key) to a file; the bodies can contain your data and prompts. --login prints a browser sign-in URL so --provider chatgpt uses your ChatGPT plan. --another-account starts a new registration, --accounts lists saved registrations, --account <client-id> selects one, --remove-account <client-id> signs it out and forgets it, and --logout signs out. Without --use-saved-secrets, the command line has no system keychain: it uses a sign-in an earlier version saved in the settings folder, but not one the desktop app keeps in the keychain, and its own sign-ins last for the command only. A later --logout or --remove-account of such a sign-in clears it on this computer but can't end its session at OpenAI (its token is gone); disconnect RustGIS in ChatGPT's settings for that. Without the flag, those commands refuse an account whose token is in the keychain, and --login never replaces such a sign-in. With --use-saved-secrets, the CLI uses, remembers, signs out and removes keychain sign-ins as the app does. See Signing in with ChatGPT.

items.title: Serving AI agents
items.text:
mcp runs RustGIS as a Model Context Protocol server for agents such as Claude Code, Cursor and VS Code, which then run commands, look at the map and search the documentation themselves:

claude mcp add rustgis -- rustgis-cli mcp --sample

To use the already-open desktop project instead, enable its MCP Relay and register rustgis-cli mcp --attach. Do not combine --attach with --sample, --project or --data. File and network commands require --yes unless the app's agent-control setting grants access.

mcp-register --client claude registers the open desktop app's MCP over HTTP with Claude Code, for when agents are turned on in the app. Without --client, it prints the configuration; --name (default rustgis-live) and --port (default RUSTGIS_MCP_HTTP_PORT, else 8768) change the entry:

rustgis-cli mcp-register --client claude

See MCP Server.

items.title: Contributing
items.text:
Contributions are welcome. See AGENTS.md for the conventions.

  1. Fork the repository and create a branch.
  2. Make your change with tests. Engine behaviour is a command in crates/engine/src/cmd/; UI-only commands (ui.*) live in crates/ui-egui/src/lib.rs.
  3. Run cargo xtask ci and pre-commit run --all-files.
  4. Open a pull request. Rust CI runs on Linux by default. A maintainer can label it ci:windows, ci:macos or ci:full to test those platforms before merging; pushes to main test all three. ci:full also builds the release apps. The nightly workflow tests and release-builds all three when there are new commits, and opens an issue on failure.
  5. The docs workflow builds a site and web-app preview. A first-time fork contributor's preview needs a maintainer to add preview or re-run the workflow; returning contributors' previews publish automatically.

A maintainer's automerge label approves and squash-merges a pull request after its required checks pass. Pushing again removes the label and disables auto-merge; removing the label also disables it.

A maintainer's claude-autofix label has Claude bring a pull request up to date: it merges the base branch and resolves any conflicts, then fixes the open review comments it agrees with, replies to each and resolves the ones it fixed or found already fixed, and pushes the commits to the branch (a fork's too, when edits by maintainers are allowed). The label comes off when it's done; add it again for another round.

items.title: Developer checks
items.text:
cargo xtask ci runs cargo fmt --all --check, cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings, cargo test --workspace -q and cargo xtask layers. The pre-commit hooks also check TOML, YAML, JSON, whitespace and large files. CI separately builds rustgis-web for wasm32-unknown-unknown and runs cargo deny --locked check licenses against deny.toml.

Other workspace tasks:

Task Purpose cargo xtask layers Check crate dependency direction and keep UI dependencies out of lower layers cargo xtask notices Regenerate the shipped THIRD-PARTY-LICENSES.txt files after changing dependencies, or after adding code or data from another project to INCLUDED in xtask/src/notices.rs (with its licence text in third-party/); requires cargo-about cargo xtask notices --check Check the notices without writing them; stale notices warn in CI but block releases cargo xtask web-pwa <dir> Generate the service worker in a Trunk build output directory, such as dist/web

Interface strings must be translatable: use tl!("…") for literals and i18n::fmt("… {name} …", &[("name", value)]) for messages with values. New strings can fall back to English until the catalogs are updated; see Languages.

items.title: Faster local builds and test runs
items.text:
All of this is optional and on your side: the repository's profiles stay as they are, and cargo xtask ci is still the check before each commit and pull request.

Less debug information. Much of a debug build's size and link time is debug information, most of it the dependencies'. In your user-level ~/.cargo/config.toml:

[profile.dev]
debug = "line-tables-only"   # backtraces keep file:line

[profile.dev.package."*"]
debug = false

On Linux, split-debuginfo = "unpacked" under [profile.dev] also keeps the linker from copying what is left of it, and mold links faster still than the rust-lld Rust already uses on x86-64 Linux. Install mold first (the link fails without it), then:

[target.x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu]
rustflags = ["-C", "link-arg=-fuse-ld=mold"]

The settings change every build's fingerprint, so the next build is a full one.

Build only what you're testing. cargo test --workspace builds every crate's library, test binaries and examples; a change in ui-egui alone means its library twice (plain and for its unit tests), fifteen integration test binaries and the examples. While you work, name what you need: cargo test -p rustgis-ui-egui --lib, cargo test -p rustgis-engine --test project_save, or cargo clippy -p rustgis-ui-egui --all-targets to check without linking.

cargo-nextest. cargo-nextest (cargo install cargo-nextest --locked) runs the test binaries side by side, each test in its own process, and filters tests by expression:

cargo nextest run --workspace --no-fail-fast -E 'not (package(rustgis-engine) and test(hostile_params_never_panic))'
cargo test --workspace --doc   # nextest doesn't run doctests

The engine's hostile_params_never_panic, which runs every command with junk parameters, is by far its slowest test; leaving it out while you iterate keeps a run short. Run it before you push, with cargo nextest run -p rustgis-engine -E 'test(hostile_params_never_panic)' or cargo xtask ci. A test that fails now and then can be retried with --retries 1.

opt-level 0 for UI work. The workspace crates build at opt-level = 1. With CARGO_PROFILE_DEV_OPT_LEVEL=0, ui-egui rebuilds after an edit about five times faster, but the engine's tests run about six times slower (rasters, geometry and the hostile-parameter test), so it suits iterating on the interface only. Switching the level rebuilds the workspace crates.

cargo clean now and then. target/ keeps the artifacts of every branch and setting you have built, and can grow past a hundred gigabytes.

items.title: Ribbon guidelines
items.text: These guidelines decide where a ribbon control goes and what kind of control it is. They guide new features and small, tab-by-tab improvements; they are not a claim that the current ribbon already follows every rule. Decisions about particular controls live in their issues.

items.title: Start with the task and the tab's purpose
items.text:
Use the tab's purpose to decide where a feature belongs, rather than putting it wherever there is space. Agree on that purpose before reorganising a tab.

Tab Purpose Home The basics of working with a map: starting a map or layout, adding data, moving around, and selecting and inspecting features. Data Working with the content and structure of data: looking at records, changing fields and values, connecting tables, and bringing data in and out. Exports here produce data, such as features and rasters. Style Deciding how a layer looks on the map: how its features are drawn and shown at different scales. Labeling How the map is labelled: what gets a label, with which text, where, and at which scales, plus the label settings for the whole map. Edit Creating and changing features and graphics on the map, and managing those edits. Analyze Turning existing data into new results, from single tools to repeatable workflows, scripts and automation. View How the map and workspace are displayed: map appearance and view configuration, and which panes and windows are open. Basic navigation stays on Home. Publish Getting work out to others: printing, exporting or sharing products such as maps, layouts, reports and packages, including on the web. Plugins Finding, installing and using plugins that extend RustGIS. Settings Preferences that apply to every project, such as language, appearance and start-up. Help Learning RustGIS, finding commands and shortcuts, and getting information about the app.

Keep Data, Style and Labeling fixed, rather than making the tab strip change with the selected layer. Their target should be explicit: a layer chooser at the left of each layer-dependent tab (for example, “Styling: Countries ▾”) is planned, with a useful hint when no suitable layer is selected. Where a class chooser is needed, the layer comes first, then the class.

If a control seems to fit two tabs, or none, clarify its task and destination before placing it. Home is not a catch-all for anything described as “frequently used”. Data exports data; Publish exports products. A control kept on a tab its purpose doesn't cover, until another tab is reorganised, is an interim exception: record it in the issue that tracks the move.

items.title: Keep useful shortcuts, not duplicate destinations
items.text:
• One button per destination, not per pane. Buttons that open the same pane at different sections are useful task shortcuts. Merge controls that land in the same place with the same context.
  • Keep View › Windows complete. Every pane must be reachable there. Working tabs may repeat the panes their tasks need; do not replace those shortcuts with a generic Panes dropdown just to reduce the button count.
  • Keep modes with their tools. Measurement units belong with Measure because they are chosen while measuring. Application-wide preferences such as Dark Mode belong in Settings.
  • One name and icon per thing. Use the same label and icon for the same command wherever it appears: ribbon, panes and Command Search. Do not give one tool different names, or expose one setting as two differently named toggles.
  • Labels say what happens. Name a control for what it does, not for a similar feature elsewhere. A coordinates-only action should say “By Coordinates”; the “Locate” menu covers both coordinates and place/address search. End a label with “…” when it opens a dialog or file picker that asks for input.
  • Keep a route to every feature. Removing a ribbon control must not remove access to its action. Name and check the remaining route, including for UI-only actions.

items.title: Choose controls for the workflow
items.text:
• Put everyday actions and quick adjustments on the ribbon; keep deeper, less frequent options in a pane. A pane holds the full set of settings; its ribbon controls are shortcuts to the same settings and selected layer or class, not separate state.
  • Use a split button only when there is a clear everyday default. The main action stays fixed; choosing an alternative never changes it to “last used”. The arrow opens related alternatives. Without an obvious default, use a plain dropdown. For example, Select's main action is click or box selection; Polygon, Lasso and Radius are in its arrow menu.

For split-button implementation and enabled-state handling, see Architecture.

items.title: Check workflows before shipping
items.text:
Improve the ribbon in small pull requests, tab by tab, rather than replacing the whole layout at once. Clear naming and duplicate-destination fixes can land independently of a larger reorganisation.

Check everyday workflows such as adding data, selecting by location, buffering, symbolising and exporting a map. When moving, removing or regrouping controls, record clicks and tab switches for these before and after; fewer controls is not an improvement if those tasks become harder. Check the tab at 1366 px wide with the ui_shot example and look at the image. Keep everyday controls reachable without horizontal scrolling; move deeper options to their pane rather than packing more controls into the strip.

A pull request that adds a ribbon control should state:

  • the task it serves, its tab and group, and how it fits the tab's purpose;
  • whether it runs immediately, selects a tool, opens a dialog or opens a pane, including the pane section and layer/class context;
  • the fixed default and alternatives if it uses a split button;
  • a screenshot of the tab at 1366 px wide.

A pull request that moves, removes or regroups controls should also state:

  • where each removed control's action remains reachable, and any Command Search location or label updates;
  • why any repeated destination is useful in its workflow;
  • the workflows checked, with their click and tab-switch counts before and after.

Changing ribbon placement does not require changing command ids or parameters: keep CLI, shortcuts and scripts working.

items.title: Test data
items.text:
Generate small datasets during tests instead of committing fixture files. The shared generator in tests/support/ogc.rs builds OGC landing pages, collection lists and GeoJSON in memory; tests/support/ogc_server.rs serves them locally for engine and UI tests. The sorting smoke test similarly generates its KML, KMZ, CSV and GeoJSON inputs. These run automatically with cargo test --workspace --locked and cargo xtask ci, without a separate setup step or a public service. Extend these generators when adding cases.

crates/engine/tests/workflows.rs runs everyday jobs from start to finish: join, overlay, summarise, map, save, reopen and export, and the same saved job twice. Its real-data case, Shelby County's census tracts checked against the areas the Census Bureau publishes, is #[ignore]d: the nightly build downloads the public-domain files, pinned by checksum, and runs it with RUSTGIS_WORKFLOW_DATA naming their folder (the list of files is in nightly.yml). To run it locally, download the files listed there into one folder, check them with sha256sum against the checksums beside them, and run RUSTGIS_WORKFLOW_DATA=<folder> cargo test -p rustgis-engine --test workflows -- --ignored.

items.title: Documentation
items.text:
The site is built with Zensical:

pip install -r requirements_docs.txt
zensical serve        # http://localhost:8000

Images live in rustgis-assets and are linked by URL; don't commit images to this repository.

For PR screenshots, GitHub web attachments are fine. The optional gh image extension can automate uploads and return image links; gh itself has no native standalone attachment-upload command.

The screenshots are rendered by the app itself. From the repository root, run crates/ui-egui/examples/shots/render.sh; it needs ImageMagick (magick) and network access for tiles, plugins and the sample DEM. It runs the ui_shot scripts beside it and writes WebP files to target/shots/; copy them to images/ in rustgis-assets. The assistant shot asks a real model, so set RUSTGIS_ASSISTANT_PROVIDER and the provider's key first, or it shows an empty pane (see AI Assistant).

items.title: Releases
items.text:
1. Bump version in the workspace Cargo.toml and merge it.
  2. Refresh third-party notices if dependencies changed (cargo xtask notices).
  3. Run the Release dry run workflow, which checks the version and builds the desktop/CLI packages without publishing anything: gh workflow run release-dry-run.yml -R opengeos/RustGIS --ref main -f version=<version>
  4. When it passes, publish a GitHub release tagged v<version> (the tag must match Cargo.toml).

The Release workflow then builds and attaches the Windows installers, zip and MSIX, the macOS DMGs, the Linux tarballs, .deb and .rpm packages and AppImages, and SHA256SUMS. To try the packaging locally:

cargo build --release --locked -p rustgis -p rustgis-cli
packaging/package.sh <version>  # writes dist/ for the host platform

items.title: Open the app
items.text:
• In the browser: open web.rustgis.app. Nothing to install.
  • On the desktop: install RustGIS and start it. On first launch it opens the World Atlas sample: countries, cities, rivers and lakes from Natural Earth.
  • From source:
cargo run --release -p rustgis -- --sample    # always opens the World Atlas sample
cargo run --release -p rustgis -- places.geojson
cargo run --release -p rustgis -- atlas.rgis   # a saved project
cargo run --release -p rustgis -- lesson.rgispkg   # a project package, opened unsaved

items.title: Five minutes with the World Atlas
items.text:
If you already changed the start-up settings, use Project › New › World Atlas to open the sample again. Settings › Start-up › Start With chooses what opens next time.

  1. Explore. Drag to pan, scroll to zoom, and click a country to see its attributes in a pop-up. Press Home for the full extent, or pick a place from Home › Bookmarks.
  2. Style a layer. Click Countries in the Layers pane, then open Style › Symbology. In the Symbology pane, choose Graduated Colors, set Field to pop_est and pick a colour scheme. Unique Values instead colours categories such as continent.
  3. Select. Open Home › Select By Attributes, choose Countries under Input Rows, enter continent = 'Asia' under Where, and press Apply. Open the attribute table with Ctrl+T. Rows and map features stay in sync.
  4. Analyze. Open Analyze › Buffer. Set Input Features to Cities, Distance to 300, Units to Kilometers and Dissolve to All, then press Run. The result is added as a new layer, and the run is listed under Analyze › History.
  5. Change the view. View › Globe turns the map into a 3D globe; View › Projection offers Equal Earth, Robinson and other projections. Home › Add › Basemap switches the basemap or adds a web tile layer, and its Celestial Bodies take the map to the Moon or Mars. Right-drag (or Ctrl-drag) turns and tilts the map; click the north arrow to reset it.
  6. Share. Publish › Export Map saves a PNG with labels and a scale bar. Home › New Layout offers page sizes and Publication Layout presets for sheets (in one of six styles) and figures. Choose a page size for a page with a map frame, legend, north arrow and scale bar. Project › Save As writes a .rgis project.

Command search

Press Ctrl+K to find any command or geoprocessing tool by name. On macOS, use Cmd in place of Ctrl for shortcuts.

items.title: Your own data
items.text:
Home › Add › Add Data opens data files directly; its arrow offers other ways to add data, including delimited text, URLs and services. Shapefiles work in the browser too: pick or drop the .shp and .dbf together, with .shx and .prj if available, or use a ZIP containing them. Home › Add › Data Sources opens saved data connections and recent sources.

Project › New › Map starts a blank project. Home › Add › Web Data finds public satellite imagery, Overture Maps, OpenStreetMap, NASA Earthdata, open-data portals and more (see Web Data). Desktop database connections include PostGIS, MySQL/MariaDB and SQL Server/Azure SQL. See Data and Supported Data Formats for format and platform limits.

items.title: Ask the AI Assistant
items.text: Analyze › AI Assistant opens a chat pane. Choose a model provider (Anthropic, OpenAI, your ChatGPT account, Gemini, OpenRouter, a local Ollama, or any OpenAI-compatible server) and ask, for example, "Which 5 countries have the largest GDP?" or "Label the cities and zoom to Tokyo". By default, the assistant asks before file, network and plugin operations. Undo restores project changes, not files already written. See AI Assistant.

items.title: Next steps
items.text:
• The User Guide walks through every part of the app.
  • Command Line shows how to script RustGIS with rustgis-cli.
  • Plugins shows how to add tools from the plugin registry, or write your own.
  • Python covers sessions, rendering and the interactive notebook map.
  • MCP connects external AI agents to RustGIS.

items.title: Languages
items.text:
RustGIS's interface is available in 19 languages:

Language Code Language Code English en Русский (Russian) ru Deutsch (German) de Türkçe (Turkish) tr Español (Spanish) es Azərbaycanca (Azerbaijani) az Français (French) fr Bahasa Indonesia (Indonesian) id Italiano (Italian) it Tiếng Việt (Vietnamese) vi Nederlands (Dutch) nl 简体中文 (Chinese, Simplified) zh Polski (Polish) pl 日本語 (Japanese) ja Português (Portuguese) pt 한국어 (Korean) ko ქართული (Georgian) ka বাংলা (Bengali) bn فارسی (Persian) fa

items.title: Choosing a language
items.text:
By default RustGIS follows the first supported language in your system's preferences (your browser's on the web) and falls back to English. The Chinese catalog is Simplified Chinese; Traditional Chinese locales are not mapped to it. To choose a language yourself, open Settings › Language. The choice is remembered in prefs.json in the desktop app's settings folder, or in browser storage on the web. When following the system language, you can override its detection for one desktop run with RUSTGIS_LANGUAGE:

RUSTGIS_LANGUAGE=de cargo run --release -p rustgis

Only the interface is translated. Your data, layer and field names, command ids and the command line stay as they are, so scripts work in every language.

Chinese, Japanese and Korean need a CJK font. The desktop app uses one you have installed (Noto Sans CJK, Microsoft YaHei, Yu Gothic, Malgun Gothic, PingFang, Hiragino or Apple SD Gothic Neo); the web app downloads Noto Sans from assets.rustgis.app the first time you pick one of these languages. Map labels in images exported from the desktop app and the command line draw CJK text with the same installed font, whatever the interface language. Images exported from the web app have no CJK font yet, so CJK characters are left out of their labels.

Persian needs a font with both Arabic-script and Latin letters. The desktop app uses one you have installed (Segoe UI, Tahoma, Arial, Vazirmatn or DejaVu Sans); the web app downloads Vazirmatn from assets.rustgis.app the first time you pick Persian.

items.title: Translating
items.text:
Each non-English language is a UTF-8 catalog of English<TAB>Translation lines in crates/ui-egui/src/i18n/<code>.tsv. English is the source language and has no catalog. Blank lines and lines beginning with # are ignored. Within either field, \n, \t and \\ represent a line break, tab and backslash. A missing entry shows in English, so translations can grow one line at a time, and corrections from native speakers are welcome.

Pull requests can leave new strings out of the catalogs: the maintainer translates them before each release. To translate a new string, add a line with the exact English text, a tab, and the translation. Keep {placeholders} such as {n} or {name} (they may move), keep the line break (\n) in two-line ribbon labels, and leave product, format and key names (RustGIS, GeoJSON, CSV, Ctrl…) in English. To add a language, add its catalog and a row in LANGUAGES in crates/ui-egui/src/i18n/mod.rs. The i18n tests check catalog format and placeholders, and require translations for some established interface strings:

cargo test -p rustgis-ui-egui i18n

Persian text uses the toolkit's script shaping, with Latin runs and brackets adjusted by crates/ui-egui/src/i18n/rtl.rs. Long paragraphs are broken into lines before drawing. Panes and widgets retain their left-to-right layout. Arabic, Hebrew, Hindi and Thai are not included in the language picker.

items.title: Install with an agent
items.text: Point your agent at the RustGIS skill and ask it to install RustGIS. The skill picks the platform, installs the app and rustgis-cli, checks the release checksum, and registers the MCP server. The same skill is how an agent manages the desktop app that is already open.

items.title: Microsoft Store
items.text: On Windows 10 and 11, the easiest way to install RustGIS is from the Microsoft Store, which signs the app and keeps it up to date:

items.title: Download
items.text:
Each GitHub release carries ready-to-run builds of the desktop app and rustgis-cli. The same files, grouped by platform, are mirrored at downloads.rustgis.app:

Platform File Windows x64 (installer, no admin rights) RustGIS-<version>-windows-x86_64-setup.exe Windows x64 (installer for all users) RustGIS-<version>-windows-x86_64.msi Windows x64 (no install) RustGIS-<version>-windows-x86_64-portable.zip (unzip and run rustgis.exe) Windows x64 (Microsoft Store package) RustGIS-<version>-windows-x86_64.msix macOS Apple Silicon RustGIS-<version>-macos-aarch64.dmg macOS Intel RustGIS-<version>-macos-x86_64.dmg Linux x64 / arm64 (Debian, Ubuntu) rustgis_<version>_amd64.deb / rustgis_<version>_arm64.deb Linux x64 / arm64 (Fedora, RHEL, openSUSE) rustgis-<version>-1.x86_64.rpm / rustgis-<version>-1.aarch64.rpm Linux x64 / arm64 (any distribution, no install) RustGIS-<version>-linux-x86_64.AppImage / RustGIS-<version>-linux-aarch64.AppImage Linux x64 / arm64 (other) RustGIS-<version>-linux-x86_64.tar.gz / RustGIS-<version>-linux-aarch64.tar.gz

On macOS the command-line tool is a separate rustgis-cli-<version>-macos-<arch>.tar.gz; the other packages include it (the Windows installers and the MSIX add rustgis-cli to every new terminal). SHA256SUMS lists the checksum of every file.

The AppImages carry update information, so tools such as Gear Lever can update them to the latest release. AppImageUpdate, and AppImageLauncher through the AppImageUpdate library, download only the parts that changed, with the .zsync file published beside each AppImage.

On Windows, setup.exe installs for your account in %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\RustGIS and needs no admin rights; the .msi installs for every user in Program Files and suits managed deployment (msiexec /i RustGIS-<version>-windows-x86_64.msi /qn). Both add a Start menu entry, open .rgis projects, list RustGIS under Open with for .geojson, and uninstall from Settings › Apps.

The .msix is the package submitted to the Microsoft Store, which signs it. It is unsigned on the release page, so Windows only installs it from the Store; outside the Store, download an installer or the portable zip instead.

The macOS app needs macOS 11 or later. It is signed and notarized by Apple, so it opens without a warning; the command-line tool is too, but macOS checks it online the first time it runs. The setup.exe, .msi and portable zip are not signed: if SmartScreen warns about an unknown publisher, choose More info › Run anyway.

items.title: Package managers
items.text:
RustGIS is also published to these package managers, which keep it up to date:

Platform Command Windows (winget) winget install OpenGeos.RustGIS macOS (Homebrew) brew install --cask opengeos/rustgis/rustgis macOS and Linux, command-line tool only (Homebrew) brew install opengeos/rustgis/rustgis-cli Arch Linux (AUR) yay -S rustgis-bin (or any AUR helper) Fedora (COPR) sudo dnf copr enable giswqs/rustgis && sudo dnf install rustgis

winget installs for your account with the setup.exe; add --scope machine for the .msi. On Homebrew 5.1 and later, run brew trust opengeos/rustgis once before installing from the tap. Each package is the same build as the release page, and a new release reaches the package managers shortly after it is published (winget after Microsoft's review).

items.title: From source
items.text:
RustGIS builds from source with a recent stable Rust toolchain (1.90 or later), a C compiler (for the C code some dependencies bundle; see Architecture) and curl (to download the sample data).

git clone https://github.com/opengeos/RustGIS.git
cd RustGIS
cargo run --release -p rustgis            # the desktop app
cargo build --release -p rustgis-cli      # the command-line tool

The build downloads the Natural Earth sample data from rustgis-assets. To build offline, download countries.geojson, countries_chn.geojson, cities.geojson, rivers.geojson and lakes.geojson from https://assets.rustgis.app/data/ once and point the build at them:

RUSTGIS_DATA_DIR=/path/to/data cargo build --release

items.title: Platforms
items.text: Platform Status Linux (X11 and Wayland) Supported macOS Supported Windows Supported Web browser Supported: web.rustgis.app (WebGPU or WebGL2), installable as an app on iOS, Android and desktops (how)

items.title: Web app
items.text:
RustGIS also runs in the browser, compiled to WebAssembly: open web.rustgis.app. It is the same app, with these differences:

  • Open and Add Data use the browser's file picker, and you can drop files on the page. GeoJSON, CSV, GeoTIFF, ASCII grids, .rgis projects and the other formats in Data formats work; pick or drop a Shapefile's .shp and .dbf together (with its .shx and .prj if it has them), or its zip.
  • Save and Export download the file. Save As, and the first Save of a project, ask for the file name first; the browser decides which folder downloads go to (Firefox, for one, saves to its Downloads folder unless told to ask). A project opened from a file is named after it, and Save downloads it under that name again.
  • The interface uses the built-in font, because a web page can't read installed fonts. Choosing Chinese, Japanese, Korean or Persian downloads a font for that script.
  • Process plugins (including Python plugins), and the formats read through GDAL or DuckDB, need the desktop app or rustgis-cli.

The web app opens the way Settings › Start-up says (remembered in the browser). The URL can override that for one visit: add ?blank to start with an empty project, ?projection=EPSG:3010 (a supported projected EPSG or ESRI code, a preset id such as robinson, or globe) to start in another projection, ?extent=10.5,55,24.5,69.5 (west, south, east, north in degrees) to open on an area, ?lang=de (or any language code) to pick the interface language, ?gpu (or ?gpu=0) to turn GPU Rendering on (off) for the visit, or ?webgl to force WebGL2. Combine them with &, so a self-hosted build can link to ?blank&projection=EPSG:3010&extent=10.5,55,24.5,69.5.

?registry=<address> opens the Plugin Manager's Browse tab on another plugin registry for the visit; installing still asks first.

Links can carry data too: ?data=<address> adds a file by its web address (any format Add Data reads, downloaded in the background; repeat it for up to 16, and the map zooms to the first that lands with something to show), ?style=<address> adds a MapLibre style (opening at the style's own place, zoom, bearing and pitch unless the link places the map), ?tiles=<template> a tile layer, and ?zarr=<address> opens Add Zarr Variable on a Zarr store. Percent-encode an address holding &, # or spaces (encodeURIComponent); a + stays a +. The server must allow the browser to fetch the file (CORS); a file that can't be added is said in a notice. For example, ?blank&data=https://earthquake.usgs.gov/earthquakes/feed/v1.0/summary/2.5_week.geojson opens the past week's earthquakes.

A MapLibre-style position after a # places the map: #zoom/latitude/longitude/bearing/pitch, the last two optional, so ?style=<address>#15.5/40.7484/-73.9857/30/60 opens a style tilted over Midtown Manhattan.

?project=<address> opens a whole project by its web address: a .rgis file (or a .rgispkg package), or any address that answers with a project's JSON, such as an API that builds the project on the fly. Its maps, layers, symbology and view open as saved, so one link shares a styled map. The project replaces the start-up one, so ?data=, ?stac=, ?style=, ?tiles= and ?zarr= are left out beside it (a notice says so). The data the project points to is read as it would be from a saved file, and its servers must allow the browser to fetch it (CORS), as must the project's.

?stac=<address> opens STAC Search on a STAC item or collection: an item's footprint is drawn and its default asset (its true-colour visual image, else its first GeoTIFF) added, signed first when it is a Microsoft Planetary Computer one; a collection is chosen in the dialog, with its API, ready to search. For example, ?stac=https://planetarycomputer.microsoft.com/api/stac/v1/collections/sentinel-2-l2a/items/S2B_MSIL2A_20240727T102559_R108_T32TLS_20240727T131405 opens a Sentinel-2 scene of Lake Geneva.

?embed runs the app inside another page, as the Python package's notebook widget does: it starts blank, keeps its settings in memory rather than in the browser, and exchanges the project with the page that frames it through postMessage (the messages are described in apps/rustgis-web/src/embed.rs).

items.title: Install the web app
items.text:
The web app installs like an app on phones, tablets and computers, with its own icon and a window without the browser's toolbars, and starts without a network connection once it has been opened online. Nothing is downloaded from an app store, and it updates itself from web.rustgis.app.

Platform How iPhone and iPad Open web.rustgis.app in Safari, tap Share, then Add to Home Screen Android Open it in Chrome, tap the ⋮ menu, then Install app (or Add to Home screen) Windows, macOS, Linux, ChromeOS In Chrome or Edge, click the install icon at the right of the address bar (or ⋮ › Cast, save and share › Install page as app) Mac (Safari 17 or later) File › Add to Dock

To remove it, delete it like any other app: long-press the icon on a phone or tablet, or use Uninstall in the app window's menu on a computer.

Offline, the installed app opens the World Atlas sample and the files you open, but not basemap tiles, web data, plugins or the AI Assistant, which need the network. When a new version has been published while the app is open, a notice offers to reload into it; otherwise the next launch picks it up. Two things to know on iPhone and iPad: iOS gives a web page less memory than a desktop browser, so very large rasters may not open, and it can clear the offline copy when the device runs short of storage, so the next launch then needs a connection.

To build it yourself, install Trunk, the wasm32-unknown-unknown target and clang (it compiles the Zstandard decoder used for GeoTIFFs to WebAssembly). Linux distributions' clang can; on macOS, Apple's can't, so install llvm with Homebrew and put its bin first on your PATH. Then:

cd apps/rustgis-web
trunk serve          # http://127.0.0.1:8772
trunk build --release   # output in dist/web
cargo xtask web-pwa ../../dist/web   # add the service worker (offline start), as the deploy does

The service worker is left out of trunk serve, so a development build is never served from a stale cache.

items.title: Self-host the web app with Docker
items.text:
A ready-made image of the web app, served by nginx, is published to the GitHub Container Registry for x86-64 and arm64, so you need only Docker:

docker run --rm -p 8080:8080 ghcr.io/opengeos/rustgis   # http://localhost:8080

latest (also tagged edge) is the newest build of main; 0.5.0 or 0.5 is a given release (releases have images from 0.5.0 on).

To build the image yourself, the Dockerfile at the root of the repository builds the web app the way the deploy does:

docker build -t rustgis .
docker run --rm -p 8080:8080 rustgis

The image holds only the built files and runs nginx as a non-root user on port 8080. Its pages check for a newer build on every load, so the app's new-version notice offers the next image you deploy. Unlike web.rustgis.app, it carries no analytics. Put it behind a reverse proxy that serves HTTPS: browsers install the app and start its service worker only over HTTPS (or on localhost). The app's addresses are relative, so the proxy can also serve it under a path, such as https://example.com/rustgis/, passing requests on without the path. Signing in to ArcGIS from your copy needs an OAuth app of your own whose redirect URLs list the copy's oauth-callback.html, as RustGIS's own app accepts only web.rustgis.app's (see Secured ArcGIS services).

The image is for the platform of the machine that builds it. To build it for another, such as on an Apple silicon Mac for an x86-64 server, add --platform linux/amd64 to docker build. With a builder that can build several platforms (one made by docker buildx create --use, or Docker Desktop's containerd image store), docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 -t <registry>/rustgis --push . publishes one image for both. The app itself is WebAssembly, so it is compiled once, on the machine that builds it, whichever platforms the image is for.

items.title: The command line in Docker
items.text:
ghcr.io/opengeos/rustgis-cli holds the command line, rustgis-cli, on a slim Debian, for x86-64 and arm64, with the same tags. It runs in /data, so mount the folder to work on there:

docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/data" ghcr.io/opengeos/rustgis-cli info cities.geojson
docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/data" ghcr.io/opengeos/rustgis-cli render cities.geojson map.png --basemap ocean

It runs as a user with ID 1000, the first user on most Linux systems, so the files it writes are yours; elsewhere, add --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" -e HOME=/tmp. The optional GDAL, DuckDB and GeoLibre programs aren't in the image. To build it yourself: docker build -f packaging/docker/cli.Dockerfile -t rustgis-cli .

items.title: Fonts
items.text: RustGIS uses an installed sans-serif when it finds one (Segoe UI, San Francisco, Arial, Inter, Noto Sans, Open Sans or DejaVu Sans) and falls back to a built-in face. Set RUSTGIS_BUILTIN_FONTS=1 to always use the built-in face.

items.title: Settings, data and cache folders
items.text:
The desktop app and the command line keep their files in three folders:

Folder Holds Windows macOS Linux Settings preferences (prefs.json), the crash log, AI Assistant sign-ins and skills %APPDATA%\RustGIS ~/Library/Application Support/RustGIS $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/rustgis (~/.config/rustgis) Data installed plugins, the GeoLibre runner and recovery copies of unsaved work %LOCALAPPDATA%\RustGIS ~/Library/Application Support/RustGIS $XDG_DATA_HOME/rustgis (~/.local/share/rustgis) Cache GDAL and DuckDB conversions %LOCALAPPDATA%\RustGIS\cache ~/Library/Caches/RustGIS $XDG_CACHE_HOME/rustgis (~/.cache/rustgis)

Set RUSTGIS_CONFIG_DIR, RUSTGIS_APP_DATA_DIR or RUSTGIS_CACHE_DIR to use another folder instead, for a portable install on a USB drive, for example. The folder is used as is, and RustGIS keeps the same files in it (plugins/, geolibre/ and recovery/ in the data folder, gdal/ and duckdb/ in the cache folder). RUSTGIS_PLUGINS_DIR, RUSTGIS_GDAL_CACHE and RUSTGIS_DUCKDB_CACHE name the plugins folder and the GDAL and DuckDB caches themselves, ahead of these.

items.title: If RustGIS closes unexpectedly
items.text:
The desktop app writes its internal errors to crash.log in its settings folder: one that closed the app, and also one it recovered from (an error in the AI Assistant, for example, stops the request and says so in the chat instead of closing the app). The next launch moves the log to crash-last.log and names the file in a notice.

Attach it to a bug report. It holds the version, the operating system, the error message and where in RustGIS it happened. An error message can quote what RustGIS was working on, such as a file path or a layer name, so read the log first and remove anything you don't want to share.

Unsaved work isn't lost with it: the next launch offers the copy autosave kept (see Autosave and recovery).

items.title: If the app doesn't start
items.text:
The desktop app draws its window with the graphics card through Direct3D 12 on Windows, Metal on macOS and Vulkan on Linux, with OpenGL as a fallback. A graphics driver that crashes there closes the app before it can open a window or write crash.log. Choose another graphics interface with --backend (dx12, vulkan, gl or metal, or several separated by commas), from a terminal or in the target of a shortcut to rustgis.exe:

rustgis --backend gl       # OpenGL
rustgis --backend dx12     # Direct3D 12 (Windows)
rustgis --backend vulkan   # Vulkan
rustgis --backend metal    # Metal (macOS)

The WGPU_BACKEND environment variable takes the same names, for every launch. On Windows, RustGIS uses Vulkan only when asked like this: some Vulkan drivers, such as Intel's for UHD 600 series graphics, crash as the app starts. Updating the graphics driver may also help.

items.title: MCP Server
items.text:
rustgis-cli mcp runs RustGIS as a Model Context Protocol server, so an AI agent such as Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor, VS Code or Codex can make maps with it. The agent opens data, runs RustGIS commands and geoprocessing tools within the access policy below, reads attribute tables, looks at the map as an image and searches this documentation. RustGIS needs no model API key in this mode: the MCP client supplies the model.

rustgis-cli mcp --sample                # the World Atlas sample
rustgis-cli mcp --data parcels.geojson  # your own data (--data more than once, or --project p.rgis)
rustgis-cli mcp --yes                   # also allow file and network access
rustgis-cli mcp --attach [--yes]        # the desktop app that is already open (its MCP Relay)

The server talks over standard input and output, so you don't start it yourself: you tell your agent how to start it (below), and the agent runs it. Each agent gets its own project, held in memory until the agent saves it. --sample, --project and repeated --data options initialize a private project. They cannot be combined with --attach, which uses the desktop app's existing project. Use absolute paths for data, projects and executables in client configurations: clients may start the server in a different working directory.

items.title: Adding it to an agent
items.text:
Claude Code:

claude mcp add rustgis -- rustgis-cli mcp --sample

Codex:

codex mcp add rustgis -- rustgis-cli mcp --sample

Claude Desktop (claude_desktop_config.json), Cursor (~/.cursor/mcp.json) and other clients that use an mcpServers object:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "rustgis": {
      "command": "rustgis-cli",
      "args": ["mcp", "--sample"]
    }
  }
}

VS Code (.vscode/mcp.json):

{
  "servers": {
    "rustgis": {
      "type": "stdio",
      "command": "rustgis-cli",
      "args": ["mcp", "--sample"]
    }
  }
}

If the agent can't find rustgis-cli, give its full path (see Installation). Then ask, for example:

  • "Which 5 countries have the largest GDP? Show them on the map."
  • "Buffer the cities by 200 km, colour the result by population and show me the map."
  • "Load ~/data/parcels.geojson, label the parcels with their owner and export the map to parcels.png." (this reads and writes files, so it needs --yes)

items.title: Managing the open desktop app
items.text:
By default each agent gets its own project in memory. To drive the project that is open in the desktop app instead, tick Let your Agents Control RustGIS in the AI Assistant's settings. It starts the relay and shows what an agent needs to connect: the MCP server configuration, and the claude mcp add / codex mcp add commands. While it's ticked, attached agents may also read and write files and use the network, without --yes. RustGIS remembers the choice and starts the relay with the app. The MCP Relay command (Help menu, or Command Search with Ctrl+K) starts the relay too, without that: attached agents then have the access their --yes asks for. The relay is off until the box is ticked or that command runs. While it runs, the status bar shows MCP relay · n attached, where n is the number of authenticated clients. For ten seconds after an attached agent runs a tool, the label also names it (MCP relay · 1 attached · layer.addSample, in red when it failed); hovering shows Stop MCP relay and the last call with its parameters, and clicking it stops the relay. Agents attached through the relay are told, when they connect, that this is the project you have open and that you watch the map change as they work.

Under it, Full access (off unless you tick it, for this session only) lifts every refusal for agents attached with the relay's own token. They may then also run scripts, tasks and models, and install, remove and run plugins: what you could do yourself in RustGIS. It isn't remembered: it's off again at the next launch, and when agents are turned off. While it's on, the status bar reads MCP relay · full access · n attached in red. Full access also lifts the project-replacement and undo-ownership refusals described below; it is not just file and network access. Agents the app starts itself keep their own grants' rules.

rustgis-cli mcp --attach                 # the open app on 127.0.0.1:8767
rustgis-cli mcp --attach 9000 --yes      # another port, with file and network access
rustgis-cli mcp --attach --timeout 300   # wait up to 5 minutes for each call (5 to 600 seconds)

The port is 8767 unless the RUSTGIS_MCP_PORT environment variable names another, for the app and for --attach alike (a second copy of RustGIS, or a port another program holds). When the port is taken, the relay's error says so and names that variable; a value that isn't a port number is an error too, not a quiet fall back to 8767. While the relay runs, the app publishes endpoint.json in the relay's private folder: schema, host, port, url, pid, started_at, the app version, the token_file path (not the token), the attach command, and once MCP over HTTP runs, its http_url and http_token_file. Setup scripts can read it instead of hard-coding the port. It's removed when the relay stops. With two copies of RustGIS on different ports it describes the one started last, and a crash can leave it behind: check that its pid is still running before trusting it.

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "rustgis-app": {
      "command": "rustgis-cli",
      "args": ["mcp", "--attach", "--yes"]
    }
  }
}

Attached calls run on the open app's session through the same tools and refusal policy as the private server. snapshot additionally supports a real window capture with mode: "screen". If the map is not on screen, it falls back to an offscreen render and explains why in note. The relay holds a screen request until the app has taken the picture, and runs nothing else meanwhile. File and network commands need --yes, unless Let your Agents Control RustGIS is ticked.

Without Full access, an attached agent cannot replace the open project: project.new, project.open, project.openText, project.sample and project.fromTemplate are refused, with or without --yes. Commands are recorded in your undo history as agent 1, agent 2… with the relay run's identity. An agent's edit.undo and edit.redo work only on its own steps: when the top step is yours or another agent's, they are refused. They run on their own through run_command, or as a one-line run script. You can still undo anything. Full access lifts both these restrictions for the relay's own token.

Undo ownership and the active layer are scoped to a token, not a client connection. Ordinary --attach clients share the relay's token, so they share one agent identity and active layer; local agents with separate grants are kept apart. Selecting a layer through an agent (layer.select, or a command that makes a layer active) does not change your Layers pane selection. Once that token has chosen a layer, commands that omit layer use it while you select others; until then they use your current selection.

Every tool call an attached agent makes is written to an audit log, one JSON line per call in a file per day (2026-10-18.jsonl) in the mcp-audit folder of the app-data folder (~/.local/share/rustgis/mcp-audit on Linux, ~/Library/Application Support/RustGIS/mcp-audit on macOS, %LOCALAPPDATA%\RustGIS\mcp-audit on Windows). Each line holds ts, source (mcp for the relay and MCP over HTTP, file for the file bridge), tool, command or script when there is one, args, success, duration_s and error. Passwords, keys and tokens in the arguments, a run script's lines included, are replaced before they are written. On Linux and macOS the folder and files are readable by you only; on Windows they're protected by your user profile's permissions. A batch's calls share the batch's duration_s and are marked "batch": true. An error whose text mentions a credential (a token, a password, a bearer…) is logged as withheld rather than risk keeping the credential. Days older than 30 are removed.

items.title: MCP over HTTP
items.text:
While Let your Agents Control RustGIS is on, the app also serves MCP over HTTP ("Streamable HTTP", stateless, JSON replies) on http://127.0.0.1:8768/mcp, beside the relay. The RUSTGIS_MCP_HTTP_PORT environment variable names another port. Clients that speak HTTP connect without rustgis-cli. Every request needs Authorization: Bearer <token>. The token is made once and kept in mcp-http.token in the settings folder (readable by you only), so a client registered with it keeps working across launches; delete the file to make a new one. Requests that name another host, or that come from a web page (an Origin header), are refused before the token is read. Calls go through the same queue, refusals and one-at-a-time rule as the relay's. HTTP clients count as agents attached with the relay's own token: they share that agent's access, active layer and name in the undo history, and the token lasts across launches where the relay's lasts one run.

rustgis-cli mcp-register --client claude registers it with Claude Code (claude mcp add --transport http rustgis-live http://127.0.0.1:8768/mcp --header "Authorization: Bearer …"), and the settings section shows that command. Without --client it prints the configuration for any HTTP client. --name and --port change the registration's name and port. Either way the token leaves its file: claude mcp add takes it as an argument (other users of the computer can see a running program's arguments for the moment it runs), and the printed configuration shows it, so keep it out of shared logs. Whoever holds the token can do, while agents are on, what an attached agent can, files and the network included. If it leaks, stop the relay, delete mcp-http.token, and turn agents on again to create and load a new token; each registered client then needs registering again. Deleting the file alone does not revoke the token already loaded by a running listener. On Windows the token file is protected by your user profile's permissions, not by a mode of its own.

An agent the app starts itself gets a run-scoped token instead of the relay's own: rustgis-cli mcp --attach PORT --token-file FILE. Each such grant carries its own file and network permission, and the app revokes it when it's done with the agent; that closes its connections and removes its file.

items.title: The file bridge
items.text:
For an agent that can't use MCP, or when the relay's port is taken, the app also runs scripts written to a file. It's on while Let your Agents Control RustGIS is ticked, even if the relay couldn't start: agents then stay on, and the status bar says only the file bridge is running.

  1. Write a script to bridge-command.txt in the relay's private folder ($XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/rustgis on Linux, a rustgis-mcp-<user> folder in the temporary folder elsewhere). The settings section shows the full path. The script is in the script.run format: one command-id {json} per line, # for comments.
  2. Once the file has stopped changing for half a second, RustGIS runs it on the open project. (To be sure a half-written script never runs, write it to another file in the folder and rename it to bridge-command.txt.) It runs as one undo step, with the same rules as the run tool: a refused or failing line stops it, and nothing it did to the project is kept. Files written by an earlier line stay written.
  3. The outcome is written to bridge-result.json in the same folder: {success, result, lines, layersAdded, notices, error, duration_s, timestamp}. The status bar says whether it worked.

Only one RustGIS at a time runs the bridge: a second copy's is refused while the first's runs (it holds bridge.lock). The bridge runs a script each time the file changes. Whatever the file held when the bridge started isn't run. While the bridge is on, bridge-ready.json there holds its pid, the two files' paths, started_at, the app version and a schema number. The folder is readable by this user only, like the relay's token. Scripts run through the bridge are written to the audit log (source: "file"), and Full access applies to them as to agents attached with the relay's own token. The bridge is named file bridge in your undo history. Without Full access, a script's edit.undo (alone on its line) takes back only the bridge's own steps. It also keeps its own active layer.

items.title: Relay requirements
items.text:
• Off until asked.
