Only ui.mcpRelay starts a listener: run directly, or by ticking Let your Agents Control RustGIS (also at launch, when it was left ticked). ui.mcpRelay with no parameters or with the same port reports the address it already listens on. A different explicit port is refused until the relay is stopped. ui.mcpRelay {"stop": true} stops it and is idempotent. The default port is 8767.
  • Loopback only. Relay::bind refuses any non-loopback address before a socket is opened; the app's ui.mcpRelay binds 127.0.0.1.
  • Private token. Each run draws 16 bytes from the operating system's random source, written as 32 hex characters. The token file is {port}.token in $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/rustgis when that is an absolute folder, otherwise in a per-user folder under the system temporary folder. The folder must be owned by the current user and not accessible to others. The file must be a regular file owned by the current user, without group or other access. A file that is a symlink is refused. rustgis-cli mcp --attach reads it with read_token(port). The token never appears on a command line. The file is removed when the relay stops.
  • App-granted access. Relay::set_allow_access(true) lets connections attached with the relay's own token use files and the network whether or not they asked; the desktop app sets it while Let your Agents Control RustGIS is ticked. This includes any process running as the same user that can read that token, not just agents launched by RustGIS. It is checked for every call. Turning the setting off stops the relay and disconnects its clients, including a relay started manually. If the relay fails but the file bridge starts, the saved setting stays on and the app reports the relay error; if both fail, the setting is cleared.
  • Grants. Relay::grant(access) writes a run-scoped token to {port}-{run}-{n}.token in the same private folder (run is random per relay run). A grant asked for after the relay stopped is refused. A connection that attaches with it gets the grant's permission. Dropping the grant removes the file, forgets the token and closes its connections. Stopping the relay removes every grant's file.
  • Attach first. A connection's first non-empty line must be a rustgis/attach message carrying the token. It must arrive within 5 seconds, measured from connection, and be at most 4096 bytes including its newline. The token is compared without early exit. A connection that fails this is closed. The access flag sets what that connection may do; the per-call refusal policy still applies. A repeat attach may change access.
  • Handshake and idle limits. Attached clients that send nothing for 300 seconds are closed. A reply write that takes longer than 10 seconds closes the connection.
  • Connection caps. At most 16 open connections, and at most 4 that have not attached. A connection beyond either cap is dropped without a reply.
  • Queue cap. Up to 64 ordinary messages wait for the app's frame; messages held for local-agent approval have a separate cap of 64. A request beyond either cap gets error -32001 (the app is busy; try again) if it expects a reply.
  • Bounded request waits. A request waits up to 60 seconds for the app to run it, or as long as the client's attach asks (timeout_s, 5 to 600 seconds; --timeout on the command line). If it is still pending then, it is cancelled and never runs; the client gets error -32002. If it is already running, the client waits one more interval of the same length. If the reply still has not come, the client gets error -32003 (its outcome is unknown), and the command may still complete later.
  • Busy app. When the app has drawn no frame for 10 seconds since a request was queued (a file dialog is open, a long tool is running, or the window is minimized or hidden and the system has stopped drawing it), the request is cancelled at once and the client gets error -32004 saying RustGIS is busy (apart from the full queue's -32001). It never runs, and the connection stays open. An app that was only idle before the request isn't busy: the request wakes it. This comes before a long timeout_s: a stalled app answers after 10 seconds whatever the client's wait, and a client waiting less than 10 seconds gets -32002 instead. A timeout_s outside 5 to 600 is clamped to that range, and one that isn't a number is ignored (the 60-second default).
  • Stop. Stopping the relay, or dropping its last owner, closes the listener and every client, drops queued messages unrun, and removes the token file. A waiting request ends at once, checked every 25 milliseconds.
  • Wake. A queued message or a change in the attached-client count wakes the UI thread so it draws a frame. A relay started before the first frame installs its wake on the first logic call after that frame exists.
  • Shared framing. Each message is one JSON-RPC message per line. After attach, messages and replies are read with read_message_max at 64 MiB (MAX_LINE), the limit counting the newline. The attach line is read at most 4096 bytes including its newline (see Attach first). After an oversized line on a socket the relay sends a -32700 error and closes that connection. On standard input the reader skips the rest of the line and continues. IO errors name neither standard input nor a socket.

items.title: Tests
items.text:
These behavioral tests in crates/assistant/src/relay.rs check the requirements above:

  • Loopback bind and command run: relay_runs_a_command_on_the_target_session
  • Token required: relay_drops_connections_without_the_token
  • Parse error after attach: relay_returns_parse_error_after_attach_and_stays_usable
  • File commands need --yes: relay_refuses_file_commands_without_yes
  • Separate active layers: relay_keeps_the_agents_active_layer_apart_from_the_users
  • Agents undo only their own steps: relay_agents_undo_only_their_own_steps
  • Agents of an earlier relay run aren't this run's: relay_agents_of_another_run_cant_undo_earlier_steps
  • Busy app: relay_says_the_app_is_busy_early
  • Client-chosen waits: relay_waits_as_long_as_the_client_asks
  • Endpoint file and port variable: relay_publishes_its_endpoint_and_names_the_port_variable
  • Full access, for the relay's own token only: relay_full_access_lifts_the_refusals_for_its_own_token_only
  • Screen snapshots go to the app: relay_hands_screen_snapshots_to_the_app
  • Snapshots without the screen: relay_draws_snapshots_offscreen_without_the_screen
  • Saved snapshots need access: relay_refuses_a_saved_snapshot_without_access
  • The agent's last call, for the status bar: relay_records_the_agents_last_call
  • MCP over HTTP with the token: relay::http::tests::http_clients_with_the_token_drive_the_session
  • HTTP refusals (no token, other host, web page, method, size): relay::http::tests::http_refuses_requests_without_the_token_or_from_elsewhere
  • Stable, private HTTP token: relay::http::tests::http_token_is_stable_and_private
  • Audit log: relay_writes_each_call_to_the_audit_log
  • The open project stays the user's: relay_keeps_project_commands_for_the_user
  • Timed-out command never runs: relay_cancels_a_timed_out_command_so_it_never_runs
  • Stop cleanup: relay_stop_closes_clients_and_removes_the_token
  • Last owner drop: relay_last_owner_drop_closes_the_listener
  • Unauthenticated cap: relay_caps_unauthenticated_connections
  • Oversized pre-attach line: relay_refuses_an_oversized_unauthenticated_line
  • Token random and private: relay_token_is_random_and_private
  • Client count and wake: relay_counts_authenticated_clients_and_wakes_on_change
  • Stop ends a reply wait: relay_stop_ends_a_reply_wait_and_the_command_never_runs
  • Running command reported as unknown: relay_reports_a_running_command_past_its_wait_as_unknown
  • Handshake deadline: relay_closes_a_trickling_handshake_at_its_deadline
  • App-granted access: relay_app_lets_agents_use_files_without_yes
  • Grants are scoped and revocable: relay_grants_are_scoped_and_revocable

items.title: Tools
items.text:
Tool What it does list_layers The whole project in one call: path and unsaved changes, the view (centre, longitude/latitude extent, scale, projection), the active layer, layers in table-of-contents order (group, type, source, extent, feature count, selection, definition query, renderer, labels, fields, visibility), web tile layers, basemap, tables and layouts with their map frames. name_filter keeps the layers and tables whose name holds it; include_fields: false leaves fields out view_map The map as a PNG image at the current view; width and height default to 1024 × 640, each clamped to 64–2048 pixels snapshot The map as a PNG with JSON metadata: mode, width, height, extent (longitude/latitude), center, scale, projection, render_settled, saved and note. mode: "screen" captures the RustGIS window through the relay, once the map has finished drawing or after wait_s seconds (default 5, clamped to 0–30); overlays: false leaves out the map's controls, scale bar, north arrow and sketches. mode: "render" draws offscreen at max_width (default 1024, clamped to 64–2048 pixels); height follows the view's shape, with each side capped at 2048. It works while the window is hidden. mode: "auto" (default) takes the screen when the map is on it. Unavailable screen captures fall back to render. save_path also writes the PNG to a file, which needs file access search_commands Finds RustGIS commands by words: their ids, ribbon locations and parameters run_command Runs a command by id with JSON parameters; each run is one undo step. The result names the layers it added (layersAdded) and what the command said beside it (notices), including any parameters it ignored (layer.moveDown ignores 'steps' (it reads layer)) run Runs several commands in one call, as one undo step: a script in the script.run format (one command-id {json} per line, # comments). A failing line stops it, nothing it did to the project is kept, and the error names the line; files an earlier line wrote (an export) stay written. Answers {success, result, lines, layersAdded, notices, error, duration_s}, where result is the last command's. Each line follows run_command's rules, checked before any line runs search_tools Finds geoprocessing tools by words describe_tool A geoprocessing tool's parameters run_tool Runs a geoprocessing tool; its output is added to the map as a new layer (with layersAdded and notices as for run_command), or to the project as a standalone table, which the result names (table) read_features A vector layer's or a standalone table's attribute rows: layer (name or id) or table (a standalone table's name or id; a layer name that no layer has reads the table of that name), optional where, fields, order_by, descending and selected (layers only); limit defaults to 20, capped at 200. Returns the matching count and rows with _row, and a layer's _lon and _lat search_docs Searches this documentation and returns the best matching sections read_doc Reads a documentation page or section as Markdown; offset (1-based line) and limit (default 2000 lines) page through long results using next_offset

MCP exposes these twelve tools: the nine shared AI Assistant tools, plus view_map, snapshot and run. The assistant-only delegate and load_skill tools are not exposed through MCP. Instead, enabled skills are offered as MCP prompts (prompts/list and prompts/get). Every built-in documentation page is also a resource (rustgis://docs/cli.md, rustgis://docs/user-guide/maps.md…) that a client can attach to a conversation. Successful JSON tool results use the default tool-output budget: an estimated 10,000 tokens per result. Read large documentation results in sections or continue with next_offset.

items.title: What the agent may do
items.text:
Your MCP client's approval settings determine when it asks you. The server adds its own limits:

  • Commands that read or write files, connect to an address on the internet or run a plugin's command run only when the server was started with --yes, as does opening a project from text (it could bring in web layers). Without it, the agent can still work with the data you gave the server and with the built-in sample, basemaps and geoprocessing. view_map draws the web tile layers the project you opened already has, fetching their tiles.
  • Plugin management, scripts, tasks, models and the GeoLibre runner are never run from here, unless you turned on Full access for agents in the desktop app. That applies only to agents attached to it with the relay's own token.
  • In private-server mode, replacing and undoing in the project are allowed: it is the agent's own. With --attach, project replacement and undo ownership follow the desktop restrictions above, unless Full access is enabled. ui.* commands that only open panes and dialogs are unavailable to the tools.

Installed plugins load first, as with the other subcommands (--no-plugins skips them). Notes such as "MCP server ready" go to standard error; standard output carries only the protocol.

items.title: Local-agent approvals
items.text:
Local agents launched by the assistant use Relay::grant_reviewed(auto), not an unrestricted run grant. With automatic approval off, gated tool calls wait in a RustGIS-side queue scoped to that grant and exact message, including all tool calls in a batch. --yes and the general relay checkbox do not bypass it. An approval cannot revive an expired request; revoking the grant or stopping the relay cancels pending work. The approval wait has a separate 15-minute bound; other clients' reads can still run while it waits. Explicit automatic approval bypasses this extra queue for that run, but not the reserved-command refusals. Ordinary MCP clients retain the access policy described above.

Stopping the relay through its command or status-bar control also turns off its remembered agent-control choice. Copyable setup commands are labelled for POSIX shells or PowerShell and quote the executable path literally; use the matching shell.

items.title: Plugins
items.text:
Plugins add commands, geoprocessing tools and assistant skills to RustGIS. A plugin has a plugin.json manifest and is packaged as a .rgplugin file. WebAssembly plugins run sandboxed in the desktop app, on the command line and in the web app. Process plugins run a local program instead and need the desktop app or command line.

Browse the plugin catalog. opengeos/rustgis-plugins holds the registry, blocklist and rustgis-plugin SDK, not plugin source. Plugin sources live in their own repositories; start one from the Rust WebAssembly, Rust process or Python process template.

items.title: Using plugins
items.text:
Open Plugins › Plugin Manager. The Plugins tab also has Install From File and Browse Plugins buttons.

  • Browse lists the plugins in the registry, with search and a category filter. Install downloads the plugin, checks its SHA-256 and id against the registry entry, and shows what the plugin may do before it loads. Descriptions stay on one line; hover over one to read its full text and, for a withdrawn plugin, the withdrawal reason in a single tooltip.
  • Installed lists your plugins: turn them on or off, update them, or uninstall them.
  • Settings has Install From File… for a .rgplugin file; you can also drop the file on the window. It also sets the registry address (empty means the RustGIS registry). On the desktop, Add Plugin Folder… loads an unpacked plugin while you develop it.

A plugin's commands and tools appear on the Plugins tab, in a group named after the plugin, or on the plugin's own tab if it has one. Its commands are also in command search, and its tools are in the Tools pane under Plugins ›.

The desktop app keeps installed packages in plugins/ in its data folder (overridden by $RUSTGIS_PLUGINS_DIR) and loads them at startup. The web app remembers the plugins you installed from the registry and downloads them again on your next visit. Packages installed from files are remembered when they are at most 1.5 MiB; larger ones last for the current session only.

On the command line:

rustgis-cli plugins                          # installed plugins
rustgis-cli plugins browse                   # the registry
rustgis-cli plugins get vector-toolkit       # install from the registry
rustgis-cli plugins install my.rgplugin      # install a file (or a plugin folder)
rustgis-cli plugins disable vector-toolkit   # enable / disable / uninstall <id>

rustgis-cli run --sample \
  --cmd 'gp.run={"tool":"plugin:vector-toolkit/hexagon-grid","params":{"input":"Countries","size":300}}' \
  --cmd 'share.exportMap={"path":"hex.png"}'
rustgis-cli run --plugin ./dev-plugin/ --sample --cmd 'plugin:my-plugin/hello'   # load for one run

Use --no-plugins to skip loading installed plugins. plugins browse and plugins get accept --registry https://…/registry.json for another registry.

items.title: Safety
items.text:
Plugins run in a sandbox: an interpreter (wasmi) with no access to files, the network, the clock or anything else outside the module. A plugin reaches RustGIS only through the requests described below, and RustGIS checks each one:

  • Every plugin can read the map: its layers, their features and the view.
  • With the edit permission, it can change the project. It can run commands that edit it and add layers. A plugin command that changes the project is one undo step, and it is rolled back if the command fails.
  • With the files permission, it can run commands that read or write files the user names, and its tools can take a file the user picks (a file parameter). SQL, database and Zarr commands require both files and network, since they can reach local files or remote servers.
  • With the network permission, it can reach the web: read a small document from a web address (host.fetch) and run the commands that fetch (adding data or services by their address). With edit too, it can add web tile layers (map.addTiles). The addresses are the plugin's choice and can carry what it read from the project, so this is a permission of its own. A command that would bring in a tile layer some other way (importing a map file) has it taken out again without network.
  • No plugin may run the user's scripts, tasks or models, create or save models, install or locate other software, manage plugins or connections and logins, replace the project, or step through undo history. It cannot call another plugin's command directly.

A process plugin is the exception: it is a program on your computer, not sandboxed, and the install prompt says so.

The install prompt lists these permissions. Each call has a fuel budget, so a plugin stuck in a loop is stopped. Memory is capped at 512 MB, and requests and replies are size-limited. A plugin that traps, panics or returns garbage produces an error message, never a crash.

The registry is curated: plugins are reviewed before they are listed, and packages are hash-pinned. A blocklist.json beside a registry withdraws a plugin (every version, or one package). RustGIS checks it when you browse that registry. Desktop and command-line startup apply the cached blocklist; the web app fetches it when restoring plugins.

items.title: Writing a plugin
items.text:
Start from the Rust WebAssembly template, or the Rust or Python template for a process plugin, and read the official plugins for examples, such as Hello RustGIS. A WebAssembly plugin uses the rustgis-plugin SDK crate:

use rustgis_plugin::{Kind, Request, ToolOutput, Value, geojson, host, json};

fn handle(req: Request) -> Result<Value, String> {
    match (req.kind, req.id.as_str()) {
        (Kind::Command, "layer-report") => {
            let n = host::layers()?.as_array().map_or(0, Vec::len);
            host::notify(&format!("{n} layers"));
            Ok(json!({"layers": n}))
        }
        (Kind::Tool, "bounding-boxes") => {
            let boxes: Vec<Value> = req.features("input")?.iter().filter_map(|f| {
                let b = geojson::bbox(&geojson::positions(&f["geometry"]))?;
                Some(geojson::feature(geojson::polygon(&[[b[0], b[1]], [b[2], b[1]], [b[2], b[3]], [b[0], b[3]]]), json!({})))
            }).collect();
            Ok(ToolOutput::new().layer("Boxes", geojson::collection(boxes)).into())
        }
        (_, other) => Err(format!("unknown '{other}'")),
    }
}

rustgis_plugin::export!(handle);

rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown
cargo build --release --target wasm32-unknown-unknown

items.title: plugin.json
items.text:
{
  "id": "hello-rustgis",
  "name": "Hello RustGIS",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "description": "What it does, in a sentence or two.",
  "author": "You",
  "homepage": "https://github.com/you/your-plugin",
  "license": "MIT",
  "entry": "plugin.wasm",
  "abi": 1,
  "minRustgisVersion": "0.1.0",
  "permissions": ["edit"],
  "commands": [
    { "id": "layer-report", "label": "Layer\nReport", "help": "Shown on hover.", "icon": "stats", "params": "{}" }
  ],
  "tools": [
    {
      "id": "bounding-boxes", "name": "Bounding Boxes", "summary": "One line.", "toolbox": "Hello",
      "params": [
        { "name": "input", "label": "Input features", "kind": "vectorLayer", "required": true },
        { "name": "whole", "label": "One box for the whole layer", "kind": "bool", "default": false }
      ]
    }
  ],
  "i18n": { "de": { "Layer\nReport": "Ebenen-\nbericht" } }
}
  • id: 1 to 64 lower-case letters, digits and hyphens, starting with a letter. Command and tool ids follow the same rules. Their full ids are plugin:<id>/<command-or-tool>; run commands directly and tools through gp.run.
  • runtime: wasm (the default), process or skills. For WebAssembly plugins, entry defaults to plugin.wasm and must name a .wasm file relative to the manifest, using forward slashes with no . or .. path segments. abi defaults to 1 and must equal 1.
  • version and optional minRustgisVersion are numeric versions such as 1.2.3 or 1.2. RustGIS compares their numeric components, ignoring prerelease and build suffixes, and refuses a plugin that needs a newer RustGIS.
  • permissions: edit, files and network (see Safety); empty by default. Ask only for what you use.
  • commands[].params: a string describing the command's parameters for scripts and agents, not a JSON object or a form definition; it defaults to "{}".
  • commands[].icon: the name of one of RustGIS's own icons (stats, zoom_full, bookmark, buffer…), or a puzzle piece when it isn't one.
  • Tool parameter kinds: layer, vectorLayer, polygonLayer, pointLayer, field, numericField, number, text, choice (with 1 to 64 choices), bool and file (see File parameters). Each has name, label, optional help, required (default false) and an optional JSON default. Parameter names start with a lower-case letter and may also contain upper-case letters and underscores after it.
  • panel (optional) gives the plugin a pane of its own, with widgets bound to its commands. See A panel.
  • i18n translates the plugin's own text into the interface language, by language code (de, zh-CN…). See Translations.
  • skills (optional) lists skills for the AI Assistant that the package carries. See Skills.

A manifest can declare at most 256 commands, 64 tools and 32 parameters per tool.

A package is a zip archive, conventionally named <id>-<version>.rgplugin. It holds plugin.json at its root or inside one top-level folder; entry is relative to that manifest. Packages are at most 64 MiB with at most 4,096 entries, modules at most 48 MiB, and the manifest at most 512 KiB.

items.title: File parameters
items.text:
A tool can read a file the user picks, such as a NetCDF model run, with a file parameter. The plugin needs the files permission:

{ "name": "model", "label": "Model output", "kind": "file", "required": true, "extensions": ["nc", "nc4"] }
  • The Tools pane shows a path box with a Browse button. extensions filters the picker: at most 16 extensions, each 1 to 16 letters or digits without the dot. Leave it out for any file.
  • On the desktop and the command line the value is a path, and RustGIS reads the file. In the web app, which has no paths, the user picks the file and its contents go with the run. A script can do the same with {"name": "run.nc", "data": base64}.
  • The tool gets the file in the request's files, by parameter name, as {"name": "run.nc", "data": base64}. The parameter itself holds just the file name.
  • Files are at most 64 MB. The Geoprocessing history keeps the file's name, not its contents.
  • RustGIS versions before file parameters refuse a plugin that has one, so set minRustgisVersion to the first version with them.

items.title: Translations
items.text:
A plugin speaks the interface language through its i18n table: for each language code, its English strings and their translations, written exactly as they appear in plugin.json (\n included):

"i18n": {
  "de": { "Bounding Boxes": "Begrenzungsrahmen", "Input features": "Eingabe-Features" },
  "zh-CN": { "Bounding Boxes": "边界框", "Input features": "输入要素" }
}
  • It covers the plugin's name and description, command labels and help, tool names, summaries and toolboxes, parameter labels and choice values, the tab, group and menu labels, and the panel's title, help and widget labels. A string with no translation shows in English.
  • Alongside English (en), RustGIS's interface languages are de, es, fr, it, nl, pt, ru, tr, az, id, vi, fa, zh, ja, ko and ka. A code with a region matches its language: zh-CN serves zh.
  • The registry copies the name and description translations into registry.json, so the Plugin Manager lists plugins in the interface language before they are installed.
  • Messages a plugin builds while it runs can follow the interface language too: every request carries its code as lang. In the SDK that is req.lang, and req.tr looks a message up in i18n.
  • Up to 64 languages and 20,000 translated strings in all.

items.title: A tab of its own
items.text:
By default a plugin's commands and tools get a group on the Plugins tab. A plugin can have a ribbon tab of its own instead. The tab sits at the end of the tab strip, and Settings › Customize › Ribbon can hide it like any other. Declare it in plugin.json:

"tab": {
  "label": "Explorer",
  "groups": [
    {
      "label": "Go To",
      "items": [
        {
          "menu": "Continent",
          "icon": "zoom_world",
          "help": "Go to a continent.",
          "layout": "small",
          "items": [
            "go-africa",
            { "menu": "Europe", "items": ["go-europe", "go-france"] }
          ]
        },
        "random-place"
      ]
    },
    {
      "label": "Inspect",
      "layout": "small",
      "items": [
        "layer-report",
        "tool:field-summary",
        { "menu": "More", "items": ["feature-report", "tool:statistics"] },
        { "menu": "Overview", "layout": "large", "items": ["map-report"] }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
  • items lists the buttons. An item is a command id, tool:<id> (which opens that tool in the Tools pane), panel (which opens the plugin's panel), or a dropdown menu whose items may also contain nested menus.
  • A group's layout is "large" by default: full-height ribbon buttons, as in existing manifests. Use "layout": "small" for compact controls, stacked three per column. A menu's optional layout overrides its ribbon trigger's size; when omitted (or null), it inherits the group's layout. Consecutive small controls share three-row columns, including small menu triggers in a large group. A large trigger starts a new column. Column widths follow the translated labels; manifests neither need nor support pixel widths. Layout affects ribbon triggers only: all entries and nested submenu triggers inside a popup remain standard menu rows, regardless of any nested layout. Popup labels stay on one line: line breaks in labels or their translations become spaces.
  • A tab has 1 to 8 groups. A large group has 1 to 16 direct items; a small group has 1 to 48. Each menu has 1 to 32 direct items. Menus may nest up to 4 levels, counting the outer menu as level 1. Across the entire tab there may be at most 16,384 items, counting every command/tool/panel entry and every menu at every level. Every entry must name one of the plugin's own commands or tools, or its panel.
  • The label is one line of 1 to 32 characters and can't be the name of one of RustGIS's tabs (Home, Data, Style, Analyze, Plugins…), including their older names. The i18n translations apply to the tab, group and menu labels too.

Map Explorer is an example.

items.title: A panel
items.text:
A plugin can have a panel: a pane on the right of the map with texts, checkboxes, sliders, buttons and trees bound to its commands. Declare it in plugin.json:

"panel": {
  "title": "Historical Imagery",
  "icon": "history",
  "help": "Step through the archived releases of World Imagery.",
  "state": "panel-state",
  "items": [
    { "kind": "text", "id": "selected", "label": "Selected release" },
    { "kind": "checkbox", "id": "local", "label": "Only versions with local changes", "command": "panel-state" },
    { "kind": "slider", "id": "release", "label": "Release timeline", "steps": true, "command": "go-to-release" },
    { "kind": "button", "command": "older" },
    { "kind": "button", "command": "newer" },
    { "kind": "text", "id": "metadata", "label": "Location metadata" }
  ]
}
  • title is the pane's tab and the label of the button that opens it: one line of 1 to 48 characters. RustGIS puts the button first in the plugin's group on the Plugins tab. On a tab of its own, put panel among a group's items. Command search lists the panel too. icon and help are for that button.
  • items lists the widgets, top to bottom (1 to 32). Buttons that follow each other share a row. Each has an id (lower-case letters, digits and hyphens; a button's is its command's unless given), and label and help (on hover) where they apply:
    • text: a caption (label) over text the plugin sets (text is what it shows first).
    • checkbox: a box with a label, default false unless given.
    • slider: whole numbers from min to max, both within ±1,000,000,000 (both default to 0; default is min unless given), with a caption, the value's label, and its two ends' labels. steps: true adds ‹ and › buttons that move it by one.
    • button: runs its command; its label is the command's unless given.
    • tree: nodes the plugin gives (themes, their datasets, say), each branch opened or closed with its triangle or a double click. search: true adds a box above it that keeps the nodes whose label holds every word typed (case and accents aside), with the branches above them open; a branch found with nothing found below it opens to all its children.
  • A checkbox runs its command when it changes, a slider when it is let go, or stepped (never while it is dragged, while the pane shows the label of the value it would take), and a tree when a node is chosen. Without a command, a widget's value just goes with the plugin's next request.
  • state (optional) is a command RustGIS runs each time the panel is opened, to answer its state.
  • Every command reference, including state, must name one of the plugin's own commands. Widget ids are independent of command ids. A plugin with a panel can't have a command called panel.

A plugin keeps nothing between calls, so RustGIS keeps the panel's state. Every request of a plugin with a panel carries the widgets' values, whatever ran the command (the panel, a ribbon button, a script or the command line):

"panel": { "values": { "local": false, "release": 196 }, "changed": ["release"] }

values has each checkbox (true or false), slider (a whole number) and tree (the chosen node's id, or null), and changed the ones this call set: the widget the user just moved. A widget's command is run with {"panel": {"release": 196}} as its parameters, which sets the values before the call and is taken out of the request's params, so a script or rustgis-cli can do the same:

rustgis-cli run --sample --cmd 'plugin:historical-imagery/go-to-release={"panel": {"release": 40}}'

Any command can answer the panel's new state, beside the rest of its answer:

{
  "panel": {
    "values": { "release": 196 },
    "items": {
      "selected": { "text": "2025-12-18\nRelease 13192" },
      "release": { "min": 0, "max": 196, "labels": ["2014-02-20", "…", "2025-12-18"] },
      "newer": { "enabled": false },
      "metadata": { "text": "Source: Maxar (Vivid)\nResolution: 0.3 m" }
    }
  }
}
  • An item can set label (null brings back the declared one), enabled and visible; a text its text; a slider its min, max and labels, one per value from min (the numbers when there are none); a tree its nodes. What an answer leaves out stays as it was.
  • A tree's nodes are [{"id": "env", "label": "Environment", "count": 67, "children": [...]}]: id is the value the node gives when chosen, unique in the tree; label defaults to the id; count (a whole number) shows at the right of the row. The nodes come before the values in an answer, so one can give a tree and choose a node of it; a chosen node no longer among them leaves nothing chosen.
  • RustGIS checks the answer like any other: unknown ids and fields and values of the wrong type are ignored, a slider's value stays within its ends and a tree's among its nodes, texts are clipped to 4,000 characters, labels to 200, and a slider has at most 2,000 labels of 80 characters. A tree holds at most 5,000 nodes, 8 levels deep; a node without an id, or with one longer than 200 characters or taken already, is left out with its children.
  • A plugin words what it sets in the request's lang; RustGIS translates only what the manifest declares.
  • A command that fails leaves the values as they were. The panel's state command is no undo step when it changes nothing in the project (it only reads the map); other commands keep theirs.
  • RustGIS asks for the state only when the panel opens, and takes in what the plugin's own commands answer. It doesn't run the plugin when the map changes in other ways: undo, another plugin, a project opened. A state command that reads what it shows from the map (which release is on it) puts the panel right when it is opened again.
  • The values are kept while RustGIS runs, not saved with the project.
  • plugin.panel {"id": "<plugin>"} answers a panel's state (values and items), and sets values or, with "refresh": true, runs the state command first. On the command line, which has no panes, the commands still run with the values given.
  • RustGIS versions before panels ignore panel (and refuse a tab that names it): keep the commands usable from the ribbon too, or set minRustgisVersion.

items.title: What a plugin can ask for
items.text:
Inside a request, host::call(op, params) sends one of these to RustGIS:

Request Answer host.info {rustgis, abi, plugin, permissions}: version, ABI, plugin id and permissions host.layers [{id, name, raster, visible, geometry, features, selected, active, fields: [{name, type}]}] host.features {layer, selected?, limit?} the layer's features as GeoJSON; each feature has its row host.view {center: [lon, lat], scale, projection} host.notify {text, error?} shows a message in the status bar host.addLayer {name, geojson} adds a layer (edit) host.fetch {url} {url, text, json?}: the document at a web address (network; see Fetching a document) map.addTiles {url, kind?, name?, attribution?, maxZoom?, overlay?, replace?, blend?, …} adds a tile layer (edit and network); accepts the built-in command's parameters any command id (layer.zoomTo, select.byAttributes, layer.symbology…) what the command returns, within the plugin's permissions

In the apps a plugin's command (from the ribbon, command search or a panel's widget; not its panel's state command) doesn't wait for a download, so where layer.addUrl has to download a file whole it answers {"pending": true, "url": …}: RustGIS downloads the data off the frame, saying so in the status bar, and adds the layer when it lands (its own undo step), as Home › Add › Add Data › From URL does. On the desktop that goes for reading a GeoTIFF's, FlatGeobuf's or GeoParquet's header too; in the web app a PMTiles archive, a cloud-optimised GeoTIFF or a FlatGeobuf or GeoParquet whose header was fetched already is added at once. Up to 16 downloads wait at a time: a request past 16 fails, and if the command then fails too, none of its downloads start. Run by rustgis-cli, a script or a task, the command waits and answers what was added.

rustgis-cli commands lists every command id and its parameters.

items.title: Fetching a document
items.text:
host.fetch {"url": "https://…"} reads a small text document, such as a web API's JSON answer, with a GET request. It needs the network permission. The answer is {"url", "text", "json"?}: url is the address fetched, text the document, and json the document parsed when it is a JSON object or array.

  • Only http:// and https:// addresses on the internet: not this computer, the local network or cloud metadata addresses, and no redirect may lead there or from https to http. Names are checked as written and again where they resolve, on every redirect too, so a name that resolves to this computer or the local network is refused on the desktop and the command line (in the web app, the browser decides what it may reach). Requests carry no credentials (an S3 connection's included) and no headers of the plugin's. On the desktop and the command line they never go through a proxy (HTTPS_PROXY and the like are ignored), since a proxy would reach addresses RustGIS can't check.
  • At most 2 MB, in UTF-8 (a byte-order mark is dropped). An answer that isn't a success (404, 500…) is an error ending in HTTP <status>.
  • Answers are kept for 10 minutes (up to 256 documents and 16 MB in all) while RustGIS runs, so asking for the same address again costs nothing. Each plugin has answers of its own: one never reads what another fetched. Errors are kept for 30 seconds, so every command waiting for an address sees its error; after that it is fetched again.
  • On the desktop and the command line the request waits for the answer: at most 20 seconds for one, and 60 seconds for all the fetches of one plugin call. A call makes at most 64 fetches.
  • In the web app nothing may wait. A fetch that isn't kept yet answers {"pending": true, "url"} and starts in the background. The command should then return straight away, before doing anything outside the project (writing a file): RustGIS undoes what the call did to the project (its notices stay, and so does anything done outside it), and runs the command again with the same parameters once every pending answer has landed (up to 8 per call), when host.fetch answers from what was kept. A command that walks a chain of documents, each address taken from the one before, runs once per step, up to 64 times. The browser follows redirects itself, and the server must allow requests from web pages (CORS).

Use host::call("host.fetch", json!({"url": url})) in the Rust SDK.

Tools work differently. A tool receives its layer parameters' features as GeoJSON (only the selected features when a layer has a selection), and its file parameters' files. It returns new layers and standalone tables, or a selection, plus messages for the Geoprocessing history. RustGIS adds the results as it does for built-in tools, with undo; returning these results does not require edit. Tools can log, but they make no host requests.

In the desktop app a plugin tool runs in the background, so the map and the rest of the window stay usable: the Tools pane shows the line the tool last logged, or a process plugin's last progress message, and a Cancel button. Cancel stops a process plugin's program; a WebAssembly tool runs on to its end and its result is dropped. One plugin tool runs at a time. gp.run, scripts and rustgis-cli still wait for the result.

items.title: The ABI (version 1)
items.text:
The SDK implements this; it is described here for other languages.

The module is wasm32 with no imports except these three, in module rustgis:

  • call(ptr: i32, len: i32) -> i32 runs the host request at ptr ({"op": "...", "params": {...}}). It returns the length of the reply, which is {"ok": value} or {"error": "text"}, or -1 when there is none. A new call replaces any reply not yet copied.
  • result(ptr: i32) copies that reply to ptr and consumes it. Allocate the length call returned first.
  • log(ptr: i32, len: i32) logs a UTF-8 line.

The module exports:

  • memory.
  • rustgis_alloc(len: i32) -> i32, which returns room for len bytes. RustGIS writes the request there.
  • rustgis_call(ptr: i32, len: i32) -> i64, which handles the request and returns reply_ptr << 32 | reply_len. The reply is {"ok": value} or {"error": "text"}.

Command requests are {"abi": 1, "kind": "command", "id": "...", "params": {...}, "lang": "de"}. id is the local command id from the manifest, not its plugin:…/… id. lang is the interface language's code (en for English). Commands of a plugin with a panel also get panel, and may answer panel beside the rest of their ok value.

Tools get "kind": "tool" and their local tool id, plus layers, which maps layer names (not parameter names) to FeatureCollections. When they have file inputs, files maps each parameter name to {"name": "...", "data": "..."}, with the contents in standard padded base64. A tool's ok value can contain:

  • layers: [{"name": "...", "geojson": {...}}].
  • tables: the same shape, using FeatureCollections whose features have no geometry.
  • selection: {"layer": "<layer name>", "rows": [0, 2, ...]}. If present, it takes precedence over layers and tables.
  • messages: an array of strings.

RustGIS takes at most 64 layers, 64 tables and 200 messages, with at most 5,000,000 features in each output dataset.

Each call gets a fresh instance, so a module keeps no state between calls and need not free memory. Host requests and module replies are limited to 128 MiB.

items.title: Process plugins
items.text:
A process plugin is a program on your computer instead of a WebAssembly module: a Python script, or an executable in any language. It can use the file system, threads and any library, which lets existing analysis code (numpy, xarray, GDAL…) become a plugin without a rewrite. It is not sandboxed: it can do anything you can. The install prompt says so, and the Plugin Manager marks it Not sandboxed, in Browse too, before it is installed (with the Python version its environment downloads, if it has one). Process plugins run on the desktop and the command line, not in the web app: its Browse list shows them as Desktop and command line only, with no Install button.

{
  "id": "hello-python",
  "name": "Hello Python",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "runtime": "process",
  "run": { "windows": ["python", "main.py"], "default": ["python3", "main.py"] },
  "permissions": [],
  "commands": [{ "id": "layer-count", "label": "Count\nLayers" }],
  "tools": [{
    "id": "feature-count", "name": "Count Features", "summary": "Counts a layer's features.",
    "params": [{ "name": "input", "label": "Input layer", "kind": "vectorLayer", "required": true }]
  }]
}
  • "runtime": "process" and run: the program and its arguments, started in the plugin's folder. A bare name (python3) is looked up on PATH; a relative path (bin/tool) is in the plugin's folder. run can name a program per platform (windows, macos, linux, and default when the platform has no entry). Omit entry; process plugins use run instead. Each argument list contains the program and at most 63 arguments.
  • Commands, tools, tabs, translations and permissions work as for WebAssembly plugins. Permissions still decide which host requests RustGIS answers, but they don't limit what the program itself can do.
  • A .rgplugin holds the plugin's files (the manifest, scripts, executables). Installing it unpacks them to unpacked/<id>/ in the plugins folder, keeping Unix execute bits and rejecting unsafe paths or more than 1 GiB of unpacked files. A plugin folder installed for development (Plugin Manager › Settings, or rustgis-cli plugins install ./folder) runs where it is.

items.title: The protocol
items.text:
The Rust process template provides a command, a tool and a reusable JSON-line transport module, with packaging and release builds for Linux, Windows and universal macOS. Users run the packaged executable without Rust or Python installed. Native plugins are not sandboxed and do not run in the web app.

Each command or tool call starts the program once. It speaks the ABI's requests and replies over its standard input and output, one JSON object per line:

  1. RustGIS writes the request as one JSON line, including panel for a command of a plugin with a panel, and layers and optional files for a tool.
  2. The program writes lines:
    • {"call": {"op": "...", "params": {...}}}: a host request. RustGIS answers with one line, {"ok": value} or {"error": "text"}.
    • {"log": "text"}: a line for the log (and a tool's run messages).
    • {"progress": "text"}: what a tool is doing now, shown while it runs and not kept in its messages: a line per step of a long run, say.
    • Last, {"ok": value} or {"error": "text"}: the result.
  3. RustGIS then closes the program's input; a program still running a few seconds later is stopped.

Output lines that aren't protocol messages are logged and skipped, since libraries print (even JSON), and so is the program's error output. A command is stopped after 2 minutes; a tool runs until it finishes or is cancelled (the desktop app runs it in the background: see What a plugin can ask for).

The plugin above, in Python with no SDK:

import json
import sys


def call(op, params):
    """Sends a request to RustGIS and returns its answer."""
    print(json.dumps({"call": {"op": op, "params": params}}), flush=True)
    reply = json.loads(sys.stdin.readline())
    if "error" in reply:
        raise RuntimeError(reply["error"])
    return reply["ok"]


req = json.loads(sys.stdin.readline())
try:
    if req["id"] == "layer-count":
        n = len(call("host.layers", {}))
        call("host.notify", {"text": f"The map has {n} layers."})
        result = {"ok": {"layers": n}}
    elif req["id"] == "feature-count":
        layer = req["params"]["input"]
        n = len(req["layers"][layer]["features"])
        result = {"ok": {"layers": [], "messages": [f"{layer} has {n} features."]}}
    else:
        result = {"error": f"unknown command '{req['id']}'"}
except Exception as e:
    result = {"error": str(e)}
print(json.dumps(result), flush=True)

items.title: Python environments
items.text:
A Python plugin can have RustGIS make its environment, so its users don't install Python or any package themselves:

"runtime": "process",
"python": { "version": "3.12", "requirements": "requirements.txt" },
"run": ["python", "main.py"]
  • python, python3 or python.exe as the program in run becomes that environment's interpreter, on every platform. The Python version defaults to 3.12; omit requirements for an environment with no extra packages.
  • RustGIS prepares the environment when the plugin is installed: in the background in the desktop app (the Plugin Manager shows how it's going, with a Prepare button if it is not ready), and before the command returns in rustgis-cli plugins install and get. rustgis-cli plugins prepare <id> and the plugin.prepare command make it on demand.
  • It uses uv, which RustGIS downloads once (a pinned version, checked against its pinned SHA-256; RUSTGIS_UV names one to use instead, which is then trusted as it is, unchecked). uv installs a standalone Python of the version asked for and the packages in the requirements file, from PyPI. Pythons and uv's cache are shared in tools/ in the plugins folder; each plugin's environment is in envs/<id>/. One environment is made at a time per plugin, even across the app and rustgis-cli.
  • The environment is made again when the Python version or the requirements change (a plugin update), and removed with the plugin. Until it's ready, the plugin's calls fail with a message saying how to prepare it.
  • The first install downloads Python and the packages: tens to hundreds of MB, depending on them. The install prompt says so.

items.title: Skills
items.text:
A plugin can carry skills for the AI Assistant: instructions for a kind of task, which the assistant reads when a request needs them. Put each in skills/<name>/SKILL.md in the package and list the names in plugin.json:

"skills": ["flood-map"]

A SKILL.md starts with front matter giving the same name and a description that says when to use it, then the instructions in Markdown (the Agent Skills format). The assistant knows it as <plugin id>:<name> (hello-rustgis:flood-map) while the plugin is enabled. A SKILL.md is at most 64 KB, and a plugin has at most 32 skills.

A package of skills alone, with no code, says "runtime": "skills". It has no module, commands, tools, tab, panel or permissions, and must list at least one skill. Nothing in it runs, and it installs from a file in the desktop app, on the command line and in the web app:

{
  "id": "flood-skills",
  "name": "Flood mapping skills",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "runtime": "skills",
  "skills": ["flood-map", "gauge-report"]
}

items.title: Publishing a plugin
items.text:
1. Write the plugin in your own repository, starting from the Rust WebAssembly, Rust process or Python process template. See Write a plugin.
  2. Release it: the templates' Release workflow attaches the .rgplugin and its registry entry to a GitHub release.
  3. Open a pull request on opengeos/rustgis-plugins adding that entry as registry/<id>.json:
{"id": "...", "source": {"url": "https://…/<id>-<version>.rgplugin", "sha256": "…"}, "categories": ["Analysis"]}

Every plugin is listed by source; the registry build refuses path entries. 4. CI downloads the package, checks its hash, validates its manifest and module (or a process plugin's files), and runs it in RustGIS. A maintainer reviews it before merging. 5. Once merged, the registry lists the plugin and serves its package at https://packages.rustgis.app/<id>/<id>-<version>.rgplugin. Published packages never change, and every version stays available. To update, release a new version and submit a pull request updating the entry's source.url and source.sha256.

Pull requests get a preview with an Open in RustGIS link; process plugins must be tried in the desktop app instead. The nightly workflow runs every published plugin in the latest RustGIS. See the registry's publishing instructions for details.

The file you submit is only a pointer to the release. The registry build turns it into the published registry.json that RustGIS reads, whose entries carry package (the package's address) and sha256 in place of source. A registry entry contains id, name, version, description, author, homepage, license, permissions, minRustgisVersion, i18n (the name and description translated), categories, package, lower-case hexadecimal sha256, and size in bytes. package is an HTTPS address or a path relative to registry.json; plain http://localhost and http://127.0.0.1 addresses are accepted for local test registries. Entries without a valid id, name, version or SHA-256 are skipped. A process plugin's entry also has "runtime": "process" and, when it has a managed Python environment, "python": "3.12" (the version); a WebAssembly plugin can omit both. Registries can list skills packages with "runtime": "skills". The Plugin Manager checks the package's hash and id before installing; rustgis-cli plugins get also checks its runtime. rustgis-cli plugins browse prints runtime for every entry (wasm when the registry leaves it out).

items.title: Privacy
items.text: The RustGIS desktop app and command line collect no analytics, telemetry or usage data. Local files and projects are processed on your device. Features that use remote services can send searches, coordinates, data or assistant context to those services, as described below.

items.title: Online services
items.text:
• Locate › By Place or Address and place search send your query to OpenStreetMap's Nominatim by default. By Place or Address and Geocode Addresses can also use Komoot's Photon or a server you specify; geocoding sends the address values you choose from your table or layer.
  • Directions sends the route's start, stops and destination to FOSSGIS's public Valhalla server by default. The Directions pane asks for consent before sending places and remembers that choice. The map.route command can also use a server you specify.
  • Web basemaps and tile layers request tiles for the area you view; vector styles can also request their tile sources and sprites. These requests reveal the requested map area to the servers even when your local layers are not uploaded.
  • Web data, remote rasters, cloud storage, database connections and online catalogs contact their configured servers. Searches may send keywords, coordinates, an area of interest, dates or filters; authenticated connections also send the credentials or tokens required by that service. See Web data.

Servers receive ordinary connection information, including your IP address and request headers. Their own privacy and retention policies apply. Working with local files does not itself upload their contents to RustGIS.

items.title: AI Assistant and connected agents
items.text:
When you use the AI Assistant, requests go to the provider and endpoint you configure, which may be a local model server. They include your messages, conversation history, map context (including the map centre, layer names, counts and field names), tool results and any skills the assistant reads. Tools can read feature attributes and geometry, so those results can become part of the conversation sent to the provider.

Signing in with ChatGPT contacts OpenAI's authentication services and Responses API. Local agents you connect or let the assistant delegate to use their own model services and tools, under their own configuration and policies. Approval prompts for file, network and other restricted actions do not stop ordinary assistant context and tool results from being sent to the configured model.

items.title: Plugins and downloads
items.text:
Browsing the Plugin Manager fetches a registry and its blocklist; installing or updating a plugin downloads its package. The default registry is plugins.rustgis.app. The web app also checks the registry's blocklist at startup and may download packages saved by URL in an earlier visit. Preparing a Python process plugin can download uv from PyPI, Python and the plugin's dependencies.

WebAssembly plugins need the network permission to make web requests through RustGIS. A plugin with that permission can send information it can read to addresses it chooses. Desktop process plugins are not sandboxed and can access files and the network as ordinary programs. Review the permissions and publisher before installing; see Plugins.

On the desktop, Help › Check for Updates contacts GitHub's latest-release API only when you ask. It does not upload your project. The web app checks its own site for service-worker updates when it loads and returns to view, and fetches app icons from assets.rustgis.app. It downloads language fonts from that asset server when needed. The web GeoLibre tools download their runner from jsDelivr when needed; the tool list is cached between visits.

items.title: Website analytics
items.text:
The websites we host, the documentation at rustgis.app and the web app at web.rustgis.app, use Google Analytics 4 to count page visits and see which pages are used. Google receives your IP address, the page you are on, the referring page and general device and browser information, and sets its own cookies in your browser. It is governed by Google's privacy policy.

RustGIS does not send layer contents, files or projects to Google Analytics. The web app's page-view event reports its address trimmed to the site and path (https://web.rustgis.app/), without the query string or map hash; its referring address is trimmed the same way. The documentation reports the standard page address, which can include a query string, such as the words of a site search.

You can block analytics with a content blocker or your browser's tracking protection; the sites work normally without them. Analytics run only on the sites we host: the measurement ID is added when those sites are deployed, so the desktop app, the command line and any copy you build yourself never load them.

items.title: Python
items.text:
The rustgis package runs the RustGIS engine inside Python, headless. It opens data and projects, runs engine commands and geoprocessing tools, styles layers, renders maps and saves projects that the desktop app opens as they are. There is no app to install and no server to run: the engine is a native module for Python 3.12 and later. Release wheels cover Windows x64, macOS Intel and Apple Silicon, and Linux x64 and arm64 (glibc 2.28 or later).

pip install rustgis               # pip install "rustgis[geopandas]" for GeoDataFrames

A getting-started notebook walks through what follows; open it in Colab to try it without installing anything.

items.title: A first session
items.text:
import rustgis

s = rustgis.Session(sample=True)                    # the World Atlas sample
s.layer_names()                                     # ['Cities', 'Rivers', 'Lakes', 'Countries']
buffers = s.run_tool("buffer", input=s["Cities"], distance=100)
s["Countries"].style("graduated", field="pop_est")
s.zoom_to(buffers)
s.to_png("map.png", width=1600, height=900)
s.save("atlas.rgis")

In Jupyter, a session on the last line of a cell shows its map as a picture. For the app itself, use a Map.

items.title: Layers
items.text:
s["Cities"] (or s.layer("Cities")) is a Layer: one layer of the active map. It is kept by its id, so it is still the same layer after a rename, and its properties read the session each time.

cities = s["Cities"]                                # by name (any case) or id
cities.count, cities.type, cities.fields, cities.bounds
"Cities" in s                                       # True
[layer.name for layer in s]                         # every layer, top first

cities.style("proportional", field="pop_max")       # layer.symbology; returns the layer
cities.visible = False
cities.set_transparency(30)
cities.filter("pop_max > 1000000")                  # a definition query; None clears it
cities.rename("Towns")
s.undo()                                            # restore the name "Cities"
cities.zoom_to()
cities.remove()
s.undo()                                            # restore the removed layer

Selections work by SQL where clause:

n = cities.select("pop_max > 10000000")            # mode="add", "remove" or "subset"
cities.to_geojson(selected=True)                    # only the selected features
cities.clear_selection()                            # clears selections in every layer

items.title: PMTiles archives
items.text:
Session.add_pmtiles and Map.add_pmtiles add a raster or vector PMTiles archive by web address or local file path. source_layers chooses the vector source layers; style is an array of MapLibre style layers (or its JSON text), using the same supported style properties as other vector tile layers. A custom style chooses what it draws through its own source-layer properties, overriding source_layers. Omit both for the archive's default look. Other map.addTiles parameters, such as opacity, can be passed as keyword arguments.

s.add_pmtiles("https://example.org/atlas.pmtiles", name="Atlas")
s.add_pmtiles(
    "atlas.pmtiles", name="Water", source_layers=["water"],
    style=[{
        "id": "water", "type": "fill", "source-layer": "water",
        "paint": {"fill-color": "#336699"},
    }],
)

The result gives the tile layer's name, kind and position; it is not a feature Layer. Web archives need a server supporting byte-range requests (and CORS for the notebook app). Local archives can be read by Python, but are not embedded in the notebook app: use a web address accessible to the browser to show one there.

items.title: The app in a notebook
items.text:
rustgis.Map shows the RustGIS app (ribbon, panes, map) in the cell, kept in step with its session: what Python adds or styles appears in the app, and what you do in the app (an edit, a new layer, a pan) is back in the session for Python to read. It needs anywidget, and works in JupyterLab, Notebook, VS Code and Colab.

pip install "rustgis[jupyter]"

m = rustgis.Map(sample=True)                         # height="800px"; lang="de" sets the language
m                                                   # the app, in the cell

m.add_geojson("sites.geojson", name="Sites")        # appears in the app
m["Sites"].style("unique", field="name")
m.set_center(10, 50, scale=5_000_000)
m.add_tiles("https://tile.openstreetmap.org/{z}/{x}/{y}.png", name="OpenStreetMap")

m.info()["center"]                                  # where the app's map is now
m.save("sites.rgis")                                # with what was done in the app
m.run_in_app("ui.language", code="de")              # a command only the app has

Map shares the command, data and view methods of Session (run, run_tool, add_data, m["Sites"], to_png, ...); its layers' changes also appear in the app. m.session is the underlying session; Map(session=s) displays an existing one. Make changes through m, rather than directly through m.session, to send them to the app.

Supported files up to 2 MiB added through Map travel with the project. Larger files and formats that cannot be embedded are read from a path only Python can see: they draw in to_png but not in the app. Use a zip for a Shapefile. The whole project goes across after each change, so simultaneous changes do not merge: the later one wins. A change made in the app replaces Python's project, so m.undo() undoes only what Python did since.

The app is the web app, loaded from https://web.rustgis.app, so the notebook needs to be online. Map(url=...) or the RUSTGIS_WEB_URL environment variable points it at another copy (a self-hosted one, such as one built with the Dockerfile, or trunk serve in apps/rustgis-web). Settings you change in the widget last until the cell is run again: an embedded app keeps nothing in the browser.

The project, with the data that travels with it, goes to that app through the browser (postMessage); nothing goes to a server. The app runs in your browser, so with the default address your data stays on your machine. Point url= only at a copy of the app you trust.

items.title: The app in a Qt application
items.text:
rustgis.qt.MapWidget is the same app in a Qt widget, for a desktop tool or a script that opens a window: it shows the web app in Qt WebEngine and keeps it in step with its session, as Map does in a notebook. It needs PySide6 (or PyQt6 with PyQt6-WebEngine).

pip install "rustgis[qt]"

from rustgis.qt import MapWidget                     # import it before the QApplication
from PySide6.QtWidgets import QApplication

app = QApplication([])
w = MapWidget(sample=True)                           # lang="de", url=... as for Map
w["Countries"].style("graduated", field="pop_est")   # appears in the app
w.show()                                             # or add it to a layout
app.exec()

w.info()["center"]                                   # where the app's map was left

MapWidget has the methods of Map (run, run_in_app, add_data, w["Sites"], to_png, notices, ...) and is a QWidget, so it goes in a layout or a dock like any other; w.view is the QWebEngineView the app runs in. Call its methods from the Qt main thread. What the notebook section says about files, merging and the app's address holds here too.

In a conda environment that also has conda's own Qt, PySide6 from pip may find conda's Qt plugins instead of its own and fail to start ("Could not find the Qt platform plugin"). Use a separate environment for it, or point QT_PLUGIN_PATH at the Qt/plugins folder of the PySide6 package (and QTWEBENGINEPROCESS_PATH at its Qt/libexec/QtWebEngineProcess).

items.title: Commands
items.text:
Engine actions are commands with an id and JSON parameters: the same ids the ribbon, the command line and the AI Assistant use. Session.run(id, ...) runs them, with parameters as keyword arguments, a positional dict, or both (keyword arguments win). It returns the decoded command result and raises rustgis.RustGISError when the command fails. UI-only commands (ui.*) need Map.run_in_app, as in the notebook example above.

A command runs to its end before run returns, but not holding Python's interpreter lock (the GIL): other Python threads keep running while it works, as do renders, layer reads and the keychain reads of use_saved_secrets. Native RustGIS calls, including calls on different sessions, take turns because connection activations are shared by the process. Waiting for another native call also releases the GIL; unrelated Python threads remain free to run. Ctrl+C (KeyboardInterrupt) is raised only once the command has ended. So a trend over a data cube (cube.trend) keeps the Script pane's bounds here (2 billion pairs compared, a STAC search of 2,000 items); run a larger one, such as a trend over a state, with rustgis-cli run (see the command line).

s.commands()                                        # every command, with its parameters
s.tools()                                           # the geoprocessing tools
s.describe("layer.symbology")                       # one command's (or tool's) parameters
s.run("labels.field", layer="Cities", field="name")
s.run("map.goToXY", {"lon": 114.1, "lat": 22.4, "scale": 2_000_000})
s.notices()                                         # drains (text, is_error) pairs since last call
s.undo()
s.redo()

run_tool runs a geoprocessing tool and returns the layer it made (a list when it made several), or the tool's own result for one that selects or makes a table. Layers can be given as Layer objects or by name; tools take layers by name, so of two layers with the same name the upper one is used:

s.describe("buffer")["params"]                      # input, distance, units, dissolve, output
rings = s.run_tool("buffer", input=s["Cities"], distance=50, units="Kilometers")
rings.style("single").set_transparency(50)

The common view commands have shortcuts too:

s.set_center(114.1, 22.4, scale=2_000_000)          # bearing= and pitch= tilt and turn it
s.zoom_to(s["Cities"])                              # or a box: (west, south, east, north)
s.bounds                                            # what the map shows now
s.set_basemap("paper")                              # paper, midnight, ocean, atlas, blank
s.add_tiles("https://tile.openstreetmap.org/{z}/{x}/{y}.png", name="OpenStreetMap")

The GeoLibre and Whitebox tools run as they do in the app, through the geolibre program (see Analysis). rustgis.load_plugins(), or Session(plugins=True), loads the plugins installed for the desktop app.

items.title: Saved connections and secrets
items.text:
rustgis.Session(use_saved_secrets=True) loads the desktop app's saved connection definitions and lets connection.login and project sources use their remembered database passwords and S3 keys, and files on NASA's Earthdata data servers the remembered Earthdata Login token (which, like a token given with earthdata.login, then serves every session of the process). Secrets are read lazily from the system keychain, only when a command needs one, under the desktop's rules: the same connection ID, kind and address or S3 endpoint. Parameters given to a command, and environment credentials selected by a connection, take precedence over saved secrets. Changes to the connection definitions aren't saved back to the desktop preferences.

The default is False: nothing reads the keychain or desktop preferences, so scripts and CI remain opt-in. If the keychain is unavailable, locked or refuses access, the session emits one WARNING record through logging.getLogger("rustgis") on its first failed access. With no logging configured, Python prints it to stderr. Unreadable or malformed desktop preferences produce a separate diagnostic during session construction; a missing preferences file is normal.

These are log records, not Python warnings: warning filters cannot replace a successful result or hide the original RustGISError. Each session reports its own failure. A logging handler or filter that raises cannot change the operation's result; the diagnostic falls back to stderr. A command that doesn't need a secret neither touches the keychain nor emits a keychain diagnostic. On macOS, Keychain may ask once per item whether the Python executable may read it; Always Allow stops that question for that executable and item. Until such a question is answered (or a locked Secret Service on Linux responds), the command that asked waits, and so do other RustGIS calls in the process, even on other sessions; other Python threads keep running.

items.title: Data in and out
items.text:
s = rustgis.Session(sample=True, data=["parcels.gpkg"])
roads = s.add_data("roads.fgb", name="Roads")
sites = s.add_geojson({
    "type": "FeatureCollection",
    "features": [{"type": "Feature", "geometry": {"type": "Point", "coordinates": [10, 50]},
                  "properties": {"name": "Site A"}}],
}, name="Sites")

gdf = s["Cities"].to_geopandas()                    # a GeoDataFrame in EPSG:4326
big = s.add_geopandas(gdf[gdf.pop_max > 5_000_000], name="Big cities")
s["Cities"].to_geojson()                            # a FeatureCollection dict
big.to_file("big-cities.gpkg", crs="EPSG:3857")     # GeoJSON, CSV, FlatGeobuf, GeoParquet, …

GeoPackage exports through Layer.to_file or share.exportLayer require a new filename. An existing .gpkg is refused to preserve its tables; export does not append or replace tables.

add_geojson also takes any object with __geo_interface__ (a Shapely geometry, a GeoSeries). add_data, add_geojson and add_geopandas return a Layer for a single layer, a list for multiple layers, or the command result for standalone tables. For example, a CSV without geometry is a table. Extra add_data keyword arguments go to layer.addData, such as layer= to choose a GeoPackage table, or x= and y= to choose coordinate columns.

Every format the app reads works here: GeoJSON, CSV, Shapefile, GeoPackage, GeoParquet, FlatGeobuf, KML/KMZ, GPX, GeoTIFF and the rest of Supported Data Formats. A large file read in place keeps only the features of the last view in memory; run layer.loadAll on it before to_geojson or to_geopandas to get all of them.

Open an existing project with Session(project="atlas.rgis") or s.open("atlas.rgis"). s.project_json() returns its JSON text; s.run("project.openText", text=...) opens project JSON without an intermediate file. to_png() returns PNG bytes even when it also writes a file; omit the path to keep the image in memory.

items.title: From source
items.text:
The package lives in apps/rustgis-python, built with maturin. Install the source-build prerequisites and use a Python 3.12+ virtual environment. From the repository root:

python -m pip install "./apps/rustgis-python[test]"
python -m pytest apps/rustgis-python/tests

For an editable development install, activate the virtual environment, then:

python -m pip install "maturin>=1.9.3,<2"
cd apps/rustgis-python
maturin develop --release

Saved-credential regression tests use an injected store, so they never access your keychain:

maturin develop --release --features test-stores
python -m pytest tests/test_saved_secrets.py

Rebuild without --features test-stores afterward to restore the OS backend. CI builds one test wheel with the injected store and runs the suite once; distributed wheels keep default features.

To require the Qt tests, install the qt extra too and set RUSTGIS_TEST_QT=1. They run offscreen with one QApplication kept alive for the test session, and with WebEngine's GPU turned off (--webEngineArgs --disable-gpu): otherwise WebEngine sets up EGL on a thread of its own, where Mesa reads the environment, and a test or library adding an environment variable at that moment can crash the process (glibc's setenv may free the environment array that getenv is reading). Qt tests create widgets with the make_widget fixture, which destroys each widget and its message bridge at test teardown.

Its version is the RustGIS version, and each release publishes wheels to PyPI.

items.title: Become a Sponsor
items.text:
RustGIS is free and open-source software, released under the Apache License 2.0 and developed in the open. There is no paid tier or seat licence. The desktop app and command line collect no analytics or usage telemetry; the hosted websites use analytics, as described in Privacy.

That model only works if the work behind it is sustainable. If RustGIS saves you or your team time, sponsorship is the most direct way to keep it moving.

items.title: RustGIS vs. other GIS platforms
items.text:
How RustGIS compares to its sibling project GeoLibre and to the GIS platforms people most often ask about: QGIS, ArcGIS Pro and ArcGIS Online.

RustGIS is not trying to replace any of these. It fills a narrower spot: a free and open-source desktop GIS compiled to a single native program, with a ribbon interface familiar from desktop GIS, almost every action available as a scriptable command, and the same app running in a browser tab through WebAssembly.

How to read this

Comparisons like this age quickly and are written by an interested party. The RustGIS column reflects what ships in the current source as of October 2026; the other columns describe each product's mainstream, out-of-the-box behaviour, not what is reachable with every add-on or plugin. The GeoLibre, QGIS and ArcGIS columns draw on GeoLibre's own comparison, where those products are described in more depth. Found something wrong or out of date? Please open an issue.

Coming from QGIS? RustGIS and QGIS goes deeper: the pros and cons of each, how QGIS concepts map onto RustGIS, and how to use the two together. Deciding between RustGIS and its sibling? RustGIS and GeoLibre compares the two in detail.

items.title: RustGIS and GeoLibre
items.text:
RustGIS and GeoLibre are both opengeos projects, and they share more than a maintainer: both can run the suite of over 1,000 GeoLibre and Whitebox geoprocessing tools, through an optional desktop runner or WebAssembly in the browser.

They differ in how they are built and who they suit:

  • GeoLibre is built on web technology (Tauri, React, MapLibre GL JS, DuckDB-WASM, deck.gl). It reaches further: cloud-native formats (GeoParquet, PMTiles, Zarr, STAC), databases, OGC and Esri services, native Android and iOS apps, a Jupyter widget, a Python package and real-time collaboration.
  • RustGIS is written entirely in Rust and draws its own interface on the GPU (egui). It is one native program with no browser engine or JavaScript runtime inside, a ribbon laid out in the order of the work, and an engine whose commands run the same way from the ribbon, rustgis-cli, Python, notebooks, models and the AI Assistant.

They complement each other rather than compete: GeoLibre is web and mobile first, RustGIS desktop first and built for automation and AI agents. If you want the widest data access and the most platforms, choose GeoLibre. If you want a compact native desktop GIS with a classic ribbon workflow and a scriptable command engine, choose RustGIS. Both work on local files on your machine; remote features, such as web data and AI providers, send requests over the network. See RustGIS and GeoLibre for a closer look.

items.title: Where each one is the right choice
items.text:
Choose RustGIS when you want a compact, native desktop GIS that installs as one program, a ribbon interface without a licence, engine commands scriptable from the command line with the same ids the interface uses, sandboxed WebAssembly plugins, or an AI assistant whose project edits use the same undo system as the interface.

Choose GeoLibre when you need the widest data access from a browser tab (cloud-native formats, STAC, databases, OGC and Esri services), the same app on Android, iOS and in Jupyter, real-time collaboration, or its Jupyter widget.

Choose QGIS when you need the widest format support through GDAL/OGR, the deepest open-source cartography, a mature plugin for a niche task, or heavy local processing of large datasets.

Choose ArcGIS Pro when you are in the Esri ecosystem, need enterprise geodatabases and versioned editing, the deepest 3D and imagery workflows, or organizational support.

Choose ArcGIS Online when the priority is hosted layers, organizational sharing and the surrounding Esri app family.

They also compose: RustGIS reads and writes GeoJSON, CSV, GeoPackage, GeoParquet, Shapefile and GeoTIFF, which every tool above opens, and writes MapLibre styles and OGC API Features collections for the web.

items.title: Where RustGIS is not the strongest option
items.text:
Stated plainly, so the tables above are worth trusting:

  • Format breadth. MySQL/MariaDB and SQL Server/Azure SQL are read only; PostGIS and GeoPackage support table write-back on desktop. Live database connections and DuckDB files are desktop only. The web app doesn't write GeoPackages. The native File Geodatabase reader is 2D and does not read compressed tables, raster fields or sparse row layouts; GDAL can fill these gaps on desktop. DWG and rasters such as JPEG 2000, NetCDF and HDF also need GDAL. SQL queries need DuckDB; both are external programs.
  • Coordinate systems. Vector data is stored in longitude/latitude; there is no full PROJ.
  • Editing depth. Vertex move, insert and delete are supported, but not versioned multi-user database editing. Desktop GeoPackage and PostGIS layers loaded for editing can save back to their source tables with row-conflict checks; other edits stay in the project until exported.
  • Specialized analysis. Built-in spatial joins, overlays (intersect, identity, union, symmetrical difference, update) and shortest paths on line networks are available, but full network datasets and advanced spatial statistics depend on the external suite or another GIS.
  • Python. The rustgis package runs commands headlessly, but there is no Python console inside the app. Python process plugins are supported on desktop and CLI, without a sandbox.
  • Maturity. RustGIS is young. Many features are first versions; see the roadmap.
