items.title: RustGIS and GeoLibre
items.text:
RustGIS and GeoLibre are sibling opengeos projects with the same maintainer, so people often ask how they differ and which to use. This page answers that: what each is built for, where each is stronger, and how to use them together. For RustGIS beside QGIS, ArcGIS Pro and ArcGIS Online as well, see the full comparison.

How to read this

This page is written by the RustGIS project. It reflects RustGIS as of October 2026 and GeoLibre 3.4 as described in its documentation, not every plugin either one can load. Both projects move quickly, so details here age fast. Found something wrong or out of date? Please open an issue.

items.title: The short answer
items.text:
GeoLibre and RustGIS serve similar purposes, but take different approaches and suit different workflows. Neither is meant to replace the other (discussion #951).

GeoLibre is web and mobile first. It is built with web technology (Tauri, React, MapLibre GL JS, DuckDB-WASM, deck.gl) and runs in a browser tab with nothing installed, as a desktop app, and as native Android and iOS apps. Its strengths are access from anywhere, cloud-native data, interactive visualization and sharing. GeoLibre is mature, with a broad set of features; as its maintainer put it in discussion #951, its development now centres on stability, performance and usability.

RustGIS is desktop first, built for automation and AI agents. It is a single program written entirely in Rust that draws its own interface on the GPU, with no browser engine or JavaScript runtime inside; the same program, compiled to WebAssembly, also runs in the browser. Its interface is a ribbon laid out in the order of the work, and almost everything in it is a command that scripts, the command line, Python and AI agents can run. It goes deeper in the classic desktop GIS jobs of data design, reports and print layouts. RustGIS is young and changing quickly: expect frequent releases, new capabilities and some significant changes.

The two complement each other. Both can run the 1,000+ GeoLibre/Whitebox geoprocessing suite, both read and write common open formats, RustGIS imports .geolibre projects as new maps, and GeoLibre opening .rgis projects is planned for later (see Using them together). Choose GeoLibre for web-first work, phones and notebooks, choose RustGIS for a scriptable desktop GIS, or use both.

items.title: Where each is stronger today
items.text: These lists compare features as of October 2026, and RustGIS's features change quickly. The differences in the short answer, in platform, technology and focus, are the ones that last.

items.title: Where GeoLibre is stronger
items.text:
• More platforms. GeoLibre runs as a web app, an installable PWA, a desktop app on Windows, macOS and Linux, native Android and iOS apps, a Docker image, a Chrome extension and a Jupyter widget. RustGIS runs on the desktop and in the browser; it has no mobile app and no touch-first layout.
  • Data reach. GeoLibre opens more formats in the app itself, including File Geodatabase, DWG, MapInfo TAB, NetCDF-4/HDF5, Kerchunk and Icechunk, ICESat-2 and GEDI. It connects to SQL Server and Apache Iceberg as well as PostGIS and DuckDB, and its plugins browse dozens of catalogs and portals, from NASA Earthdata and Planet to Hugging Face and about 150 US local agencies. RustGIS reads a focused set natively, including 2D File Geodatabase feature classes and tables, GeoRSS and LandXML. It also has NASA Earthdata discovery and live SQL Server/Azure SQL connections. Other formats and File Geodatabase tables the native reader cannot read need GDAL (see Data formats).
  • SQL in the browser. GeoLibre runs DuckDB Spatial, PGlite/PostGIS and Apache Sedona inside the browser. RustGIS's SQL pane uses DuckDB on the desktop; its web app has no SQL engine.
  • Cartography depth. GeoLibre has rule-based and expression renderers, heat maps, clustering, diagrams, blend modes, layer groups, a data-defined label engine, and style interchange with SLD, QGIS QML and Mapbox GL JSON. RustGIS covers the common renderers and SQL-filtered label classes, stacked line symbols, symbol levels, blend modes and layer groups, symbol size, colours, outline width and angle by expression, but not rule-based renderers or data-defined labels.
  • 3D. GeoLibre has a Cesium globe with terrain, 3D Tiles, I3S, Gaussian splats, CZML and Google Photorealistic 3D Tiles. RustGIS has a globe, terrain-draped tilted views, 2.5D extrusion and LiDAR point layers.
  • AI and imagery models. Besides an AI assistant, GeoLibre has SAM segmentation, in-browser ONNX/YOLO object detection and an object-based image analysis workbench. RustGIS has pixel classification (k-means, minimum distance and a trainable neural network).
  • Sharing and collaboration. GeoLibre shares projects through links with roles, expiry and passwords, has review comments anchored to the map, story maps, dashboards, and an experimental real-time collaboration mode. RustGIS shares by writing files: web map pages, packages and static exports.
  • Python, R and notebooks. The geolibre Python package is a two-way Jupyter widget with a leafmap-style API, the geolibre R package works in RStudio, Quarto and Shiny, and the notebook panel runs JupyterLite or JupyterLab. RustGIS has a Python package that runs commands headlessly and built-in notebooks of command cells, but no Python console in the app and no R package.
  • Opening other projects. GeoLibre imports QGIS (.qgs/.qgz) and ArcGIS Pro (.aprx/.mapx) projects. RustGIS opens supported QGIS projects as maps (see QGIS projects) but not ArcGIS Pro ones.
  • Editing. GeoLibre edits vertices and writes edits back to their sources (GeoPackage, PostGIS, ArcGIS feature services). RustGIS moves, inserts and deletes vertices, but edits stay in the project until exported rather than being written back to those sources.
  • Languages. GeoLibre's interface comes in 21 languages, including right-to-left Arabic, Hebrew and Persian. RustGIS has 17, including Persian text support; its widget layout is not right-to-left.

items.title: Where RustGIS is stronger
items.text:
• A native program, not a web view. RustGIS is memory-safe Rust compiled to one native program with no browser engine, JavaScript or Python inside the core app. Large GeoPackage, GeoParquet, FlatGeobuf and Shapefile files are read a view at a time rather than loaded whole; the cloud-native readers also work in the browser.
  • Commands for scripts and AI agents. Ribbon actions dispatch commands with ids and JSON parameters. Engine commands run from rustgis-cli, the rustgis Python package, notebooks, models, the Script pane, the MCP server and the AI Assistant. UI-only pane/dialog commands stay in the app. A batch of maps can be rendered in CI with one command line. GeoLibre is driven through its interface, its Python and R packages and its MCP server; it has no general command-line tool.
  • Sandboxed WebAssembly plugins. These RustGIS plugins use declared, approved permissions and run on desktop, in rustgis-cli and in the browser. Plugins can add commands, tools, ribbon tabs, panels and assistant skills. Native process plugins, including Python environments managed by RustGIS, are also supported on desktop and CLI, but are not sandboxed. GeoLibre's TypeScript plugin API states that its plugins "run as trusted code in the app window" and that its policy "is not a security boundary".
  • Data design. RustGIS defines domains, subtypes, attribute rules, contingent values, relationship classes, archiving, topology rules and traverse/COGO in the project itself, the geodatabase design work of ArcGIS Pro. GeoLibre has attribute forms with constraints and honours the domains and subtypes of the ArcGIS feature services it edits, but doesn't define its own.
  • Reports and layouts. RustGIS builds grouped reports with statistics, charts and subreports, and layouts with publication presets, shaped map frames, legends, colorbars, grids, tables, charts, extent indicators and map series, exported to PDF or PNG. GeoLibre's print layout and atlas cover the common cases, and it has no report builder.
  • A ribbon interface. Tabs follow the order of the work (Home, Data, Style, Labeling, Edit, Analyze, View, Publish), with Command Search (Ctrl+K) to find any command or tool by name. People coming from ArcGIS Pro often find it familiar. GeoLibre uses menus and panels, with a command palette and beginner, intermediate and advanced interface levels.
  • Offline local workflows. RustGIS's local-file readers, built-in tools and rendering work without a network or server (remote and cloud sources need the network); offline areas sync edits back to the corresponding map in the project, not to the underlying source data or a remote database. GeoLibre tools, GDAL, DuckDB and process plugins use separate programs. GeoLibre works offline too, but some features need a remote host (GDAL export, ONNX detection and story map HTML export among them), and on the desktop its raster tools and some vector tools use an optional Python sidecar.

items.title: Using them together
items.text:
The two read and write the same open formats, so data moves between them without conversion: GeoPackage, GeoParquet, FlatGeobuf, Shapefile, GeoJSON, KML/KMZ, GPX, CSV and cloud-optimised GeoTIFF (GeoPackage export is desktop only in RustGIS).

RustGIS imports .geolibre projects as new maps, keeping supported data, styles and views and reporting differences. See GeoLibre projects for supported content and limits. GeoLibre opening .rgis projects comes later, once RustGIS's project format and the data types it supports settle: RustGIS is still changing quickly, and GeoLibre would otherwise be reading a moving target.

They also share their geoprocessing. RustGIS's Analyze › Tools offers the GeoLibre and Whitebox suite through the optional geolibre program on desktop and an on-demand WebAssembly runner in the browser. The available tools come from that runner's manifests. See Analysis.

A common split is to explore, share and collaborate in GeoLibre, especially from a browser, a phone or a notebook, and to use RustGIS for repeatable desktop work: a project scripted command by command, maps rendered by rustgis-cli in CI, data with domains and attribute rules, or reports and map series printed to PDF.

items.title: Common questions
items.text:
Why are there two? To explore different ways of making geospatial tools accessible and powerful. GeoLibre uses the web platform to reach as many places and data sources as possible. RustGIS explores what a desktop GIS looks like as one native Rust program that scripts and AI agents can drive. Each project borrows ideas from the other, and they are meant to be used together, not chosen between.

Which one should I start with? If you want to open a dataset in a browser tab or on a phone right now, or work in Jupyter or R, start with GeoLibre. If you want a desktop GIS with a ribbon, scriptable engine commands, or reports and data design, start with RustGIS.

Do they run the same geoprocessing tools? RustGIS can load the GeoLibre/Whitebox suite of over 1,000 tools from geolibre-rust, with the available list depending on the runner. RustGIS also has built-in vector tools, A5 grids, interpolation and guided workflows; GeoLibre adds its Toolbox (routing, H3 grids, spatial statistics).

Can a GeoLibre plugin run in RustGIS, or the other way round? No. GeoLibre plugins are TypeScript modules for its web interface. RustGIS has its own WebAssembly and native process-plugin interfaces, including Python process plugins.

Can I open a GeoLibre project in RustGIS? Yes. Open or Project › New › GeoLibre Project… imports a .geolibre (or .geolibre.json) as a new map, preserving supported data, styles and the saved view. The command project.importGeolibre also accepts a URL, text or base64 JSON. It reports unsupported sources and appearance differences per layer; see GeoLibre projects for the limits.

items.title: RustGIS and QGIS
items.text:
"How does RustGIS compare to QGIS?" is the question people ask most. This page answers it directly: where each one is stronger, how QGIS concepts map onto RustGIS, and how to use the two together. For RustGIS beside GeoLibre, ArcGIS Pro and ArcGIS Online as well, see the full comparison.

How to read this

This page is written by the RustGIS project, so read it with that in mind. It reflects RustGIS as of October 2026 and QGIS's out-of-the-box behaviour, not everything reachable through its plugins. Found something wrong or out of date? Please open an issue.

items.title: The short answer
items.text:
QGIS is the mature, complete open-source desktop GIS. Over twenty years it has grown the widest format support (through GDAL/OGR) and full coordinate-system support (through PROJ), the deepest open-source cartography, thorough editing, GRASS and SAGA processing, QGIS Server, mobile companions (QField, Mergin Maps) and thousands of Python plugins, with a large community, training material and books behind it.

RustGIS is younger and narrower, built differently. It is one native program written entirely in Rust that also runs as a WebAssembly app in a browser tab. Its interface is a ribbon laid out in the order of the work, its engine commands run from the command line, Python or an AI agent, and its WebAssembly plugins run sandboxed.

RustGIS is not a QGIS replacement, and doesn't aim to be. If your work depends on what QGIS does best, keep using QGIS. RustGIS suits people who want something lighter to install, a browser version with nothing to install, a command-driven engine, or a ribbon workflow without a licence, and the two read and write the same open formats.

items.title: What they look like
items.text:
The same World Atlas data, styled the same way, in each app.

RustGIS: the ribbon, the Layers pane and the AI Assistant. QGIS with the same data and styling: toolbars and the Browser and Layers panels.

items.title: Where RustGIS is stronger
items.text:
• Installing it. RustGIS's core app is a single program with no Python, Qt or GDAL inside. Packages include a portable Windows zip, a macOS DMG, AppImage, .deb/.rpm, Homebrew, winget, the AUR and Fedora COPR. Optional GeoLibre tools, GDAL, DuckDB and process plugins use separate programs. QGIS installers bundle a Python interpreter, Qt, GDAL, GRASS and more. See Installation.
  • In the browser. The WebAssembly app runs at web.rustgis.app: add files, style them, load the optional 1,000+ GeoLibre/Whitebox suite, build layouts and export. Live database connections and external programs are desktop only, and GeoPackage export is not available on web. You can serve the static build yourself. QGIS has no official browser version; QGIS Server and qgis2web publish maps made on the desktop.
  • A shared command engine. Ribbon actions dispatch commands with ids and JSON parameters. Engine commands run from rustgis-cli, the rustgis Python package, notebooks, models, the Script pane, the MCP server and the AI Assistant. UI-only commands open panes and dialogs inside the app rather than running headlessly. QGIS's processing algorithms are scriptable through qgis_process and PyQGIS, but much of its interface (styling, layouts, project setup) is reached through the PyQGIS object model rather than the same actions the buttons run.
  • An AI Assistant that uses the command engine. The AI Assistant works with Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, OpenRouter, Ollama or any OpenAI-compatible model with your own key, or with a ChatGPT sign-in. Project edits use the same undo system as the interface; file, network and plugin commands wait for your approval, and external side effects are not undone. An MCP server lets agents such as Claude Code, Cursor and VS Code drive RustGIS. QGIS has AI through third-party plugins.
  • Sandboxed WebAssembly plugins. These RustGIS plugins use declared, approved permissions and run on desktop, in rustgis-cli and in the browser. Plugins can add commands, tools, ribbon tabs, panels and assistant skills. RustGIS also supports unsandboxed process plugins, including managed Python environments, on desktop and CLI. Like QGIS's Python plugins, these are trusted programs, not contained.
  • Cloud-native data without extra libraries. Cloud-optimised GeoTIFF, GeoParquet, FlatGeobuf, PMTiles and Zarr are read in place by RustGIS's own readers, over HTTP byte ranges and from s3:// buckets, on the desktop and in the browser alike. QGIS reads all of these too, through GDAL on the desktop.
  • A ribbon interface. Tabs follow the order of the work (Home, Data, Style, Labeling, Edit, Analyze, View, Publish), with Command Search (Ctrl+K) to find any command or tool by name. People coming from ArcGIS Pro often find it familiar; people who know QGIS's toolbars may not want it, which is a matter of taste.
  • A permissive licence. RustGIS is Apache-2.0, so its crates can be embedded in proprietary or differently licensed software. QGIS is GPL-2.0-or-later, which requires derived works to stay under the GPL. For running either program, both are free.
  • Memory-safe core. RustGIS's workspace forbids unsafe Rust, checks file and parameter inputs, and has hostile-input tests for registered commands and built-in tools. This does not make external programs or unsandboxed process plugins a security boundary.

items.title: Where QGIS is stronger
items.text:
• Format and database breadth. QGIS opens the formats its GDAL/OGR build supports, natively, and writes many of them. RustGIS reads a focused set of formats with its own code (see Data formats), including a native, read-only 2D File Geodatabase reader; compressed tables, raster fields and sparse row layouts need GDAL. DWG, JPEG 2000 and NetCDF also need GDAL's programs. QGIS connects to PostGIS, SpatiaLite, Oracle and SQL Server and edits in them directly; RustGIS reads PostGIS, MySQL/MariaDB and SQL Server/Azure SQL tables live (read only) and DuckDB databases through DuckDB, on the desktop.
  • Coordinate systems. QGIS uses full PROJ: every CRS, datum transformations and grids, and layers kept in their own CRS. RustGIS holds vector coordinates as WGS 84 longitude/latitude and reprojects rasters and the map by EPSG code, which covers mapping and most analysis but not survey-grade work in a local datum.
  • Editing. QGIS has a complete digitizing toolkit: reshape, offset curves, advanced digitizing with constraints, topological editing and geometry checkers. RustGIS creates, moves, rotates, scales, splits and merges features with snapping and templates, and moves, inserts and deletes vertices. Edits stay in the project until exported; RustGIS does not write them back to live databases.
  • Processing. RustGIS has built-in spatial joins, geodesic buffers, A5 grids, IDW, ordinary kriging and shortest paths on line networks, plus the optional 1,000+ GeoLibre/Whitebox suite. QGIS combines its native algorithms with GDAL, GRASS and SAGA providers and has more complete built-in overlays, network datasets and spatial statistics. RustGIS's external suite is strong on terrain, hydrology, LiDAR and image analysis; its available tools depend on the installed runner.
  • Cartography. QGIS's styling is the richest in open source: rule-based renderers, data-defined overrides on nearly every property through its expression engine, blending modes, geometry generators, a refined labeling engine. RustGIS covers the common renderers (single, unique values, graduated, proportional, aggregation, raster stretch/RGB/classified/hillshade), stacked line symbols, symbol levels, blend modes, layer groups and SQL-filtered label classes, without that depth.
  • Print layouts. QGIS's layout designer and atlas are mature and detailed. RustGIS has publication presets, shaped map frames, legends, colorbars, scale bars, grids, tables, charts, map series, reports and PDF/PNG export.
  • Plugins and integrations. QGIS has thousands of Python plugins for niche tasks, an in-app Python console, QGIS Server for OGC services, and QField and Mergin Maps for field work. RustGIS's plugin registry is new and small, and it has no server or mobile app.
  • 3D and point clouds. QGIS's 3D map views, mesh layers and point-cloud rendering go further than RustGIS's globe, terrain-draped tilted views, 2.5D extrusion and LiDAR point layers.
  • Maturity and community. QGIS has two decades of releases, a long-term-release cycle, translated documentation, courses, books, user groups and commercial support. RustGIS released its first version in 2026; many features are first versions and some workflows will have gaps. See the roadmap.

items.title: Side by side
items.text: RustGIS QGIS Licence Apache-2.0 GPL-2.0-or-later Written in Rust (egui, wgpu, tiny-skia) C++ and Python (Qt) First release 2026 2002 Download One core program; optional external tools installed separately Hundreds of MB (bundles Python, Qt, GDAL, GRASS…) Platforms Windows, macOS, Linux, and the browser (WebAssembly) Windows, macOS, Linux Interface Ribbon with Command Search Toolbars, menus and docked panels Formats A focused set read natively; more through GDAL when installed Whatever its GDAL/OGR build supports (read/write varies by driver) Coordinate systems Vectors in WGS 84; rasters and the map by EPSG code Full PROJ Geoprocessing Built-in tools plus optional 1,000+ GeoLibre/Whitebox suite 1,000+ (native, GDAL, GRASS, SAGA) Editing Create, move, rotate, scale, split, merge, vertex move/insert/delete, snapping; export edits Complete digitizing and topology tools Scripting Engine commands: CLI, Python package, notebooks, Script pane, MCP; UI-only commands stay in the app PyQGIS, qgis_process, Python console Plugins Sandboxed WebAssembly; unsandboxed desktop/CLI process and Python plugins; registry Python, thousands in the official repository AI Built-in assistant using engine commands and project undo; MCP server Through plugins Server and mobile Static web build or Dockerfile you can host QGIS Server; QField and Mergin Maps Project file .rgis (open JSON) .qgs / .qgz (open XML)

items.title: RustGIS for QGIS users
items.text:
Most QGIS ideas have a counterpart under a different name:

In QGIS In RustGIS Layers panel Layers pane (left) Browser panel, Data Source Manager Browser pane, Home › Add › Data Sources, the Data Sources pane Processing Toolbox Tools pane (Analyze › Tools), or Command Search (Ctrl+K) Graphical Modeler ModelBuilder: a node canvas of inputs, tools and outputs, which can also build a model from your history qgis_process rustgis-cli run --cmd 'gp.run={…}' Python console, PyQGIS The Script pane and notebooks inside the app; the rustgis Python package outside it Layer Styling panel Style tab and the Symbology pane Expressions (select, filter) SQL WHERE clauses for selections and definition queries Field Calculator Calculate Field Print Layout, Atlas Layouts, Map Series Plugin Manager Plugins › Plugin Manager Project (.qgz) Project (.rgis), or a package (.rgispkg) with its data inside; a QGIS project opens as a map

The User Guide walks through the interface, and Getting Started is a short tour.

items.title: Using them together
items.text:
You don't have to choose. RustGIS reads and writes the formats QGIS works in, so data moves between them without conversion:

  • Vector data: GeoPackage, GeoParquet, FlatGeobuf, Shapefile, GeoJSON, KML/KMZ, GPX and CSV, in both directions (GeoPackage export is desktop only).
  • Rasters: GeoTIFF and cloud-optimised GeoTIFF.
  • Colour ramps: RustGIS reads QGIS Style Manager exports (.xml) and the colour ramp or raster colour map in a layer style (.qml); see Custom color ramps.

  • Web maps: MapLibre styles and OGC API Features collections exported from RustGIS can be served and opened anywhere, QGIS included.

  • Projects and layer styles: RustGIS opens QGIS projects (.qgs, .qgz) as maps and applies QGIS layer styles (.qml), carrying over the layers, their order and visibility, renderers, symbols, labels and reference scales, and listing what it draws differently; see QGIS projects and styles. It doesn't write them back.

A common split is to do heavy editing, PROJ-dependent work and detailed cartography in QGIS, and use RustGIS where a light install, the browser, scripting by command id or the AI Assistant helps: a quick look at a GeoParquet on a laptop without QGIS, a map shared as a web app, a batch of maps rendered by rustgis-cli in CI, or the optional 1,000+ GeoLibre/Whitebox suite loaded in a browser tab.

items.title: Common questions
items.text:
Is RustGIS a replacement for QGIS? No. It covers the everyday work of a desktop GIS (adding data, styling, labelling, geoprocessing, layouts, sharing) and does some things QGIS doesn't, but QGIS is far more complete. Use RustGIS alongside QGIS, or instead of it only if the gaps above don't touch your work.

Is RustGIS faster than QGIS? It starts quickly and is light to install, and its own readers draw large cloud-native files a view at a time. We haven't published benchmarks against QGIS, and speed depends on the data and the task, so try your own data in both.

Can I use my QGIS plugins in RustGIS? No. QGIS plugins are written against PyQGIS. RustGIS has its own WebAssembly and process-plugin interfaces, including Python process plugins; see Plugins.

Does RustGIS need GDAL like QGIS does? No. Its common formats, cloud-native formats and GeoTIFF are read by its own Rust code, which is also why the browser version works. GDAL is optional: when its programs are installed, RustGIS uses them for the formats it doesn't read itself.

Can I open a QGIS project? Not yet. Open the project's data in RustGIS (GeoPackage is the easiest route) and restyle it.

items.title: User Guide
items.text:
This guide walks through RustGIS by task. Each page covers one part of the app:

Page What it covers Data Adding files, databases, saved connections, Data Sources, large files, rasters, Zarr and project items Web Data Public web services and catalogs: STAC, Overture Maps, OpenStreetMap, NASA, open-data portals, satellite embeddings Supported Data Formats Every format RustGIS reads and writes, how to add it, and its limits Maps and Basemaps Basemaps and web tile layers, projections, the 3D globe, view effects and navigation Cartography Symbology, labeling, layer effects and graphics Editing Creating and modifying features, data design, the clipboard and pop-ups Analysis Selection and SQL queries, geoprocessing, the GeoLibre tools, guided workflows, imagery, data cubes and time series Expressions The expression language of queries, filters and Calculate Field: grammar, operators, functions Layouts and Reports Page layouts, map series, reports, presentations and notebooks Sharing Exports, packages and open-format web maps, layers, styles and scenes Workspace Linked views, the Browser view, animation, profiles, offline areas, customizing the ribbon AI Assistant A chat pane that answers questions and acts on the map through commands RustGIS with the World Atlas sample in the Equal Earth projection.

items.title: The window
items.text:
• Ribbon: tabs of commands grouped by task. The Project button opens the backstage (Start, New, Open, Save, Save As and About).
  • Quick Access Toolbar (top left): New, Open, Save, Undo and Redo, plus any commands you add under Settings › Customize › Quick Access.
  • Layers pane (left): the map's layers in drawing order, with their legends. A new layer goes on top, whatever its kind (a feature, raster or web layer, an analysis result). Tick a layer to show or hide it; drag it up or down to change the drawing order; right-click it to zoom to it, rename or remove it and more. The entire layer block, including its expanded legend and classes, is split 50/50: drop in its upper half to insert above, or its lower half to insert below. The insertion line shows the destination. Drop inside the first block's upper half to move to the top, or inside the final block's lower half to move to the bottom. Type in the box at the top to show only the layers and tables whose names contain the text (Esc clears it); a selected layer it hides is no longer selected, and layers can be reordered again once it is cleared. The buttons beside the list's title list the layers by drawing order, by data source (grouped under the file, web address or database each comes from) or by selection (selectable layers first, each with a box to make it selectable or not and its count of selected features); only the drawing order reorders layers. A layer that isn't selectable is skipped by the Select tool's clicks and boxes on the map; Select By Attributes, Select Layer By Location and the attribute table still select in it, since they name the layer. Pick several layers with Ctrl (Cmd on a Mac) and click to add or drop one, or Shift and click to take the rows from the last one clicked; the layer clicked last, outlined, is the one the Style and Data tabs act on. Right-click one of them to zoom to them all, show or hide them, allow or block selecting their features on the map, move them to the top or bottom of the drawing order (one in a group, to the top or bottom of its group), put them in a group or take them out of one, or remove them; a layer the filter hides is left out. A new group made from the menu asks for its name. In scripts, layer.select takes a list and a mode (replace, toggle or extend), and the commands that remove, show, move, group or zoom to a layer take a list in layer, or the picked layers when it is left out. Group layers to keep related ones together, such as one dataset drawn as several layers with their own visibility ranges: right-click a layer and pick Group › New Group, or move it into a group that already exists. Groups nest, up to eight levels (Base map › Hydrography › Rivers): a new group made from layers that are all in one group goes inside it. A group folds open and closed with its arrow; its box shows or hides all its layers at once, its subgroups' too (each keeps its own box), and its menu renames it, sets a transparency over its layers' own, ungroups it (its layers and subgroups go up one level) or removes it with its layers and subgroups. The visibility, transparency and visibility range of every group above a layer apply to it. Drag a layer or group onto a group's row to put it in that group, or between rows to put it in the group of the row below; drag it out of the group's rows to take it out. Drag a group's row to move all its layers in the drawing order. Like a word processor's outline, a layer's or group's menu has Indent (into the group just above it, as its last item) and Outdent (out of its group, just below it); Alt+Shift+Right and Alt+Shift+Left indent and outdent the active layer, Alt+Shift+Up and Alt+Shift+Down move it one step, past a subgroup at once. Scripts and the AI Assistant build groups with group.add (parent puts it in another), group.set, group.scaleRange (a visibility range on top of each layer's own), group.move, group.setParent, group.indent, group.outdent, group.expand, group.ungroup, group.remove, layer.group, layer.indent and layer.outdent. Copy Layer (or Copy Group, with its layers and subgroups) from its menu and Paste Layer (or Paste Group) it on a layer (above it), a group or the map's name above the list (at the top, also when the map has no layers yet), after switching to another map if you like, or on a map in the Browser (at the top). The copy keeps its source, symbology, labels, transparency, scale range, definition query, display filters and mask, but not its selection, and a name the map already has gets " copy". Pasting into the same map duplicates the layer. A mask whose layer the map lacks is cleared, and said. Pasted into a group (on it, or on one of its layers), the copies go in it at the top, copied groups too. Scripts use layer.copy and layer.paste. The Style and Data tabs act on the layer selected here. The tabs at the top of the left pane switch it between Layers, Browser and Data Sources (also in View › Windows). The planet button above the list switches the map between the Earth and other celestial bodies.
  • Map view: one tab per map and layout. The buttons at the top right zoom in, zoom out and go to the full extent; the north arrow and scale bar sit in the corners (on a rotated or tilted map, click the north arrow to face north and look straight down); tile credits at the bottom right.
  • Panes (right): Tools (geoprocessing), Symbology, Labeling, History, Details, Bookmarks, Editing, Workflows, Script, SQL, the AI Assistant and more. Open them from View › Windows or the commands that use them. Each pane opened gets a tab at the top, in the order opened: click a tab to show its pane, and its ✕ to close it (the next tab shows; closing the last hides the side). Right-click a tab to close it, the others or all; the ✕ at the header's end closes every pane. Tabs that don't fit are listed under ». A ribbon button for a pane shows it when it is open but not in view, and closes it when it is. Pane Sets keep the tabs open.
  • Status bar: the scale (type one, or pick from the list), the zoom level, bearing and pitch (click them to face north and look straight down again), the pointer's coordinates (click them to switch between decimal degrees and DMS), the coordinate system (click it to change the projection), the selection count (with a button to clear it), the latest notice, the last draw time, the frame rate and a GPU/CPU renderer switch. While agents control the desktop app, it also shows the MCP relay or file bridge.

Command Search (Ctrl+K, or the box at the top right) finds commands and geoprocessing tools by name. Commands with an interactive entry point open their dialog, file picker or pane to collect input: for example, Basemap, Add Tile Layer, Rename, Select By Attributes and exports. Workflow tools such as Georeference and Classification Wizard open in the Workflows pane. Workflows can also be found by their translated titles or section ids, such as deepLearning. A command that needs input but has no interactive entry point stays listed greyed out, with the reason on hover, instead of running without its required parameters. Desktop-only database connections are also disabled in the browser.

To give the map more room, collapse the ribbon to its tab row with the chevron at its right end, by double-clicking a tab, or with Ctrl+F1 (Cmd+F1 on macOS, where F1 may need the Fn key). Click a tab to peek at its commands while collapsed. When the window is narrower than the ribbon, arrows at its ends scroll it.

The tabs stay the same whatever is selected: Style, Labeling and Data act on the layer selected in Layers.

Menus with checkboxes stay open while you change options: stack or show web basemaps, combine Visual and Camera Effects, or customize Ribbon tabs and Quick Access buttons. Click outside the menu to dismiss it. The time slider's Layers menu likewise stays open while binding layers.

items.title: Projects
items.text:
A project (.rgis) holds maps, layouts, reports, presentations, notebooks, styles, tasks and models. Vector data loaded whole is stored inside the project. On the desktop, linked local files (large vector files read in place, rasters and tile archives) are saved relative to the project's folder: moving the folder whole keeps the links. Save As recomputes those paths for the new location. Files on another drive or a network share stay absolute. Web addresses, databases and embedded data are unchanged; files uploaded in the web app are embedded. A project opened as text, as in the web app, has no folder against which to resolve local links. Saved web addresses drop passwords, keys and tokens. A project package (.rgispkg) also embeds linked rasters within a size limit, while large files read in place, database and web layers stay linked; it opens as a new, unsaved project.

Relative linked paths, including bare paths in older or hand-written files, are interpreted against the project's folder, never the process's working directory. Resolution is lexical: it does not follow symbolic links. Avoid .. after a symlinked directory; choose the direct data location instead.

On the backstage's Start or New page, choose a blank Map, the World Atlas sample or Open…. Save and Save As write the project, named after its file; a project opened from a file is named after that file too. See Project items for the other files RustGIS reads and writes.

Changes to the project are commands, and each can be undone (Ctrl+Z) and redone (Ctrl+Y). Undo keeps the last 40 changes; starting or opening another project clears it. The desktop app also keeps a copy of unsaved work and offers it back after a crash: see Autosave and recovery. Exports and other files already written are not undone.

items.title: Repair Data Source
items.text:
If a linked file moved or was renamed, right-click its layer or local PMTiles/MBTiles tile archive and choose Repair Data Source…. For the selected layer, use Data › Data Source › Repair Source, or find Repair Data Source (or Repair Tile Archive) in Command Search. Choose the replacement file or folder. For a container such as a GeoPackage, List Datasets reads its tables in the background; choose a table when there is more than one. The existing table is retained when available. Repair keeps the layer's identity and configuration, marks the project unsaved and can be undone or redone. A raster drawn with its own color table requires a replacement with a color table; incompatible rasters are rejected without changing the saved style. If a tile archive is removed or reordered out of its captured slot while the dialog is open, the dialog closes rather than applying the replacement to another archive. It does not change embedded data, databases or web links. The web app cannot link to files on your computer: add the file again with Add Data.

CLI and Python use the same commands: layer.repairSource with {"layer":"Cities","path":"/data/towns.fgb"} (and optional "table"), or map.repairTiles with {"index":0,"path":"/data/tiles.pmtiles"}. Tile archives can also be selected by "name" or catalog "id".

items.title: Keyboard shortcuts
items.text:
Keys Action Ctrl+K Command search Ctrl+N / Ctrl+O / Ctrl+S New / Open / Save project Ctrl+Shift+S Save project as Ctrl+Z Undo Ctrl+Y / Ctrl+Shift+Z Redo Ctrl+T Attribute table Ctrl+F1 Collapse or expand the ribbon Ctrl+= / Ctrl+- Zoom in / out Home Full extent Esc Back to Explore; cancel a sketch Del Delete selected features; with Edit Vertices, the chosen vertex; in a layout, the selected element Ctrl+D Duplicate the selected layout element Arrow keys / Shift + arrow keys Nudge the selected layout element / nudge it further Alt+Shift+Right / Alt+Shift+Left Indent the active layer into the group above it / outdent it out of its group Alt+Shift+Up / Alt+Shift+Down Move the active layer up / down one step in the Layers pane Ctrl+C / Ctrl+X / Ctrl+V Copy / Cut / Paste features

On macOS, Cmd takes the place of Ctrl. Help › Shortcuts lists them all in the app, from the same table the app runs them from. While you type in a text field, undo and redo take back its typing, not the project's last change.

items.title: Selection and queries
items.text: Home › Select picks features by clicking or dragging a box. Open Select options to choose Select by Polygon (click vertices; click the first vertex or double-click to finish), Select by Lasso (drag a freehand outline), or Select by Radius (drag from the centre to set a distance). Shift adds to the selection; Ctrl/Cmd removes; Esc cancels an unfinished outline. Area tools use even-odd fill, so a self-crossing outline selects its alternating filled regions. Radius uses the Neighborhood Explorer's local Mercator distance and retained geographic prefilter; its outline and readout are approximate and some features near the outline may be excluded. The main Select button remains click/rectangle selection. All selection tools take only features that are drawn, in selectable layers: a definition query or a display filter hiding a feature keeps it out, and a click picks the feature drawn on top among the selectable layers. Select By Attributes takes a SQL clause and checks it as you type; Select By Location picks features that touch another layer's features or lie within a search distance of them (or, inverted, those that don't). Selected features draw in cyan and are highlighted in the attribute table, and the selection is synced both ways. Switch, clear or zoom to the selection, or make a new layer from it (Make Layer From Selected Features, select.layerFromSelection).

items.title: The attribute table
items.text:
Ctrl+T (or Home › Selection › Attributes) docks the active layer's table under the map. Click a column header to sort by it (a second click reverses the order, a third unsorts), click a row to select it (Ctrl or Shift toggles it without clearing the other rows), and double-click a cell to change its value. Selected only keeps to the selected rows and Filter rows… keeps rows where any value contains the text typed, ignoring letter case. The toolbar opens Select By Attributes and zooms to, switches, clears or deletes the selection, adds or calculates a field, and calculates geometry attributes.

The attribute table, with a selection highlighted on the map and in the table.

Select By Attributes and definition queries use SQL WHERE clauses, written in the expression language:

pop_est > 100000000 AND continent = 'Asia'
name LIKE 'S%'
iso_a3 IN ('FRA', 'DEU', 'ITA')
gdp_md IS NULL
"OR" = 1          -- double quotes name a field, even a keyword

items.title: Geoprocessing tools
GeoLibre tools
items.text:
The desktop app and the command line can also run the GeoLibre tool suite: over 1,000 tools from Whitebox and GeoLibre for terrain analysis (slope, aspect, hillshade, curvature), hydrology (fill depressions, flow direction and accumulation, watersheds), image processing, interpolation and vector work. They run on the map's layers and add their outputs as new layers.

The suite is an optional download, so RustGIS itself stays small: the GeoLibre runner, a single geolibre program (about 20 MB to download). In the Tools pane, click Install Whitebox and GeoLibre tools under Whitebox and GeoLibre tools: RustGIS downloads the latest runner for your platform from the geolibre-rust releases, checks it against its published SHA-256 checksum (which catches a corrupted download; the release itself is trusted as when you download it by hand) and installs it in its data folder (by default ~/.local/share/rustgis/geolibre on Linux, ~/Library/Application Support/RustGIS/geolibre on macOS, %LOCALAPPDATA%\RustGIS\geolibre on Windows). RUSTGIS_APP_DATA_DIR overrides the data folder; Linux also honours XDG_DATA_HOME. From the command line, gp.installGeolibre does the same.

To remove it, click Uninstall beside GeoLibre at the top of the Tools pane, then Confirm uninstall (gp.uninstallGeolibre from the command line): RustGIS deletes the runner it installed and removes the geolibre folder only if it is empty. Other files there, a runner you located yourself, and one on your PATH are left alone; RustGIS looks for a runner again. You can install the tools again at any time. In the browser, Remove unloads the tools and stops loading them when RustGIS starts.

To install it yourself instead, download the archive for your platform (geolibre-<version>-<platform>.tar.gz, or .zip on Windows), unpack it anywhere, and click Locate… to pick the geolibre program; RustGIS remembers it.

RustGIS also finds the runner without asking when it is next to the RustGIS program (or in a geolibre folder beside it), on your PATH, or named by the RUSTGIS_GEOLIBRE environment variable (the command line uses these). The tools then appear under GeoLibre in the Tools pane and the Browser's toolboxes, grouped by the category and subcategory the runner gives each tool (Conversion, Hydrology, LiDAR, Projection, Raster, Remote Sensing, Terrain, Vector, then e.g. GeoLibre › Terrain › Derivatives). A runner too old to list subcategories groups them by category only. Find Tools searches them.

  • Raster inputs are passed as their own files; vector layers (or their selection) are written in the first raster input's coordinate system, or, with no raster input, the UTM zone around the data. The latter uses metres; data spanning more than 40° of longitude stays in degrees.
  • Tools that take several layers (a composite's bands, a mosaic's tiles) list them in order: Add picks a layer, and ▲ ▼ change its place (the order of the bands, for a composite). From the command line, name them separated by ;: "inputs":"red;green;blue". In the desktop app a file not open as a layer can be added too: type its path below the list and press Enter.
  • Raster outputs are kept inside the project, so they save and reopen with it. Table outputs become standalone tables; text reports appear in the tool's messages.
  • LiDAR and other inputs RustGIS doesn't open as layers take a file path, read like Add Data reads one. Outputs are written to a fresh scratch folder and loaded from there.
  • Each run is a separate geolibre process, so a tool that fails can't take RustGIS down.
  • From the command line: gp.run={"tool":"geolibre:slope","params":{"input":"dem"}}; gp.tools lists every tool's parameters, gp.geolibre shows the runner in use and gp.setGeolibre={"path":"…"} picks one.

In the web app, click Load Whitebox and GeoLibre tools in the Tools pane instead. RustGIS loads geolibre-rust's WebAssembly runner (the geolibre-wasm package, from jsDelivr, about 25 MB the first time, then from the browser's cache) and the tools run in the page, in an in-memory folder: nothing is uploaded. The web app remembers this and loads them again on your next visit. The runner's code comes from jsDelivr, pinned to one geolibre-wasm release, the same trust as installing that package. Tools that read files by path (LiDAR files, for instance) need the desktop app, since a web page has no file system.

In the desktop app and on the command line, RustGIS waits while a tool runs, so a long run on a large raster or point cloud keeps the window busy until it finishes. In the web app the run is started in the background and the result is added when it ends, but the tool itself runs in the page, so the page is busy while it computes.

items.title: Analysis workflows
items.text:
The Analyze tab's Workflows pane holds guided analyses. Where one needs points, it asks you to click them on the map:

Workflow What it does Raster Functions Slope, aspect, hillshade, NDVI, band math ((b4-b3)/(b4+b3)), remapping, thresholds, resampling Function Editor Chains raster functions, each on the previous output Suitability Modeler Scores rasters 1–10 and adds them with weights Visibility Analysis A viewshed from a point on an elevation raster Exploratory 3D Analysis A line of sight between two points, split into seen and hidden parts Geostatistical Wizard An IDW surface from feature values, using 12 nearest neighbours by default Network Analysis The shortest (or cheapest, by a cost field) route over a line layer Neighborhood Explorer What lies within a distance of a point, with sums of numeric fields Simulation Random points in polygons (a fixed number, or from a field × rate) Data Engineering Counts, nulls, distinct values, min, max and mean of every field Exploratory Analysis Histograms and correlations of numeric fields Embeddings The features most like the selected one, by their numeric attributes Data Interop KML, GPX, CSV with WKT, GeoJSON or CSV

Rasters these make are kept in the project. Environments (gp.env) set an extent from the map view, full extent, a layer or a longitude/latitude box (or null to clear it). For tools that honour it, this restricts an unselected main feature input by bounding-box intersection, not by clipping its geometry; an existing selection takes precedence and overlay inputs stay whole. The Geostatistical Wizard uses the environment's extent and raster cell size (degrees). IDW Interpolation and Ordinary Kriging instead use their own extent and pixelSize parameters; the environment does not set their output grids. Project Raster (raster.project) puts a raster on a grid of any coordinate system, cell size and extent; Raster Functions › Resample matches a target raster's grid.

The Script pane runs commands from text, one per line (id {json}); its box grows with the script down to the bottom of the pane, short of the buttons, and then scrolls, so Run stays in view; Ctrl+Enter (⌘+Enter on macOS) in the box runs the script too. Above a run's results, a line tells its number, how long it took and when it started (Run #2 (0.84 s), and 14:04 UTC on the right), so a run made again by mistake shows (Undo takes a whole run back). It colours the commands as you type, in both themes: # comments in green italics, the command id, and the JSON's strings, numbers and true/false/null; an id no command has, or one that can't run in a script (ui.*, script.*, notebook.run), and parameters that aren't valid JSON are red and underlined. A script is read to its 10,000th line; any further are dimmed, as Run doesn't read them. Typing a line's first word opens a list of the commands it starts, under the cursor: ↑/↓ to move, Enter or Tab to accept, Escape to close, or a click. Beside it, the highlighted command's help: its signature (keys with ? may be left out), its name, its parameters one per line, and where it sits in the interface. Accepting a command on a line of its own adds its braces: with its required keys ready for their values, the cursor at the first (map.goToXY {"lon": , "lat": }), or empty with the cursor inside when every key may be left out; a command with no parameters gets none, and a line that has parameters keeps them. While you type a command's parameters (the cursor inside its {…}), the same help stays by the cursor; Escape closes it. A quote that starts a key in a command's braces opens the list of its keys not given yet, beside the highlighted key's description; accepting one closes it with its colon ("size":). The same goes in a key's own object, or in each object of its list, for the keys the command's description gives it (topology.rules {"add": {"rule": …}}). In a gp.run line, a quote after "tool": opens the list of the tools, beside the highlighted tool's help; accepting one closes it. In its "params": {…}, the keys offered are those of the tool its "tool" names (by id or name, before or after params), beside the highlighted key's kind, name, default and help; there the help by the cursor is the tool's. A task.addStep line works the same way: its "command": " offers the commands, and its "params" that command's keys and help. For a command that takes them, "layer": " offers the map's layers, top first, each with its kind's icon and beside it what it holds; "field": " offers the fields of the layer the line names (before or after it), or of the active layer when it names none, with each field's type beside it. So do the other keys a command describes as taking a field or fields, also inside their arrays (without the fields the array already lists): "fields": [" in data.explore (only the numeric ones, as it says), "sort": " in report.new, "address": [" in layer.geocode (the fields of its "table" when it names one). "map": ", "layout": " and "table": " offer the project's maps, layouts and standalone tables, with their layer counts, page sizes and row counts. "class": " offers the line's layer's label classes (or the active layer's), with each class's SQL clause, or All features. Default is included under its current name, except for commands that cannot remove or move it. In a gp.run line's "params", a value offers what the tool's parameter takes, as the tool's form does: the layers of its kind (polygon, point, raster, vector; any layer, then the tables), the fields of the tool's input that it takes (numeric, holding coordinates), or its choices ("units": " offers Kilometers, Meters, …). Accepting one writes its name as the line's JSON needs it ("Big \"lakes\""). A { or [ typed closes itself, the cursor inside, unless text follows it or it's in a string or a comment; so does a " where a string can start (after a space, {, [, , or :). A } or ] typed before the same one steps over it, as does a " typed before the quote that ends its string, and Backspace in an empty {}, [] or "" deletes both. The lists open in a quote that closed itself, and accepting keeps that quote. Pasting adds nothing.

items.title: ModelBuilder
items.text:
A model after its run: each node is ticked, and its outputs are layers on the map.

Analyze › Model Builder opens a model in a view of its own, a tab beside the maps and layouts. A model is a graph of three kinds of node: inputs (blue) name layers of the map, tools (amber) are geoprocessing tools, and outputs (green) keep a result as a layer of their name.

  • Drag a tool from the palette on the left onto the canvas, or click it; + Input and + Output add the other nodes.
  • Drag from a node's right port to another node's left port to connect them. A tool's left ports are its layer parameters; a parameter that isn't connected can name a layer of the map instead, in the settings on the right.
  • Select a node to set its parameters there; Keep this result adds an output for it.
  • Drag the background to pan, Ctrl+wheel (or pinch) to zoom; Arrange lays the nodes out along the flow and Fit shows the whole model. Delete removes the selected node or wire, Ctrl+D copies a node, Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+Y undo and redo.
  • Problems are listed below the canvas as you build (an input without a layer, a required parameter left empty, a loop) and the nodes concerned are marked; Run waits until there are none. The tools then run in flow order, and each node shows how it fared. A result that only feeds other tools is removed once the model has run; the outputs, and tools at the end of the flow, stay on the map. A run that fails is undone as a whole.
  • Save keeps the model in the project; Export writes it as a *.model.json file, which Import (or dropping the file on the window) opens again. A model from a file may not read or write files. Copy Command copies a model.run command that runs the model from the Script pane, the command line or Python.

The Workflows pane's Models section lists the project's models, and New Model From History turns the geoprocessing you've run into one. Models made as steps (model.new with steps, where %1 stands for step 1's output) run as they always have until they are saved from ModelBuilder, which shows them as a graph and saves them as one. The model.* commands build, check (model.validate), save and run models without the canvas:

{"graph": {"nodes": [
   {"id": "i1", "kind": "input", "layer": "Cities"},
   {"id": "t1", "kind": "tool", "tool": "buffer", "params": {"distance": 50}},
   {"id": "o1", "kind": "output", "name": "City zones"}],
 "edges": [
   {"from": "i1", "fromPort": "out", "to": "t1", "toPort": "input"},
   {"from": "t1", "fromPort": "out", "to": "o1", "toPort": "in"}]}}

items.title: Imagery
items.text:
The Analyze tab's imagery groups open their tools in the Workflows pane:

  • Ortho Mapping and Reality Mapping workspaces mosaic georeferenced images into an orthomosaic, or elevation rasters into a surface model that exports as a 3D mesh (OBJ).
  • Georeference places a raster from control points (column, row, longitude, latitude) or stretches it over the map view. Those only shift and scale a north-up grid, as RustGIS's geotransform has no rotation. With transform (raster.georeference) the points are fitted by any of the Control Point Fit transforms and the raster is warped onto a new north-up grid covering the warped image: {"layer": "scan", "transform": "spline", "points": [[column, row, x, y], …], "pointsCrs": "EPSG:4326", "crs": 32613, "resampling": "bilinear", "cellSize": 5, "name": "warped", "path": "warped.tif"}. pointsCrs is the coordinate system the points' x and y are in (default EPSG:4326) and crs the output's (default pointsCrs, so nothing is reprojected unless asked). Each output cell is taken back through the fit, after reprojection, to the image and sampled there with nearest, bilinear (the default) or cubic; cells that fall outside the image are no data, or see-through for a colour image, which gains an alpha band for it (a grey byte image becomes grey with alpha; alpha is 0–255 in every pixel type). An image warped into a geographic crs gets square cells in degrees, and one that would span more than 180° of longitude is refused: give a projected crs. The cell is about the source pixel's size on the ground unless cellSize (output units) says otherwise. The result replaces the layer's raster, or becomes a new layer with name; path also writes it as a cloud-optimised GeoTIFF, which then is the layer's file. A raster opened from an overview is warped at that reduced resolution, and the result says so.
  • Control Point Fit (raster.gcpFit) fits a similarity, affine, projective, second- or third-order polynomial, or thin plate spline transform to control points and reports how well it holds: each point's residual in pixels and map units, the RMSE, and each point's error when it is left out of the fit. With compare it fits them all and recommends the simplest whose leave-one-out error is close to the best.
  • Change Detection (difference, ratio, percent), Spectral Analysis (every band at a pixel), Indices (NDVI, NDWI, SAVI, NBR, NDBI, EVI), Process (clip to the view, to a box, or to a polygon layer's selected or all polygons, with the cells outside them no-data; resample) and the Pixel Editor (set the pixels inside a polygon).
  • Mosaic Rasters (raster.mosaic) merges tiles of one grid, such as the 1 km tiles of a state elevation model, into one raster in their own coordinate system and cell size, optionally written to a GeoTIFF: {"inputs": ["dgm_1.tif", "dgm_2.tif", …], "path": "dem.tif"}. Inputs are layers or file paths; where they overlap, the first one with data wins. Tiles in different coordinate systems or cell sizes, or opened from an overview, are refused rather than quietly resampled, as are tiles whose cells don't line up; the mosaic has to fit in memory (120 million values: cells times bands).
  • Project Raster (raster.project) puts a raster on a grid of your choosing, so rasters from different sources line up cell for cell (for map algebra, the Suitability Modeler, a series for Trend Analysis, or the inputs of a model): {"layer": "ndvi", "crs": 31983, "cellSize": 100, "extent": "Study area", "resampling": "average", "path": "ndvi_100m.tif"}. It has no pane yet: run it from the Script pane, the AI Assistant, the command line or Python. The result is a new layer (name, by default the layer's name with "projected"), and with path a cloud-optimised GeoTIFF too.
  • The grid: crs (by default the layer's), cellSize in its units (one number, or [x, y]; by default about the layer's pixel there), origin, a point a cell corner falls on ([0, 0] by default, so cell corners are whole multiples of the cell size and any two rasters projected with the same crs and cellSize line up), and extent: a polygon layer (its selected features' bounds, or all of them), [west, south, east, north] in degrees or "view", by default the layer's footprint. The extent is widened to whole cells.
  • Another raster's grid: "grid": "dem_100m" takes its coordinate system, cells and extent exactly, instead of crs, cellSize, origin and extent.
  • Resampling: nearest (the default: it never invents a value, which is right for classes), bilinear or cubic sample each cell at its centre. average and mode take every pixel whose centre falls in the cell (no-data skipped), its mean or its most frequent value (of those tied, the one that reaches the top count first, the pixels taken row by row, as in GDAL), which is what a coarser grid of elevation or land-cover classes should hold. A cell no pixel centre falls in, on a grid finer than the raster, takes the pixel under its centre. Classes take nearest or mode, continuous values bilinear or cubic, or average going coarser. A whole-number pixel type keeps its type, so its mean is rounded. On a colour image the colours count as much as their pixels are opaque, and mode is taken band by band (each channel's most frequent value among the pixels that show).
  • Cells off the raster are its no-data value. A raster without one keeps its bands as they are, with NaN there in a floating-point type and 0 in a whole-number one, as GDAL leaves them; a colour image gains an alpha band instead, so they are see-through.
  • Datums are shifted as everywhere in RustGIS, through each system's transformation to WGS 84 (a Helmert step for SAD69 or Córrego Alegre, a few metres from the IBGE's grid shifts).
  • The result has to fit in memory (120 million values, cells times bands; 32 million in the web app): a grid past that is refused, naming the limit. A raster read from its overview is projected at that resolution, and the result says so.
  • Classification Wizard (unsupervised k-means) and Classification Tools (minimum distance from training polygons).
  • Mensuration: distances along the surface, heights between two points, areas, and volumes above or below a base height, with a list of results.

items.title: Trend analysis
items.text:
Trend Analysis (cube.trend, in the Workflows pane after Change Detection) asks of a series of rasters whether each cell is changing, how fast, and how surely: an NDVI series greening or browning, a temperature series warming. Each cell gets Sen's slope, the median of the slopes between every two dates, which holds up against outliers such as a cloud left in an NDVI scene, and a Mann–Kendall test of whether the trend is significant.

  • The series (a data cube) is any of:
  • raster layers, a date each, dated by their names or their files' (ndvi_2024-06-01, MODIS's A2024153, 2024-06, a year) or by the dates given: {"layers": ["ndvi_2015", "ndvi_2016", …]}. A layer on another grid than the first one listed is resampled onto it (nearest neighbour, as Raster Functions › Resample does) as it is read, so a scene with another cell size or coordinate system takes part. The first layer sets the cell size: a finer layer gives one of its pixels to each cell, not their mean. Cells a layer doesn't cover are empty that date. The Workflows pane's Dates field takes the dates separated by commas;
  • a Zarr variable along its time dimension, by its layer or its store, as for Summarise over time (see Data): {"path": "air.zarr", "variable": "t2m"};
  • a raster of several bands, a date each, as Earth Engine and openEO export, dated by the bands' names (the descriptions GDAL writes in the file, or in an .aux.xml next to it: NDVI 2024-06-01) or dates: {"layer": "ndvi_2015_2024", "dates": ["2015", "2016", …]};
  • a STAC collection's band (desktop), read in place from its cloud-optimised GeoTIFFs over an area, as Add as Time Series finds them (see Web data): {"url": "https://data.inpe.br/bdc/stac/v1", "collection": "mod13q1-6.1", "asset": "NDVI", "bbox": [-46, -10.95, -40.35, -2.7], "start": "2001", "end": "2025"}. Each date's files (a grid tile each, MODIS's h13v09 and h13v10 for Piauí) are put together on one grid, each scaled as its own metadata says (NDVI's 0.0001). "cellSize" reads the level of the files' overviews nearest it (1000 reads MODIS's 926 m one), which reads far fewer bytes; by default the full images. An overview is often one pixel taken from each block (the Brazil Data Cube's are), so a cell is then one 250 m pixel, which can differ much from the place's mean; "resampling": "average" makes each cell the mean of the full images' pixels in it, reading those (16 times the bytes at 1 km from 250 m). It needs every file's corner on a cell's corner, as MODIS's tiles are; a file on a grid shifted by part of a cell is refused: set "resampling": "nearest" and run it again. A file's no-data value is skipped, from its header or from its asset's metadata (raster:bands nodata). Where two tiles' files overlap on a date (items without a tile name are told apart by footprint), a cell is the mean of their values, while the data cube on the map shows one of them. This source is given as parameters (a script, the assistant, the command line); cube.trend waits for the search and the reads with no Cancel, the app with it, as for a Zarr store's address, so keep the area and period small there, or run a large one from the command line (see Long runs below).
  • an entry of the catalog of data cubes (see Web data), by its id: {"cube": "bdc-mod13q1-ndvi", "bbox": [-46, -10.95, -40.35, -2.7], "start": "2001", "end": "2025"} fills in the collection's API, band, cell size and cloud cap, or a Zarr entry's store and variable. In the app, Trend Analysis… on a cube of Home › Add › Web Data › Data Cubes opens this section on it: a STAC cube is read where the map is, a Zarr cube whole.

For the mean of a finer layer's pixels in each cell, or for a grid of your own, put the rasters on one grid first with Project Raster ("grid", the first one's, and "resampling": "average"). - The test: NDVI and temperature series are autocorrelated, which makes the plain test report too many significant cells, so the default is the modified Mann–Kendall test of Hamed & Rao (1998): the variance of S is corrected by the autocorrelation of the detrended series' ranks, at the lags significant at the test's level. The others: - Yue & Wang (2004), from the lag-1 autocorrelation of the detrended series; - Seasonal (Hirsch et al. 1982), for a series with a yearly cycle: the test is made within each season ("seasons": 12 for months, 23 for 16-day composites) and summed, and Sen's slope comes from pairs within a season; - Mann–Kendall for independent values.

The definitions follow pymannkendall's, ties included. - Options: the significance level ("alpha", 0.05), the slope per year or per decade (from the real dates, so uneven spacing is handled), a period (start, end; a whole number from 1000 to 9999 is a year, and an end given as a year or a month takes all of it), a season across years ("months": [12, 1, 2]), and the dates a cell needs ("minValid", by default half of them, at least 4). Missing values and no-data are skipped cell by cell. - Outputs: four 32-bit layers, kept in the project as GeoTIFFs: Sen's slope, the test's Z, the p-value, and the slope where p < alpha (no-data elsewhere), the one a map usually shows on a diverging ramp centred on 0. - Size: the cube is read into memory a slice at a time, up to 64 million values (cells times dates; 16 million in the web app) and 2,000 dates. A STAC collection's area is read in pieces instead, bands of rows each within that block (a whole number of the files' tile rows where they fit), eight dates at a time, and the outputs are put together: Piauí at about 1 km over 25 years of 16-day composites (645 × 984 cells × 576 dates) is six pieces. Its area is up to 25 million cells. The seasonal test compares only pairs within a season, so its time limit counts those. It runs in the background with progress and Cancel. - Long runs: in the app, a trend run from the Script pane or the assistant waits with no Cancel, so it takes a tenth of the panes' limit on pairs compared (2 billion), as Python does. rustgis-cli run, where nothing but a shell waits on it, takes the panes' limit (20 billion): Piauí's 576 composites at about 1 km with the seasonal test (about 4.4 billion pairs) run in one call there, and rustgis-cli run prints its progress (cube.trend: 42%). There, a STAC collection's search also takes up to 10,000 items for a trend or a summary (a state's four MODIS tiles over 25 years are 2,304). In the app, whose Script pane and assistant wait for the search with no Cancel, and in Python, it takes 2,000, as a data cube on the time slider does.

rustgis-cli run --cmd 'cube.trend={"layers":["ndvi_2015","ndvi_2016","ndvi_2017","ndvi_2018"],"per":"decade"}'
rustgis-cli run --cmd 'cube.trend={"url":"https://data.inpe.br/bdc/stac/v1","collection":"mod13q1-6.1","asset":"NDVI","bbox":[-46,-10.95,-40.35,-2.7],"start":"2001","end":"2025","cellSize":1000,"test":"seasonal","seasons":23,"per":"decade"}' --save piaui.rgis

items.title: Summarising a data cube over time
items.text:
Summarise a Data Cube over Time (cube.reduce) makes rasters of one statistic of each cell over the dates of any of the series Trend Analysis takes (layers, a raster's bands, a Zarr variable, a STAC collection's band): mean, min, max, sum, std (the population standard deviation), count of values, or countAbove a threshold ("above"), as Summarise over time does for a Zarr variable (see Data).

  • Classes: a series of categorical rasters, such as yearly land-cover maps (MapBiomas, ESA WorldCover), is summarised as classes with eight more statistics:
  • mode, each cell's most frequent class, the least of those tied ("majority" too);
  • modeCount, at how many dates it had that class;
  • variety, how many classes it had;
  • changes, how many times its class changed from one date with a class to the next, in date order. A date with no data is skipped, so A, no data, B is one change. Within each group, so by year a change is one within the year;
  • longestRun, the class it kept for the most dates in a row, in date order, the least of those tied. A date with no data neither breaks a run nor adds to it, so A, no data, A is a run of two;
  • longestRunLength, how many dates that run lasted;
  • frequency, a layer for each class met (… frequency 1985–2023 class 3), each cell's count of dates in that class. By year or month, a layer for each class of each group;
  • countIn, at how many dates it was one of the classes given ("classes": [3, 4, 5], whole numbers from 0 to 255), such as the years a cell was forest.

They take the values as classes: a value that isn't a whole number (an NDVI) is refused with the value, as is a run with more than 1,000 classes, or more than 64 million cells × classes in the groups being read at once (16 million in the web app; for frequency, whose classes are each a layer, the outputs' 32 million values). These are the data cube summary's only: Summarise over time for a Zarr variable refuses them and points here. Mode, modeCount, variety and frequency keep a count of each class in each cell while they read, 2 bytes a class, for each group being read: by month, every month's at once, so a large area by month may need a smaller area or a group by year. changes, longestRun and longestRunLength read a STAC collection one date at a time, in order, so they are slower there than the other statistics, which read several dates at once.

  • Groups: "by": "all" (the default) makes one layer of the whole period, "year" one for each calendar year (an annual mean NDVI from 16-day composites), "month" one for each month of the year across the years (a climatology). "start", "end" and "months" pick the dates as for a trend.
  • Missing values: no-data and missing values are skipped cell by cell. A cell keeps no value where it had fewer values than "minValid" (a share of its group's dates, 0 by default: 0.5 wants half of a year's composites); with the default, count, countAbove, countIn, modeCount, variety, changes, longestRunLength and frequency give 0 where a cell never had a value, and mode and longestRun give none.
  • Size: the slices are folded into running totals as they are read, so a long period takes no more memory than a short one; a STAC collection's area is read in pieces, as for a trend. The outputs hold up to 32 million values (cells times groups; 8 million in the web app). A summary by month keeps every month's totals while it reads, up to five times the outputs' memory for std (three for mean, min, max, sum and countAbove), so a large area by month may need a coarser cell size or a smaller area. rustgis-cli run takes a STAC collection's search up to 10,000 items, as for a trend (the app and Python 2,000), and prints a summary's progress (cube.reduce: 42%). The layers are named after what they hold (NDVI mean 2001, NDVI mean 2001–2025 month 03, or the "name" given and the group) and kept in the project as GeoTIFFs.
rustgis-cli run --cmd 'cube.reduce={"layers":["ndvi_2015","ndvi_2016","ndvi_2017","ndvi_2018"],"stat":"max"}'
rustgis-cli run --data cobertura_1985.tif --data cobertura_1986.tif --data cobertura_1987.tif --cmd 'cube.reduce={"layers":["cobertura_1985","cobertura_1986","cobertura_1987"],"stat":"changes"}'
rustgis-cli run --cmd 'cube.reduce={"url":"https://data.inpe.br/bdc/stac/v1","collection":"mod13q1-6.1","asset":"NDVI","bbox":[-44.8,-7.5,-44.3,-7.0],"start":"2001","end":"2025","cellSize":1000,"stat":"mean","by":"year","minValid":0.5,"name":"NDVI"}' --save urucui.rgis

items.title: Zonal statistics and polygon clipping
items.text:
Open Zonal Statistics through Command Search, or choose it in the Workflows pane.

Zonal Statistics uses the selected polygon features when the layer has a selection. It keeps original geometries and fields, and reports features with missing or rejected polygon parts. If any polygon part fails validation or transformation to WGS 84, the feature receives count 0 and null statistics. If a part subsequently fails projection onto the raster grid, it is omitted and reported; statistics cover the remaining valid parts. Large overlapping zones each require a separate pass over their raster window.

For raster.process polygon clipping, selectedOnly: true requires a selection, selectedOnly: false uses every polygon, and omitting it uses the selection when present. The Process pane initially checks Selected only when the chosen layer has a selection, and sends the choice explicitly. Clipping and Zonal Statistics share polygon transformation rules so a failed hole cannot silently enlarge the sampled area. A malformed ring or a failed projection rejects its complete polygon part in all raster masking operations. Clipping skips invalid features and reports their count in the command result; its output bounds cover the valid polygons only.

An empty band field or bands: "" selects band 1. The pane disables calculation when raster data is unavailable, shows the available band range for invalid band input, and indicates when only selected polygons will appear in the output. Both tools report parts omitted during raster-grid projection while retaining the valid parts.

Field parameters in Dissolve, XY Table to Point, IDW, Kriging, Summary Statistics and Pivot Table accept case-insensitive names. An exact spelling takes precedence; otherwise a name matching several fields is rejected as ambiguous. This prevents silently using the wrong field.

items.title: Deep learning and hosted imagery
items.text: Analyze › Deep Learning Tools trains a neural network (a multilayer perceptron) on the pixels under training polygons and classifies every pixel, adding a class raster with a confidence band and reporting the accuracy on held-back pixels. Trained models stay in the project; Publish › Share As › Deep Learning saves one as a package to apply in other projects. Analyze › Create Hosted Imagery cuts a raster into XYZ web map tiles (PNG, transparent outside the raster) with a TileJSON file and a viewer page.

items.title: AI Assistant
items.text:
The AI Assistant selects the five most populous African countries and zooms to them.

Analyze › AI Assistant (also View › Windows, or Command Search) opens a chat pane. Ask a question about your data or say what to do with the map, and the assistant answers by running RustGIS commands and geoprocessing tools for you:

  • "Which 5 countries have the largest GDP?" reads the Countries table and answers.
  • "Label the cities with their names, and zoom to Tokyo."
  • "Buffer the cities by 200 km and colour the result by population."
  • "Switch to a dark basemap and hide the rivers."

Each step it takes shows in the conversation (click one to see its parameters and result). Project edits use the usual undo history, so Ctrl+Z takes them back; undo does not remove exported files or reverse actions outside the project. Check the tool results and map rather than relying only on the model's reply. Commands that would read or write files, connect to an address on the internet, run a plugin, script, task or model, or replace the project wait for you: Allow or Decline. SQL queries also ask, because SQL can access files and the network. Allow such actions for this conversation remembers the exact command and all its parameters, not general access to a file or server. Plugin commands, user automation and project replacement ask every time.

Enter sends, Shift+Enter starts a new line, and Up and Down recall earlier messages when the message box is empty or showing a recalled message. Drag the grip above it to resize it. Stop ends the current assistant run; background local-agent threads have their own Stop controls.

From the command line, rustgis-cli ask sends one request (see Command Line).

items.title: Choosing a model
items.text:
Click the model name or the gear to open the settings. The assistant works with:

Provider Default model Key Anthropic claude-opus-5-5 console.anthropic.com, or ANTHROPIC_API_KEY OpenAI gpt-5.5 platform.openai.com, or OPENAI_API_KEY ChatGPT (sign in) the first model in your account’s current catalog none: Continue with ChatGPT to use your ChatGPT plan (desktop app and command line) Google Gemini gemini-3.8-flash aistudio.google.com, or GEMINI_API_KEY / GOOGLE_API_KEY OpenRouter openrouter/auto openrouter.ai, or OPENROUTER_API_KEY Ollama (local) qwen3 none; the server from OLLAMA_BASE_URL (default http://localhost:11434) OpenAI-compatible — LM Studio, vLLM, llama.cpp…: OPENAI_COMPATIBLE_BASE_URL (default http://localhost:1234/v1), with an optional OPENAI_COMPATIBLE_API_KEY

The ↻ button lists the provider's models. The provider and model you last chose in the settings are used at start. Until you choose one, RUSTGIS_ASSISTANT_PROVIDER and RUSTGIS_ASSISTANT_MODEL pick them, and otherwise the desktop uses the first provider with a key in the environment, falling back to Anthropic when none has a key. ChatGPT sign-in is used only when you choose that provider. Saved settings win over the environment. The Address field changes the endpoint for providers other than ChatGPT; use the OpenAI-compatible API path (usually /v1) for local servers. Models that call tools well give the best results; small local models may stop early or skip steps.

items.title: Signing in with ChatGPT
items.text:
With a ChatGPT plan you can use the assistant without an API key, through OpenAI's Sign in with ChatGPT for open-source apps. Choose ChatGPT (sign in) and click Continue with ChatGPT: your browser opens OpenAI's sign-in page, where you approve RustGIS using your plan (the first time, OpenAI registers RustGIS as an app of your account; you can rename it there). Afterwards the settings show the account's email, Using ChatGPT plan, and a Weekly usage link to your ChatGPT usage settings, where you can see and limit what RustGIS uses or disconnect it. Sign out clears local tokens and attempts to revoke the remote session. If OpenAI does not confirm revocation, RustGIS says so; disconnect RustGIS in ChatGPT settings to ensure that remote access ends. The registration remains for signing in again. The account picker retains separate registrations, even when their emails match. Use another account adds a registration; choose an existing one to reuse its issued client ID. Remove account signs the selected one out and forgets it. From the command line:

rustgis-cli ask --login                 # continue with ChatGPT in the browser
