rustgis-cli ask --login --another-account  # or register RustGIS for another account
rustgis-cli ask --sample --provider chatgpt "Zoom to Tokyo"
rustgis-cli ask --accounts              # list saved registrations
rustgis-cli ask --account oaiapp_...      # select one by its issued client id
rustgis-cli ask --login --account oaiapp_... # reauthorize that registration
rustgis-cli ask --remove-account oaiapp_...  # sign out and forget it
rustgis-cli ask --logout

The model catalog loads after sign-in, on startup when signed in, and when switching to this provider or another account. The first model is chosen when the current one is not offered. The ↻ button reloads the catalog. The CLI uses the catalog's first model unless --model or RUSTGIS_ASSISTANT_MODEL is set. While waiting for sign-in, Open browser again and Copy sign-in link let you recover a closed tab or failed browser launch. Requests go to the OpenAI API (https://api.openai.com/v1/responses) and use your plan's usage; when a limit is reached, the assistant says so and points to the usage settings. Signing in needs the desktop app or the command line (it runs a short-lived server on 127.0.0.1, port 1455 when it's free, for the browser to return to); the web app doesn't offer it.

Live testing of this integration was limited to a ChatGPT Pro account on Windows 11. Plus, Team/Business, Enterprise and Edu accounts, macOS and Linux have not been live-verified. Plan usage limits and model catalogs depend on the selected account and workspace. Team/Business, Enterprise and Edu workspace policy may block plan usage.

Weekly usage opens ChatGPT's settings page. RustGIS does not show a live percentage: there is no documented usage endpoint, and the tested live responses supplied no rate-limit headers.

items.title: Tool output limits
items.text:
The assistant can search_docs and read_doc to look up RustGIS features and commands. Each tool result defaults to an estimated 10,000 tokens, following Codex's default output budget. A result is capped at an absolute 24,000 tokens. Like Codex's truncation utilities, the budget uses a byte-based estimate (four UTF-8 bytes per token), rather than an exact tokenizer. It includes JSON escaping and truncation metadata. This bounds individual results, not the entire conversation or all results from a batch.

RUSTGIS_ASSISTANT_TOOL_OUTPUT_TOKEN_LIMIT changes the requested per-tool budget; it cannot bypass the 24,000-token ceiling. Embedding callers can set Config::tool_output_token_limit. MCP uses the 10,000-token default.

Oversized successful results return an explicit, bounded text preview inside valid JSON, preserving the beginning and end; ask for fewer rows or a narrower search to get complete structured data. Documentation reads preserve complete lines and return next_offset when more remain: call read_doc again with the same page/section and that offset. limit defaults to 2000 lines, following Pi's line-oriented read convention. Invalid offsets (including zero, negative numbers, fractions and strings) return an error. Tiny output budgets use minimal truncation metadata or a diagnostic string prefix rather than returning bare null; extremely small budgets can only retain an abbreviated marker. Reading a section avoids loading an entire page. A single line that cannot fit produces an explicit error rather than silently skipping text.

items.title: Skills
items.text:
Skills are instructions for a kind of task. The assistant sees only each skill's name and a line on when to use it, and reads its instructions on demand, so skills cost little until used. Loaded instructions share the configured tool-output budget; oversized results are explicitly marked as truncated. Split long skills or raise that limit (up to its existing ceiling) when complete instructions do not fit. RustGIS comes with these:

Skill For thematic-map Styling a layer by its data (graduated colours, categories, proportional symbols), labelling it and exporting the map explore-data What's in a layer: fields, value ranges, top records, counts, filters and summary statistics print-layout A page layout with a map frame, title, legend, north arrow and scale bar, exported to PDF or PNG geoprocessing Running and chaining tools: buffer, clip, erase, dissolve, select by location, summarize within add-data Adding files, web addresses, DuckDB SQL queries, STAC catalogs and Overture Maps share-web-map Sharing the map or a layer as files that work without a server: a web map, a web layer, a style, an image

On the desktop, the settings' Skills list shows every skill and where it comes from, with a switch to turn each one on or off:

  • Built in: the skills above.
  • Plugins: skills a plugin carries, named <plugin>:<skill>, while the plugin is enabled (see Plugins).
  • Yours: on the desktop, Add skill… adds a SKILL.md, a skill's folder, a folder of skills or a .zip of them. They are kept in the skills folder of the app's settings folder (Open folder), and Remove deletes one's SKILL.md (files you keep beside it stay). A skill of yours replaces a built-in one of the same name.
  • Shared: skills in ~/.agents/skills, where other AI agents keep theirs. They are listed but off until you turn them on, since they were written for other tools.

A skill's description and instructions reach the model as instructions you trust, like a message of your own, so turn on only skills you trust. Whatever a skill says, the commands that need your approval (files, the network, plugins) still ask.

A skill is a folder holding SKILL.md in the Agent Skills format: front matter giving its name (lower-case letters, digits and hyphens) and a description that says when to use it, then the instructions in Markdown. Each SKILL.md is at most 64 KiB; the assistant reads only that file, and importing a folder or ZIP does not copy its other files. Descriptions can be single-line values or indented blocks introduced by > or |. For a description spanning several lines, use a block; plain multiline YAML values are not supported.

---
name: flood-map
description: Map flood depth and extent from a depth raster and the river network.
---

# Flood map

1. ...

From the command line:

rustgis-cli skills                      # every skill, where it comes from, and whether it's on
rustgis-cli skills add ./flood-map      # a SKILL.md, a folder or a .zip
rustgis-cli skills disable explore-data # enable / disable / remove <name>

items.title: Skill folders and ZIP names
items.text:
Skill folders may be symbolic links, including shared ~/.agents/skills folders. Enabling a shared skill trusts the instructions at that linked location; shared skills are off by default. The SKILL.md file itself must be a regular file, not a symbolic link. Removing one of your skills removes its SKILL.md, including from a linked folder's target; it does not remove the folder link or other files.

ZIP imports recognize SKILL.md regardless of letter case and accept slash or backslash path separators. Paths that collide after separator/case normalization are refused. Nested skills remain part of their containing skill. Entries are read in memory, never extracted as paths. The ZIP dependency is native-only; browser builds do not include the installer.

Skill front matter supports top-level name and description fields, plain or single/double- quoted one-line values, and indented >/| description blocks (joined into one line). This reader implements those forms rather than full YAML: trailing inline comments, multiline quoted scalars, escapes, anchors and advanced block modifiers are not interpreted. Keep comments on their own lines and put literal # text inside the intended value. Descriptions are collapsed to one whitespace-separated line before catalog insertion. On Windows, reserved device names such as con, nul, com1 and lpt1 cannot be installed; rename the skill. Unknown-name errors show up to 20 names; Settings shows the full available list.

An archive with SKILL.md at its root represents that one outermost skill: nested SKILL.md files belong to its examples/references and are not installed separately. To import several skills, put each in a sibling folder and omit a root SKILL.md. A failure during the final rename phase can leave earlier skills installed; the error names those completed installs.

items.title: Subagents
items.text: For a self-contained task, the assistant can use delegate to start a fresh conversation with the same provider and model, acting on the same project. The subagent receives the task, not the whole conversation, and returns a short report. Its tool calls appear in the main transcript, and file, network and other gated actions still need approval. It inherits the conversation's exact-command approvals. This works without installing a local coding agent; it is distinct from the background threads below.

items.title: Agents on this computer
items.text:
On the desktop, the assistant can hand a task to a coding agent you already have, such as Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot CLI, Cursor, OpenCode or goose. RustGIS talks to it through the Agent Client Protocol (ACP), as code editors do. The agent works on the map open here through RustGIS's tools, and with its own: calling a web API RustGIS doesn't have, running a script, writing files. It suits tasks RustGIS's own tools can't do.

It is off until you turn it on: in the settings, tick Let the assistant hand tasks to agents on this computer. The settings list the agents found. Starting a task or sending a follow-up waits for your approval in the assistant, unless automatic approval is enabled. Then ask, for example: "Have Claude Code fetch the USGS stream gauges in Texas and add them to the map."

  • It works in the background. The assistant hands over the task and carries on talking with you. A small window shows what the agent says and does until it finishes; its report then comes back into the conversation, and the assistant tells you what came of it. Several agents can work at once, each in a thread of its own (codex-1, claude-code-2…), listed above the message box with Show, Hide and × to close one.
  • Threads take follow-ups. A thread that has finished waits for more, with what it did in its context: "Now colour the gauges by flow" goes to the same agent. Threads end with New conversation, when you close them, or after half an hour of waiting.
  • You approve what it does. Each action the agent asks to take (a command, a web request, a file it writes) waits for Allow, Always allow (when the agent offers it) or Decline in its window. Allow never becomes a persistent approval: if no once-only option exists, use the explicitly labelled Always allow or decline. Approve agents' actions without asking lets them through instead. Turn it on only if you trust the agent with your computer.
  • RustGIS checks its own tools. File, network, plugin-command and project-replacement requests from a local agent wait for a separate Allow or Decline in its window. Approval applies only to that exact MCP message and that agent's run; a batch is approved or declined as a whole. The agent's --yes and the general relay checkbox cannot bypass this queue. Requests that expire, or whose agent ends, never run. Plugin management, scripts and other user-only commands remain unavailable through MCP. Approve agents' actions without asking explicitly bypasses this queue for these local agents and allows subsequent delegations without confirmation; turn it on only if you trust the agent and its inputs. It also selects the agent's own full-access mode where available.
  • Its work is kept. Each task gets a folder in Documents/RustGIS/Agent work, and what the agent adds to the map comes from there. The assistant's reply names the folder.
  • On the map, it has its thread's permission only. It reaches the map through the MCP relay with a token of its own, which RustGIS revokes when the thread ends. Stop in its window, or × in the list, revokes its token immediately and terminates its live process tree on a background thread. A reaped leader's old process ID is never signalled.
  • No console windows. On Windows, agents start without a terminal window; their window in RustGIS shows what they do.
  • Signing in is the agent's. The agent uses its own account and sign-in. If it isn't signed in, sign in with it once (for example, codex login).
  • Claude Code and Codex need Node.js. They speak ACP through an adapter (@agentclientprotocol/claude-agent-acp, @agentclientprotocol/codex-acp), which npx downloads from npm the first time, at the version RustGIS names. Agents with ACP built in need nothing more. The web app doesn't offer agents.

items.title: Privacy
items.text:
Assistant requests go directly to the provider and address you chose, using your API key or ChatGPT sign-in. They carry your messages, the map's layer names, fields and extent, and tool results such as rows the assistant reads. Local agents use their own providers and tools, with their own data handling. A key typed in the settings is used for the session only unless you tick Remember the key on this computer. On the desktop, this saves it in the system keychain (macOS Keychain, Windows Credential Manager, or the Secret Service on Linux). Clearing the key or unticking Remember deletes the saved key; a failed deletion is shown in settings. Keys from the environment are never saved. If the keychain is unavailable, locked, or access is refused, a new key stays in memory for this session and the settings explain why it was not remembered. On upgrade, an existing keychain key takes precedence over an old key in the preferences; otherwise the app moves the old key into the keychain. The plaintext preference is cleared only after the keychain key is read or the old key is saved successfully. If either operation fails, the old preference is retained and the unencrypted-storage warning stays visible. In the web app, Remember still saves the key unencrypted in the browser's storage, with a note in settings. A ChatGPT sign-in's refresh token is kept in the system keychain, never in the preferences or a project file, and no token is ever logged. The short-lived access token stays in the memory of the RustGIS window that got it, so each time RustGIS starts it renews the sign-in once before its first request; after a restart, the browser may ask you to choose the account again when you sign in. chatgpt-auth.json in the app's settings folder keeps only the saved accounts (their client id, account, email, permissions, when the tokens expire, and which one is selected), no token. A sign-in from an earlier version, whose tokens are in that file, keeps working: they move to the keychain the first time they are used, and leave the file only once the keychain has taken them. If the keychain is unavailable, they stay in the file until it is, and the settings say so. A new sign-in the keychain can't take lasts until RustGIS closes and is never written to the file; the settings say it won't be remembered, and it never replaces a sign-in the keychain still holds for that account. Sign out revokes the session at OpenAI and deletes its token; if the keychain can't be read, you are still signed out on this computer, and the settings say the session couldn't be ended at OpenAI. Remove account also forgets the account, once any keychain item it had is deleted: while the keychain can't be read or can't delete it, removal refuses, so no token is left behind in it. Without --use-saved-secrets, the command line has no keychain (it uses a sign-in from an earlier version still in the file), so its sign-ins last for the command only, and it can't use, sign out or remove an account whose token is in the keychain. With the flag, it uses the keychain as the app does. Python's Session(use_saved_secrets=True) similarly opts connection commands into the system store; it does not add an assistant API. The ChatGPT provider's address is fixed, so only the OpenAI API receives the tokens. Renewals are serialized across RustGIS processes (a refresh token can be used only once), and the keychain is read under the same lock. Plain HTTP is only used for servers on your computer or local network.

In the web app, the browser calls the provider directly. Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini and OpenRouter accept that; a local Ollama server must allow the page's origin (OLLAMA_ORIGINS=https://web.rustgis.app ollama serve).

items.title: Retries and long conversations
items.text:
The assistant stops after 16 rounds of tool use per message, shared with subagents. Provider retries and conversation summaries are separate. Reply "continue" to go on.

RustGIS first trims older tool results and reasoning when the conversation grows too large. If that is not enough, or the provider rejects the context length, it asks the same model to summarize earlier turns. Compact requests this explicitly while the assistant is idle; New conversation clears the chat and its remembered approvals and ends local-agent threads, without resetting the map.

Live streaming text is available on the desktop. The browser currently buffers the complete response (up to the response limit, 64 MiB for SSE) before displaying it; it has no live streaming preview. Cross-origin retry timing headers are available only when the provider exposes them through CORS; otherwise ordinary backoff applies.

A failed compaction shows an error and keeps the original conversation, then stops. It does not retry continuously in the background. Sending another message or pressing Compact explicitly tries again; if the history still cannot fit, use New conversation or choose another model.

Connection failures and explicit provider overload/rate-limit failures are retried at most three times, including errors reported inside an HTTP-200 stream. The failed reply and its preview are discarded before retrying; no tool calls from it run. Usage limits, authentication failures, browser fetch failures (which can be permanent CORS refusals), timeouts and interrupted streams without an explicit retryable provider error stop without replay. Stop cancels a pending retry.

Summary requests have a total input bound, retaining the newest history if older text must be omitted. If the provider rejects a summary as too long, RustGIS halves that bound and tries again, down to 1,024 bytes; further failure stops and preserves the original conversation. This learned bound lasts for the conversation. A cut, refused or failed summary never replaces history. The summariser treats retrieved text as data, not instructions. Internal summary markers in user messages are escaped in model input; the visible transcript keeps the user's exact text.

Background agent reports are quoted as untrusted data, with markup escaped and the report payload constrained by the configured tool-output budget. The main assistant uses observations relevant to your task, rather than treating a report as a new user instruction.

ACP input uses a bounded background writer queue, so a stalled agent cannot block permission buttons or follow-up submission. Queue overflow reports an error instead of blocking. On Linux and macOS, an exited leader is observed without reaping until cleanup; its reserved identity lets Stop terminate surviving process-group descendants before finally reaping the leader.

items.title: Symbology
Symbols by expression
items.text:
By Expression, under the symbol in the Symbology pane, sets parts of the symbol per feature from an expression: a point's Size (points), the Fill and Outline colours (a line's Color), the Outline width (a line's Width, in points) and a point's Angle (degrees clockwise, in place of the Rotation field; where it gives null, the field's). A colour is text: '#d7301f', a CSS colour name such as 'navy', or 'r,g,b[,a]' as color_rgb() and color_rgba() give it. A point with Marks scales them all with its Size, their sizes and offsets in proportion to the symbol's own size (each mark keeps its colours); a size of 0 or less draws nothing. Where an expression gives null (or, for a colour, text that isn't one), the feature takes the symbol's own, so a CASE without ELSE changes only the features it names. @map_scale is the scale the map is drawn at, so a width can change with the zoom (in a shared web map, whose reader zooms freely, it is null). They apply on top of the renderer: a Unique Values class's colour, then the expression's. An expression applies when its box loses focus; one that doesn't read shows why and isn't applied. A layer styled by expression is drawn on the CPU; points drawn as counted bins (aggregation) keep the bins' own symbol, and a line's stacked strokes keep the colour and width each sets. A shared web map draws each feature's colours, outline width and size as styled (points as circles, without their angle or marks); a layer's MapLibre style (a web layer's, or one exported alone) carries the renderer's symbol, without the expressions. By command:

layer.symbolBy={"layer":"Cities","size":"scale_linear(pop_max, 0, 2e7, 4, 24)","fill":"CASE WHEN pop_max > 1e7 THEN '#d7301f' END"}
layer.symbolBy={"layer":"Rivers","strokeWidth":"if(@map_scale < 5e6, 2, 0.5)"}
layer.symbolBy={"layer":"Cities","fill":null}

Pick a colour scheme from the pane's swatches, listed in groups: Perceptually Uniform (Viridis, Plasma, Inferno, Magma, Cividis, Batlow and Aurora: even steps in lightness, so they read in greyscale and for colour-blind viewers), Sequential, Diverging (Red–Blue, Vik, Roma, Balance), Topographic and Bathymetric (Terrain, Oleron, Topo and Deep; Oleron and Topo change colour sharply at the middle of the range, sea level for data centred on 0), Qualitative, Matplotlib (the whole matplotlib colour map library as GeoLibre lists it, cmocean's maps included, by name from Accent to YlOrRd) and the project's own Custom ramps. Commands take a scheme by name; matplotlib's names are case-sensitive where they meet ours (terrain is matplotlib's, Terrain ours). A project's own ramp named like a built-in one (an older project's jet, say) is renamed with (custom) when the project opens; layers drawn with it keep their colours, as each holds its own copy. Click a group's name to show or hide it. The Style tab sets the fill Color, the Outline width, Transparency and a Visibility Range (the scales between which the layer draws; a large file read in place is not read at all outside them); points can be circles, squares, triangles, diamonds or stars. Data › Definition Query draws only the features matching a SQL clause; Unique Values, Graduated Colors and Proportional Symbols take their values, classes and sizes from those features when you apply them (apply the symbology again after changing the query), and Full Extent zooms to them. A layer with subtypes can be symbolized by them. Style › Styles saves symbology as styles to reuse on other layers and in other projects.

For polygons, No Fill in the Symbology pane or Style › Drawing draws only the outlines. It keeps each symbol's outline colour and width, including in Unique Values and Graduated Colors, without changing the classes. Change the outline with Outline color and Outline width in the Single Symbol editor, or layer.outline for all classes. Undo restores the previous fills; the colour picker's opacity control can also make a fill visible again. By command:

layer.noFill={"layer":"Countries"}

A GeoJSON with mixed geometry keeps its points, lines and polygons in one layer, classified by its most common geometry family. No Fill and the Fills editor are also available when that layer contains polygons. No Fill leaves point and line symbols unchanged; use the Fills editor to change the polygon fill's colour or remove its transparent fill to restore the symbol's fill. For layers read in place, these controls recognise polygon features in the currently loaded view as well as the layer's declared geometry family.

The ribbon's Color control changes Unique Values or Graduated Colors back to Single Symbol. To keep the classification, edit a class's colour in the Symbology pane instead. A polygon's fill and outline are independent: changing its fill leaves its outline intact. For raster renderers and band stretches, see Rasters.

items.title: Edit a class
items.text:
With Unique Values or Graduated Colors, each class in the Symbology pane's list has a colour button and a legend label. Pick a colour and opacity to give that class its own. Type a label to show in the Layers pane and in layout legends instead of the value or range (for example High income for 1. High income: OECD); clear it to show the value again. <all other values> can be edited the same way. Applying the symbology again on the same field keeps the colours, outlines and labels you set by hand on the classes that are still there (the others take the scheme's colours again); picking another colour scheme recolours every class but keeps the labels. A Graduated Colors class keeps its colour and label while its range stays the same. By command:

layer.classStyle={"layer":"Countries","value":"1. High income: OECD","color":"#2E6B4F","label":"High income"}
layer.classStyle={"layer":"Countries","index":0,"label":"Under 1 million"}
layer.classStyle={"layer":"Countries","index":0,"color":"#2E6B4FFF"}
layer.classStyle={"layer":"Countries","other":true,"label":"No data"}

value names a Unique Values class, index a Graduated Colors class (0 is the lowest) and other the <all other values> class; outline sets a class's outline colour. #RRGGBBAA sets the fill opacity exactly for every geometry type: FF is fully opaque for print choropleths, 00 fully transparent, and intermediate values partly transparent. The class colour picker includes opacity and sends all eight digits, including FF. Changing opacity keeps the class's RGB colour, even when making a fully transparent class visible again. For fully transparent fills, the numeric controls temporarily use linear 0–1 values so you can edit the hidden RGB colour without losing it. Other colour pickers keep their numeric settings.

For polygons, six-digit #RRGGBB retains the existing translucency, with the legacy minimum alpha of 150; new polygon layers still default to 170. Colour schemes preserve a polygon's fill opacity when classes are first created or recoloured with layer.ramp. Reapplying the same field, ranges and scheme also preserves opacity, including edits that change only alpha. As with other class colour edits, changing the field or graduated ranges starts fresh; choosing a different scheme through layer.symbology resets polygon opacity to its default. Layer/group transparency still applies on top of the symbol's opacity in maps and exports.

items.title: Line strokes
items.text:
A line layer draws one stroke by default. The Strokes section of the Symbology pane stacks up to 16 in one symbol, for road casings, parallel lines and offsets: Add Stroke puts one on top, and each stroke has its own Color, Width, Offset, Cap (round, flat or square) and Join (round, miter or bevel), with buttons to move it up or down or remove it. The list shows the top stroke first, and the preview above it shows the symbol along a line drawn left to right. A colour or width set to From symbol follows the renderer, so the strokes take each Unique Values or Graduated Colors class's colour. Use a Single Stroke goes back to one.

Widths and offsets are in points: they keep their size on screen at every scale, and the features keep their coordinates. A positive offset shifts the stroke to the right of the line's direction (the order of its vertices) and a negative one to the left, so two copies of an edge drawn in opposite directions land on opposite sides of it. Strokes are saved with the project and drawn in exports. By command, bottom stroke first ([] goes back to the single stroke):

layer.lineStrokes={"layer":"Rivers","strokes":[{"color":"#000000","width":11.5,"offset":8.5},{"color":"#FF8C00","width":7,"offset":8.5,"cap":"round","join":"round"}]}

A stroke without color or width takes the renderer's.

A Unique Values or Graduated Colors class can stack strokes of its own, so a motorway gets a casing and a centre line while a path stays a single thin line on the same layer. Pick the class under Strokes for at the top of the Strokes section (All classes edits the layer's strokes); a class with strokes of its own is marked with •. A class without its own is drawn with the layer's strokes, and changing them while it is picked gives it its own copy. Use the Layer's Strokes gives the class back to the layer's. A class keeps its strokes when the same symbology is applied again on the same field (a Graduated Colors class, while its range stays the same). By command, name the class as layer.classStyle does, with value, index or "other": true:

layer.lineStrokes={"layer":"Roads","value":"Motorway","strokes":[{"color":"#5A3A1E","width":7},{"color":"#F28C28","width":5},{"color":"#FFFFFF","width":0.6}]}

A stroke can be dashed: Dash takes the lengths in points, dash and gap in turn (4 2, or 4 2 1 2 for dash-dot; an odd list is repeated, as in SVG), and its menu offers dashed, dotted, dash-dot and long-dash patterns sized to the stroke's width. Empty is a solid line. With flat caps the dashes are as long as given; round and square caps add half the width at each end. By command, "dash" on a stroke (null for solid):

layer.lineStrokes={"layer":"Paths","strokes":[{"color":"#000000","width":1.2,"cap":"flat","dash":[6,3]}]}

By default, each feature draws its whole stack in turn, so where two roads meet, the second one's casing cuts across the first one's core. Draw strokes in levels (symbol levels) draws all stacked strokes at a lower level before those at a higher one, so the casings join underneath and the cores run through. A stroke's level is its place in the stack (the bottom one 0) unless it is given one: a Level row shows on each stroke while levels are on; turn off Auto to set it from 0 to 255. Strokes of different classes that share a level go down together, such as the casings of all road classes before any core. A layer read in place from its file draws its levels a batch of features at a time. By command ("level" on a stroke, null for its place in the stack):

layer.lineStrokes={"layer":"Roads","value":"Motorway","strokes":[{"color":"#5A3A1E","width":7,"level":0},{"color":"#F28C28","width":5,"level":1}]}
layer.strokeLevels={"layer":"Roads","on":true}

A stroke can draw markers or hash marks along the line instead of a line, as railways, boundaries and directions of flow are drawn: its Draw menu picks Line, Markers or Hash marks. Markers take a Shape (a character of a font too, as for points) and a Size; hash marks a Length, crossing the line square at an Angle of 0°. Place puts them at intervals along the line (Interval apart, counted from its start), at its vertices or its inner ones, at either end or both, or in its middle. With the line turns each mark with the line's direction; the Angle turns it further, clockwise. Marks take the stroke's colour, its width as a hash mark's line (or a marker's outline, by command), and its offset to either side. Stack them with line strokes: a casing, a core and ticks across it. By command, "markers" on a stroke:

layer.lineStrokes={"layer":"Railways","strokes":[{"color":"#333333","width":1.5},{"color":"#333333","width":1,"markers":{"mark":"hash","size":6,"interval":10}}]}
layer.lineStrokes={"layer":"Rivers","strokes":[{"width":1},{"markers":{"mark":"triangle","size":7,"at":"middle"}}]}
layer.lineStrokes={"layer":"Trails","strokes":[{"markers":{"mark":"character","char":"»","font":"DejaVu Sans","size":8,"interval":16}}]}

"at" takes "interval", "vertices", "innerVertices", "first", "last", "middle" and "segmentMiddles", or a list of them; "offsetAlong" moves the marks along the line (from its start, back from its end, on from its middle), "averageAngle" turns a mark at an interval with the line over that stretch of it (smoother on a line of many short bends), "rotate": false keeps marks upright, and "outline" gives markers an outline as wide as the stroke.

items.title: Fills
items.text:
A polygon layer fills with one colour by default. The Fills section of the Symbology pane stacks fills inside the outline, as a wetland gets a pale green under blue hatch lines: Add Fill puts one on top (the first is the symbol's colour, the next hatch lines over it), the arrows move one up or down and the cross removes it; the top fill is listed first. Draw picks Solid, Hatch lines (parallel lines at an Angle, anticlockwise from east, Spacing apart, of a Line width, shifted across by an Offset), Markers (a Marker shape of a Size on a grid Spacing across and Spacing down apart, Rows shifted to stagger them), Gradient or Shapeburst. A gradient shades each feature from its colour to a Second color: by default top to bottom, of a Type that runs Linear (straight across), Radial (in rings from its first point) or Conical (round its first point), turned by an Angle (anticlockwise), and past its points a Spread of Pad (its end colours), Reflect or Repeat. A shapeburst shades from its colour at the polygon's edge to the second colour inside, a Distance in, or over the Whole shape to the point deepest inside; Blur softens it and Ignore holes shades from the outer edge alone. Each part of a multi-part feature is shaded on its own, in its own box (an island its own gradient). Zoomed far into a polygon shaded over the whole shape, its deepest point is found on a coarser picture of it. A colour set to From symbol follows the renderer, so the fills take each class's colour. The polygon's outline is drawn over the fills. Patterns are fixed to the map, so neighbouring polygons' hatch lines meet, and keep their size in points as the map zooms. A Unique Values or Graduated Colors class can stack fills of its own, picked under Fills for as for strokes. By command, layer.fillLayers:

layer.fillLayers={"layer":"Wetlands","fills":[{"color":"#DDEEDD"},{"color":"#3366CC","pattern":"hatch","angle":0,"spacing":6,"width":0.8}]}
layer.fillLayers={"layer":"Orchards","fills":[{"color":"#F2F5E6"},{"color":"#4E7A2E","pattern":"dots","marker":"circle","size":3,"spacing":[8,8],"displacement":[4,0]}]}
layer.fillLayers={"layer":"Land use","value":"Forest","fills":[{"color":null},{"color":"#2D5A27","pattern":"hatch","angle":45}]}
layer.fillLayers={"layer":"Lakes","fills":[{"color":"#1F5FA8","pattern":"shapeburst","color2":"#CFE3F7","distance":12,"blur":4}]}
layer.fillLayers={"layer":"Countries","fills":[{"color":"#FFFFFF","pattern":"gradient","shape":"radial","from":"centroid","to":[1,0.5],"color2":"#88AA66"}]}

A gradient's from and to are places in the feature's box ([across, down], 0 to 1) or "centroid", or in the map view's box with "inView": true; stops adds colours between the two ([[0.5, "#RRGGBB"], …]), held rather than blended with "discrete": true.

[] goes back to the single fill (for a class, to the layer's fills). Fills draw on the CPU (on the globe, patterns keep to the screen rather than the map as it turns); the legend shows the symbol's colour.

items.title: Reference scale
items.text:
Symbol and label sizes are set in points, and normally keep that size on screen at every scale. A layer with a Reference scale (Symbology pane, under Layer) has its sizes set for that scale instead, as on a printed map: zoomed in to half of it, its lines, markers and labels are drawn twice as large; zoomed out to twice it, half as large (within 1/100 and 32 times). Pick a scale, Current scale to keep the sizes as they are now, or None. A topographic map designed for 1:25,000 then keeps its proportions as you zoom. By command (a scale, "current" or null):

layer.referenceScale={"layer":"Roads","scale":25000}

Scales in RustGIS take a screen pixel to be 0.28 mm (the OGC standard pixel). Programs that take 96 pixels to the inch (0.2646 mm) call the same view a larger scale; to match their sizes, multiply their reference scale by 0.2646 / 0.28 (about 0.945).

items.title: Custom color ramps
items.text:
Besides the built-in color schemes, a project can hold your own color ramps: an organization's palette, a published scheme such as a ColorBrewer or cmocean ramp not built in, or one designed in a tool like Phosphor. Add them from a color ramp file with Style › Styles › Add Color Ramp File (or Add Color Ramp File under the swatches in the Symbology pane). They appear under Custom in the Symbology pane, for feature layers and rasters (Stretch, Classify, Unique Values and Shaded Relief) alike, and under Color Ramps in the Browser, where right-click deletes one. Publish › Save As › Color Ramps saves the project's custom ramps to a file.

A color ramp file (.rgisramp) is JSON: a list of ramps (or one ramp on its own), each with a name, a kind (sequential, the default, diverging or qualitative) and its stops:

[{
  "name": "Phosphor Frostfire",
  "kind": "diverging",
  "stops": ["#eff6ff", "#abc5e8", "#87a0d7", "#7b5ca6", "#ca7482", "#f5b88e", "#fff5da"]
}]

Stops are #RRGGBB or #RRGGBBAA colors, evenly spaced from the first to the last. For uneven spacing, give a stop as {"pos": 0.25, "color": "#87a0d7"}, with pos from 0 to 1; plain stops between two positioned ones are spaced evenly between them. A ramp has 2 to 256 stops (a qualitative one can have 1), and can't take the name of a built-in scheme; adding a ramp with the name of one already in the project replaces it. Scripts, the CLI and the AI Assistant add ramps with the ramp.add command ({"path": "ramps.rgisramp"}, or the JSON itself as {"text": …}), and then name them like built-in schemes, for example layer.ramp={"ramp":"Phosphor Frostfire"}.

items.title: Color ramps from other tools
items.text:
Add Color Ramp File also reads the color ramp files other tools write, so a palette from QGIS, GDAL, GMT or a tool like Phosphor can be added without converting it first:

Format Extension What RustGIS reads QGIS style .xml Every gradient ramp (discrete ones as steps) and preset ramp (as a qualitative ramp) in a Style Manager export, with its name. ColorBrewer, cpt-city and random ramps hold no colors and are skipped. QGIS layer style .qml The layer's color ramp, or a raster's color map. GDAL color-relief text .txt value R G B [A] lines (as gdaldem color-relief takes them), separated by spaces, tabs, commas or colons; values may be percentages and colors may be names; nv lines are skipped. A QGIS color map export reads the same way. GMT palette .cpt z0 color0 z1 color1 lines, with colors as r/g/b, r g b, #RRGGBB, grey levels, names or HSV; B, F and N lines are skipped.

These formats tie colors to data values; the ramp keeps their spacing, from the lowest value to the highest, and a sharp change between two colors stays sharp. A ramp from a GDAL or GMT file is named after the file and is sequential; the ramp.add command takes a name and a kind to change that ({"path": "relief.cpt", "kind": "diverging"}), and a format (rgisramp, qgis, gdal or cpt) for text without a file name. A file with more than 256 colors is resampled to 256 evenly spaced stops.

Sequential and diverging ramps blend between their stops; when there are as many classes as stops, each class takes a stop's color exactly, so a stepped palette keeps its colors. A qualitative ramp gives each class the next stop, starting again after the last. A layer keeps its own copy of the ramp it uses, so layer files, map files and packages keep their colors in projects that don't have the ramp, and deleting a ramp from the project leaves layers that use it unchanged.

items.title: Labeling
items.text:
The Labeling pane brings together the label classes and the chosen class's field, SQL clause, text symbol, placement and visibility limits. Under its header (the layer, labels on or off, and the class chosen), a tab per topic shows one part at a time: Content (the label field, with a search in its list, above the SQL query), Symbol, Position and Range. Open it for a feature layer with Layers › right-click › Labeling Properties…, View › Windows › Labeling, or Labeling › Labels › Properties. It runs the same commands as the ribbon, so each setting change undoes on its own (a dragged size or a colour pick is one step). Label classes are described below.

Turn labels on per layer (Labeling › Labels › Label), then:

  • Label field and text: the field the labels show (labels.field={"layer": "Cities", "field": "name"}), and the text symbol's size (4–72 points), colour, halo, bold and italic (labels.style={"layer": "Cities", "size": 12, "color": "#5A1E0A", "halo": true}).
  • Halo and letter spacing: a halo is white behind dark text and dark behind light, and thin, unless it is given a colour and a width of its own (Labeling pane › Symbol › Halo color, Halo width: how far it reaches beyond the letters, 0–10 points). The letters can be set apart, or closer with a negative spacing (Letter spacing, −5 to 50 points), along lines too. The width and the spacing grow with the labels at a reference scale (labels.style={"layer": "Rivers", "haloColor": "#FFFFFF", "haloWidth": 1.4, "spacing": 0.5}; "haloColor": "" and "haloWidth": null go back to the automatic colour and the thin halo).
  • Background: a rectangle behind the text (Labeling pane › Symbol › Background), white with a thin dark outline when turned on: its Fill and Outline (each can be none), the outline's width, its padding across and up and down (how far it reaches past the text, 0–50 points) and its Corner radius. Other labels keep off it as they keep off a halo, and it turns with a label along a line; a label curved along a line, character by character, has none. Its sizes grow with the labels at a reference scale (labels.style={"layer": "Roads", "background": {"fill": "#FFFFFF", "stroke": "#262626", "strokeWidth": 0.3, "padding": [1.2, 0.3], "radius": 0.7}}; "background": true turns on the default one, false takes it away, and what an object leaves out is kept).
  • Offset: a label moved from where its position puts it, right and down in points (Labeling pane › Position › Offset right, Offset down, −200 to 200; negative moves it left or up), growing with the labels at a reference scale. A label along a line isn't moved (labels.placement={"layer": "Cities", "position": "aboveRight", "offset": [5.7, -2.8]}; an offset can be given without a position).
  • Wrapping: a label's text broken into lines (Labeling pane › Symbol): Wrap at a character (or a few, up to 8), a line break wherever it occurs, left out (a space puts each word on its own line, / breaks Zürich/Winterthur), and Wrap length, the longest line in characters, broken between words (a longer word keeps a line of its own). Line alignment lines the lines up left (as labels always have), centred or right. A label curved along a line, character by character, isn't wrapped (labels.style={"layer": "Cities", "wrapChar": " ", "wrapLength": 12, "lineAlign": "center"}; "" and 0 wrap none).
  • Repeat along lines: a label placed along a line (Parallel or Curved) repeated every so many points (Labeling pane › Position › Repeat, 10 to 10,000): the one at the line's middle where it always is, and more either side of it, nearest first, at most 32 a line. Each is a label of its own: it collides like any other (one that doesn't fit is left out, the others stay), and Lock keeps the ones placed. The distance grows with the labels at a reference scale (labels.placement={"layer": "Rivers", "position": "curved", "repeat": 144}; null or 0 is the one at the middle).
  • Font: the labels' font family, any installed on the computer (Labeling pane › Symbol › Font; type part of a name to find it), or the label font the interface uses. Bold and italic take the family's own bold and italic faces where it has them. The family is saved by its name, so a project keeps it on a computer that lacks it, drawing its labels in the label font there (the pane shows it as not installed), and in the browser, which reads no installed fonts (labels.style={"layer": "Rivers", "font": "Liberation Serif"}; labels.fonts lists the installed families, {"font": ""} goes back to the label font).
  • SQL: label only the features that match a SQL clause (the language of definition queries), such as pop_max > 5000000. In the Labeling pane, Class › SQL › New expression: write the clause (the field and operator buttons add to it), Check says whether it reads and how many of the features the layer draws at the map's scale match (after its definition query, display filters and time window), and Apply sets it in one undo step; Clear removes the chosen class's clause, leaving other classes unchanged (labels.class.update={"layer": "Cities", "where": "pop_max > 5000000"}).
  • Visibility Range: draw labels only between two scales (Out Beyond / In Beyond), or between two viewing distances (Closest / Farthest). Clear Limits removes all four.
  • Placement: automatic (above points, centred on lines and polygons), centred, or one of eight positions around the feature (labels.placement={"layer": "Cities", "position": "aboveRight"}). Lines can be labelled along them (Position › Along lines): Parallel sets the text straight, turned to the line's direction across it; Curved turns each character with the line where it bends. Both sit at the middle of the line's longest stretch in view, centred on the line and kept upright, and may run past its ends by about a letter; a line too short for its text, or (curved) one bending more than 25° from one character to the next, is left unlabelled. A text over 200 characters long is set straight rather than curved. Points and polygons with these placements are labelled as automatic (labels.placement={"layer": "Rivers", "position": "curved"}).
  • Other places round points: a point's label whose place another label takes tries the other places round the point, corners first (above right, above left, below right, below left, right, left, above, below, leaving out its own), and goes to the first where all of it shows; where none is free it is left out, as before (Labeling pane › Position › Try other places round the point, for point layers). Off by default: a label that moves can take the place a less important one had. The class's offset applies to every place, and Lock keeps the place each label took (labels.placement={"layer": "Cities", "otherPositions": true}).
  • Lock keeps the labelled features fixed while you pan and zoom; Pause stops drawing labels for faster navigation; View Unplaced draws the labels that didn't fit in red. They apply to the whole map, so they are on the ribbon (Labeling › Map Labeling), not in the pane.
  • Convert (Labeling › Map Labeling, or Layers › right-click › Convert To Annotation) turns a layer's labels into an annotation layer: one point per label, carrying its text in a TEXT field, which you can then edit, move or delete like any other features.
  • Label classes label different features differently, such as large cities in larger text. Each class has a SQL clause choosing its features, and its own field, text symbol, placement and visibility range. Each class labels every feature its clause matches, the Default class too (with no clause, every feature). A feature matched by two classes produces a label candidate for each; collision rules still determine which labels fit. To avoid duplicate labels, use clauses that do not overlap: pop_max > 5000000 for Large cities and pop_max <= 5000000 for Default. Classes are placed in list order, Default last; a hidden class or one outside its visibility range labels nothing without excluding features from other classes. There can be up to 64 classes besides Default. In the Labeling pane, the Class list at the top, in a card with the class's actions, chooses the class every tab shows and edits, and Visible under it hides or shows that class. The row under the list has New, which adds a class with the chosen class's field, text symbol, placement and range, listed before Default; Rename and Move Up / Move Down (the arrows) for the chosen class; and, at its far end, Remove (Default can be renamed or hidden, not moved or removed). The ribbon's label groups edit the same chosen class, and Labeling › Label Class › Class chooses it as the pane's list does. By command, make them with labels.class.add (a new class copies Default's field, text symbol, placement and range, or those of the class named by from), then labels.class.rename, labels.class.update (where or visible), labels.class.move (to: 0 first), labels.class.remove and labels.class.clear (removes every class but Default, even when it has been renamed; no error when there are none). Field, text symbol, placement and range commands take a class; without one they change Default, whatever its name. For example:
labels.class.add={"layer":"Cities","name":"Large cities","where":"pop_max > 5000000"}
labels.class.update={"layer":"Cities","where":"pop_max <= 5000000"}
labels.style={"layer":"Cities","class":"Large cities","size":14,"bold":true}

Convert keeps the classes, with a point for each matching class and a CLASS field identifying it. Web Style and Web Layer exports (Publish › Share As) use Default only, and have no labels when Default is hidden.

City labels placed above and to the right of their points, beside the country labels.

items.title: Layer effects
items.text:
On the Style tab, Masking shows a layer only inside another layer's polygons; Display Filters show different features at different scales (a SQL condition per scale range); Aggregation draws points as hexagon or square bins coloured by count. Extrusion raises polygons by a constant height or numeric field (in metres), multiplied by Factor, with Face Culling, Lighting and Cast Shadow controls. It draws in an oblique view on an untilted flat map and in perspective on a tilted map; the globe draws the polygons flat. See Rotating and tilting the map.

For a raster layer, the Style tab also has Layer Blend (multiply, screen, overlay, darken, lighten, difference), Swipe (the layer shows only left of a divider you slide, to compare it with what's beneath), Masking and Rotation.

items.title: Graphics
items.text: Edit › Graphics draws shapes in a graphics layer (Home › Add › Add Data › Graphics Layer, or one is made with the first graphic). Click once for a Point. Line, Curve and Polygon are clicked vertex by vertex (double-click to finish); Freehand, Lasso, Rectangle, Circle and Ellipse are dragged. Edit › Graphics and Text › Text places a text where you click, as a layout's text is placed: it says "Text", is selected, and opens in the Format pane (beside the other right-hand panes) with its text selected, so you type over it. Shift+Enter starts a new line, and Enter ends the text. Dynamic Text is a menu of values that update as the map changes (map name, scale, date, time, coordinate system, number of layers, map centre): pick one, then click the map, and the text starts with its token ({map}, {scale}, {date}, {time}, {crs}, {layers} or {center}); the pane's Insert Dynamic Text menu adds more. Picture: drag a rectangle, then pick a PNG or JPEG image to stretch over it. Tools return to Explore after each graphic unless Keep Tool is on. Each graphic keeps its own fill, outline, width, text size, bold, italic, alignment and letter spacing in the layer's attributes, so you can edit them in the attribute table or with graphics.style. To change a text later, click anywhere on it (with Explore or Select): selected alone, it opens in the Format pane, with the same form a layout's text has there: text, size, colour, bold, Italic (slanted), Alignment (how the lines of a text of several lines line up; the text stays centred on its point) and Letter spacing in points (spaced-out names such as O C E A N O, or a negative value to tighten). A text looks the same on the map and in an exported map. Each change is one undo step on that text only (graphics.edit does the same by layer and row, with text, fontSize, fill for the colour, bold, italic, align and letterSpacing). Once a text is selected, drag it by its text to move it, as one undo step (points on graphics.edit); a drag anywhere else, or on a text that isn't selected, pans the map as usual. A graphics layer that isn't Selectable keeps its texts from being picked, moved or edited. Closing the pane keeps the text selected; double-clicking it or right-clicking it › Edit Text… opens the pane again. Text sizes go from 2 to 400 points, on the map as on a layout page.

items.title: Supported Data Formats
items.text:
This page lists the data formats RustGIS reads and writes, how to add each one, and the main limits. Data covers adding data, large files and rasters in more detail; Maps and Basemaps covers web tile layers.

Most native readers work in the desktop app and the web app. Formats read through external GDAL or DuckDB programs need the desktop app or rustgis-cli; they aren't available in the web app. Database connections and folder-based File Geodatabases are desktop-only too. Browser files are uploaded rather than opened by path; GeoPackages use a pure-Rust SQLite file reader there. Reprojection supports the coordinate systems RustGIS knows, not every EPSG code; azimuthal equidistant systems such as Equi7 need the desktop app.

items.title: Vector and tabular files
items.text:
Format Extensions or source How to add it Notes GeoJSON .geojson, .json Home › Add › Add Data, or drop the file Features with typed attributes; a GeometryCollection keeps its first readable member. A FeatureCollection's legacy crs member ({"type": "name", "properties": {"name": "urn:ogc:def:crs:EPSG::28992"}}) is honoured for EPSG codes (EPSG:28992, urn:ogc:def:crs:EPSG::28992, urn:ogc:def:crs:EPSG:6.6:28992) and for CRS84: a projected or other non-WGS 84 system converts the coordinates to longitude/latitude and the layer keeps it as its coordinate system (Layer properties, export in it, Define Projection); CRS84 and EPSG:4326 are longitude/latitude already, so the coordinates stay as they are and the layer has no other coordinate system. Coordinates are x/y (easting/northing, or longitude/latitude) whatever the EPSG axis order. A crs that isn't understood (a link, WKT or PROJ text, any other name, an unknown code) is named in a notice and the coordinates are read as longitude/latitude. A feature whose coordinates can't be converted, or convert to beyond ±180.5° longitude or ±90.5° latitude (the declared system doesn't fit the numbers), is left out and counted in a notice, and Define Projection then asks for the file to be added again. A crs on a feature, a geometry or a lone Feature is ignored. GeoJSON is always written in WGS 84 without a crs. Desktop FeatureCollections larger than 32 MiB use an in-place reader (which honours crs too, reading the file once more to check the features convert); layers with more than 100,000 features stream a view at a time. Other GeoJSON files load whole, up to 256 MiB. Delimited text .csv, .tsv, .txt Add Data, or Home › Add › Add Data › Delimited Text… to choose the columns from the file's header Comma, semicolon, tab or pipe separated (found from the header, or "delimiter"); info.fileColumns lists the columns and the ones found. Points from x/y columns (named like longitude/latitude or easting/northing, or chosen with "x" and "y"), or any geometry from a WKT/EWKT column (named like wkt or geometry, or "wkt"). Coordinates in another system are converted from "crs" (EPSG:2263, or WKT) or an EWKT SRID=; without either, coordinates outside longitude/latitude are pointed out. A file without coordinates opens as a standalone table. Shapefile .shp with .dbf (and .shx), or zipped (.zip) Add Data or drop the file; in the web app, pick or drop the .shp and .dbf together, with the .shx and .prj if there are (they open as one layer), or the zip A zip may hold several Shapefiles, in folders, and other vector files (GeoJSON, CSV, GeoParquet, FlatGeobuf); each becomes a layer, at most 32 for the whole archive (Shapefiles first, so other files are left out when Shapefiles fill it). .txt files and macOS __MACOSX entries are passed over, and a member that can't be read is skipped and named in a notice. Converted to longitude/latitude from the coordinate system in its .prj (EPSG, Esri or OGC WKT, or WKT2 as PROJ and QGIS write it; Web Mercator, UTM, State Plane and other common projections); without a .prj it must be in longitude/latitude. On the desktop, one with more than 100,000 shapes (counted from its .shx) is read in place, a view at a time. KML / KMZ .kml, .kmz Add Data, drop the file, or upload it in the web app A layer for each kind of geometry (points, lines, polygons), with each placemark's name, description, folder path and extended data. Styles are kept: the layer is drawn by unique values of its style field, with each KML style's line and fill colours, widths and icon colours (up to 64 styles). Multi-geometries and gx:Tracks are read. Ground overlays (pictures on a LatLonBox, turned by its rotation) are raster layers kept in the project: the picture inside a KMZ, or a file beside a KML (not a web address, nor outside its folder); a gx:LatLonQuad isn't drawn. GPX .gpx Add Data, drop the file, or upload it in the web app Waypoints, routes, tracks (one line per track, its segments as parts) and track points (with elevation and time) as separate layers. Spreadsheets .xlsx, .xlsm, .xlsb, .xls, .ods Add Data (or Delimited Text… to choose the columns), drop the file, or upload it in the web app One sheet at a time, read like delimited text: the first non-empty row names the columns, and x/y or WKT columns (found, or given with "x", "y", "wkt" and "crs") make the geometry; a sheet without them is a table. The first sheet is added and the others named in a notice; "layer" picks one, and info.fileLayers lists them. Dates read as ISO 8601. GeoRSS .rss, .atom, .georss, or .xml Add Data, drop the file, upload, or From URL… RSS 2.0, RSS 1.0 and Atom feeds with GeoRSS Simple, GeoRSS GML or W3C Basic Geo places: points, lines and polygons layers with each item's title, link, description, date, id and category. LandXML .landxml, or .xml Add Data, drop the file, or upload Coordinate geometry points, parcels (polygons), alignments (lines; curves as chords) and TIN surfaces (a triangle per face, with its mean elevation), converted from the file's epsgCode or "crs". Encoded polylines text layer.addEncodedPolyline with "polyline" (one or a list) Google's encoding, precision 5, or 6 ("precision") as OSRM and Valhalla can give: a line layer. GML .gml Add Data, drop the file, or upload Simple features in GML 2 and 3 (WFS answers, OGR's GML): a layer per feature type, its simple elements as fields. Converted from the srsName (EPSG codes, URNs and URLs; the URN and URL forms of geographic systems are latitude first). MapInfo Interchange .mif with its .mid (or both zipped) Add Data, drop the file, or upload the zip Points, lines, polylines, regions (holes found by nesting), rectangles and ellipses; text and arcs are rows without geometry. Converted from the CoordSys: longitude/latitude, Transverse Mercator, Lambert Conformal Conic, Albers or Mercator. A loose .mif upload has no .mid attributes; zip both files to keep them in the web app. OpenStreetMap PBF .osm.pbf, or .pbf containing OSM data Add Data, drop the file, or upload Points (tagged nodes), lines and multipolygons (closed ways that are areas, and multipolygon and boundary relations), with common tags as fields and the rest in other_tags, as GDAL gives them. Up to 40 million nodes (4 million in the web app); on the desktop, extracts over 256 MiB open through GDAL when it is installed. Vector-tile .pbf files use Add Tile Layer instead. TopoJSON .topojson, or .json Add Data, drop the file, or upload Shared arcs (quantized or not) are rebuilt into geometries. A .topojson adds a layer per object, up to 64; a topology named .json adds its first object and names the others in a notice. Use .topojson to add them all. AutoCAD DXF .dxf (ASCII) Add Data, drop the file, or upload Points, lines and polygons layers from the drawing's entities: POINT, LINE, LWPOLYLINE and POLYLINE (bulges drawn as arcs; closed ones stay lines; polyface meshes become polygons), CIRCLE, ARC, ELLIPSE, SPLINE, HELIX, LEADER, MLINE (its centre line), TEXT, MTEXT, ATTRIB and constant ATTDEF (points with their text, at the alignment point of justified text), HATCH boundaries (holes found by nesting), SOLID, TRACE and 3DFACE (polygons). Blocks (named in any case) are drawn where INSERTs place them (scaled, rotated, in arrays, nested up to 8 deep), and so are DIMENSIONs' blocks (a linear dimension without one draws its lines and measured text). Entities in an object's own coordinate system are turned into the drawing's. Fields: layer, entity, color (ACI, BYLAYER and BYBLOCK resolved), linetype, text, height, rotation, block, elevation and paperspace. The drawing's layouts (paper space: title blocks, viewport frames) are left out, with a notice, unless "paperSpace": true. A drawing never says its coordinate system: give "crs" (such as EPSG:2263), or its coordinates are kept as they are, with a notice. "layer" picks one of the drawing's own layers, and info.fileLayers lists them. Up to 2 million features (500,000 in the web app). Not read: binary DXF, MULTILEADER, WIPEOUT, IMAGE and ACIS solids (3DSOLID, REGION), named in a notice. Geotagged photos .jpg, .jpeg Add Data (several at once in the web app), drop them, upload, or layer.addPhotos with "paths" or a "folder" JPEGs with a GPS position in their EXIF become points in the Photos layer (photos added one at a time join it): each with its name, file, time (when it was taken), altitude, direction (where the camera faced), camera and a thumbnail of at most 160 pixels, kept with the feature so the project needs no other file. Identify shows the thumbnail. Photos without a position are named in a notice and left out; a layer holds up to 2,000 photos. A JPEG is always read as a photo unless layer.addData or layer.addDataBytes is given "as": "scan" (a phone photo of a paper map, say: see Scans with no coordinates). LiDAR point clouds .las, .laz (COPC too) Add Data, drop the file, upload, or From URL… LAS 1.0–1.4 (point formats 0–10) and LAZ, on desktop and web: points with z, intensity, classification, return and colour (red, green, blue), coloured by ASPRS class or elevation. An evenly spread sample is read once, at most 2 million points (500,000 in the web app); views use that sample, not the COPC spatial index. LAZ decompression reads at most the first 400 million points (40 million on the web), with a notice when capped. Converted from the file's WKT or GeoTIFF-key record; without one, coordinates are kept with a notice. A local project keeps the path; uploads keep the file bytes. Remote files download whole. GeoPackage .gpkg Add Data, or upload in the web app Local files and browser uploads add every feature table, up to 32 (with the rest counted in skippedCount and up to 100 named in skipped); "layer" picks one, and info.fileLayers lists them. Desktop byte uploads and downloads add the first table unless "layer" names another. Large local tables use their R-tree and reproject supported EPSG systems. Browser tables are scanned, testing each geometry header's envelope first; UTF-16 databases aren't read there. Raster tile tables aren't imported. GeoParquet .parquet, .geoparquet Add Data, or upload in the web app WKB geometry, with the CRS from the file's geo metadata. A binary geometry column is required; plain non-spatial Parquet tables and GeoArrow-native geometry encodings aren't read by this importer. Row groups are pruned by the bbox covering. Snappy, gzip, LZ4 and zstd compression are read, in the browser too; Brotli isn't. FlatGeobuf .fgb Add Data, or upload Read in place by its packed R-tree. Esri File Geodatabase .gdb folder (desktop) In Add Data pick a .gdbtable file inside it; or double-click the .gdb in the Browser, or drop the folder The native reader loads up to 512 feature classes and tables, up to 2 GiB per table. Feature classes become layers and non-spatial tables standalone tables; dates are text. Coordinates use the EPSG/Esri code, else WKT. "layer" picks one; info.fileLayers lists them. Multipatches become footprints with z_min, z_max and height; large or wall-only ones may use a convex hull. Curves become straight segments between their ends. Unreadable tables (compressed storage, raster fields or unsupported row indexes) are tried through GDAL when installed; otherwise they are named in a notice. Standalone tables CSV, or any layer without geometry Add Data Listed under the map in Layers; join or relate them to layers.

Shapefile text uses the encoding in its .cpg sidecar first, then the language-driver code in the .dbf header. Include the .cpg when picking or dropping loose files in the web app. UTF-8 (including 65001), DOS code pages such as CP437 and CP850 (numeric, CP or IBM labels), Windows code pages such as 1252, CP1252 and Windows-1252, ISO-8859 encodings and common East Asian encodings are supported. The Esri 0x57 DBF marker is read as Windows-1252. An unreadable, empty, invalid, oversized or unsupported .cpg gives a notice and falls back to the DBF code page; an unsupported DBF code page gives a notice and falls back to UTF-8. Files without encoding metadata keep the UTF-8 default. Unsupported characters become replacement characters. This applies to zipped files and large files read in place too. See the DBF language-driver support inventory for every recognized marker and the legacy code pages that still use the UTF-8 fallback.

Files with more than 100,000 features (GeoPackage, GeoParquet, FlatGeobuf, and Shapefile on the desktop) are read in place, a view at a time, rather than loaded whole: see Large files. They draw, label, identify and run through tools like any layer; Load All Features loads one to edit it.

items.title: Formats read through GDAL
items.text:
With GDAL installed (its ogr2ogr and ogrinfo on the PATH, GDAL 3.7 or later), the desktop app also reads the vector formats below. Each layer is converted once into a cached, indexed FlatGeobuf, so large ones stream too: see Formats through GDAL.

Format Extensions or source Notes AutoCAD DWG .dwg Through GDAL's CAD driver, when it is built in. Give "crs" (such as EPSG:2263) when the drawing doesn't say its coordinate system. MapInfo tables .tab Keep the companion files together. OpenStreetMap XML .osm GeoJSON Lines, GMT .geojsonl, .geojsons, .gmt

items.title: Files on the web
items.text:
Home › Add › Add Data › From URL… (layer.addUrl with "url") downloads a file by its https:// (or http:// or s3://, see S3 buckets) address and adds it like an uploaded file. Native formats include GeoJSON, delimited text, GeoParquet, FlatGeobuf, GeoPackage, zipped Shapefiles, KML/KMZ, GPX, spreadsheets, GeoRSS, GML, DXF, TopoJSON, LiDAR and rasters. Downloads are limited to 512 MiB on desktop and 256 MiB on the web; individual readers may have lower limits (the whole-file vector readers use 256 MiB). In the web app the server must allow requests from web pages (CORS). On the desktop, with GDAL installed, a JPEG 2000 file (.jp2, .j2k: Sentinel-2's imagery on S3) is downloaded too, converted to a GeoTIFF that the project keeps, and added. Desktop byte uploads (layer.addDataBytes) of .jp2 and .j2k use the same conversion. The web app rejects both JPEG 2000 uploads and downloads with an explicit GDAL limitation; convert them to GeoTIFF first. The format comes from the address, or from the contents when the address has no extension (an API endpoint, say), JPEG 2000 included: its signature is recognised in the contents, so the desktop converts it and the web app gives the same GDAL limitation. The app downloads in the background and adds the layer when the file arrives (to the project it was started in: opening another meanwhile drops it). A .pmtiles address is added as a tile layer and read a tile at a time instead.

For JPEG 2000 uploads and downloads on the desktop, the converted GeoTIFF must fit within 512 MiB. The private conversion workspace (source file, output and GDAL scratch files together) is monitored every 50 ms against a budget of the input file's byte length plus three times that output limit (1.5 GiB). Conversion stops when the workspace exceeds the budget, but files can grow between checks: this is not a strict operating-system disk quota. Ordinary conversions of files opened from disk do not use this workspace budget.

Conversion runs synchronously while the layer is added and can temporarily make the app unresponsive. The original JPEG 2000 byte buffer is released once it has been staged on disk, before GDAL runs or the GeoTIFF is read back. The converted GeoTIFF and decoded raster still occupy memory together; the 512 MiB file limit is not a limit on total process memory.

A tiled GeoTIFF is read in place rather than downloaded: its header first, then, by HTTP range requests, the tiles of the overview each part of the view needs. Overviews make zoomed-out reads smaller. It is a tile layer (map.addTiles kind cog, saved by its address), drawn under the map's own layers: RGB(A) 8-bit images in colour, other images stretched between the 2nd and 98th percentiles of their coarsest overview. Planar files (bands stored apart), signed-byte data and bottom-up images work too. map.setTiles selects one or three "bands" (from 1) and a fixed "range"; see Satellite embeddings. A GeoTIFF in strips, a rotated image or an unsupported tiled image downloads whole as a raster layer, as does a GeoTIFF added with "whole": true (for raster tools and symbology). The web app needs the server to allow range requests (CORS with the Range header).

A GeoParquet or FlatGeobuf file by its address is read in place too, a view at a time, however large: the layer is streamed like a large local file, and the view's features are fetched in the background by HTTP range requests and drawn as they land. A FlatGeobuf's header and packed R-tree index are read first (a level of the tree per round of requests), then only the features in the view. A GeoParquet's footer is read first, then the row groups the view meets, by their bounding box covering column (bbox) and its statistics: the covering of groups on the view's edge, then the geometry and attribute columns of the rows taken. A view holding more than a read takes (60,000 features on the desktop, 30,000 in the web app) shows an evenly spread sample of it, in patches; zoom in for more detail. The project keeps the address and reads it the same way when it opens. A FlatGeobuf without an index, a GeoParquet without a covering column, or a server that doesn't answer range requests means the file is downloaded whole instead, as is any file added with "whole": true; Load All Features and the geoprocessing tools fetch the whole file on the desktop, while in the web app they need the file downloaded first.

On desktop, layer.addUrl waits for downloads, up to a minute; the From URL… dialog (ui.addUrl) and a plugin's layer.addUrl work in the background. In the web app the same dialog handles asynchronous downloads. layer.addUrl can add PMTiles and COG tile layers directly, but an ordinary download returns {"pending": true, "url": "…"} and is added later by the app. To open a remote GeoParquet or FlatGeobuf whose header hasn't been fetched yet, use the From URL… dialog or a ?data= link.

items.title: Map and feature services
items.text:
Home › Add › Add Data › From Service… connects to a service by its address, lists what it offers from its capabilities. For OGC API feature collections, enter a group name (initially My OGC Layer) and choose Import All. The group expands into ordinary point, line and polygon layers with the same legends, styling and attribute tables as file imports. Other offerings have individual Add buttons (service.layers and service.add from scripts, the command line and MCP). An OGC API landing page works directly: RustGIS follows its advertised JSON collections link, so you don't need to append /collections. If the landing page also offers map tiles, they remain listed alongside the collections. A failed collections request leaves any available map layers usable and shows the error.

When a service can't be reached or refuses the request, the dialog says what happened in plain words and what to try next: a sign-in or token it needs (401), access refused (403), nothing at that address (404), too many requests (429), a problem on the server (5xx), or a server that couldn't be reached or took too long. When a firewall in front of the server (Cloudflare, Akamai, Imperva, Sucuri or AWS WAF) blocked or challenged RustGIS itself, told by its own block page or a header it sends only then, it says so: only the service's administrator can let RustGIS through. A firewall that only passed on the service's own refusal (a private service wanting a token) isn't blamed for it. Details, folded below, lists what the server said for an expert or the administrator: the address (without keys or tokens), the status, the server, the firewall and the request's id, the User-Agent RustGIS sent, and the title or first words of the server's answer (as text). Copy details copies them to send. In the web app the browser hides most of a refused answer, so it tells the status only.

Right-click the group and choose Refresh to rediscover its collections and update them all, including newly added or removed collections. Right-click a child and choose Refresh to update only that collection. Existing children keep their names, styles and visibility (a changed geometry type gets a suitable default symbol); selections are cleared because row positions can change. Refresh replaces local feature edits with the service's data. Failed imports or refreshes leave the map intact; a successful operation is one undo step. Groups and their source connections are saved in the project. Group downloads are limited to 2000 collections and 64 MB in total and use the existing per-collection feature limits.

Scripts use service.import {"url":"…","name":"My OGC Layer"} and service.refresh {"group":id} or service.refresh {"layer":id}. The browser uses service.groupPlan to discover the requests, then supplies text, documents, and responses: [{"url":"…","text":"GeoJSON"}] to import or refresh without blocking network calls.

Service What it lists How a layer is added WMS 1.1.1 / 1.3.0 Named layers offered in Web Mercator or in a coordinate system RustGIS can transform (an EPSG code, CRS:84) A layer of GetMap images (PNG when the service offers it, else JPEG): one picture of the view, or tiles; see One picture of the view, or tiles and Services in other coordinate systems WMTS Layers whose tile matrix set is Web Mercator's pyramid, or a tile matrix set in a coordinate system RustGIS can transform A tile layer from the tile template (or KVP GetTile) WFS 1.1 / 2.0 Feature types Their features downloaded as GeoJSON, in the output format the service names (up to 50,000) OGC API Features Collections Their items downloaded as GeoJSON, following the service's next pages up to 100,000 features (a command such as service.add waits a minute at most) OGC API Tiles Collections' map and vector tiles; a landing page's dataset map tiles A tile layer in WebMercatorQuad, from the tile template the tileset advertises (its item link; …/tiles/WebMercatorQuad/{z}/{y}/{x}, the usual path, when that can't be read), keeping the tiles link's query (a token), map tiles in the server's image format, vector tiles drawn layer by layer in colours of their own WCS 1.0 / 2.0 (a 1.1 service is asked in 1.0) Coverages, with their bounds A raster: GetCoverage of the map's view within the coverage's bounds (or its whole extent: "bbox": "full"), as a GeoTIFF in EPSG:4326, at most 2048 pixels on a side ArcGIS REST FeatureServer and MapServer layers; a MapServer's map; an ImageServer; a VectorTileServer Layers queried as GeoJSON, page by page past the server's record limit (resultOffset) up to 100,000 features (a command such as service.add waits a minute at most), where the layer supports paging (ArcGIS Server 10.3 and later; otherwise up to the record limit); a map as its tile cache when it is Web Mercator's pyramid, else exported images; an ImageServer as exported images; a VectorTileServer as its MapLibre style

A WMS or WMTS layer's tiles are asked for down to the detail its service gives, and stretched only past it: a WMTS layer's over the zooms of its tile matrix set (or those its TileMatrixSetLimits name; swisstopo's SWISSIMAGE goes to zoom 20), a WMS layer's between the scales it is drawn at (WMS 1.3.0's MinScaleDenominator and MaxScaleDenominator, 1.1.1's ScaleHint, its parent's when it gives none), else down to zoom 22 (about 4 cm a pixel at the equator), since a WMS draws at any scale. service.layers lists these zooms, minZoom and maxZoom, for each WMS and WMTS layer.

The type is guessed from the address (?SERVICE=, /wmts, /wfs, /wcs, /collections, /rest/services…) or chosen (select OGC API Features and Tiles when a landing page's address doesn't identify its type). A WebMercatorQuad tileset is found by its tile matrix set, whatever the server calls it. A service that asks for a token says so. In the web app the server must allow requests from web pages (CORS).

A coverage is read once, for the view when it was added (its DescribeCoverage first, for its axes, format and bounds; service.coverage gives the GetCoverage address alone). Moving the map doesn't ask for it again: add it again for another area. The server reprojects it to EPSG:4326 (WCS 2.0 through its CRS extension); one that can't answers with an error, which is shown.

A feature type is asked for in CRS84 when it offers it, else in EPSG:4326. Every server tried answered those requests longitude first, but a server may answer latitude first (deegree does when asked in the URN form, urn:ogc:def:crs:EPSG::4326). The crs a GeoJSON answer names doesn't tell the order (GeoServer names its longitude-first answers urn:ogc:def:crs:EPSG::4326), so the features' positions are turned round only when they miss the layer's longitude/latitude bounds from the capabilities and fit them turned (give or take a tenth of the bounds' size, or half a degree). An OGC API collection's extent counts as such bounds only in CRS84, the standard's default. A layer listed without bounds, or whose features fit both ways, is read as it comes.

A WFS, OGC API Features or ArcGIS feature layer comes whole, as in other GIS programs. A large one (a country's municipalities, hundreds of megabytes) can be asked for over an area instead: tick Only the map's area in the dialog, or give service.add a "bbox" ([west, south, east, north] in longitude/latitude, or "view"). The service then sends only the features that cross the area, whole, not clipped. service.add then zooms to the box given (not to the whole layer's bounds), and leaves the view as it is for "view". The box is asked in each service's own terms:

  • WFS 1.1 and 2.0: BBOX, in CRS84 when the feature type offers it, else in urn:ogc:def:crs:EPSG::4326, latitude first as that name fixes.
  • OGC API Features: bbox, longitude first; the next pages keep it.
  • ArcGIS: an envelope in EPSG:4326 the features intersect; the pages past the record limit keep it.

A WFS 1.0 service reads its box in the feature type's own coordinate system, so it is asked for the whole layer, as is an area across the antimeridian; a note says so. When a whole layer takes longer than service.add waits (a minute), the error suggests "bbox":
