rustgis-cli run --cmd 'service.add={"url":"https://geoservicos.ibge.gov.br/geoserver/wfs","layer":"CGMAT:qg_2024_030_munic","bbox":[-45.99,-10.93,-40.37,-2.74]}'

The layer holds the features of the area it was added for: moving the map doesn't ask for more.

For callers that fetch documents themselves (including the web app), service.layers accepts text for the initial document and documents: [{"url": "…", "text": "…"}] for subsequent responses. It returns next while another collections document is needed; supplied documents never cause a blocking capabilities fetch. Each listed layer includes source_url; pass it and the same documents to service.add to distinguish layers with the same name. Discovery follows at most four documents and rejects loops and disallowed addresses. Collection lists aren't paged. On the desktop, feature downloads follow their next pages (see the table above).

items.title: One picture of the view, or tiles
items.text:
A WMS layer and an ArcGIS map or image service's export draw their pictures on request, for any area and size. Added from Add Service, the Library or the National Map (its drawn maps; its imagery stays in tiles), such a layer is asked for one picture of the view: the service lays out its symbols and labels over the whole view, so none is cut at a tile edge, and it is asked once a view instead of for every tile (#1162). So is one added by its address (map.addTiles with a GetMap or export address that has its size: WIDTH and HEIGHT, or size), unless it's given "singleImage": false or a "tileSize".

  • The picture reaches past the view, its middle on a grid, so small pans and zooms (most of a quarter of a level) ask for nothing new; while the next picture loads, the last one stays in place.
  • It is asked for in the map's logical pixels, as tiles are, so the service's symbols keep their size on a high-density screen; at most 4096 pixels a side (2048 for five minutes after a larger picture of the layer fails), coarser for a view larger than that. A picture the service fails to draw leaves the layer drawn in tiles there.
  • Nothing is asked for zoomed out past the layer's scale range or outside its bounds, and closer in than its finest zoom its picture there is stretched, as its tiles are.
  • It is drawn so on a flat map, north up or turned, in Web Mercator or in a projection with an EPSG code. The picture is asked for in the map's own system when the service offers it (a map service's export takes any: the service projects it); otherwise in one it does offer (Web Mercator, or the WMS layer's own system), and warped into place piece by piece. On the globe, a tilted map, a projection without an EPSG code (the presets), or a Web Mercator or longitude/latitude picture across or near the antimeridian (a little larger than the view, it would cross it; tiles wrap), the layer is drawn in tiles. Exports and layouts ask for their own picture.

Right-click the layer in the Layers pane, Draw as, to switch to Tiles and back to Single image (map.setTiles with "singleImage"). A layer asked for in Web Mercator takes tiles of 256, 512 or 1024 pixels ("tileSize"): larger tiles cut fewer labels and ask fewer times. Tiles are fetched while the map moves, and kept for panning back. A layer in a project saved before keeps its tiles until you switch it.

items.title: Services in other coordinate systems
items.text:
National and regional services often draw their maps in a coordinate system of their own (Switzerland's LV95, EPSG:2056; Austria's EPSG:31287) and sometimes not in Web Mercator at all. A WMS layer offered in any system with an EPSG code that RustGIS can transform (or in CRS:84), and a WMTS layer whose tile matrix set is in one, is listed and added like any other (#769):

  • On a Web Mercator map, a layer the service offers in Web Mercator is asked for in it, as before. Otherwise a WMS layer drawn as one picture of the view is asked for one picture in its own system, warped into place; drawn as tiles (and a WMTS layer), each of the map's tiles is made from what the service gives for its area in the layer's own system, warped into place on your computer: one GetMap image, or the tiles of the WMTS matrix nearest the map's detail (a coarser one where that would take more than 16 tiles; of a set of more than 40 matrices, its 20 coarsest and 20 finest are kept). A WMS layer is asked for in the projected system it lists first, else in CRS:84, else in another longitude/latitude system.
  • On a map in another projection (View › Projection, map.projection) that the layer is offered in, a WMS layer is asked for in that system, as one picture of the view or, drawn as tiles, in tiles of its own 256 pixels a side, and drawn as the service draws it: nothing is warped, so its lines and labels stay sharp. A WMTS layer is drawn so on a map in its tile matrix set's system. Change the map's projection and the layer follows: in Web Mercator again, it is asked for in Web Mercator (or warped), and in a projection the layer isn't offered in, it is drawn warped as before. A WMS layer is drawn so in up to 64 of the systems it lists that RustGIS can transform (projected ones first, then CRS:84, then other longitude/latitude ones, each kind in the order listed), and warped in the rest. A tilted map draws every layer warped.
  • Identify asks a WMS layer drawn in a system of its own (GetFeatureInfo) in that system.
  • Axis order. A WMS 1.3.0 bounding box and a WMTS TopLeftCorner are in the order of the system's axes as EPSG defines them, as the standards ask: latitude first in EPSG:4326 and other longitude/latitude systems (not in CRS:84), north first in EPSG:3035 (LAEA Europe), the German Gauss-Krüger zones, SWEREF99 TM, Poland's CS92, Austria's Lambert and the ETRS89 "UTM (N-E)" codes (EPSG:3040 and its neighbours), east first in Web Mercator, the other UTM codes and LV95. RustGIS carries that order for the systems it knows (from the EPSG dataset); for a system newer than its table, the layer's own BoundingBox is read the way that holds the layer, and a WMTS corner the way its matrix covers the layer. A longitude/latitude WMTS corner, which services often write longitude first, is read longitude first when its first number can't be a latitude, or when its matrix read in EPSG's order misses the layer and read the other way doesn't; otherwise in EPSG's order.

A layer offered in no system RustGIS can transform (an AUTO: system, a planet's) is still left out, and the dialog says how many were.

rustgis-cli run --cmd 'service.add={"url":"https://wmts.geo.admin.ch/EPSG/2056/1.0.0/WMTSCapabilities.xml","layer":"ch.swisstopo.pixelkarte-farbe"}' --cmd 'map.projection={"type":"EPSG:2056"}' --cmd 'map.goToXY={"lon":7.4474,"lat":46.948,"scale":20000}' --cmd 'share.exportMap={"path":"bern-lv95.png"}'

items.title: Secured ArcGIS services
items.text:
A secured ArcGIS service answers error 499, "Token Required". There are two ways in:

  • Sign in to ArcGIS (in Add From Service, shown for ArcGIS addresses; arcgis.signIn) signs in to ArcGIS Online, an ArcGIS Online organization (https://myorg.maps.arcgis.com) or an ArcGIS Enterprise portal (https://gis.example.org/portal) on the portal's own page, with its single sign-on and multi-factor checks: RustGIS never sees the password. It uses OAuth 2.0 with PKCE. ArcGIS Online needs no setup: leave Client ID blank and RustGIS's own app is used. An Enterprise portal needs the client ID of an app registered on it (Content › New item › Developer credentials › OAuth 2.0 credentials) whose redirect URLs list RustGIS's callback: http://127.0.0.1:7290/arcgis/callback for the desktop app and the command line (give "port" to arcgis.signIn for another port, and register that address instead), and oauth-callback.html next to the web app's page for the browser (for example https://web.rustgis.app/oauth-callback.html), where the sign-in opens in a pop-up window. ArcGIS accepts only an address the app registers, port and path included. The portal and client ID are remembered; the session is not.
  • A token with the address: a service address given with ?token=… (from the portal, or arcgis.token with "url" and "token") keeps the token for that ArcGIS Server and takes it out of the address the layer keeps.

A token is sent (in the X-Esri-Authorization header; in the browser, as the request's token parameter, since ArcGIS's query endpoints refuse the header from web pages) only where its session reaches: the portal and, for ArcGIS Online, the organization's own hosted services (services*.arcgis.com/<org id>/…, tiles.arcgis.com/tiles/<org id>/…), or, for ArcGIS Enterprise, the portal's host and its federated servers; a token given with an address goes to that server alone. Its layers, tiles and feature pages are then read with it. Tokens live in memory for the session, never in a project or a connection, and a sign-in renews itself until the portal's session ends (two weeks at most). Sign out (arcgis.signOut) forgets it (and, on the desktop, revokes it with the portal); arcgis.status lists the sessions.

items.title: Catalogues
items.text: The same dialog's Catalogue search (CSW) type searches a CSW 2.0.2 catalogue (GeoNetwork, pycsw, geocat.ch…) by words anywhere in its records and, if you like, the map's area (catalog.search). Its records are listed 20 at a time (More asks for the next), with their titles, abstracts (on hover) and bounds (Zoom), and a button per link RustGIS can follow: a WMS, WMTS, WFS, WCS, OGC API or ArcGIS service connects in the dialog, a download is added as From URL… does. Links pointing where a document on the web may not send RustGIS (the local network) are left out.

items.title: PostgreSQL and PostGIS
items.text:
The desktop app reads the geometry and geography columns of a PostGIS database live, talking to the server itself: see PostgreSQL and PostGIS.

Source How to add it Notes PostGIS table or view Home › Add › Add Data › Database… (layer.addDatabase) with a libpq connection string or postgresql:// address Large tables read a view at a time by their spatial index, others loaded whole. Converted to longitude/latitude by the server; "crs" for geometry that doesn't say. A column of mixed types becomes a layer per type. The password is kept for the session only.

items.title: MySQL and MariaDB
items.text:
The desktop app reads the spatial columns of a MySQL (8 or later) or MariaDB (10.2 or later) database live, talking to the server itself: see MySQL and MariaDB.

Source How to add it Notes MySQL or MariaDB table or view Home › Add › Add Data › Database… (layer.addDatabase) with a mysql://user@host:3306/database or mariadb://… address Large tables read a view at a time by their spatial index, others loaded whole. Converted to longitude/latitude by RustGIS from the column's SRID; "crs" for an SRID of 0. A column of mixed types becomes a layer per type. ssl-mode sets the encryption. The password is kept for the session only.

items.title: SQL Server and Azure SQL
items.text:
The desktop app reads SQL Server 2012 or later and Azure SQL spatial tables live, without an external client: see SQL Server and Azure SQL.

Source How to add it Notes SQL Server table or view Home › Add › Add Data › Database… (layer.addDatabase) with an mssql://user@host:1433/database address Read only; large tables read a view at a time. Geometry and geography, including curves, are converted to longitude/latitude. "crs" supplies SRID 0; mixed types become separate layers. TLS and certificate checking are on by default. SQL Server logins on every desktop platform; Windows logins on Windows only. Passwords are kept for the session, never in projects.

items.title: SQL queries and DuckDB databases
items.text:
With DuckDB installed (the duckdb program on the PATH, DuckDB 1.5 or later), the desktop app adds the result of an SQL query as a layer, and opens DuckDB database files. Results are written as cached GeoParquet, so large ones stream too: see SQL queries and DuckDB databases.

Source How to add it Notes SQL query layer.addSql with "sql" One DuckDB SELECT with DuckDB Spatial: Parquet, CSV, GeoParquet and ST_Read files, web addresses (https://, s3://). Give "crs" for a geometry that doesn't say its coordinate system. DuckDB database .duckdb, .ddb: Add Data Every table with a geometry column becomes a layer ("layer" picks one). Converted once, until the file changes.

items.title: Rasters
items.text: Format Extensions or source How to add it Notes GeoTIFF / Cloud-optimised GeoTIFF .tif, .tiff Add Data, or upload Regular or cloud-optimised, striped or tiled; grey, RGB(A), palette (with its colour table) or multiband; Deflate, LZW, PackBits, JPEG or Zstandard compression. Supported EPSG systems or the file's own GeoKey projection are reprojected as it draws. Rotated or skewed images are resampled north-up. Large files open from an overview, or one made while reading. Browser uploads over 256 MiB read only the parts needed for a fitting overview, provided those parts fit the upload limit; the project keeps those parts, not the full-resolution file. JPEG 2000 .jp2, .j2k Add Data, byte upload (layer.addDataBytes), or From URL… (desktop, with GDAL installed) Converted through GDAL. Uploads and downloads keep the converted GeoTIFF in the project, so reopening it needs neither GDAL nor the original file or address; their output and workspace limits are described under Files on the web. The web app rejects JPEG 2000 uploads and downloads with an explicit GDAL limitation: use GeoTIFF instead. Scans with no coordinates an untagged .tif or .png; any .tif, .png or .jpg/.jpeg with "as": "scan" Add Data, or upload (layer.addData, layer.addDataBytes) Grey or RGB(A), 8- or 16-bit pixels. An untagged TIFF or PNG opens as a scan by default; a JPEG needs "as": "scan" (otherwise it is a photo). This also discards a GeoTIFF's coordinates. The scan initially covers the current view and is marked not georeferenced (georeferenced: false) until Georeference places it. Export and tools needing ground coordinates refuse it until then. PNG/JPEG decoding is bounded and may reduce the image; large TIFFs can be read at reduced resolution. ASCII grid .asc (with an optional .prj on desktop) Add Data, or upload A single numeric band with square CELLSIZE or separate DX and DY pixel sizes. Desktop files use the neighbouring .prj; uploaded and downloaded grids have no sidecar and must have coordinates that fit WGS 84 longitude/latitude. Zarr a store's folder (.zarr, desktop) or web address (desktop and browser), format 2 (consolidated) or 3 Home › Add › Add Data › Zarr… (layer.addZarr), Add Data on a local folder, or a ?zarr= link A variable's latitude/longitude (or y/x) map at the steps picked of its other dimensions (time, level), read chunk by chunk in pure Rust (blosc, zlib, gzip, zstd, LZ4; sharded arrays too). See Zarr stores. Rasters GDAL reads .img, .hgt, .dem, .dt0–.dt2, .nc, .nc4, .hdf, .hdf5, .h5, .he5, .bil, .bsq, .bip, .envi, .grd, .rst, .sdat, .kea, .ers, .ntf, .nitf, .ecw, .sid, .gsb, .bt, .rsw Add Data (desktop, with GDAL: gdal_translate, gdalinfo and gdalwarp; the installed build must include the driver) Converted once to a cached cloud-optimised GeoTIFF. NetCDF/HDF variables are subdatasets: the first is added, the others named in a notice; "layer" picks one. Without a declared coordinate system, longitude/latitude-like coordinates use WGS 84 (0–360° longitudes are moved to −180–180°); otherwise give "crs". JPEG 2000 is listed separately above.

items.title: Tiles and web services
items.text: Format Extensions or source How to add it Notes Raster tiles XYZ/TMS template ({z}/{x}/{y}, {-y}, {s}, {q}), WMS ({bbox-epsg-3857}) Home › Add › Basemap › Add Tile Layer PNG, JPEG and WebP. Vector tiles Mapbox Vector Tiles (.pbf, .mvt) template, or TileJSON Add Tile Layer Drawn in a built-in style that knows the OpenMapTiles, Protomaps and Shortbread schemas. MapLibre styles style.json Add Tile Layer A supported subset of vector and raster sources, sprites, expressions and zoom functions; see Maps and Basemaps for styling limits. PMTiles .pmtiles: a web address, or a desktop file Add Tile Layer (or Tile Archive File…), Add Data, or drop a local file on desktop Version 3 archives only: PNG, JPEG or WebP rasters, or MVT vectors; uncompressed, gzip, Brotli or Zstandard. Read a tile at a time by byte ranges (CORS on the web). Browser local-file uploads aren't supported; use an archive's web address. The map moves to the archive's bounds, except a world archive. Vector archives use the built-in basemap style, or a colour per layer when added as an overlay. MBTiles .mbtiles: a file Add Data, drop the file, Add Tile Layer's Tile Archive File… button, or upload in the web app Raster (PNG, JPEG, WebP) or vector tiles, as its metadata says, drawn as PMTiles archives are. The desktop reads the file in place, a tile at a time. The web app reads an upload into memory (the plain tiles table and the deduplicated layouts of mbutil, TileMill and Planetiler) and keeps it for the session: a project saved there asks for the file again.

items.title: Writing
items.text:
Format How to write it Notes GeoJSON (.geojson, .json), CSV Data › Export (share.exportLayer) The Export Features dialog picks the format; the chosen extension is appended when needed. In the web app it downloads any vector format below except GeoPackage (a Shapefile as one zip). Feature export loads a streamed layer's whole source; remote sources on the web must be downloaded first. GeoPackage Data › Export to .gpkg (desktop) A new file with one feature table (an attributes table for a layer without geometry) in the layer's coordinate system (see below), with an R-tree and GeoPackage 1.4 triggers to maintain it. An existing destination is refused; adding or replacing tables in an existing GeoPackage is not supported. Unique feature ids that fit signed 64-bit integers are kept; otherwise SQLite assigns new ids. GeoParquet (.parquet, .geoparquet) Data › Export GeoParquet 1.1: WKB geometry in WGS 84, Snappy compression, row groups of 65,536 features and a bbox covering column. A standalone table without geometry writes plain Parquet. Shapefile Data › Export to .shp (or .zip for the files zipped) Writes .shp, .shx, .dbf, .prj (the coordinate system, see below) and .cpg (UTF-8). Field names are cut to 10 characters (made unique), text to 254 bytes, and numbers too wide for a dBase field are left empty; features without geometry, and lines of a single point, are left out (and reported). FlatGeobuf Data › Export to .fgb In the layer's coordinate system (see below), with a spatial index; features without geometry are left out (and reported). KML, KMZ, GPX Data › Export to .kml, .kmz or .gpx Placemarks named by a name field, if there is one; features without geometry are left out. GeoJSON, KML, GPX, CSV, CSV with WKT Analyze › Workflows › Data Interop (data.convert; "format": "geojson", "kml", "gpx", "csv" or "wkt") Returns text when "path" is omitted; writes a file on desktop when it is given. GeoTIFF / Cloud-optimised GeoTIFF Data › Export Raster (share.exportRaster) Untiled GeoTIFF by default; "cog": true writes 512-pixel tiles, Deflate compression and overviews. Writes the loaded raster's resolution (an overview when that is what was opened), the selected band or its colour bands. The web app's Export Raster downloads an ordinary GeoTIFF. PNG Publish › Export Map (share.exportMap) Configurable DPI, with labels, scale bar and tile credits. PDF Layouts, reports and presentations Wavefront OBJ, glTF Publish › Export To 3D, Share As › Web Scene Polygons extruded by a field. Web map, OGC API Features, MapLibre style Publish › Share As Open-format files that need no server: see Sharing. Raster tiles imagery.hostedImagery A zip of tiles/z/x/y.png tiles, tiles.json and a viewer page; at most 5,000 tiles and 256 MiB of tile data.

GeoPackage, Shapefile and FlatGeobuf exports default to the layer's original coordinate system when it has an EPSG code. Shapefiles can also retain a custom WKT system; GeoPackage and FlatGeobuf need an EPSG code and otherwise default to WGS 84. A layer made in RustGIS defaults to WGS 84. share.exportLayer takes "crs" to choose another, such as {"layer": "Parcels", "path": "parcels.gpkg", "crs": "EPSG:4647"}. GeoJSON, KML, GPX, GeoParquet and CSV are always written in WGS 84.

RustGIS keeps x and y only. When a source has Z or M values (heights or measures), adding it says they were dropped, and exporting or converting the layer, or sharing it as a web map, web layer or OGC API Features, says what's written lacks them. Shapefile, GeoPackage, GeoParquet, FlatGeobuf, PostGIS, File Geodatabase, GeoJSON, KML (altitudes other than 0), GML and CSV WKT columns are checked; sources read through GDAL or DuckDB, and SQL Server tables, aren't yet. GPX elevations and LiDAR heights are kept as fields, and a File Geodatabase multipatch's heights as z_min and z_max. Where a source doesn't declare its dimensions, only a sample is checked: the first 16 rows of a GeoParquet file without geometry types (in its first row group), and the first 16 rows with a geometry of a GeoPackage table with optional Z or M (in the web app, its first 16 rows) or of an unconstrained PostGIS column.

items.title: Define Projection
items.text:
When a Shapefile's .prj is missing or incorrect, right-click its layer and choose Define Projection… (also in Command Search). Enter the source coordinate system, such as EPSG:2263 or a WKT/PROJ definition, then Apply. This reinterprets the native coordinate numbers: it changes the layer's position, preserves attributes and selection, and can be undone in one step. Use Zoom To Layer to see its corrected position. It does not modify the original file. Saving the project keeps the definition. Shapefile exports use it by default; GeoPackage and FlatGeobuf exports do so when the definition has an EPSG code. Custom definitions without an EPSG code can be exported in their native coordinates as Shapefiles.

This differs from changing the map's coordinate system, which only changes the display, or exporting to another CRS, which converts coordinate numbers while preserving locations. RustGIS stores geometry in longitude/latitude, so Define Projection first reconstructs native numbers through the previous CRS; small floating-point rounding differences are possible. Edits already made to the layer are reinterpreted too. If the wrong CRS already discarded or clamped coordinates, import the original file again to recover them accurately.

If the incorrect .prj prevented geometry from being read, Define Projection cannot restore it. Choose Import Original File… in the dialog, or search for Import Shapefile with Projection…. Enter the correct CRS before choosing the file. In the browser, pick the .shp and .dbf together, with any sidecars, or choose a ZIP. The override replaces the .prj before any conversion and applies to every Shapefile in a ZIP; other formats keep their own CRS. This adds a new layer, so existing layer edits and styles are not transferred.

A streamed layer cannot be changed by Define Projection. Use Load All Features first (up to the read limit), or import again with the override; streamed Shapefiles remember that override when the project reopens. Layers whose import lost geometry must be imported again.

The same operations are available to scripts and the CLI:

{"cmd":"layer.defineProjection","params":{"layer":"Parcels","crs":"EPSG:2263"}}
{"cmd":"layer.addData","params":{"path":"parcels.shp","crs":"EPSG:2263"}}

layer.addDataBytes, layer.addUrl and layer.addDownload also accept crs for zipped Shapefiles. The source files and their .prj sidecars are never rewritten by either operation.

items.title: RustGIS files
items.text: File Extension Notes Project .rgis (older .rgisx open too) Saves streamed layers' local file paths relative to the project, not their features; a browser upload is kept inside. Map, layer, style, color ramp, template, task, bookmark and layout files .rgismap, .rgislyr, .rgisstyle, .rgisramp, .rgistemplate, .rgistask, .rgisbookmarks, .rgislayout See Project items. Project package .rgispkg Everything, rasters included. Plugin .rgplugin See Plugins. Color ramps from other tools QGIS style .xml and layer style .qml, GDAL color-relief .txt, GMT .cpt Read as custom color ramps; see Custom color ramps.

items.title: Formats
items.text:
Every format, with how to add it and its limits, is listed on Supported Data Formats.

Format Read Write GeoJSON (.geojson, .json) Yes Yes Delimited text (.csv, .tsv, .txt) with x/y columns in a supported coordinate system, or WKT geometry Yes Yes Shapefile (.shp + .dbf, or zipped in a .zip) Yes (the web app also accepts sidecar files picked or dropped together) Yes (share.exportLayer) GeoPackage (.gpkg, feature tables) Yes Yes (desktop) GeoParquet (.parquet, .geoparquet, WKB geometry) Yes Yes FlatGeobuf (.fgb) Yes Yes (share.exportLayer) KML/KMZ (with their styles), GPX Yes Yes Spreadsheets (.xlsx, .xls, .ods), GeoRSS feeds, LandXML, encoded polylines Yes No GML, MapInfo MIF/MID, OpenStreetMap PBF, TopoJSON, AutoCAD DXF (ASCII) Yes No LiDAR point clouds: LAS, LAZ, COPC (an evenly spread sample) Yes No Geotagged photos (JPEG with EXIF GPS): points with their thumbnails Yes No Esri File Geodatabase (.gdb folder; 3D multipatches as footprints) Yes (desktop) No Through GDAL: AutoCAD DWG, MapInfo TAB, OpenStreetMap XML, File Geodatabases RustGIS can't read itself… Yes (desktop, when GDAL is installed) No PostgreSQL/PostGIS databases, read live (large tables a view at a time) Yes (desktop) No MySQL and MariaDB databases, read live (large tables a view at a time) Yes (desktop) No SQL Server and Azure SQL databases, read live (large tables a view at a time) Yes (desktop) No DuckDB databases (.duckdb, .ddb) and SQL queries Yes (desktop, when DuckDB is installed) No GeoTIFF and cloud-optimised GeoTIFF (.tif, .tiff) Yes Yes ASCII grid (.asc, with an optional .prj) Yes No Unreferenced TIFF and PNG scans; JPEG with "as": "scan" Yes GeoTIFF after georeferencing Through GDAL: JPEG 2000, ERDAS Imagine, SRTM HGT, DTED, NetCDF, HDF, ENVI, SAGA… Yes (desktop, when GDAL is installed) No Web tiles: XYZ/TMS/WMS rasters, Mapbox Vector Tiles, MapLibre styles, PMTiles and MBTiles archives Yes Yes (Analyze › Create Hosted Imagery) RustGIS project (.rgis; older .rgisx files open too) Yes Yes

Add data with Home › Add › Add Data: its main button opens the file picker, and its menu offers other ways to add data, including Delimited Text…, From URL… and From Service…. Files can also be dropped on the window or passed on the command line (rustgis places.geojson). The file picker opens formats listed on Supported Data Formats, including cloud-optimised GeoTIFF, GeoParquet and FlatGeobuf (read in place, a view at a time; see Files on the web). Home › Add › Data Sources opens the pane with saved connections, favourites, recent data and the public-source library. On the desktop, a file that holds several layers (a File Geodatabase, a GeoPackage, a DuckDB database or a file read through GDAL) asks which to add when it is picked, dropped or double-clicked in the Browser: Choose Layers lists them, all ticked, with Select All, Select None and a filter for a long list. Turn Ask Which Layers to Add off in the Add Data menu to add every layer, as before. Scripts pick one with layer.addData's "layer"; info.fileLayers lists them. On the desktop, Home › Add › Add Data › Add Folder… connects a folder to the Browser; the web app does not offer folder connections. Home › Add › Add Data › Delimited Text… asks for a CSV or a spreadsheet first, then lists its columns to pick the x and y (or WKT) ones from, with the coordinate system (such as EPSG:2263) and the separator (changing it reads the columns again); info.fileColumns lists them for scripts. Add Data finds them itself (columns named like longitude/latitude, easting/northing or geometry, and EWKT's SRID=) and says when coordinates aren't longitude/latitude. A CSV without coordinate columns, or a layer without geometry, opens as a standalone table, listed under the map in Layers; right-click it to open or remove it. Tables can share a name: commands and tools take a table's id (info.project lists them) as well as its name, which stands for the first table of that name. An id given as a number is never taken for a name. The Tools pane and Geocode Addresses send the id of the table picked; a tool's run keeps the table's name beside it (input_name). The XY Table To Point tool (Geoprocessing, and a table's right-click menu) makes points of a table already in the project, from two fields of coordinates and their coordinate system. In a text field a single comma is the decimal separator (1,234 is 1.234); thousands separators are not read. Home › Add › Add Data › Graphics Layer adds a layer for drawn graphics, and Data › Layer Templates adds empty layers with ready-made schemas to draw into.

Vector geometry is stored as WGS 84 longitude/latitude. Data in another supported coordinate system is converted as it is read; Shapefiles use their .prj, and formats such as GeoPackage, GeoParquet and FlatGeobuf carry their coordinate system in the file. Rasters keep their own coordinate system and are reprojected as they draw. The map uses Web Mercator by default, but View › Projection can change it; see Maps.

ESRI .prj files without an EPSG code use their projection parameters and, for ED50, Monte Mario (from Greenwich or from Rome), OSGB36, DHDN, Amersfoort, GGRS87, CH1903/CH1903+ and S-JTSK, the same built-in Helmert datum transformation as the EPSG definition. A TOWGS84 transformation in the file takes precedence. RDN2008 and IGM95 are treated as WGS 84-like datums. These transformations do not replace regional grid corrections for survey accuracy. An unrecognized datum keeps its ellipsoid and produces a notice when no transformation is available. Swiss oblique Mercator and the standard Krovak East/North variant are supported from their parameters.

Shapefile text uses a supported .cpg encoding, otherwise the .dbf code page, with UTF-8 as the fallback. Keep the sidecar files together.

items.title: Attribute tables and fields
items.text:
Open a feature layer's table with Ctrl+T (Cmd+T on macOS), Home › Selection › Attributes or Attribute Table on a feature layer's Data tab (table.open). Rows and map selections stay in sync. Standalone tables open from their right-click menu; their cells are read only. See The attribute table for sorting, filtering, selection and the SQL WHERE clause syntax used by Select By Attributes and Definition Query (the full grammar is in Expressions). These clauses filter a layer; they are not DuckDB queries.

For an editable feature layer, double-click a cell to change it. The table's toolbar also adds fields, calculates field expressions and opens Calculate Geometry (edit.calculateGeometry). The geometry calculator fills a new double field or an existing numeric field with area, perimeter, length or point X/Y, for all or selected features. Point coordinates can be WGS 84 degrees or a supported projected EPSG system's units. See Editing for field calculations and data-design rules. Streamed layers must first be loaded with Load All Features.

items.title: Formats through GDAL
items.text: When GDAL is installed (its ogr2ogr and ogrinfo programs on the PATH, or the folder holding them in RUSTGIS_GDAL_BIN; GDAL 3.7 or later), the desktop app also opens the vector formats GDAL reads: DWG, MapInfo TAB, OpenStreetMap XML, File Geodatabases RustGIS can't read itself (compressed ones, or ones with raster fields) and more. RustGIS doesn't link to GDAL: each layer is converted once, by ogr2ogr, into a FlatGeobuf with a spatial index in WGS 84 (GDAL reprojects it), kept in the cache folder (~/.cache/rustgis/gdal on Linux, ~/Library/Caches/RustGIS/gdal on macOS, %LOCALAPPDATA%\RustGIS\cache\gdal on Windows, or RUSTGIS_GDAL_CACHE). Adding the file again reuses the conversion until the file changes, and large layers stream like any large FlatGeobuf (below). Every layer of the file is added; a layer mixing geometry types is added as one layer per type. Curves become straight segments, and 3D surfaces (an Esri multipatch, such as the buildings of swissBUILDINGS3D, is read as a TIN) become flat polygons, one part per face, without their heights. Projects remember the original file and convert it again if the cached copy is gone.

items.title: SQL queries and DuckDB databases
items.text:
When DuckDB is installed (the duckdb program on the PATH, or the folder holding it in RUSTGIS_DUCKDB_BIN; DuckDB 1.5 or later), the desktop app adds the result of an SQL query as a layer, with the layer.addSql command (Add Data From SQL in command search):

{"sql": "SELECT name, geometry FROM read_parquet('places.parquet') WHERE country = 'FR'", "name": "French places"}

Analyze › SQL opens the SQL pane, a workspace for these queries: an editor (Ctrl+Enter runs the query) that completes table and column names of the database named above it and DuckDB Spatial's common functions, the result's first 200 rows as a table, Add to Map for a result with a geometry column, and a history of the queries run (kept by the app with its preferences, without the database's password; a query that seems to hold a credential, such as user:password@ in an address, a signed URL or a secret, isn't kept). Queries run in the background, so the app keeps drawing while DuckDB works. The commands behind it are sql.query (a query's first rows, up to 1,000, without adding a layer) and sql.schema (a database's tables and their columns); both take "database" as layer.addSql does. The web app has no DuckDB, so the pane says to open the project in the desktop app.

The query is one DuckDB SELECT (or FROM …, WITH …), with DuckDB Spatial's ST_ functions: it can read Parquet, CSV, JSON and GeoParquet files, anything ST_Read reads, and web addresses (https://, s3://), so a bounding box of Overture Maps is one query:

SELECT id, names.primary AS name, geometry
FROM read_parquet('s3://overturemaps-us-west-2/release/2026-09-23.1/theme=places/type=place/*', hive_partitioning = 1)
WHERE bbox.xmin BETWEEN -83.95 AND -83.89 AND bbox.ymin BETWEEN 35.94 AND 35.98

The first geometry column becomes the layer's geometry; other columns become its attributes (types RustGIS doesn't read, such as dates and lists, as text). A geometry that says its coordinate system is converted to longitude/latitude; give "crs" (such as EPSG:2263) for one that doesn't. A result mixing geometry types becomes a layer per type, and rows without a geometry are left out. "database" opens a DuckDB database (read only) so the query names its tables plainly; the database is trusted like the query, since its views run as part of it.

Home › Add › Add Data opens a DuckDB database file (.duckdb, .ddb): every table with a geometry column becomes a layer ("layer" picks one).

items.title: PostgreSQL and PostGIS
items.text:
Home › Add › Add Data › Database… (layer.addDatabase, desktop) connects to a PostgreSQL database with PostGIS and reads its tables live. The dialog takes a saved connection or a typed one, a password, a table (List Tables, or all tables with geometry) and a coordinate system for geometry that doesn't say its own. RustGIS talks to the server itself (nothing else to install; TLS as libpq does it). sslmode=prefer (the default) uses TLS only when the server offers it, and otherwise connects without encryption, so a server in the middle can force a plaintext connection. require always uses TLS but doesn't check the server's certificate. On networks you don't trust, use verify-full or verify-ca; both check the host name here. The certificate is checked against sslrootcert (a private authority's PEM file) or the web's roots. disable turns TLS off. The connection is a libpq connection string (host=localhost port=5432 dbname=gis user=postgres) or a postgresql://user@host/dbname address; what it leaves out comes from PGHOST, PGPORT, PGUSER and PGDATABASE, as with libpq. List Tables (info.databaseTables) shows the tables and views with a geometry or geography column, and every one of them becomes a layer unless one is chosen (table, schema.table, or table:column for one of several geometry columns). The connection is read only.

A table of more than 100,000 rows (or any, with "stream": true) is read in place a view at a time, like a large GeoParquet: the view's box is matched against the column's spatial index, and when more rows match than a view draws, an evenly spread sample of them is numbered on the server, so only those cross the network. Smaller tables are loaded whole, so they can be edited. The server converts geometry to longitude/latitude (ST_Transform, so every coordinate system in its spatial_ref_sys works) and curves to lines; give "crs" (such as EPSG:2263) for a column whose geometry doesn't say its coordinate system. A column of mixed geometry types becomes a layer per type, and empty tables (such as the TIGER geocoder's) are left out. Features keep their ids between views: the table's integer primary key, else the row's place in the table (the rows of a view or a partitioned table without a key are numbered as read, so theirs can change between views).

Passwords are never written to the project. By default, an entered password lasts until RustGIS closes. For a named desktop connection, Remember on this computer is an unchecked opt-in to the operating system's password store; see Named connections for reconnect, selection and forgetting rules. Opening a project can use a remembered password only for a unique, exact saved-address match, or an explicit session selection. Otherwise a waiting layer offers Log In…, or a chooser when several remembered connections match. Without a matching connection, connect again with Home › Add › Add Data › Database…. PGPASSWORD or libpq's password file (~/.pgpass, or %APPDATA%\postgresql\pgpass.conf) can serve when you explicitly add a table without a password; opening a project never newly authorizes these ambient credentials. A small table's features are kept in the project as they were when added.

layer.addSql takes a connection as its "database" too, through DuckDB's postgres extension (installed the first time, like DuckDB Spatial), so a query names its tables plainly; the password reaches DuckDB in its environment (PGPASSWORD), never on its command line:

rustgis-cli run --cmd 'layer.addSql={"sql":"SELECT name, geom FROM roads WHERE lanes > 2","database":"postgres:host=localhost dbname=gis user=postgres","password":"…"}'

RustGIS doesn't link to DuckDB: it runs duckdb, which writes the result as GeoParquet in the cache folder (~/.cache/rustgis/duckdb on Linux, ~/Library/Caches/RustGIS/duckdb on macOS, %LOCALAPPDATA%\RustGIS\cache\duckdb on Windows, or RUSTGIS_DUCKDB_CACHE), sorted along a Hilbert curve with a bounding-box covering, so large results stream like any large GeoParquet (below). DuckDB Spatial is installed the first time (a download from DuckDB's extension repository). A database table is converted once and reused until the file changes; a query runs afresh each time. Projects convert a table again if the cached result is gone, but never run a query when they open: run it again. A database is read on its own, shut out of other files and web addresses, so a view in it that reaches elsewhere fails rather than reading them.

A query can read any file the app can and fetch any web address, and a database is a file or a server, so the AI Assistant asks before it runs a query or reads a database, and plugins need both the files and network permissions.

items.title: Editing PostGIS tables
items.text:
On the desktop, a PostgreSQL table with PostGIS can be loaded to be edited and its edits saved back to it. In Home › Add › Add Data › Database…, give a PostgreSQL connection, choose a table (List Tables) and tick Load for editing.

  • The connection (pg.connect) lasts until RustGIS closes, or until Disconnect in the same form (pg.disconnect). It isn't saved with the project, and neither is the password. Without a password, PGPASSWORD or libpq's password file serve.

  • The table (pg.addLayer; pg.tables lists those with a geometry or geography column) loads whole, up to 100,000 rows a layer, in the order of its key. A table whose geometries are of several types loads each type as its own layer, each up to that many. A condition (an SQL expression on its columns, such as population > 10000) loads only the rows it keeps. The layer is an ordinary layer in memory, so every editing tool works on it.

  • Edit › Manage Edits › Save to PostGIS… (pg.saveEdits), there while a layer is loaded for editing, shows how many of the layer's rows are new, changed and deleted, and writes them to its table in one transaction. Discard PostGIS Edits… (pg.discardEdits) loads the rows again as they are in the database, dropping the edits (Undo brings them back).

A table needs a single-column integer primary key to be added this way. The key becomes each feature's id, and the layer keeps each row's version (PostgreSQL's xmin) and what it held as it was read. Saving locks the rows you changed or deleted and checks them first: when one was changed or deleted in the database since you loaded it, or a new row's key is already taken, nothing is saved, and the message lists those rows. Discard PostGIS Edits then loads them as they are now. A row someone else changed that you didn't edit is no conflict, and stays as they left it.

Undo doesn't reach into the database: undoing a save brings back the layer as it was before, but the rows stay saved. Saving that layer again is refused, since it would write the same edits twice (its new rows as more new rows); Redo, or Discard PostGIS Edits, brings the layer back in step.

Only what you changed is written: the columns whose values differ, and the geometry when it moved (converted back to the table's coordinate system, single or multi type and dimensions). A new row takes the value of its key field, else the table's default key (serial, identity), else its feature id, and its feature takes the key it was saved with. A new row's empty fields take their column's default, NULL when it has none. Fields the table has no column for aren't saved, and the message names them. The layer says when the database's user can't insert, update or delete the table's rows; saving is then refused.

rustgis-cli run --cmd 'pg.connect={"host":"localhost","database":"gis","user":"postgres"}' \
  --cmd 'pg.addLayer={"table":"public.roads","where":"lanes > 2","name":"Roads"}' \
  --cmd 'edit.enable={"on":true}' \
  --cmd 'edit.setValue={"layer":"Roads","row":0,"field":"name","value":"Main St"}' \
  --cmd 'pg.saveEdits={"layer":"Roads"}'

Connecting and adding a layer read the database, so the AI Assistant asks before it connects or adds a table, and asks every time before it saves edits. Plugins can't connect or save at all.

items.title: Editing GeoPackage tables
items.text:
On the desktop, Home › Add › Add Data › Edit GeoPackage Table… (gpkg.addLayer) loads one feature table of an existing local .gpkg for editing. Choose its table with List Tables when the file has several. The table needs one INTEGER PRIMARY KEY. At most 100,000 rows are loaded; Most rows can lower that limit. Whole numbers may use comma-grouped thousands (for example, 1,000); fractional values are rejected. RustGIS does not directly edit rows outside that load, including rows with unreadable geometry. File-owned triggers can change other rows.

Edit › Manage Edits › Save to GeoPackage… (gpkg.saveEdits) writes pending inserts, updates and deletes to that table in one SQLite transaction. If any row you changed or deleted has changed or disappeared in the file since it was loaded, nothing is saved. A constraint or trigger failure also rolls everything back; pending edits remain in the layer. New features get source-assigned keys that cannot alias loaded rows, and unrelated columns and tables remain intact. The saved rows are read back within the transaction, so the layer keeps values assigned by defaults and triggers before it starts tracking its next edits. If a DELETE trigger recreates a target row, that stored row reappears in the layer and is not counted as deleted. If triggers change or remove other rows already loaded in the layer, those rows are refreshed or removed before the next edits; rows outside the load are not added.

New-feature saves also check the table's persisted last_change revision. If it changed since the layer was loaded, the save is refused rather than risking duplicate inserts from an older project or an undone save reopened in another session. Pending edits remain available to export; Discard Edits reloads the source and drops those pending edits. Identical feature values are not used to guess whether a new row was saved before.

Spatial indexes use the final stored geometry after table triggers run. Bounds are refreshed from the whole table's readable native extents after inserts, geometry edits or deletes; they can shrink, and become NULL when no readable nonempty geometry remains. Attribute-only saves keep known bounds unless a trigger writes feature rows. Such trigger writes require a whole-table spatial rebuild in the transaction; unreadable nonempty geometry, including a body hidden behind a valid header envelope, makes that rebuild refuse the entire save rather than guess its index coverage. Metadata or index-repair triggers that would change features after the final snapshot are also refused, with the transaction rolled back. A geometry type, Z/M declaration or SRS that changed since the layer was loaded also refuses the save until Discard Edits reloads it.

Discard GeoPackage Edits… (gpkg.discardEdits) reloads the scoped rows as they are in the file now, including renamed columns and its current geometry type and coordinate system; Undo restores the discarded layer edits. A changed geometry family resets its renderer to a compatible default. Saving refuses a changed source SRS until the layer is reloaded. Undoing a save does not undo file writes: Redo or Discard Edits is needed before saving again. Saving the project keeps pending edits in the project only; exporting writes a new file rather than changing this table. Save and Discard dialogs remain bound to the project, map and specific layer instance where they opened. Switching maps or projects, or undoing and re-adding a layer, requires reopening or choosing again; a reused layer ID cannot retarget another file. Feature-less project templates retain the layer's schema and styling, but no source-edit binding: opening a template cannot turn its absent features into source-row deletions. The same holds for the simplified layers a publication layout's globe locator map keeps: they can't be saved back.

Geometry is converted back to the table's coordinate system and must match its declared family. Single-part columns reject multipart features; collection, curve and surface columns cannot receive geometry writes. Geometry writes that would lose existing Z/M dimensions, or insert geometry into a table requiring them, are refused; attribute-only edits can still be saved. Read-only files cannot be saved. These editing commands are desktop-only; normal GeoPackage reading remains available in the browser.

rustgis-cli run --cmd 'gpkg.addLayer={"path":"/data/roads.gpkg","table":"roads","name":"Roads"}' \
  --cmd 'edit.enable={"on":true}' \
  --cmd 'edit.setValue={"layer":"Roads","row":0,"field":"name","value":"Main St"}' \
  --cmd 'gpkg.saveEdits={"layer":"Roads"}'

The AI Assistant asks before reading the file and every time before saving edits. Plugins need file permission to load or discard rows and cannot save edits back to the table.

items.title: MySQL and MariaDB
items.text:
Home › Add › Add Data › Database… (layer.addDatabase) also connects to a MySQL (8 or later) or MariaDB (10.2 or later) database and reads its spatial columns live, as it does PostGIS tables: RustGIS talks to the server itself, with nothing else to install. The connection is an address, mysql://user@host:3306/database (or mariadb://…); what it leaves out is, as with the mysql client, localhost, port 3306 and your login name. List Tables (info.databaseTables) shows the database's tables and views with a geometry column, and every one becomes a layer unless one is chosen (table, or table:column for one of several geometry columns). An address without a database lists the tables of every database but the server's own, as database.table. The session is read only, and a server asking for a local file (LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE) is sent none.

ssl-mode in the address's query sets the encryption, as the mysql client names it: PREFERRED (the default) encrypts, connecting unencrypted only when the server offers no encryption (the layer then says so), and REQUIRED always encrypts; neither checks the server's certificate, so neither protects the password from a server in the middle. On networks you don't trust, use VERIFY_IDENTITY, which checks the certificate and the host name (against ssl-ca, a private authority's PEM file, or the web's roots); VERIFY_CA checks the certificate only. DISABLED turns encryption off:

rustgis-cli run --cmd 'layer.addDatabase={"database":"mysql://gis@db.example:3306/city?ssl-mode=VERIFY_IDENTITY","password":"…"}' \
  --cmd 'share.exportMap={"path":"city.png"}'

Large tables are read a view at a time through the column's spatial index (MBRIntersects), and a capped view is an evenly spread sample numbered on the server; smaller ones are loaded whole. RustGIS converts the geometry to longitude/latitude itself (MariaDB has no ST_Transform), from the column's SRID (MySQL's per-column SRID, MariaDB's REF_SYSTEM_ID) or else its rows'; give "crs" (such as EPSG:2263) for a column whose SRID is 0. A GEOMETRY column of mixed types becomes a layer per type. Features keep their ids between views from the table's integer primary key; a table without one has its rows numbered as read, so theirs can change between views.

Passwords are never written to the project and last for the session unless you opt in with Remember on this computer for a named desktop connection. The same exact-address reconnect, chooser and Forget rules in Named connections apply. MYSQL_PWD can serve when you explicitly add a table without a password, but opening a project never newly authorizes it. SQL queries (layer.addSql, the SQL pane) don't run on MySQL or MariaDB databases.

items.title: SQL Server and Azure SQL
items.text:
Home › Add › Add Data › Database… (layer.addDatabase) reads the geometry and geography columns of SQL Server 2012 or later and Azure SQL tables and views directly, on the desktop. Use mssql://user@host:1433/database; an empty host means localhost, and omitting the database uses the login's default database. List Tables (info.databaseTables) lists spatial columns. Choose a table as table, schema.table or table:column, or leave the choice empty to add all. For a named instance, use ?instance=SQLEXPRESS without a port so SQL Browser can discover it.

The connection is encrypted and its certificate checked against the platform's trust store by default (encrypt=mandatory, also required, true or yes). encrypt=strict selects TDS 8.0 strict encryption on servers that support it. A private authority can be supplied as ?ca=/path/to/ca.pem, and hostname-in-certificate overrides the expected certificate name. For a self-signed server, ?trust-server-certificate=true disables certificate checking; the layer reports that it is unchecked. ?encrypt=false (also optional or no) requests encryption for login only, not subsequent traffic; certificate validation still applies during login unless explicitly disabled with trust-server-certificate=true. connect-timeout sets a positive connection deadline in seconds (default: 10, maximum: 300).

rustgis-cli run --cmd 'layer.addDatabase={"database":"mssql://gis@db.example:1433/city","password":"…"}' \
  --cmd 'share.exportMap={"path":"city.png"}'

SQL Server logins work on every desktop platform. On Windows, DOMAIN%5Cuser with a password uses a Windows login: %5C is the URL encoding of \, and a literal DOMAIN\user is also accepted in the address (escape it as DOMAIN\\user inside JSON). Leaving the user out signs in as the current Windows user. These Windows logins are not supported on macOS or Linux: give a SQL Server login instead. Passwords can be supplied in user-info or the password, pass, pwd, or passwd query parameters; the separate password field overrides an address's password.

Large tables read a view at a time using their spatial index, with a server-numbered sample when more rows match than a view draws; small tables are loaded whole. Curves are linearized and coordinates converted to longitude/latitude. Only rows with the first non-null geometry's SRID are read; give "crs" for SRID 0. Mixed geometry families become separate layers. An integer primary key provides stable feature ids; without one (including views), ids are numbered as read.

At database compatibility level 100 or lower, streamed geography layers filter their whole-table read or sample locally instead of sending a viewport polygon to the server. A small view can therefore miss features in a large sampled table. geometry layers and higher compatibility levels retain server-side viewport filtering.

The provider only reads data; edits are not written back to SQL Server. Passwords are never written to the project and last for the session unless Remember on this computer is checked for a named desktop connection. The named-connection rules govern remembered reconnects and explicit selection. Secret-named query values such as pwd and access_token are removed from saved connection addresses. SQLCMDPASSWORD serves only when explicitly adding a database, not when opening a project. Windows integrated sign-in still requires that same address to have been added this session: opening a project does not authorize Windows identity. Reconnect with Home › Add › Add Data › Database… when needed. SQL queries (layer.addSql, the SQL pane) do not run on SQL Server connections.

items.title: Web Data
items.text: Home › Add › Web Data gathers public web services and catalogs: STAC imagery catalogs, Overture Maps, OpenStreetMap, NASA Earthdata, open-data portals, satellite embeddings and more. They have a page of their own: Web Data.

items.title: Geocoding addresses
items.text:
Home › Add › Add Data › Geocode Addresses… (layer.geocode) turns a standalone table's or a layer's addresses into points: a CSV of addresses without coordinates is added as a standalone table, then each row's address fields ("address": a field, or several such as street, city and country, joined with commas) are looked up, each distinct address once. The result is a new point layer holding every field plus geocoded, what the geocoder called the place; rows that weren't found stay in its table without a point.

The geocoder is OpenStreetMap's public Nominatim by default, or Photon ("provider": "photon"). Their usage policies allow light use, so RustGIS sends them at most one request a second and 100 addresses a run; give "url" of a Nominatim or Photon server of your own for more (up to 10,000, with no wait between requests). In the app the requests go out in the background, one at a time, and the layer is added when the last answer lands; layer.geocode on the command line waits for them.

rustgis-cli run --cmd 'layer.addData={"path":"stores.csv"}' --cmd 'layer.geocode={"table":"stores","address":["street","city","country"]}'

The addresses are sent to the geocoder's server, so the AI Assistant asks before it geocodes, and plugins need the network permission.

items.title: S3 buckets
items.text:
An s3://bucket/key address works wherever data is added by its address: Home › Add › Add Data › From URL… and layer.addUrl (a cloud-optimised GeoTIFF is read in place by range, other files are downloaded), PMTiles archives, ?data= links, and STAC assets whose address is an s3:// one. A public bucket needs nothing more: it is read anonymously from AWS.

Home › Add › Add Data › S3… (s3.connect) connects to a private bucket, or to an S3-compatible service (MinIO, Cloudflare R2, Wasabi, source.coop…) by its endpoint, and browses a bucket a folder at a time (s3.list), adding an object with Add. A connection names its endpoint (AWS when empty), its region and the buckets it serves: the ones it is given ("buckets") and the ones browsed through it this session. An s3:// address of one of them is read through that connection, signed (AWS Signature Version 4) with its keys; an address of any other bucket (a project's, a link's) is read anonymously from AWS, never with your keys or from your endpoint. Keys are typed, or, on the desktop and only when chosen, read from an AWS profile ("profile": ~/.aws/credentials and ~/.aws/config) or from the environment ("environment": true: AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, AWS_SESSION_TOKEN, AWS_REGION); without any, the connection is anonymous. AWS, anonymous in the dialog browses with no keys at all.

rustgis-cli run --cmd 's3.connect={"name":"minio","endpoint":"https://minio.example.org","buckets":["my-bucket"],"accessKeyId":"…","secretAccessKey":"…"}' \
  --cmd 's3.list={"url":"s3://my-bucket/rasters/"}' --cmd 'layer.addUrl={"url":"s3://my-bucket/rasters/dem.tif"}'

Keys are kept until RustGIS closes unless you ask otherwise: never in a project (which keeps the address), a command's result, a notice or the log. After Connect, Save as Connection keeps its name, endpoint, region and credential source under Data Sources › Connections, never its keys. Use Saved connection to pick it again.

On the desktop, a saved connection that uses typed keys can also keep them in your computer's credential store (the macOS Keychain, the Windows Credential Manager, or the Secret Service): tick Remember on this computer in the S3 dialog or the connection's form when you log in (it is off every time; connection.login takes "remember": true). Both keys go to the store, with the endpoint they are for, and the connection only gets a Saved keys mark; the connection's definition, the preferences and projects never contain a key. Displaying that mark does not read the store or guarantee it is available. In the next session, choosing, browsing, testing or logging in to the connection can read its keys from the store with nothing typed (the system may ask you to unlock it). Typed keys win over saved ones for that login. Temporary credentials (with a session token) are never kept: they work for the session, and keys saved earlier stay as they were. If the store is missing or refuses, the login still works for this session and says the keys weren't remembered; without keys typed, a connection with nothing available says so, and is not logged in. The web app has no system keychain; the command line and Python use it only with --use-saved-secrets / use_saved_secrets=True. Forget Saved Keys (connection.forgetSavedKeys; the connection's right-click menu or its form) deletes them from the store and keeps the session's login. Removing a connection deletes its saved keys first, and changing its endpoint or switching away from typed keys does too. With a credential store available, these actions check it even when the Saved keys indication is absent: the indication may be stale. If the store refuses deletion, the forget, removal or edit doesn't happen. Without a store, a connection marked as holding saved keys cannot be removed or have its endpoint changed. Renaming, grouping, buckets and region keep the keys, and a copy of a connection has none. A profile, the environment or anonymous access never read saved keys.

A saved connection's login reads only what is added through it: its listings, and the objects Add takes from them, are kept as addresses that name that connection (and its endpoint), so a project reads a bucket through the connection it was added with, never with another connection's keys because the endpoint or bucket is the same. Opening a project (or importing a map or layer) finds each bucket its S3 sources read. A single matching connection whose bucket list explicitly includes that bucket logs in and opens the sources when its credentials are available. Connections with an empty bucket list require an explicit choice, even when only one matches. When only one such connection matches, the notice names it and asks you to confirm it in Choose S3 connection…; it is not automatically authorized to read an unlisted bucket. Missing or unavailable keys leave the sources blocked until you log in. If several connections fit, Choose S3 connection… (connection.resolveS3) asks which one, with no connection selected initially; nothing is read until you choose, and Cancel leaves the sources blocked. If none fits, sources carrying saved-connection provenance stay unread (an older project's bare s3:// address is read as before). Addresses of plain s3.connect sessions keep reading as they did. A saved login belonging to another open session is not reused merely because its name matches: each session logs in through its selected saved connection. Resolving a bucket retries only that bucket's deferred sources, keeping layer styles and ordering. An older source with an unknown endpoint stays separate from an explicitly AWS-backed source, even when both name the same bucket and object. Saving and reopening while a choice is pending preserves that distinction; choosing a connection for one resource does not choose for the other. Raster reloads use the same authorized address and load their pixels in the background. Keys go only to the endpoint they're for: a signed request that is redirected isn't followed, and keys from a profile or the environment are used only with AWS or the profile's own endpoint_url. In the web app, the bucket's CORS rules must allow the page's origin (and, for a private bucket, the Authorization and x-amz-* headers). The AI Assistant asks before it connects or lists; plugins can't connect, and need the network permission to list.

items.title: Data Sources
items.text:
The Data Sources pane (View › Windows › Data Sources, ui.pane.sources; Home › Add › Data Sources also opens it) gathers the places data comes from:

  • Favourites: any source, right-clicked and added.
  • Recent: the last 20 sources added (files, web addresses, tile layers, services, database tables, Zarr variables, STAC assets, sample data), newest first. A dataset added from a connection in the tree is listed under that connection's name rather than one made from its address. Only the name changes: the entry keeps the kind, address and options of the dataset as it was added, and the layer keeps its own name. Clicking it opens it as any Recent entry of that kind opens (a service entry reopens the service's layer list). A source is one entry per kind and address, so every dataset added through one service shares an entry, as do two connections with one address. The name is the connection's when the dataset was added: renaming a connection changes it only when something is added from it again. An add that fails, or is cancelled before it lands, isn't listed.
  • Folders: the folders connected to the Browser (Add Folder…; desktop).
  • Connections: named services, databases, STAC APIs and S3 endpoints, organised by optional groups. New Connection ▾ opens a kind-specific form. Click a connection to open it: its datasets are listed under it, a level at a time as you open its folders, with Refresh (a connection's or a folder's right-click menu; ⟳ refreshes every connection) and an error with Retry (and Log In… for databases and keyed S3) when it can't be read. Click a dataset to select it (click again to clear it); double-click, or right-click › Add, adds one, and right-click › Add Selected (N) adds them all (Clear Selection empties the selection). Each dataset is added by one command, so each is one undo step. On a table, a service layer or a STAC collection, Add With Options… opens the database, service or STAC add dialog on it; on a connection, it opens the kind's add dialog. Right-click a connection to edit, test, duplicate, copy its address or remove it.
  • Library: well-known public sources: OpenStreetMap tiles, EOX Sentinel-2 cloudless and NASA GIBS (WMTS), USGS imagery, topographic and hydrography maps (ArcGIS), GEBCO bathymetry (WMS), swisstopo's maps and imagery (geo.admin.ch) as WMTS tiles and as a WMS (most of its layers answer Identify), Earth Search and Planetary Computer (STAC), and the Natural Earth sample layers.

A click on a file, a web address, a tile layer or a sample adds it at once. The lists are kept with the app's preferences, never in a project. They hold no secrets: a web address loses its password and any key, token or signature in its query (token=, sig=, X-Amz-*…), and a database is kept without its password. The commands sources.list, sources.save, sources.favourite and sources.remove read and change the lists, for the command line and the AI Assistant. On the command line they last for the run.

items.title: Named connections
items.text:
In the pane, New Connection ▾ and Edit… let you set the name, group and address; Home › Add › Add Data › New Connection opens the same form for a chosen kind. Leave a new connection's name blank to derive it from the address. Test checks the form without saving it: web-service, catalogue, STAC and S3 requests run in the background on both desktop and web; database tests run synchronously on desktop. The web app doesn't offer database kinds for new connections; saved database rows remain visible but cannot be opened or tested there. Earth Search and Planetary Computer remain available under Library.

From Service… (including Catalogue search (CSW)), Database…, STAC Search… and S3… can use saved connections directly. Service, database and S3 dialogs offer a Saved connection picker; STAC includes saved connections in its existing API/catalog list. Picking one keeps its identity, not just its address: two connections can point to the same server with different names or users.

To keep an endpoint entered by hand, click Save as Connection after it connects: after List Tables for a database, Collections or Browse for STAC, a catalogue search with results, or Connect for a service or S3. Nothing is saved automatically. The new connection is selected and the button disappears. An endpoint typed by hand can be saved even when another connection has the same address; its default name is made unique. S3 uses the session name, so choose a different name and connect again if that name is already saved. DuckDB files aren't saved database connections. Within an ArcGIS directory, the button keeps the root directory.

Changing a form field clears pending or completed Test feedback; a late response from the previous inputs is ignored. PostgreSQL accepts a bare host=… dbname=… user=… connection string, but a blank address cannot be saved or tested.

The connection.* commands keep named, reusable endpoints independently of the project. Each has a stable id (c1, c2, …), a case-insensitively unique name and an optional group. Different names may use the same address. connection.new, connection.edit, connection.duplicate and connection.remove manage them; commands that take id accept either the id or the name. connection.list can filter by kind or group, and reports availability, session login state and the commands to use to add data. Names cannot match a stored id or the reserved c + digits id pattern (case-insensitive). Loaded names that conflict get a numeric suffix; ids and endpoints stay unchanged. Clearing a name with connection.edit chooses a unique default from the address.

rustgis-cli run \
  --cmd 'connection.new={"kind":"wms","address":"https://ows.terrestris.de/osm/service","name":"OSM WMS","group":"Public"}' \
  --cmd 'connection.test={"id":"OSM WMS"}' \
  --cmd 'connection.list={"group":"public"}'

Kinds are postgres, mysql (including MariaDB), sqlserver, service (detected on connect), wms, wmts, wfs, wcs, ogcapi, arcgis, csw, stac and s3. Database connections are used on the desktop only. S3 options are region, buckets (comma-separated), credentials (keys, profile, environment or none) and profile. connection.test lists the endpoint's tables, layers, records, collections or buckets. It also accepts an unsaved definition (kind, address, name, group, options) instead of id. With probe: true, it returns the secret-free address to fetch (fetch: null for databases). For non-database kinds, pass that response text as answer with the same definition to parse it without a network request. Database kinds ignore answer and test through their driver. An anonymous S3 test needs at least one named bucket.

connection.browse lists what a connection offers, a level at a time: database roots list the schemas returned by their provider; opening a schema lists its spatial tables. Services list their layers, catalogues their records with the services and files they link to, STAC APIs their collections, items and assets (for a static STAC catalog, its catalogs, collections and items, each item opened for its assets), and S3 connections their buckets, folders and files. Each child has a key, a name and what it is (what); a child with a node is browsed by asking again with that node; one with add names the command and parameters that add it (service.add, layer.addDatabase, stac.addAsset, layer.addUrl). Database browsing adds no table-count cap of its own. MySQL/MariaDB and SQL Server providers list at most 10,000 spatial-column rows per catalog read, so larger catalogs can omit later tables or schemas; PostGIS has no such provider limit. Other levels list at most 500 children and say truncated when they leave some out. Like connection.test, it reads the address itself on the desktop and the command line; with probe: true it returns the address to fetch, and the app passes what it fetched back as answer (and further documents when a service asks for them, as next). Browsing never changes the project. When a saved database password turns out to be missing, or to have been saved for another address, the connection loses its Saved password marker; the stored entry itself is left for Forget Saved Password, an address edit or a removal to delete.

Addresses are saved without passwords or tokens. Database passwords entered through connection.login are kept separately by connection ID for this session. On desktop, Remember on this computer in the new, edit and login forms is always unchecked initially. Checking it opts that submitted password into the operating system's password store; Test never saves it. The command equivalent is connection.login {"id":"c1","password":"…","remember":true}; remember defaults to false. If the store is missing, unavailable or denies access, the login remains usable for the session and a visible warning says it was not remembered (passwordSaved:false in the result). The browser has no OS-store hook and remains session-only. The command line and Python also remain session-only unless run with --use-saved-secrets (Python: use_saved_secrets=True).

The stored database password envelope is bound to the connection's ID, kind and cleaned address, including its username. Renaming or regrouping preserves it. Changing the address or username, or removing the connection, deletes the old stored password before committing the change; if deletion fails, the definition remains unchanged. Invalid edits do not delete a password. Duplicating a connection copies neither its stored password nor its session login. Saved password marks a remembered database connection without reading the store just to display it; it is separate from an S3 connection's Saved keys marker. Forget Saved Password (connection.forgetPassword {"id":"c1"}) deletes the stored value, but leaves an explicitly entered session password and already-open layers alone. Forgetting an inactive connection never selects it or replaces another connection's active password.

Database layer origins remain address-only: projects contain neither database passwords nor saved database connection IDs. On opening a project, one exact matching remembered database connection may reconnect automatically. Matching strips passwords and outer wrappers/whitespace, but does not infer that URI and libpq forms, reordered parameters, host aliases or different usernames mean the same server. Several eligible remembered matches open a chooser with no default; cancel leaves the layers unavailable. Choose a connection explicitly, or use connection.login {"id":"c2"} to select its existing session, environment or remembered password without exposing it. Selection lasts for this session, not in the project. connection.list reports secret-free loginRequests with the reason, database label, candidate IDs and affected-layer count; ambiguous layers are not attributed to the first saved row. loggedIn means this ID has a session password, an environment password selected for it, or an already-loaded remembered password available; it does not certify successful server authentication.

Explicit command, address and session passwords take precedence over saved credentials. On the command line and in Python with --use-saved-secrets / use_saved_secrets=True, an eligible remembered connection's PGPASSWORD, MYSQL_PWD or SQLCMDPASSWORD (according to the database kind) wins over the keychain password without reading the store; the desktop app always uses the saved password. Project opening may use it only through the same exact-address remembered-connection selection; it never newly authorizes an unrelated address, password-file credentials or Windows identity. A positively refused saved or environment password is not retried automatically for the rest of the session, and no other saved password is tried automatically. Its old OS-store value is retained. The fresh login form has an empty password and Remember unchecked: an unchecked replacement is session-only and does not overwrite or delete the old value; checking Remember and successfully saving replaces it. A password the server refuses is not kept as this session's, and is not sent to the database's other layers. A refused typed login restores the previous active password, selection and activation; with no previous password, the attempted value is removed. If a password reused from this ID's session cache is refused, that cached value, its owned driver entry and activation are cleared, and a password is requested. An identical saved value is also suppressed for this session; a different saved value is not marked refused by this attempt. The OS-store entry is retained in either case. A transport error or missing table is not a wrong-password prompt. Use Forget to delete a previously saved password.

A database login reopens waiting layers at the same password-free address; connection.list reports them as waiting, and connection.login returns reopened and failed counts. Adding, editing or removing a saved connection, or adding a layer, resolves only the databases that change: an unrelated database that is down is not connected to again. connection.test never persists a password. For a named connection, if the server positively refuses a password typed for that Test, the previous per-ID session credential, selection and active address password are restored (or the attempted credential is removed if none existed). A failure after authentication, such as a table-listing error, keeps the new session login. S3 accessKeyId and secretAccessKey likewise stay session-only unless a typed-key login opts into remembering them; a nonblank sessionToken always keeps the complete temporary credential set session-only, leaving previously saved keys unchanged (see S3 buckets). With login parameters, an S3 connection.test logs in first, never remembers keys, and a failed listing does not undo that session login. S3 profiles and environment credentials remain subject to the existing endpoint restrictions; editing an S3 name, endpoint or options disconnects its session login. S3 shares the name-based session registry used by the S3 dialog and s3.connect, so editing or removing a saved connection also affects a session entry of the same name created there. Renaming clears runtime entries under both the old and new names, so the renamed connection cannot inherit an unrelated login at its destination name. Web-service logins are not supported. Plugins may list connections but cannot manage, log in to, forget passwords or S3 keys for, choose an S3 connection for, test or browse them. The in-app assistant asks for fresh approval each time for those operations, including Forget, S3 source selection and scripted calls; external assistants using MCP cannot run them. Even probe: true needs approval: connection operations cannot be approved for the whole conversation.

Desktop and web apps save connections with their preferences (connections in desktop prefs.json, rustgis.connections in web localStorage). The first load imports saved services, databases other than DuckDB files, STAC APIs and remembered S3 connections once, without changing the old lists. Legacy saved endpoint lists are no longer shown in the pane or the S3 dialog; use the imported named connections instead. Testing S3 can register or replace the session endpoint and credentials under the form's connection name, including a same-name session created in the S3 dialog. Cancel does not disconnect that login or restore the previous one. CLI and Python connections last only for the run.

items.title: Large files
items.text:
GeoPackage, GeoParquet, FlatGeobuf and (on the desktop) Shapefile files with more than 100,000 features are read in place rather than loaded whole, avoiding an in-memory copy of the entire dataset. The layer reads features in view in the background as the map moves, using spatial indexes: the GeoPackage R-tree, the FlatGeobuf packed R-tree, GeoParquet row-group bounding boxes, or a cached Shapefile R-tree built from the shapes' bounding boxes. When a local file's view holds more than 250,000 features (100,000 in the web app), the layer draws an evenly spread sample of them and its tooltip in Layers says so: zoom in to see them all. Remote files have lower limits (see Data formats). Smaller files load whole; layer.addData with "stream": true or false overrides the choice.

On the desktop, opening a large Shapefile for the first time scans its record headers to build a disposable SQLite index outside the dataset directory. Reopening an unchanged file reuses that index; its canonical path, size and modification time identify the cached generation. The record directory and R-tree stay on disk, with an 8 MiB SQLite page-cache target per open index and memory mapping disabled. Query results retain file order and the same sampling rules. Attributes and the .prj are still read from the source files.

Set RUSTGIS_SHP_CACHE to choose the cache directory and RUSTGIS_SHP_CACHE_MIB to choose the retained index budget (2048 MiB by default, clamped to 64–65536 MiB). Idle indexes are evicted in least-recently-used order. Open readers and builders hold operating-system leases, so another instance cannot evict their indexes; active files can temporarily exceed the budget. An index larger than the budget is session-only. Cache checkout and release reclaim abandoned builds and temporary indexes. A corrupt cache is rebuilt, and an unavailable cache directory falls back to the system temporary directory (a per-user directory on Unix). New Unix cache directories are created with mode 0700.
