Existing roots must belong to the effective user, forbid group/other writes, and have trusted parents; symlink roots are rejected. These checks also apply to configured locations. Unsafe locations fall back rather than changing their permissions. If neither location works, the Shapefile remains readable by scanning record headers without retaining a full in-memory index. Deleting idle cache files does not modify the dataset.

On the desktop, a GeoJSON FeatureCollection larger than 32 MB is read the same way, with no size limit: opening reads the file once, keeping each feature's place in it and its bounding box (a file over 256 MB through a buffer, so it is never held whole), and each view parses just the features it shows. A single feature, a bare geometry or TopoJSON is loaded whole.

A streamed layer works like any other for symbology, labels, pop-ups, selection and the attribute table (which lists the features read for the view). Geoprocessing tools, exports and Load All Features read the whole source, up to 2 million features (500,000 in the web app; a source that doesn't report its feature count must have fewer than that, since a read that reaches the limit is refused); a larger source is refused rather than processed as a sample. A GeoPackage, GeoParquet, FlatGeobuf or LAS/LAZ file is refused the same way when added without streaming (layer.addData with "stream": false) or given to a geoprocessing tool as a file path. If the source's feature count is known, an oversized whole read is refused before reading its features; an incomplete read is an error, not a successful sample. A tool given a streamed layer with a selection uses the selected features read for the view. Edits are refused, since the features are read again as the view moves: right-click the layer in Layers and choose Load All Features (layer.loadAll) to load it into memory and edit it. Projects save the layer's file path, not its features, and read the file again when they open; a browser upload is kept in the project.

File Features A view read GeoParquet, 0.1° grid (50 MB) 1.6 million polygons 183,000 in 0.15 s FlatGeobuf, the same grid (335 MB) 1.6 million polygons 183,000 in 0.11 s GeoPackage, the same grid (344 MB) 1.6 million polygons 183,000 in 0.18 s GeoParquet, global grid (190 MB) 6.5 million polygons a sample of 136,000 in 0.27 s

items.title: Streamed view memory
items.text:
Interaction windows share a retained-memory budget across all source layers in a map, including hidden layers: 128 MiB on the desktop and 48 MiB in the browser. The budget counts allocated row capacity, attribute strings, nested geometry buffers, projected geometry, extent arrays and optional display geometry. Complex records can therefore reduce the interaction sample even below the existing feature-count limit. Source ids, attributes and file order are retained; the sample is marked as incomplete. An individual feature that cannot fit produces a layer error instead of silently disappearing.

Projection is prepared with the window on the source worker. Optional thinned geometry uses the remaining budget, up to 64 MiB per layer; when it cannot fit, drawing uses the original projected geometry. Explicitly loaded layers retain their full source data and limit only their optional display caches.

This is a budget for installed interaction caches, not a process-RSS or GPU-memory cap. Provider decoding scratch, in-flight reads, shared snapshots and explicit full reads are outside it. The generic provider adapter probes a small sample and trims the returned window; it does not bound the provider's transient decoding allocations. Blocking map exports retain their original row limits and reread instead of reusing a budget-reduced interaction window. Full-source loading, analysis, editing, data exports and project serialization continue to use the original source data and existing read limits.

items.title: Rasters
items.text:
An elevation raster of the Sierra Nevada with shaded-relief symbology.

Add a GeoTIFF or an ASCII grid with Add Data, by dropping it on the window, or in the web app by picking it. Local ASCII grids can be up to 1 GiB; ASCII-grid uploads are limited to 256 MiB in the web app. A TIFF or PNG without coordinates opens as a scan to place with Georeference; see Supported Data Formats. An ASCII grid takes its coordinate system from a .prj file next to it (as a Shapefile does); otherwise, and always for uploads, it must be in longitude/latitude degrees. On the desktop, a GDAL .aux.xml file next to a raster (dem.tif.aux.xml or dem.aux.xml) names its bands from their descriptions, gives the no-data value when the file has none, and supplies the band statistics when only an overview of the raster is read. Its category names (GDAL's SetCategoryNames, one per value) label the classes in the legend of a Colormap or Unique Values layer; a value without a name shows the value itself. The band descriptions GDAL and rasterio write inside a GeoTIFF (its GDAL_METADATA tag) name its bands too, a sidecar's taking precedence. Exporting a raster opened from an overview writes that overview; the results of adding and of exporting it (layer.addData, share.exportRaster) give the full size as overviewOf, so scripts and the MCP server see it too. share.exportRaster writes an untiled GeoTIFF; with "cog": true it writes a cloud-optimised one: 512-pixel tiles compressed with Deflate, overviews (each half the size of the last, down to one tile), and every directory ahead of the tiles, so a reader fetches the header once and then only the tiles it needs. Overviews are averaged, except for a palette raster or one with a few whole-number classes, whose overviews take a pixel so that no class is invented; a palette keeps its colour table, though not the table's transparency, which a TIFF colour table can't hold (GDAL drops it too). The file is classic TIFF when it would fit in 4 GiB even uncompressed and BigTIFF when it might not. Exported to a file it is written tile by tile, never held whole in memory (the browser builds it in memory to download it). GeoTIFFs may be regular or cloud-optimised: grey, RGB(A), palette (coloured by the file's colour table, as land cover such as the NLCD is) or multiband, of any pixel type, tiled or striped, and compressed with Deflate, LZW, PackBits, JPEG or Zstandard. JPEG-compressed YCbCr images are shown as RGB; other YCbCr and CMYK images aren't read. A rotated or skewed image is resampled to a north-up grid as it is read. The coordinate system is an EPSG code, or the file's own projection described in its GeoKeys (Albers, Lambert conformal conic, transverse Mercator, Mercator, Lambert azimuthal, stereographic, equirectangular, sinusoidal and others), which an exported GeoTIFF keeps. A raster too large to hold in memory (more than 120 million samples, 32 million in the web app) opens from its largest overview that fits; one without overviews opens as an overview made as it is read, a strip or tile at a time (every second, fourth… pixel each way), so reading it takes as long as decoding the whole file once. A cloud-optimised GeoTIFF added by its web address is read in place instead, a tile at a time (see Files on the web).

The web app opens a picked or dropped file of up to 256 MB whole. A larger GeoTIFF is read a part at a time instead: its header, then only the tiles of the overview it opens from. A cloud-optimised file opens however large it is, as long as those parts fit in 256 MB (a 436 MB EnMAP hyperspectral scene reads about 20 MB, the 1.6 GB NLCD land cover about 14 MB). The parts read are what a saved project keeps. A file that isn't cloud-optimised (in strips, or without overviews) needs most of itself, and past 256 MB the web app says to open it in the desktop app.

With a raster layer selected in Layers, the Style and Data tabs show its groups:

Tab › Group Controls Style › Visibility Range, Effects Scale range, transparency Style › Rendering Symbology: Stretch, RGB, Classify, Unique Values, Colormap, Shaded Relief; Stretch Type: None, Minimum Maximum, Custom Min/Max (your own bounds, one pair per colour channel on an RGB layer), Percent Clip, Standard Deviation, Histogram Equalize; DRA (stretch the pixels in view); Resampling (nearest or bilinear); Band Combination (natural colour, colour infrared, or any bands) Style › Enhancement Brightness, contrast, gamma Data Raster information (size, bands, statistics, coordinate system) and Export Raster (GeoTIFF)

Masking, at the foot of the Symbology pane (raster.mask), hides pixel values from view without changing the data: values to draw as no data (a background of 0 or −9999 the file doesn't flag, QA flags, land cover classes such as 0, 254, 255), and values outside, or inside, a range. The stretch, class breaks and legend then use only the values shown. Clear mask shows every value again; the mask is saved with the project.

A single-band raster of continuous values (an elevation model, a temperature grid, an index such as NDVI) is first drawn as a grey stretch, black to white (matplotlib's gray), clipping 0.5 % at each end. To draw such rasters your own way, style one with the Stretch symbology, then click Save as Default under Resampling: rasters added from then on, opened files and analysis results (a slope, an NDVI) alike, take its color scheme, inversion, stretch type and resampling (a Custom Min/Max stretch is in one raster's own units, so it can't be saved). Reset Default goes back to the grey stretch. The app keeps the setting with its preferences, for every project; colour images, rasters with their own color table and rasters of a few categories keep their own look. Scripts use raster.setDefaultStyle, e.g. {"ramp": "Viridis", "invert": false, "stretch": "standardDeviation", "n": 2, "resampling": "bilinear"}, {"fromLayer": true} or {"reset": true}; with no parameters it returns the current setting.

Tiles of one dataset drawn as separate layers each stretch over their own values, which shows as steps where they meet. raster.stretch with {"like": "<layer>"} gives a layer the value range of another layer's stretch as fixed bounds, so the tiles match; {"type": "custom", "min": …, "max": …} sets the bounds yourself.

Clicking a raster with the Explore tool shows its pixel values. Projects remember a raster's file path relative to the project and reopen it; rasters added in the browser are stored inside the project.

items.title: Zarr stores
items.text:
Home › Add › Add Data › Zarr… (layer.addZarr) adds a variable of a Zarr store (format 2 or 3), the multidimensional arrays climate and Earth-observation data are kept in: give the store's web address, or (on the desktop) its folder, and Connect lists its variables (raster.zarrInfo). A variable's map is its latitude/longitude (or y/x) dimensions; its other dimensions, such as time or pressure level, are picked a step at a time with a slider, labelled by their coordinates (CF time units as dates, the noleap and 360_day model calendars included). Add to Map adds that step as a raster layer named after the variable and step (tas 2014-07-15), and the dialog stays open to add others. Only the chunks the step needs are fetched, a few at a time, in the background.

Stores are read in pure Rust, in the web app as well as on the desktop: Zarr 2 with consolidated metadata (.zmetadata, as xarray writes) and Zarr 3 (zarr.json, sharded arrays too), chunks compressed with blosc (LZ4, zlib or zstd, byte- or bit-shuffled), zlib, gzip, zstd or LZ4, of integer or float values, in C or Fortran order. A sharded array's shards are fetched whole. _FillValue, missing_value and a Zarr 2 array's fill value are no data; a Zarr 3 array's fill value isn't: chunks never written are left empty, but chunks missing from inside a shard show the fill value. scale_factor and add_offset are applied. The coordinates must be evenly spaced (a curvilinear grid isn't read); longitude/latitude grids of 0–360° are turned to -180–180°, and projected ones take their coordinate system from the variable's grid mapping (crs_wkt, spatial_ref, an EPSG code) or "crs". Blosclz-compressed and transposed chunks and shards inside shards aren't read yet, and say so. A store by web address must allow the browser to fetch it (CORS) for the web app; Google Cloud's CMIP6 bucket does, ARCO-ERA5's doesn't (the desktop reads both).

rustgis-cli run --cmd 'layer.addZarr={"url":"https://storage.googleapis.com/gcp-public-data-arco-era5/ar/1959-2022-full_37-1h-0p25deg-chunk-1.zarr-v2","variable":"2m_temperature","index":{"time":539100}}'

Follow the time slider (desktop; layer.addZarr with "time": true) adds the variable as one layer whose step is the time slider's. The slider turns on over the variable's dates when it is off, and the layer shows the last of its steps in the slider's window, or nothing when none falls in it. Moving or playing the slider reads that step's slice (only its chunks), keeping the last eight read. A web store's next two steps are read ahead in the background. The stretch is fixed at the first slice's range, so a colour means the same value at every step, and Export writes an animation of it. An axis longer than the slider's 20,000 steps (hourly ERA5) takes a period with "start" and "end"; given neither (as the dialog adds it), the layer takes 20,000 steps from the one picked. The project keeps such a layer by its store (a folder or a web address) and selection, not as a slice, and reads the slider's step again when it opens.

rustgis-cli run --cmd 'layer.addZarr={"path":"air.zarr","variable":"t","time":true}' --cmd 'time.export={"path":"t.gif"}'

View › Time Series (desktop; zarr.series) reads a Zarr variable's values through time at a point. Pick a Zarr layer, then Pick a Point on the map. A layer that follows the time slider gives its period, a slice the whole axis, and "start"/"end" any other. Only the chunks holding that point's cell are read. A store chunked one step at a time, such as ARCO-ERA5's map-oriented copy, reads a chunk per step: about 4,000 steps at most, so a long axis needs a shorter period. The chart draws up to six points as lines and marks the time slider's step, and a click on it takes the slider to that date. Export CSV… writes the date and value of each point.

rustgis-cli run --cmd 'zarr.series={"path":"air.zarr","variable":"t","lon":-55.7,"lat":-12.5}'

Summarise over time (in the Time Series pane; zarr.reduce) makes a raster of one statistic of a Zarr variable's steps: mean, min, max, sum, std (the population standard deviation), count of values, or countAbove a threshold (days above 30 °C, say). It reads a layer's period by default, else the "start"/"end" given, and "months" keeps one season across years ([12, 1, 2]). Slices are read one at a time and folded into running totals (12 to 20 bytes a cell, for grids of up to 32 million cells), so memory depends on the grid, not on the period: at most 20,000 steps, with progress and Cancel in the app. A cell keeps no value when it had fewer values than "minValid" (a share, 0 by default) of the steps read; with the default, count and countAbove give 0 where a cell never had a value (land in an ocean variable, say), and a "minValid" above 0 leaves such cells empty. The layer is named after what it holds (tas mean 1991-01-01–2020-12-31) and kept in the project as a GeoTIFF.

rustgis-cli run --cmd 'zarr.reduce={"path":"air.zarr","variable":"t","stat":"mean","months":[12,1,2]}'

A single step (a layer that doesn't follow the slider) from a store in a folder is saved in the project by its folder and slice (2m_temperature[time=539100]) and read again when the project opens, as Add Data on the folder does (its first variable); a single step from a store by web address is kept in the project as the slice read. ?zarr=<address> in a web app link opens the dialog on a store.

items.title: Project items
items.text:
RustGIS saves pieces of a project as files you can share and reuse:

Item Extension Made with Opened with Map file (a map with its data) .rgismap Publish › Save As › Map File Command Search (map.import), or drop it on the window Layer file (a layer with its symbology) .rgislyr Publish › Save As › Layer File Add Data Styles (saved symbology) .rgisstyle Style › Styles › New Style, then Publish › Save As › Style Items Style › Styles › Add Style File Color ramps .rgisramp (also reads QGIS .xml/.qml, GDAL color .txt and GMT .cpt) Publish › Save As › Color Ramps, or by hand Style › Styles › Add Color Ramp File Project template (the setup without features) .rgistemplate Publish › Save As, or Command Search (project.saveTemplate) Command Search (project.fromTemplate) Project package (the project, with linked raster files embedded while they fit) .rgispkg Publish › Package › Project Project › Open, or drop it on the window Map package / mobile map package .rgismpk Publish › Package › Map or Mobile Map Open the package as a project, or drop it on the window Results package (geoprocessing history and outputs) .rgisgpk Publish › Package › Results any zip tool Task (guided command steps) .rgistask Analyze › Task, Publish › Save As › Task Item Analyze › Task › Import Task Bookmarks (as longitude, latitude and scale) .rgisbookmarks Home › Navigate › Bookmarks › Export Bookmarks Home › Navigate › Bookmarks › Import Bookmarks Layout .rgislayout Publish › Save Layout File Home › New Layout › Import Layout

Packages are zip files. Project and map packages can newly embed a combined 512 MiB of linked raster files on the desktop (128 MiB in the web app); a raster that doesn't fit stays linked. Already embedded uploads are retained. Local streamed vector files, databases and web layers stay linked to their sources. A mobile map package keeps only the visible layers and simplifies their geometry, for phones and tablets. Styles can also be imported from the layers of a layer file, map file or project. Data › Layer Templates adds empty layers with ready-made schemas (places, routes, areas, observations…) to draw into. Add Folder connects a folder to the Browser, which also lists the project's layouts, styles and tasks. A task's steps each run a command; New Task From History turns the geoprocessing history into a task you can replay.

Saved projects, map and layer files, and packages keep no password, key, token or signature in layer web addresses. The open project keeps them for this session. RustGIS remembers the 32 most recent distinct saved snapshots whose addresses needed stripping. Opening a plain .rgis file whose bytes exactly match one of those snapshots restores its secrets; saving more distinct snapshots evicts the oldest. Changed files, packages, imports and files saved by another process never restore secrets. After a snapshot is evicted or RustGIS closes, add those layers again with their credentials.

items.title: Complete streamed Shapefile rendering
items.text:
The CPU renderer traverses a streamed Shapefile in source order instead of painting only its interaction sample. Shapes and attributes arrive in chunks targeting 8 MiB of owned feature storage; projection and display geometry are temporary copies of one chunk. Whole-file imports, loading for editing and other providers retain their existing read APIs. An indivisible row exceeding the chunk target is emitted alone, preserving its full geometry. A zero budget reports an error.

Styles, definition queries, display filters and label classes use the same painter as an in-memory layer. The renderer chooses geometry simplification from statistics over the whole layer, accumulates point bins across chunks, applies transparency and blend once per layer, and draws selection highlights after the whole layer. Labels share the existing global priority, stable tie ordering, collision rules and 20,000-candidate placement limit. Screen rendering and PNG/layout exports share this traversal. Live redraws of a streamed Shapefile therefore also read the complete source; line/polygon layers currently make an additional statistics pass. Interaction windows remain byte-budgeted, but they are not a shortcut for this complete painter, so redraws can be I/O intensive on large files.

Native flat extrusions use a private disposable SQLite ordering workspace (2 MiB page-cache target, memory mapping disabled, 4 GiB database ceiling), with a global shadow pass followed by globally sorted solids. It is removed when rendering finishes. Failure or incomplete traversal does not publish a partial successful frame. This workspace is not a reusable index.

This is not a fixed bound on total renderer memory: raster targets, label candidates and the existing combined polygon-mask path have separate costs. Upright perspective point markers and polygon extrusions retain the complete upstream depth renderer through an isolated full-source snapshot. Upright points require a known source total of at most 50,000 rows; larger or unknown totals use complete ground-marker traversal, independent of the current interaction-window size. Plain fills, lines and mask sources continue complete chunk traversal per band, including terrain bands; they do not consume that snapshot's feature budget. Retained complete-source feature storage across the snapshot has a separate budget (512 MiB natively, 192 MiB in the browser). Exceeding it fails the whole frame with a source diagnostic, without sampling or truncating features; raster targets, derived geometry caches and decoding scratch are outside that budget. Flat line/polygon rendering makes a statistics pass before painting and currently reads the entire source, so it trades additional I/O for complete rendering and predictable chunk storage. Geometry preprocessing and GPU preparation are separate optimizations.

items.title: Creating features
items.text:
Edit › Create draws new points, lines and polygons into the layer selected in Layers: click once for a point, or click each vertex and double-click to finish a line or polygon (Esc cancels). Delete (Del) removes the selected features across the map's layers. Edit attributes in the attribute table (Ctrl+T): double-click a cell to change it. Data › Data Design (and Data › Fields) adds and deletes fields and calculates a field from an expression; Calculate Geometry (in the attribute table's toolbar) fills a new or existing numeric field with each feature's area, perimeter, length or X/Y coordinate, in the units you choose, for all features or the selected ones. Length and perimeter include feet and miles; area includes square feet (ft2), acres (ac) and square miles (mi2). Every edit is one undo step.

Undo (Ctrl+Z) and Redo (Ctrl+Y or Ctrl+Shift+Z) restore project changes, not just feature edits; use Cmd instead of Ctrl on macOS. While typing in a text field, those shortcuts undo or redo the typing instead. Saving keeps the undo history; opening or creating a project clears it. Undo does not reverse files already written by an export.

items.title: Modifying features
items.text:
Edit Vertices: drag a square handle to move a vertex, a round one to add a vertex.

The Edit tab's Edit button turns feature editing on or off for the map; with it off, feature creation, geometry changes and attribute edits are disabled. The Editing pane (Settings, Templates, Status, Modify) holds the rest. Its Distance units selector sets the units used for Move and constant elevation. The choice is remembered independently of the live map's measurement units. The entered numbers are interpreted in the selected units when you click Move, Constant or Apply elevation. The current elevation stays in effect while you edit the value or choose units; click Apply elevation to apply the new inputs.

  • Modify: move the selected features by distances east and north, rotate them, scale them, merge them (polygons are unioned), explode multipart features, split a line where you click, and flip line direction. A single point turns and scales on itself, so Rotate and Scale leave points (text graphics included) as they are: with only points selected they change nothing, say so, and add no undo step. Edit › Tools lists every editing tool.
  • Edit Vertices (Edit › Features): reshape the selected features on the map. Their vertices show as square handles and each edge has a round midpoint handle. Drag a vertex to move it; drag a midpoint, or click an edge, to insert a vertex; click a vertex and press Del to remove it (a line keeps at least two vertices, a polygon ring three). Clicking elsewhere selects the feature there (Shift adds it). Multipart features and polygon holes work the same way, dragged vertices snap when snapping is on, and each move, insertion or deletion is one undo step. Esc finishes. From scripts and the command line, edit.vertex does the same to one vertex and edit.setGeometry (Set Geometry) replaces a feature's whole shape.
  • Feature templates: named default values for new features, made from a selected feature; the Create tool uses the chosen template.
  • Snapping (Edit › Snapping): new and dragged vertices snap to nearby vertices, edges and line ends of visible feature layers at the current scale (magenta marker; graphics and rasters are not targets). Vertices and ends take priority over edges within the tolerance. Snapping starts off; its vertex, edge and end options start on. Both Point features and individual MultiPoint members use the vertex option; they supply neither edges nor line ends. Dragging a Point or MultiPoint member excludes its entire source feature. The tolerance is how near, in screen pixels, a vertex must come to snap (10 by default, 1 to 100): edit.snapping={"on": true, "tolerancePx": 12, "edge": false} (without "on" it toggles snapping, even when other options are supplied). edit.snap={"lon":12.5,"lat":41.9} queries the current snap target without editing a feature.
  • Settings: Show Vertices marks the vertices of the selected features even when Edit Vertices isn't on (edit.settings={"showVertices": true}).
  • Elevation: new features get a z attribute, constant or sampled from a raster surface at the feature's label point; this is not a change to its geometry's coordinates.
  • Ground to grid: a scale factor and rotation applied to entered distances and directions (Move, and edit.traverse, which draws a line or polygon from distances and bearings).
  • Topology: rules (must not overlap, must not have gaps, must not self-intersect, must not have dangles, must be covered by); Validate lists the errors, and clicking one zooms to it.
  • Status: features added, changed and deleted per layer since the last save.

items.title: Moving shared polygon vertices
items.text:
Edit › Features › Shared Vertices opts polygon moves into linked editing. It starts off, lasts only for the current app session, and is not saved in projects or preferences. With it on, dragging a polygon vertex moves every polygon vertex in that layer stored at exactly the same original coordinate, including unselected and filtered-out rows, point-only contacts, other polygon parts and holes. Unrelated polygons touching by chance at that point move together too; turn the switch off to move just the source feature. Inserting and deleting vertices, and moving line or point vertices, keep their existing behaviour. Changing the switch cancels a held drag.

The command uses row positions and the same vertex addresses as edit.vertex:

{"layer":"Parcels","row":0,"part":0,"ring":0,"index":3,"lon":12.5,"lat":41.9}

Run these parameters with edit.moveSharedVertex. It returns the source part, ring and index, plus modified: the number of features whose geometry or attributes actually changed. Every matched feature runs through attribute rules and archiving in one transaction; a rejection rolls back the whole edit. A successful command is one undo step. As with edit.vertex, a direct same-position command still runs the rules and records an edit, even if modified is zero. Undo retains cumulative edit counts. Streamed layers require Load All Features first.

This moves coincident vertices, not every shared boundary. For a boundary stored as P–Q on one polygon and P–R–Q on its neighbour, moving Q moves the two stored Q vertices but leaves R in place. It does not remap intermediate vertices, insert missing ones or refuse the edit because vertex densities differ; the two boundaries can separate. There is no tolerance or nearby-coordinate matching. Use the mustNotOverlap and mustNotHaveGaps topology rules, then Edit › Manage Edits › Topology › Error Inspector (validate) (topology.validate) to inspect a coverage.

items.title: Distance units in commands
items.text:
edit.move, edit.traverse and constant edit.elevation accept "units": "Feet", "Meters", "Kilometers" or "Miles" (case insensitive). Omitting units keeps the existing metre default. All traverse legs use the command's units. Conversion to metres happens before ground-to-grid corrections and distance limits; stored elevation stays in metres. Feet mean international feet (0.3048 m), independently of the source CRS's units.

For example, edit.move={"dx":500,"dy":0,"units":"Feet"} moves selected features 152.4 metres east.

items.title: Data design
items.text:
The Data tab's Data Design pane keeps attributes valid, on every edit (creating, pasting, attribute edits, Calculate Field):

  • Domains: coded values (code=description) or a numeric range for a field.
  • Subtypes: an integer field's codes, each with a name and default values for new features; the layer is symbolized by subtype.
  • Attribute rules: calculations (a field set from an expression on every insert and update) and constraints (a SQL condition every feature must meet).
  • Contingent values: the combinations of values allowed across fields.
  • Archiving: keeps every edit with its time; restore the layer as it was minutes ago.
  • Relationships: link two layers by key fields; Related Data selects the rows related to the selection.

items.title: Clipboard and pop-ups
items.text:
Copy (Ctrl+C) and Cut (Ctrl+X) take selected features from one layer: the active layer if it has a selection, otherwise the first layer with selected features. Paste (Ctrl+V) adds them to the layer selected in Layers, matching fields by name and converting values to the destination field types; unmatched fields stay empty. Geometry types must match. Paste Special adds them as a new layer instead. Copied features also go on the system clipboard as GeoJSON, so they can be pasted into another RustGIS window or a text editor, and GeoJSON copied elsewhere pastes into RustGIS. Copy Path copies the selected layer's data source path.

Whole-layer copying is separate: use Copy Layer or Copy Group and Paste Layer in the Layers pane's context menus to preserve symbology and other layer settings, including when moving layers between maps.

Pop-ups (Home › Navigate) choose which layers a click with Explore identifies: the topmost layer under the click, every visible layer, only selectable layers, only the layer selected in Layers, or nothing. The pop-up lists every feature under the click in those layers, overlapping ones included (up to 100): step through them with ‹ ›. The feature shown is the one selected. The magnifier in the pop-up's header zooms to it. Long feature titles and layer names are shortened with an ellipsis to leave room for the header controls; hover over either name to read it in full.

The topmost and visible modes also identify the features of vector tile layers under the click: PMTiles and MBTiles archives and vector tiles added as data (not catalog basemaps or MapLibre styles), beneath the map's own layers. Each shows its tile layer and source layer (firenze › buildings) and its attributes; tile features can't be selected or zoomed to.

They ask WMS layers too (WMS tile layers that are shown and, as far as their service's capabilities say, queryable): RustGIS sends the service a standard GetFeatureInfo request for the point (WMS 1.3.0 or 1.1.1, as in the layer's address), asking for GeoJSON when it offers it, else GML, other XML, plain text or HTML. While it asks, the pop-up says "Asking the map service…". When something else is under the click, it waits up to 4 seconds for every layer asked to answer, then shows the features found and answered together, in drawing order; answers that come later join it as they arrive. When nothing else is, it waits until an answer has features, and closes once every layer asked has answered (or failed) without any. When the service answers with an error in that format (swisstopo's MapServer can't write some of its layers as GeoJSON, but answers them in GML), RustGIS asks again in the next format it offers, and keeps asking that layer in it for the rest of the session. Topmost asks only the highest WMS layer that can be asked at the point (one that covers it and is queryable), and only when it is drawn over the feature found, or nothing was found; its features then take that feature's place. A project doesn't save the request: a WMS layer from a project reads its service's capabilities again on its first click (once for all the map's layers from that service), so until then Topmost takes it as one that can be asked. identify lists the requests in featureInfo, and identify.featureInfo reads an answer (or, on the command line, asks the service and waits).

A tile layer's row in Layers can be clicked to select it, as a map layer's can (map.selectTiles; no map layer is active then, and clicking one ends it). With Selected in Layers, a click on the map then identifies that tile layer alone: a WMS layer is asked as above, and a vector tile layer, archive or MapLibre style lists its features. This works for catalog basemaps and MapLibre styles too, which the topmost and visible modes leave out.

items.title: Expressions
items.text:
One expression language serves every place that reads values from features:

  • Select By Attributes, Definition Query, display filters, label classes, attribute constraints and reports use an expression as a condition (a WHERE clause): a feature matches when the expression is true.
  • Calculate Field and calculation attribute rules use an expression as a value, stored in the field after conversion to the field's type.
  • Symbols by expression take a value per feature: a marker's size, the fill and outline colours, the outline width and a marker's angle.
pop_est > 100000000 AND continent = 'Asia'
name LIKE 'S%' OR iso_a3 IN ('FRA', 'DEU', 'ITA')
"name" || ' (' || to_string(round(pop_est / 1e6)) || ' M)'
CASE WHEN pop_est > 1e8 THEN 'large' WHEN pop_est > 1e7 THEN 'medium' ELSE 'small' END
scale_linear(pop_est, 0, 1e9, 2, 12)

items.title: Grammar
items.text:
Keywords and function names are not case sensitive. Rules are listed from the loosest binding to the tightest; [ x ] is optional, { x } repeats zero or more times, | separates choices.

expression = or ;
or         = and { "OR" and } ;
and        = not { "AND" not } ;
not        = "NOT" not | comparison ;
comparison = concat [ compare_op concat
                    | "IS" [ "NOT" ] "NULL"
                    | [ "NOT" ] ( "LIKE" | "ILIKE" ) concat
                    | [ "NOT" ] "IN" "(" expression { "," expression } ")"
                    | [ "NOT" ] "BETWEEN" concat "AND" concat ] ;
compare_op = "=" | "==" | "<>" | "!=" | "<" | "<=" | ">" | ">=" ;
concat     = sum { "||" sum } ;
sum        = product { ( "+" | "-" ) product } ;
product    = unary { ( "*" | "/" | "%" ) unary } ;
unary      = ( "-" | "+" ) unary | power ;
power      = primary [ "^" unary ] ;
primary    = number | text | "TRUE" | "FALSE" | "NULL"
           | field | variable | call | case | "(" expression ")" ;
call       = name "(" [ expression { "," expression } ] ")" ;
case       = "CASE" [ expression ]
             "WHEN" expression "THEN" expression
             { "WHEN" expression "THEN" expression }
             [ "ELSE" expression ] "END" ;

number     = digits [ "." digits ] [ exponent ] | "." digits [ exponent ] ;
exponent   = ( "e" | "E" ) [ "+" | "-" ] digits ;
text       = "'" { character | "''" } "'" ;
field      = name | '"' { character | '""' } '"' | "!" { character } "!" ;
variable   = "@" name | "$" name ;
name       = ( letter | digit | "_" ) { letter | digit | "_" } ;   (* not starting with a digit *)

So a OR b AND c is a OR (b AND c), NOT a = b is NOT (a = b), 1 + 2 * 3 is 7, -2 ^ 2 is −4 and 2 ^ 3 ^ 2 is 512 (^ groups from the right). A comparison takes one operator: write a < b AND b < c, not a < b < c.

items.title: Values
items.text:
Write Meaning 42, 3.5, 1e6, .5 Numbers; whole numbers are integers 'text', 'it''s' Text in single quotes; two quotes stand for one TRUE, FALSE, NULL Booleans and the missing value pop_est, "Pop Est", !Pop Est! A field, by name, ignoring letter case; quote a name with spaces, punctuation or the name of a keyword ("OR", "null") @map_scale, $scale The scale denominator of the map being drawn: set in symbols by expression, null in queries and Calculate Field @row_number The feature's position in the layer, from 1 $id The feature's id

An unknown field, variable or function is an error that names it.

items.title: Operators
items.text:
Operator Result + - * / Arithmetic; / always divides exactly (7 / 2 is 3.5) % Remainder ^ Power \|\| Joins the two values as text; null when either is null = <> < <= > >= Comparison; == and != are also accepted LIKE, ILIKE Text pattern: % matches any run of characters, _ one character IN (…) Equal to one of the values BETWEEN a AND b >= a AND <= b IS NULL, IS NOT NULL Whether the value is missing AND OR NOT Logic

Rules shared by all of them:

  • Comparing numbers and text. A number and text that reads as a number compare as numbers ('12' = 12 is true). Two texts compare as text, ignoring letter case, even when both read as numbers (name = 'paris' matches Paris; '10' < '9'; LIKE ignores case too).
  • Arithmetic reads text as a number when it is one ('12' + 1 is 13). + joins text that isn't (name + ' km'); -, *, / on such text give null.
  • Nulls. Arithmetic with a null gives null. A comparison with a null is unknown: it matches neither pop > 100 nor NOT pop > 100; IS NULL tests for it. AND is false when either side is false and OR true when either side is true, whatever the other side is.
  • Errors give null: a division by zero, the square root of a negative number, a result too large to represent.
  • IN compares with each value as = does; a NULL in the list matches nothing, so x NOT IN (1, NULL) is true for 2.
  • As a condition, a value that isn't true or false counts as true when it is a non-zero number or non-empty text.

items.title: Functions
items.text: Function Result if(condition, a[, b]) a when the condition is true, otherwise b (or null) coalesce(a, b, …) The first value that isn't null nullif(a, b) Null when a equals b, otherwise a abs(x) Absolute value round(x[, places]) Rounded half away from zero to places decimals (0 by default; negative rounds to tens, hundreds…) floor(x), ceil(x) Rounded down, up sqrt(x), exp(x), ln(x), log10(x) Square root, eˣ, natural and base-10 logarithm pi() π min(a, b, …), max(a, b, …) The smallest, largest number; values that aren't numbers are skipped clamp(low, x, high) x kept within low…high; null when low is above high scale_linear(x, d0, d1, r0, r1) x mapped from the domain d0…d1 to the range r0…r1, clamped to the domain scale_exp(x, d0, d1, r0, r1, exponent) As scale_linear, along a curve: 0.5 grows fast then slowly, 2 slowly then fast to_string(x) x as text to_int(x), to_real(x) x as a whole number (cut toward zero), as a decimal number; null if it isn't a number length(s) Number of characters upper(s), lower(s), trim(s) Upper case, lower case, without surrounding spaces substr(s, start[, length]) Part of s from character start (1 is the first; negative counts from the end); a negative length leaves that many characters off the end left(s, n), right(s, n) The first, last n characters replace(s, find, with) Every find in s replaced by with concat(a, b, …) The values joined as text, nulls skipped color_rgb(r, g, b), color_rgba(r, g, b, a) A colour as the text 'r,g,b' or 'r,g,b,a', each channel 0–255

items.title: Limits
items.text: A number too large to represent (1e999) is an error. An expression is at most 10,000 characters and nests at most 64 levels: each parenthesis, function call, NOT, sign before something other than a number, ^ and CASE counts (a CASE two). One chain of AND, OR, ||, +/- or *///%, and the arms of one CASE, take at most 256 terms; a function at most 32 arguments; an IN list as many as fit. Text an expression makes is cut at 64 KiB, and a LIKE pattern longer than 10,000 characters matches nothing. A LIKE that would take more than about 16 million steps to match (a very long text against a pattern of many %s) is unknown.

items.title: Calculate Field
items.text: Calculate Field also takes the forms its earlier calculator took: a field name with spaces written bare (Pop Est * 2) still works when the text isn't a valid expression, and on a layer with a field named true, false or null such forms keep reading it as the field (in other expressions, quote it: "null"). Text that starts and ends with a quote but holds more quotes now reads as an expression: 'it''s' is it's and 'a' || 'b' is ab, where both were taken as the text between the outer quotes.

items.title: Layouts
items.text:
A page layout with a map frame, title, legend, north arrow and scale bar.

Home › New Layout adds a page layout (Letter, Legal, Tabloid or A5 to A0, landscape or portrait) with a map frame, title, legend, north arrow, scale bar and a dynamic credits line. The command layout.new also accepts custom width and height in millimetres and "template": "blank". Layouts open as tabs next to the maps; while one is open, its groups lead the Publish tab:

  • Publication layouts: Home › New Layout › Publication Layout builds a finished sheet or figure of the map view in one step, with layout.publication behind it:
  • Sheets (A4, A3 or A2, portrait or landscape): a frame and margin, the title and subtitle, the map, and a footer of two boxed columns (sources, and the cartographic reference; one with nothing in it is left out, the other taking the width) with a note and the authorship under them. Text sizes follow the sheet: an A3's are 1.41 times an A4's. Given its size alone ("a4", the default, "a3" or "a2"), a sheet is turned to portrait or landscape, whichever the map comes out larger on: the area's extent east to west against north to south, on the map's projection, with the room the style leaves the map. The result names the profile chosen ("profile": "a4-landscape"); give it with its orientation ("a4-portrait") to have the other.
  • Figures for a journal (90, 140 or 190 mm wide, as tall as the map's shape asks) or a thesis (160 × 225 or 160 × 110 mm): the map edge to edge with a line of its projection and datum under it, at 7 pt. A figure's title and sources belong in its caption, so they are left out, and the result says so.
  • The map: the extent given (or the view) fitted north-up, without tilt, at a round scale, two significant figures, rounded up so it still fits within the strips the graticule's labels take inside the frame. A graticule's step follows the extent (2° for a state, 15′ for a city), with labels on every edge of a sheet. The north arrow, the legend (sized to what it lists), the scale bar with the numeric scale under it and the locator sit in the frame's corners, clear of the graticule's labels. Each takes the corner where it covers the least of what the map draws (its layers and labels, not the basemap), so a legend leaves a corner the data fills; when it makes no difference they keep theirs: the locator at the top left, the arrow at the top right, the legend at the bottom left and the scale at the bottom right. With more surrounds than free corners, one warning names those left on the data, to move by hand if that matters (data under every corner alike, such as a context layer filling the frame, isn't worth a warning); two that overlap (a frame too small) are said too. The top visible raster gets a colorbar beneath the vector legend if its renderer has a colour scale; RGB and untinted hillshade do not. If the legend or colorbar cannot fit, the result warns about clipping or resizing. A streamed layer still loading gets a fixed-size legend to adjust by hand.
  • Decimal comma: "decimal": "," prints the graticule, scale bar and colorbar numbers and {scale} with a decimal comma and points between thousands (0,05, 1:6.300.000). layout.page={"decimal": ","} sets it on any layout; "." restores decimal points. This changes generated numbers, not numbers typed into text.
  • Texts: the title, subtitle, footer lines and authorship are measured with the layout's font (the title and headings bold, as drawn) and wrapped to their box, so none runs past it, and each box grows to hold them. {projection}, {datum} and {grid} are filled from the map when the layout is made. {date} and the other dynamic text tokens stay live. The reference defaults to the projection, datum and graticule, and the authorship to "Made with RustGIS · {date}" ("author": "" leaves it out). headings renames the two columns.
  • The locator (at the frame's top left unless the data is there): "locator": "globe" (a sheet's default) adds a separate globe map with simplified copies of the map's visible polygon layers held in the project. Streamed layers, rasters, points, lines and labels are left out. It uses the map's basemap, not its web tiles, in a round frame, the globe nearly filling it and the area outlined in red; "inset" shows the surrounding region (about four times the area across) on the map itself, outlined the same way; "none" (a figure's default) leaves it out. The legend stops short of it; a frame with no room for a legend beside it leaves the legend out, with a warning. Undo takes the globe's map away with the layout; a globe map no layout shows any more (its layout deleted) is replaced by the next sheet's rather than left beside it, which a warning says.
  • The style ("style", on any sheet, portrait or landscape): "classic" (the default) sets the title over the map and the footer's boxes under it; "banner" puts the title and subtitle in a band of the accent colour across the top, the title in white; "panel" sets the map at the left and a pale panel at the right with the title, subtitle, locator and legend, and the sources and reference at its foot, the note across the bottom; "editorial" sets the title large in serif and a column at the right under a rule, with a heading (the third of headings), the note, the locator and the legend; "modular" sets cards with rounded corners on a light page: the map in one, the locator and the legend in one each beside it, the sources and reference in tinted ones under them; "poster" colours the whole page, sets the title and subtitle in light text across the top, the map in a light card and the footer in darker blocks with amber headings. "accent" (#RRGGBB) colours the band, the panel's tint, the headings and rules, and a poster's page (a deep brown, green or blue by default). A figure leaves the style to its caption. In the menu, each sheet opens a list of the six styles, each saying what it looks like, in its default accent ("accent" in the command picks another).
  • Every element is an ordinary one, to move or restyle afterwards. The command returns element IDs for layout.update, and warnings. Running it again with another profile makes another layout of the same map.
layout.publication={"profile": "a4-portrait", "extent": [-46.8, -11.6, -38.5, -2.2],
  "title": "PIAUÍ", "subtitle": "Greening and browning of vegetation: NDVI trend, 2001–2025",
  "sources": ["NDVI: MOD13Q1 v6.1 (NASA LP DAAC), via the Brazil Data Cube (INPE)", "Boundaries: IBGE 2022"],
  "note": "Only cells with a significant trend (p < 0.05) are coloured."}
  • Map frames: rectangle, circle and ellipse frames, or polygon and lasso frames drawn on the page. Each frame shows a map of the project at its own centre and scale. Turn on Pan/Zoom Map (Map Frames group, or a frame's properties) to drag inside frames to pan their maps and turn the wheel to zoom them about the pointer; Esc turns it off. Without it, Shift-drag a frame to pan its map. Double-click a frame to match the map view, or set the scale in its properties: from the whole world down to site plans at 1:20, finds at 1:1 and 2:1 (a scale of 1:0.5). A frame can be turned and tilted like the map view: a new frame, or one matched to the view, takes the view's bearing and pitch, and Bearing and Pitch in its properties (or layout.update with bearing and pitch) set them. Its north arrows turn with it. Grid draws a labelled graticule over a frame; Extent Indicator outlines another frame's extent (an overview map).
  • Extent indicators: the Extent Indicator section of an overview frame's properties sets the outline's Color and Line width (red and 2 pt to begin with), so it can sit quietly on a muted page, and Remove Extent Indicator takes it away. Scripts set the same with color and width on layout.addElement (kind extentIndicator), or layout.update with "extentIndicator": {"color": "#555555", "width": 1} (false removes it).
  • Grids: the Grid section of a frame's properties turns the grid on and sets its Interval in degrees (Auto picks one from the frame's extent), its Style (full lines across the frame, ticks along its neatline only, or both, with the Tick length), its colour and Line width, and its labels: decimal degrees (112.5°W, as many decimals as the interval needs) or degrees, minutes and seconds (112°30′W), with a hemisphere letter or a sign (-112.5°), on any of the four edges (longitudes along the top and bottom, latitudes along the left and right; the bottom and left to start with), and the side labels horizontal or running along the edge. From a command: layout.addElement={"kind":"grid","step":0.5,"style":"ticks","format":"dms","edges":["top","bottom","left","right"],"labelOrientation":"vertical"} (given again, it changes only the options it names), or layout.update with "grid": {…} (false removes the grid).
  • Measured grids: a grid's Type is a Graticule (latitudes and longitudes, as above) or a Measured grid, as ArcGIS Pro has them: eastings and northings in a projected coordinate system, for maps read with UTM or national grid coordinates (a hiking map at 1:25,000 with a line every kilometre). Its Coordinate system is the one typed (EPSG:25832, WKT or a PROJ string); left empty, the map's own when the map is in a projected system, else the UTM zone (WGS 84) at the frame's centre. Its Interval is in that system's units, metres for UTM (Auto picks 1, 2 or 5 times a power of ten that suits the frame; one too fine for the frame is widened to about 50 lines). Its lines are drawn through the coordinate system onto the map, so on a map in another projection they lean or bend as they do there; eastings are labelled along the top and bottom and northings along the sides, whole (543000) or, with Short labels, as topographic maps print them, the kilometres' last two digits (43). Style, ticks, colour, width, edges and side label orientation are as for a graticule. A system that isn't projected (a latitude/longitude one) is refused: that is a graticule's job. From a command: layout.update={"element":1,"grid":{"type":"measured","crs":"EPSG:25832","step":1000,"short":true}}; a change of type without a step picks one, as degrees and metres don't carry over.
  • Map surrounds: north arrow, scale bar, legend, colorbar, table frame (a layer's attribute table) and chart frame (a bar chart of a numeric field), plus a neatline or backdrop. A north arrow's properties pick its Style (classic arrow, compass rose, triangle or star) and its Fill and Outline colours ("style":"compass","fill":"#B91C1C"). A scale bar's pick its Style (alternating bar, stepped line or single line), its Units (metres or kilometres to suit the scale, or kilometres, metres, miles or feet) and its Divisions (1 to 10), each labelled where there is room ("style":"line","units":"miles","divisions":2). A legend shows what its frame draws: only layers with a feature at the frame's scale (through their definition query, display filters and scale range) and, for Unique Values, only the classes those features have, with <all other values> only when some feature falls in it and its symbol is not fully transparent. Graduated Colors and Proportional Symbols list their classes as they are (they are taken from the kept features when the symbology is applied). A layer that draws nothing there, such as an empty one, is left out, in layouts saved before this too. Tick All classes in its properties ("allClasses": true) to list every class of every visible layer instead, and Hide other values ("hideOther": true) to leave <all other values> out of the legend in either mode (the features it stands for are still drawn). A visible WMS or WMTS layer with a legend is listed by its name over its service's legend picture, the one for the frame's scale (as the Layers pane shows it), a pixel a point and narrowed to fit the legend's width, in the order the map draws its layers (as the Layers pane lists them); one whose picture can't be loaded (or is wider or taller than 2048 pixels) is left out. Exporting waits up to half a minute for the pictures, as it waits for the map's tiles; in the browser the page is drawn with those that have arrived, and again as the others arrive. Its Layers section has a checkbox for each layer of the frame's map (and each WMS or WMTS layer with a legend): untick one to leave it out of the legend while the map still draws it (a mask, a highlight, a basemap-like layer). Scripts give the same with "exclude": ["Graticule"] on layout.addElement or layout.update ([] lists every layer again); a renamed layer stays left out.
  • Colorbar: the colour scale of a raster layer in the frame's map, as the map draws it (its stretch, colour ramp and enhancement): a gradient bar for a stretch or a tinted hillshade, steps labelled at their breaks for Classify, and a block per value for Unique Values and colour tables. Its properties pick the Layer (the top visible raster unless one is picked), the Title (the units, such as Elevation (m); the layer's name to start with), the Orientation, which side the Labels go on, how many Ticks a gradient labels (2 to 21, the ends included) and Reverse (high values first). An RGB raster or a hillshade without a tint has no colour scale and shows a placeholder, as does a picked layer that was renamed or removed (it is kept by name, like a table or chart frame's layer) until another is picked. From a command: layout.addElement={"kind":"colorbar","layer":"DEM","title":"Elevation (m)","orientation":"vertical","ticks":3}.
  • Shapes: Rectangle, Circle, Ellipse and Line add a shape in the middle of the page, to frame, highlight or divide parts of it. The Line menu starts a horizontal, vertical or diagonal line; turn it to any angle with its rotation handle or properties. A circle is an ellipse in a square box. The properties set a shape's fill, outline and outline width (0 for none; a fill with no opacity leaves only the outline), a rectangle's rounded corners ("radius", in mm), and a line's colour, width, arrowheads and angle. From a command: layout.addElement={"kind":"line","dir":"falling","color":"#C0392B","width":2}.
  • Arrows: Arrow adds an arrow pointing right. Drag the round handle above a selected arrow or line to turn it about its centre: it snaps to level, upright and diagonal within 3°, and Shift turns it in 15° steps. Angle in its properties sets it exactly (0° points right, 90° up), and Arrowheads puts heads at its end, its start, both or neither, so any line can be an arrow. From a command: layout.addElement={"kind":"arrow","angle":30,"length":60}, or layout.update={"element":7,"angle":-90} to turn one.
  • Text and Dynamic Text: {date}, {time}, {scale}, {map}, {crs}, {page}, {pages}, {pageName} and {layout} fill in when the page is drawn; the Format pane's Insert Dynamic Text menu, under the text, lists each with what it shows. The text, its size (2 to 400 points, as text graphics on the map), colour, bold, Italic (slanted, as water and ocean names are; the built-in fonts have no italic face, so the letters are slanted 12°), Alignment (left, center or right within the element) and Letter spacing in points (spaced-out names such as O C E A N O, or a negative value to tighten) are the same form a text on the map has in the pane; Enter ends the text and Shift+Enter starts a new line. Scripts set them with italic, align and letterSpacing on layout.addElement and layout.update. A layout's text also takes a Font: Sans-serif (the default) or Serif, for a title or a classic atlas look. The serif is one installed on the computer (Georgia or Times New Roman on Windows and macOS, Noto, DejaVu or Liberation Serif on Linux), with its own bold and italic faces, so italic there is a true italic rather than slanted letters (a family with no bold or italic file draws that style from its regular face: italic slanted, bold as the regular); RustGIS bundles no font. The project saves only the family, so it opens anywhere. Where no serif is installed (the web app, a minimal Linux), the text is drawn in the sans-serif and the pane says so, as layout.addElement and layout.update do in a warning. Scripts set it with "font": "serif" or "font": "sans".

The Font list also has every font family installed on the computer, after Sans-serif and Serif, so a figure can match the typeface a journal or a series names (Times New Roman, Arial, Garamond, a condensed face for long names). Type part of a name to find one. Its bold and italic come from the family's own faces, as for the serif, and characters it lacks from the sans. A named family keeps a Fallback, Sans-serif or Serif, for a computer that doesn't have it (a project opened elsewhere, the web app): there the text is drawn in the fallback, and the pane and the commands say so. A family that is installed but whose file can't be read (too large, damaged) is drawn in the fallback too, and the command that names it says so. The fallback starts as the family's own class (a serif's is Serif). Scripts give the family's name: "font": "Garamond", with "fallback": "serif" if wanted; labels.fonts lists the installed families. The project keeps the name, never a file, and no font goes into a PNG or PDF export (their pages are pictures). Picture places a PNG or JPEG. - Map Series: one page per feature of an index layer, with the frame zoomed to each feature; step through pages, refresh, and export every page into one PDF. - Click an element to select it, drag to move, drag its handles to resize, and edit it in the Format pane, which opens as a tab beside the other right-hand panes. Closing the pane keeps the element selected; selecting an element, or clicking the selected one, opens it again. The wheel zooms the page. Delete (or Backspace, the delete key on a Mac) deletes the selected element, and Ctrl+D (⌘D on a Mac) duplicates it: the copy is placed 5 mm down and to the right, on top, and selected. The arrow keys nudge it 1 mm, or 10 mm with Shift, and keep it moving while held; a run of nudges is one step to undo. - Arrange: elements later in the layout are drawn over earlier ones, and a click picks the one on top. Under Duplicate and Delete, Bring to Front and Send to Back put the selected element over or under every other, and Bring Forward and Send Backward move it one place, to put a legend over a map frame, say. A locked element keeps its place. From a command: layout.arrange={"element":4,"to":"front"} (front, forward, backward or back). - Locked, at the top of the Format pane, keeps a finished element from being changed by mistake: it can still be selected (a lock marks its corner, and it has no handles), but not moved, resized, deleted or edited, and a locked map frame's map isn't panned or zoomed. A map series still turns its pages. Duplicate makes an unlocked copy, and a map frame isn't deleted while one of its surrounds is locked. Scripts lock and unlock with layout.update {"locked": true} or {"locked": false}. - Rulers and guides: rulers start on along the top and left and show millimetres from the page's corner. Drag out of a ruler to add a guide, drag a guide to move it, and drag it back onto a ruler to remove it. Guides are saved with the layout but never printed or exported. Clear Guides removes them all, and Rulers in the Page group hides the rulers. - Snap starts on: a dragged or resized element snaps to the guides, the page's edges and centre, and the other elements' edges and centres, and the line it snapped to is highlighted. Hold Alt to place an element freely, or turn Snap off in the Page group. - Export writes PDF (every map series page by default, up to 500), or PNG or SVG of the current page. In SVG each element is a group (an Inkscape layer) named after it: text stays text and rectangles, ellipses and lines stay shapes, while map frames and the other surrounds are pictures at the export resolution, so the page can be finished in a vector editor. SVG text uses the viewer's font (a named family where the viewer has it, else its serif or sans-serif), so its alignment and line widths can differ from PNG/PDF and can change when edited. Embedded pictures are clipped to their element boxes; layout.export accepts dpi and "allPages": false for just the current PDF page. Print opens the PDF in the system viewer on desktop; Save Layout File and Import Layout move layouts between projects (.rgislayout).

items.title: Reports
items.text:
Publish › New Report lists the selected layer's records page after page; the Report pane previews it and sets it up.

  • Data: pick the detail Fields (or Autofill Fields), Group records by up to four fields (each group gets a heading and its own statistics), add Statistics (count, sum, mean, minimum, maximum), a Dynamic Picture per record (a field holding a PNG/JPEG path relative to the saved project's folder, or base64 image data), Attachments (a field listing each record's files, separated by ;; image files show when they're inside the project's folder), and a Chart Frame (records, or a field's sum, per category).
  • Report Section: Supplemental Pages of text before or after the records, New Template and Existing Template (a page layout drawn as a report page), a Related Report appended after this one, and Subreports (each record's related records through a relationship, listed beneath it).
  • A where clause or the layer's selection limits the records; a sort field orders them within their groups.
  • Publish › Report: Export Report writes a PDF (or the first page as PNG); Save As Report File keeps the report, and Report Template its design without the data source, to start reports on other layers (Publish › Import Report).

items.title: Presentations and notebooks
items.text:
Publish › New Presentation starts a presentation with a title page; the Presentation pane previews, edits and plays it.

  • Page: a Map page shows the map view as it is now, a Blank page shows text on a coloured page, an Image page a picture with a caption, and a Video page a video file or URL with an optional poster picture.
  • Each page has a title, speaker notes and a duration (for Play), and can move up or down.
  • Publish › Output › Presentation › Export Presentation writes an HTML slideshow (arrow keys, N for notes, P to play; videos play in place), a PDF, or the first page as PNG. Video sources remain file paths or URLs, so keep them accessible beside the exported slideshow. Save As Presentation File in the same menu keeps it to import into other projects (.rgispres).

Analyze › New Notebook starts a notebook of text and command cells; Add and Open opens a RustGIS (.rgisnb) or Jupyter (.ipynb) notebook. A command cell runs one command per line (id {json}, as in scripts) and shows each command's result beneath it. Notebooks save in either format. The Notebook pane opens beside the map, on half of the room right of the left pane (at least 320 points where the window allows); drag its edge to give the notebook or the map more room. The cells of a RustGIS notebook contain RustGIS commands, not Python, even in an .ipynb file. A Jupyter notebook in another language, such as Python, or one that names no language, opens with its cells and outputs (text, results, errors and PNG images) but its code cells don't run here; saving it as .ipynb keeps its kernel, metadata, cell ids and outputs, so it still opens and runs in Jupyter. RustGIS marks the .ipynb files it saves with the rustgis language, so their command cells run when opened again. A notebook holds up to 1,000 cells of up to 200,000 characters each; a larger one is refused rather than opened in part. Notebooks opened from a file or an existing project cannot run commands that read or write files or run other scripts.

items.title: Maps and Basemaps
items.text: A project holds one or more maps (Home › Project › New Map), each with its own layers, basemap, projection, bookmarks and view settings. Maps open as tabs above the map view. In the Browser, right-click a map to rename, duplicate or delete it; the project always keeps at least one map. For selecting, grouping, reordering and copying layers between maps, see The window.

items.title: Navigating
items.text:
Drag to pan and scroll to zoom; Home (or Full Extent) shows all the data. Home › Navigate has fixed zoom steps, Previous and Next extents, Bookmarks (the World Atlas has World, Europe, Africa, Americas and East Asia), and Locate: By Coordinates… pans to a longitude and latitude; By Place or Address… finds a place or address with a geocoder. New Bookmark… saves the current view under a name, with an optional description of the place. The Bookmarks menu removes a bookmark with the button beside it, and exports or imports them as a .rgisbookmarks file. Imported bookmarks show the same place on a map in another projection; places that projection can't show are skipped. Type a scale in the status bar to jump to it: the map zooms from the whole world in past 2:1, close enough for site plans at 1:20 and finds drawings at 1:1 (type 2:1 for twice life size). Beside it are the zoom level, bearing and pitch; click them to face north and look straight down again. More navigation tools are under View effects below.

Measurement units. In Home › Inspect › Measure, choose Metric or Imperial. The choice is remembered and updates existing distance and area measurements, the live map scale bar, elevation profiles, and distance labels and presets for label visibility and view clipping. Imperial readouts use feet or miles for length, and square feet, acres or square miles for area, according to size. Profile elevations and gain/loss use feet. Feet are international feet (0.3048 m). Scripts can set ui.measurementUnits={"units":"imperial"} or {"units":"metric"}; calling it without units toggles the choice. Distance presets still send metre values to commands. Editing tools, geoprocessing tools, directions and layout scale bars have their own explicit unit controls.

Zoom To Layer in a layer's right-click menu shows that layer's extent instead of the whole map. It works for feature and raster data, PMTiles archives, cloud-optimised GeoTIFFs, and service tile layers whose capabilities advertise geographic bounds, including WMS. WMS 1.3 geographic bounds and WMS 1.1 latitude/longitude bounds are inherited from parent layers when needed and saved with the project. Re-add a service layer saved by an older version to retain its bounds. Tile layers without known bounds (such as plain XYZ/TMS or MVT templates, styles and MBTiles archives) have no Zoom To Layer action unless bounds were supplied when adding them.

Rotating and tilting the map. Drag with the right mouse button, or hold Ctrl and drag with the Pan tool, to turn the map about the centre of the view (to the right turns it clockwise) and to tilt it (up tilts it further), as in MapLibre; or hold Shift and press Left or Right to turn it, Up or Down to tilt it. The north arrow turns with the map to point north and leans back as it tilts; click it to face north and look straight down again. The bearing (the compass direction the top of the view faces, in degrees clockwise from north) and the pitch (the tilt from looking straight down, 0 to 85 degrees) work as in MapLibre. They are saved with the project, its bookmarks and bookmark files, and exported maps are drawn turned and tilted. A tilted map keeps the scale at the centre of the view: nearer ground is larger, farther ground smaller and drawn coarser, fading into fog and, past about 72 degrees, a sky above the horizon. Labels stay upright, and those too far away to read are left out. Point markers stand upright, facing you, as MapLibre's circles do, smaller with distance (aggregated, masked or blended point layers, and layers of more than 50,000 points, keep their markers on the ground). Extruded layers (Style › Extrusion) stand up in perspective on a tilted map, as in MapLibre: walls lit by the way they face and darker toward their foot, roofs at their height, with the labels of extruded features on their roofs. While a tilted map moves, the picture drawn last is laid over the ground and the extrusions and markers are moved with it, and the map is drawn again once it settles. map.setBearing sets the bearing ({"bearing": 90} puts east at the top; {"by": 15} turns it further), map.setPitch the pitch ({"pitch": 60}, or {"by": 10}), map.resetNorth faces north and looks straight down, and map.goToXY takes a bearing and a pitch too. Page layout map frames take their own bearing and pitch (see Layouts), and the globe turns and tilts the same way: tilted, its camera swings back about the centre of view, so the horizon comes into sight past the curve of the Earth.

Countries extruded by population on a map tilted 55°.

Terrain gives a tilted map relief, as MapLibre's terrain does: the map is draped over the ground's heights, labels and point markers stand on it, and nearer slopes hide what lies behind them. The heights come from a DEM raster layer of the project (heights in metres; the layer can stay hidden) or from elevation tiles: Terrarium (terrarium, as the free https://s3.amazonaws.com/elevation-tiles-prod/terrarium/{z}/{x}/{y}.png) or Mapbox Terrain-RGB (mapbox, also MapTiler's). map.terrain sets it: {"layer": "DEM"} or {"tiles": "https://…/{z}/{x}/{y}.png", "encoding": "terrarium"}, with "exaggeration" (0 to 20, default 1) to stretch the heights; {"exaggeration": 2} alone changes only that, and {"off": true} flattens the map again. Terrain is saved with the project and shows in exported maps; a flat (untilted) view, the globe and other projections stay flat, extruded layers are not lifted onto the relief yet, and identify and selection still pick on the flat ground.

Mount Rainier: USGS imagery draped over Terrarium elevation tiles.

MapLibre map links carry a view in their address, as #zoom/latitude/longitude/bearing/pitch (https://…/#15.5/40.7484/-73.9857/30/60). Go To Map Link (map.goToLink {"url": …}) takes such a link, or the part after its #, to that place, zoom, bearing and pitch, and map.link gives the current view the same way. The web app reads one from its own address (see Installation).

Manage Bookmarks (at the foot of the Bookmarks menu, or View › Windows › Bookmarks) opens the Bookmarks pane: every map's bookmarks, grouped by map (the map in view in the accent colour), with a box that filters them by name or description. On each bookmark, Zoom To shows its place at its scale and Pan To centres it at the current scale; a bookmark of another map takes the map in view to the same place. Update saves the current view into it (only on its own map, in view), and Delete removes it. The chevron shows its description: click it to write or edit it. Double-click a name to rename it, and right-click it to rename, describe, update, move it up or down, or delete it. Bookmark edits run bookmark.* commands and undo with Ctrl+Z; Zoom To and Pan To change the view without adding an undo step.

Home › Navigate › Locate › By Place or Address… (map.findPlace) looks up a place or an address by name with OpenStreetMap's Nominatim (or a Photon server, or a geocoder of your own given by its address) and zooms to the one picked. The search goes to that server over the network; see Geocoding addresses for whole tables.

The search box at the foot of the left pane searches the map as you type: a latitude and longitude (40.7, -74.0, 40.7N 74W or 40°42'46"N 74°0'21"W; latitude first unless the letters or a number past ±90 say otherwise), the map's layers and bookmarks by name, and the values in its layers' attribute tables (the best few per layer, by the feature's name where it has one). Places come from Nominatim when you press Enter on Search places, since the public servers don't allow searching as you type. The arrow keys move through the list and Enter picks: a layer is zoomed to, a feature selected and zoomed to, and a coordinate or a place is marked with a pin until the box is cleared (✕ or Esc). map.search runs the same search from the command line or a script, and goes to a hit with "go":

rustgis-cli run --sample --cmd 'map.search={"query":"Tokyo","go":true}'

Right-click the map for a menu about that place. Its first row shows the latitude and longitude; click it to copy them. Below it, Copy As GeoJSON copies the place as a point feature, Center Map Here and Zoom In Here move the view, and Directions To Here and Directions From Here open the Directions pane. Quick Analysis runs a tool at the place: a buffer of 500 m, 1 km or 5 km (¼, 1 or 5 miles when the Directions pane is set to miles; gp.bufferPoint), a viewshed of 2, 5 or 15 km or a line of sight on an elevation raster in the map, and Open In Geoprocessing… opens the Buffer tool. View In Google Maps and View In Google Earth open the place in your browser at about the same zoom.

items.title: Directions
items.text:
Directions (Home › Navigate) plans a route between places and follows it turn by turn, with the public Valhalla server run by FOSSGIS on OpenStreetMap data. Pick Drive, Bike or Walk, then set the start and the destination: type an address (Enter looks it up with Nominatim) or a latitude and longitude, press the ⌖ button and click the map, or right-click the map and choose Directions From Here or Directions To Here. + Add Stop adds places on the way (up to 20 in all), Swap reverses the trip, and a drive can avoid tolls, highways or ferries; Miles gives distances in miles and feet.

Routes are drawn as soon as every place is set. Between two places the server offers up to two other ways, drawn grey: pick one in the list or click it on the map. The steps list each maneuver with its arrow, instruction and distance; click one to zoom to it. Simulate replays the route as a drive the map follows, with the next maneuver and its distance in a banner across the top of the map, at 1× to 16× speed (pause, drag the slider to jump along, End to stop). Save as Layer adds the route as a line layer, and its maneuvers as a point layer, to style, export (GPX, GeoJSON…) or keep with the project.

The first time, the pane asks before anything is sent: planning a route sends its places to the routing server, and looking a place up sends its name to Nominatim. Travel times don't include live traffic, and the public server is shared, so it answers light use only.

map.route plans a route from the command line, a script or the AI Assistant, with places given as [lon, lat], "lat, lon" or a name to look up, and adds it and its steps as layers; ui.pane.directions with from, to (and via, mode) opens the pane on a route. map.route sends its places to the same public servers (names to Nominatim, at most five a call, a second apart; coordinates to FOSSGIS's Valhalla), so the AI Assistant asks before running it:

rustgis-cli run --sample --cmd 'map.route={"from":"Brandenburg Gate, Berlin","to":"Alexanderplatz, Berlin","mode":"bike"}'

On the web, plan routes in the Directions pane; map.route cannot fetch a route or look up place names there. On the desktop, its optional url selects another Valhalla server.

items.title: Basemaps
items.text:
An OpenFreeMap MapLibre style over Paris, and the Basemap gallery.

Home › Add › Basemap offers five built-in basemaps drawn from a world outline (Paper, Midnight, Ocean, Atlas, Blank), which need no network, and web tile layers over them:

  • Raster tiles from an XYZ or TMS template (https://…/{z}/{x}/{y}.png; {-y} for rows from the south, {s} for subdomains, {q} for Bing-style quadkeys) or a WMS through {bbox-epsg-3857}. PNG, JPEG and WebP.
  • Vector tiles (Mapbox Vector Tiles, .pbf) from a template or a TileJSON address, drawn in a built-in style that knows the OpenMapTiles, Protomaps and Shortbread schemas.
  • PMTiles archives (.pmtiles) of raster or vector tiles: a web address, read a tile at a time by byte ranges (the server must allow range requests, and CORS for the web app), or on the desktop a file (Tile Archive File…, Add Data, or drop it on the window). Version 3 archives are read, uncompressed or with gzip, Brotli or Zstandard. The map moves to what the archive covers once its header is read, unless it covers the whole world, and right-clicking its row in Layers gives Zoom To Layer. A vector archive that is a basemap is drawn in the built-in style; any other is drawn with each of its layers in a colour of its own.
  • MBTiles files (.mbtiles) of raster or vector tiles, drawn as PMTiles archives are: on the desktop read in place a tile at a time (Tile Archive File…, Add Data, or drop it on the window); in the web app added with Add Data and held in memory for the session (a project keeps the layer, and asks for the file again).
  • Map styles: a MapLibre style document (style.json), with its vector and raster sources. RustGIS draws background, fill, line, circle and raster layers, labels with their icons from the style's sprite (SDF icons in their icon-color), and fill patterns; it evaluates the style's expressions and zoom functions. Labels are placed as MapLibre places them: at points, in the middle of areas, and along lines (street names every symbol-spacing, turned to the street, where it bends less than text-max-angle; shields and one-way arrows), wrapped to text-max-width, the style's later layers first and then by symbol-sort-key, kept apart by text-padding and the *-optional, *-allow-overlap and *-ignore-placement rules. Text along a line is drawn straight rather than curved round its bends. Line patterns, hillshade and 3D extrusion are not drawn (extrusions draw flat). A label shows the lines of its text that the map's font can draw: a style's "Syria / سوريا" shows as "Syria". A style's root center, zoom, bearing and pitch say where it opens: map.addTiles with "view": true takes the map there once the style has loaded.

The gallery's Web Basemaps need no API key: the OpenFreeMap vector maps (Liberty, Bright, Positron, Dark, Fiord) and USGS Imagery. Choosing one replaces the other web basemaps; tick Stack on the current basemaps above them to add it over the others instead (clicking one that already shows then takes it off). Toggling the checkbox keeps the gallery open so you can choose a basemap; choosing one closes it. For many more (OpenStreetMap, Esri, NASA and others), follow Install the Basemaps plugin under them, which opens the Plugin Manager at the Basemaps plugin; it adds a tab of public basemaps.
