Add any other with Add Tile Layer… at the bottom of the Basemap gallery. The gallery lists the map's tile layers: show or hide them, change their opacity and order, or remove them. The Layers pane lists them too, at their place in the drawing order: a basemap under the map's layers and above the built-in basemap; an overlay (a WMS or WMTS layer, a vector tile service, Overlay ticked in Add Tile Layer) on top of the map's layers when added, as every new layer goes. Drag one, or right-click it and choose Move up or Move down, to put it between the map's layers (above a layer group, never inside one). Tick one to show or hide it, and right-click it for Zoom To Layer (when its bounds are known), opacity, Blend mode, order and Remove; a WMS or map service layer also has Draw as: one picture of the view or tiles of a size (see One picture of the view, or tiles). A blend mode (Multiply, Screen, Overlay, Darken, Lighten, Difference) combines a tile layer with what is drawn beneath it (tile layers, the basemap, and map layers when it's placed over them): stack imagery over a hillshade and set it to Multiply to let the terrain show through. Overlays stay over the basemaps; choosing a built-in basemap removes the web basemaps but keeps the overlays. Tile layers are saved with the project, and their credits are shown in the corner of the map and drawn on exports.

Use Explore to click features in vector PMTiles, MBTiles or MVT layers added as data and see their source-layer names and attributes in a pop-up. This works with Topmost Layer or Visible Layers pop-up mode, not with catalog basemaps or MapLibre styles; with Selected in Layers, click a tile layer's row to select it and a click on the map identifies that layer alone, whichever it is (a WMS layer too). Tiles are not selectable or editable; a tile not yet loaded may need another click once it arrives. Reload in the Basemap gallery (map.reloadWebLayers) clears cached tiles and styles and fetches them again.

Source layers. A vector PMTiles or MBTiles archive lists its source layers (the vector_layers its metadata names: water, roads, pois…) under its row in the Layers pane: the arrow beside it opens them, each with its own checkbox. Untick one to hide what it draws (fills, lines, points and labels, in the default look and in a style given with styleLayers alike); Explore's pop-ups then skip its features too. From scripts, map.tiles lists a vector archive's sourceLayers once its header is read, and map.setTiles takes "hiddenLayers": ["roads", …], the source layers switched off ([] or null shows them all again). Switching one off is an edit to undo, and a project keeps which are off.

Tiles load in the background and the map fills in as they arrive, with coarser tiles standing in meanwhile; exports and rustgis-cli wait for them. On the globe and in other projections the tiles are reprojected. From scripts: map.addTiles, map.removeTiles, map.setTiles, map.zoomToTiles and map.tiles. map.addTiles accepts optional "bounds": [west, south, east, north] in longitude/latitude; service.add retains the bounds advertised by map and tile services. Explicit bounds must form a finite, ordered geographic rectangle; an invalid value rejects the command without adding or replacing a layer. Invalid or malformed bounds in a saved project are instead discarded, leaving the project and tile layer usable without that coverage metadata.

Legends. A WMS or WMTS layer added from its service has its legend in the Layers pane, as ArcGIS Pro's Contents pane shows a map service layer's: the arrow beside it opens the legend under the layer, indented as a feature layer's classes are, at the size the service draws it (one wider than the pane scrolls across). A WMS layer's legend is the one its service draws from the layer's styling (GetLegendGraphic, when the service offers it in PNG or JPEG), else the picture of its default style (its LegendURL: the style named default, else its first, inherited from the layers above it as WMS has it); when one can't be shown the next is. A WMTS layer's comes from its default style, which may give one per range of scales: the one for the map's scale shows, and "No legend at this scale" where none is for it. The pictures are fetched when first shown and kept (one that couldn't be fetched is asked for again a minute later). Any tile layer can be given one: map.addTiles and map.setTiles take "legend" (an address, or a list of addresses and {"url", "minScale", "maxScale"}; null takes it away), and map.expandTiles shows or hides it (as layer.expand does a layer's classes: not an edit to undo). A project keeps a layer's legends and whether they show.

rustgis-cli run --cmd 'service.add={"url":"https://wms.geo.admin.ch/","layer":"ch.swisstopo.geologie-swissgeocover2d_lines"}' --cmd 'map.tiles={}'

items.title: Other worlds
items.text:
Mars on the globe, on the Viking mosaic: Valles Marineris crosses the middle.

A map can be on the Moon, Mars or another body instead of the Earth. Pick the body from the planet button at the top of the Layers pane, or under Celestial Bodies in the Basemap gallery: Earth, Moon, Mars, Callisto, Charon, Europa, Ganymede, Io, Mercury, Pluto, Titan and Venus. Choosing one closes the gallery and puts one of its basemaps under the map (reopen the gallery for the others: Viking, MOLA elevation and hillshade mosaics for Mars, LOLA albedo for the Moon, and the USGS Astrogeology mosaics of the rest) and measures on that body: the Measure tools, the scale bar, the map scale and layout scale bars use its radius. Coordinates stay longitude and latitude, and the map stays a Web Mercator sphere, the size of the body. Off the Earth there is no atmosphere: the globe has no glow around it, and a tilted view's sky is the black of space, with no haze toward the horizon. Choosing the Earth replaces all non-overlay web tile layers, including planetary and custom basemaps, with USGS Imagery, keeping overlay tile layers. The body is saved with the map.

The basemaps come from OpenPlanetaryMap and USGS Astrogeology. OpenPlanetaryMap's mosaics sit in storage that browsers can't read from another site, and USGS serves its mosaics in lon/lat only, so both are read through the opengeos tile service (tiles.geolibre.app, shared with GeoLibre), which adds what browsers need, reprojects the USGS mosaics and caches the tiles. From scripts: map.body={"name": "mars"} ("basemap" picks another of its basemaps, or false adds none, still taking other bodies' basemaps off) and map.bodies.

The Moon's near side on LOLA's hillshaded albedo.

items.title: Worldview
items.text: The world outline and the World Atlas sample's countries come in two worldviews: Natural Earth's default borders, and China's (Natural Earth's China point of view: Taiwan, Aksai Chin and South Tibet are part of China). RustGIS picks China's when the system's time zone is mainland China's (such as Asia/Shanghai) or its first locale is zh-CN; nothing is looked up over the network. Choose one in Settings › Language › Worldview, set RUSTGIS_WORLDVIEW (default or china), or pass --worldview to rustgis-cli. An untouched sample project switches its countries at once; others keep the layer they have.

items.title: Projections
items.text:
The flat map is drawn in Web Mercator by default. View › Projection switches it to another projection, and clicking the coordinate system in the status bar opens the Coordinate System dialog, which also takes a projected EPSG code (such as 3035, 32633 for UTM zone 33N or 2056 for Switzerland) or an ESRI code, the one .prj files and ArcGIS name (such as ESRI:102033 for South America Albers Equal Area Conic, or ESRI:54030 for World Robinson). A code whose projection method or datum grid RustGIS can't use (Polyconic such as 5880, Cassini, oblique Mercator, or a NAD27 code that needs a grid) is refused with the reason, rather than drawn in another projection. RustGIS supports a subset of Esri's projected systems, checked against PROJ at representative points; unsupported codes such as World Miller (ESRI:54003) are refused as unknown codes. The presets:

Preset Kind Equirectangular, Miller World, cylindrical Mollweide, Lambert Cylindrical Equal Area, Equal Earth, Eckert IV World, equal-area Robinson, Natural Earth, Winkel Tripel World, compromise North / South Polar Stereographic Polar Europe Equal Area (ETRS89 LAEA), USA Contiguous Albers Equal Area Regional, equal-area Albers Equal Area Conic, Lambert Conformal Conic Conic, for a mid-latitude region VN-2000 / TM-3 (Vietnam), VN-2000 / UTM zones 48N and 49N Vietnam, transverse Mercator

The world and polar presets take a central meridian, and the two conics also their standard parallels: pick the preset in the Coordinate System dialog and set Central meridian (and First and Second standard parallel) beside it. A Pacific-centred Robinson is map.projection {"type": "robinson", "lon_0": 150}, and an Albers for South America {"type": "albers", "lon_0": -55, "lat_1": -5, "lat_2": -35}. Without type, the values go to the map's current preset. The map saves them in its code (robinson +lon_0=150), which can also be typed as it is. View › Projection picks a preset in its standard form, and marks the one in use whatever its parameters. Meridians run from -180° to 180° and parallels from -89° to 89°. Parallels that average within 0.5° of the equator (mirrored, such as -30° and 30°, or both next to it) make no cone and are refused, as is a value a preset doesn't take. The two regional grids keep their standard definitions. A conic's area of use runs 35° beyond its parallels and 90° either side of its meridian.

For Vietnam, VN-2000 / TM-3 takes a central meridian (105°E by default), with province shortcut buttons in the Coordinate System dialog. A province alias such as vn2000:hanoi sets its meridian; scripts can use map.projection={"type":"vn2000tm3","lon_0":105.75}. The UTM presets use fixed zones: vn2000Utm48 (EPSG:3405) and vn2000Utm49 (EPSG:3406). These systems include the seven-parameter datum shift to WGS 84. A bare VN-2000 is ambiguous and is refused: name TM-3 or a UTM zone.

Layers are projected on the fly. A feature that crosses the edge of a world projection (the meridian opposite its central one, such as 90°E in Equal Earth Americas) is cut there and drawn on both sides of the map. Each projection has an area of use: polar projections show their hemisphere poleward of 30°, regional ones their region, transverse Mercator (UTM) zones 30° either side of their meridian, and data outside it isn't drawn. Switching keeps the centre and scale, and the choice is saved with the map (map.projection from the command line). A raster already in the map's coordinate system draws without being reprojected. To open every new session in a projection, set it in Settings › Start-up › Projection. Robinson, Equal Earth, Natural Earth, Winkel Tripel and Eckert IV are computed by RustGIS itself on a sphere, so EPSG:8857 (Equal Earth) works too. So is the sinusoidal projection, on a sphere or an ellipsoid: MODIS rasters, whose GeoTIFFs give it as their own projection, open and draw, and World, Sphere and Africa Sinusoidal (ESRI:54008, 53008, 102011) can be the map's.

items.title: Globe
items.text:
The World Atlas on the 3D globe.

View › Globe shows the map as a 3D globe seen from space instead of the flat Web Mercator map, and back again. Drag to spin the globe, right-drag or Ctrl+drag to turn and tilt it (as on the flat map), scroll to zoom, and use Full Extent to see the whole Earth. Every layer draws on the globe: vectors are clipped at the horizon and follow great circles, rasters are draped onto the sphere, and labels, selection, identify, measuring and editing work as on the flat map. The scale stays the same when you switch, and the choice is saved with each map in the project (map.projection from the command line).

While the globe turns or zooms, the map is drawn flat once and laid over the sphere by the graphics card, so it moves smoothly whatever the basemap; labels come back, and the map is drawn exactly, as soon as it stops.

The globe hangs in dark space, in the light theme too, with stars around it and now and then a shooting star passing behind it. View › Visual Effect › Stars turns them off. Exported maps and layout map frames print the globe in a light space instead, without stars, so a globe inset suits a light page (on the Midnight basemap the space stays dark).

items.title: View effects
items.text:
Dark mode on the Midnight basemap.

The View tab adds effects drawn over the map: Illumination (day and night shading for a time, with twilight), Weather (haze, fog, rain, snow), Visual Effect (vignette, edges, the stars around the globe), Camera Effect (tilt-shift blur, film grain) and Postprocessing (brightness, contrast, saturation, sepia). The Color Vision simulator shows the map as people with protanopia, deuteranopia, tritanopia or achromatopsia see it (on screen only; exports are untouched). View › Display › Graticule (map.graticule) draws latitude and longitude lines over the basemap.

Global shows a globe; Local a flat view centred where you are (azimuthal equidistant; not in the web app, which doesn't include that projection). Wireframe draws polygons as outlines; Raise Priority and Lower Priority change a layer's drawing priority independently of its order. View Clipping hides features beyond a distance from the centre, and Speed Display draws without antialiasing. The Navigator adds a compass, zoom buttons and a pan pad; Camera shows and sets the position and scale; the Magnifier shows twice the map under the pointer. On the Home tab, First-Person navigation walks with W A S D and flies up and down with Q and E. The interface follows the system's light or dark setting; View › Display › Dark Mode switches it by hand.

View › Display › GPU Rendering (beta) draws supported parts of the flat map on the GPU for smoother navigation on large datasets. Unsupported geometry and layer effects fall back to the CPU. Raster tiles and opaque vector tile styles can be drawn directly on the GPU on a north-up Web Mercator map; translucent or blended tiles use cached pictures during navigation.

GPU Rendering is off by default and remembered across sessions (ui.map.gpu is the command; RUSTGIS_GPU=1 forces it on for development). The globe, view effects and colour-vision simulation stay on the CPU, and exports are unaffected. A rotated or tilted map uses the GPU only when every visible layer can be drawn there: tiles, rasters, terrain, transparency, masking, swipe, blending, aggregation, graphics, stacked strokes, fills or labels with icons keep it on the CPU. Extrusions use the GPU only on a tilted map.

items.title: Shapefile DBF language drivers
items.text: A valid .cpg takes precedence over the language driver ID (LDID, byte 29 of the .dbf header). Without a usable .cpg, the following inventory describes RustGIS's LDID decoding. All numbers in the marker column are hexadecimal. These are language-driver identifiers, not the numeric code-page labels accepted in a .cpg.

items.title: Decoded markers
items.text:
Code page LDID markers DOS CP437 01, 09, 0B, 0D, 0F, 11, 15, 18, 19, 1B DOS CP850 02, 0A, 0E, 10, 12, 14, 16, 1A, 1D, 25, 37 DOS CP852 1F, 22, 23, 40, 64, 87 DOS CP861 67 DOS CP865 08, 17, 66 DOS CP866 26, 65 Windows-874 (Thai) 50, 7C CP932 (Shift JIS) 13, 7B CP936 (GBK) 4D, 7A CP949 (Korean) 4E, 79 CP950 (Big5) 4F, 78 Windows-1250 C8 Windows-1251 C9 Windows-1252 03, 57, 58, 59 Windows-1253 CB Windows-1254 CA Windows-1255 7D Windows-1256 7E Windows-1257 CC Mac Roman (10000) 04 Mac Cyrillic (10007; see below) 96 UTF-8 (65001) F0 No encoding metadata: UTF-8 default 00

57 deliberately means Windows-1252 in RustGIS. GDAL interprets it as ISO-8859-1; changing to that interpretation would change bytes 80–9F, such as the euro sign and an en dash, into control characters. The regression test uses 80 96 9F → €–Ÿ.

Mac Cyrillic is decoded with encoding_rs's x-mac-cyrillic (Mac Ukrainian) decoder. The shared Cyrillic letters are supported; this is not an exact mapping of every Mac Cyrillic character. The test uses 8A E8 E5 E2 → Киев, which both mappings share.

items.title: Recognized but not decoded
items.text:
Code page LDID markers DOS CP863 (French Canadian) 1C, 6C DOS CP860 (Portuguese) 24 DOS CP895 (Czech, Kamenický) 68 DOS CP620 (Polish, Mazovia) 69 DOS CP737 (Greek) 6A, 86 DOS CP857 (Turkish) 6B, 88 Mac Central European (10029) 97

These markers emit a diagnostic naming the marker and code page, then use lossy UTF-8. Unknown markers also emit a diagnostic and use lossy UTF-8. Valid UTF-8 survives, malformed bytes become replacement characters, and the records remain available. An unusable .cpg adds its own diagnostic before falling back to the LDID. Supplying a valid .cpg bypasses the LDID and its unsupported-code-page diagnostic.

The existing transitive yore 1.4.0 package has CP737, CP857, CP860 and CP863 decoders, but RustGIS's current dbase adapter does not expose them. Making these available would require decoder integration and a coordinated direct dependency declaration; their presence in the lockfile does not make the corresponding LDIDs supported today. No local conversion tables or system programs are needed for the supported decoders above.

items.title: References and regression coverage
items.text:
• Marker inventory: GDAL 3.11.4's GetEncodingFromLDIDNumber, plus 09, 7D, 7E and F0 from dbase 0.8.0's CodePageMark.
  • GDAL's Shapefile encoding documentation describes .cpg precedence and its different 57 interpretation.
  • Character mapping references: Unicode's Microsoft code-page mappings and Apple mappings.
  • yore's CodePage implementations list the available legacy decoders and lossy decoding API.

crates/data/tests/shapefile_encoding.rs specifies fixed bytes and Unicode expectations independently of RustGIS's mapping. Its matrix covers every marker above, names and values, ZIP and loose-file imports, a genuinely sampled streamed read, a complete read, and ordered chunk traversal. It also checks .cpg precedence, fallback diagnostics, and malformed multibyte text without discarding records. Test files are generated locally; the tests do not download data or call external converters.

items.title: Exporting
items.text:
Publish › Output › Export Map writes the map view as a PNG with labels, the scale bar and tile credits. The ribbon exports at 192 DPI; share.exportMap accepts width and height in pixels and a dpi value (96 by default). Print Map opens a PDF in the system viewer on desktop; Capture To Clipboard copies a map image. Export To 3D writes a layer as a Wavefront OBJ model with polygons extruded by a field.

Data › Export (or share.exportLayer, Export Features) writes a layer to GeoJSON, CSV, GeoPackage, GeoParquet, Shapefile (including a zip), FlatGeobuf, KML, KMZ or GPX (see Writing). GeoPackage, Shapefile and FlatGeobuf use the layer's source coordinate system by default; the crs parameter chooses another. A streamed layer exports its whole source, not just the features loaded for the view. share.exportTable exports a standalone table. Data › Export also writes rasters to GeoTIFF, and Data Interop converts layers to KML, GPX or CSV with WKT. Layouts, reports and presentations export from their own tabs and panes (see Layouts and Reports).

GeoPackage exports require a new filename. Exporting to an existing .gpkg is refused to protect its tables and data, even if the save dialog offers to replace the file. Export does not append a table to an existing GeoPackage or replace one of its tables.

Packages and project item files are described under Project items.

items.title: Sharing as open formats
items.text:
Publish › Share As writes open-format files to a chosen file on desktop, or downloads them in the browser. The Share As commands accept a path; without one they use the first data store (a folder added with Add Data Store… in the Shared Items pane).

  • Web Map (share.webMap): an HTML page of visible layers (rasters as embedded images), pan and zoom, a layer list and pop-ups. It uses a flat Mercator view, not the project's projection, and does not include the basemap's web tiles.
  • Web Layer (share.webLayer): the selected layer as a static OGC API – Features collection, with its style and a viewer page, in a zip. Geodata Service (share.geodataService) writes the map's non-raster, non-graphics layers and the project's standalone tables as collections. These are files, not running services with query or editing endpoints.
  • Web Style (share.webStyle): the selected layer's symbology as a MapLibre style (unique values and classes as expressions). Labels use only the Default label class, without its SQL clause; a hidden Default class exports no labels. The same limit applies to a Web Layer's style.
  • Locator (share.locator): the selected layer's names as a .rgisloc place-search file; text fields are searched by default, or specify fields. locator.find searches it and can zoom to the best match with "zoom": true.
  • Web Tool (share.webTool): the last model as a .rgistool file, which model.import adds to another project; model chooses a model by name.
  • Web Scene (share.webScene): the visible vector layers as glTF, polygons extruded by their layer's extrusion setting, with a camera that looks at the map's centre from its bearing and pitch.
  • Web Link Chart (share.linkChart): the features joined by the map's relationships as a node-link HTML page; relationship limits it to one relationship.

Publish › Share As › Jobs (the Shared Items pane) lists desktop shares; Save Web Map, Replace Web Layer, Save Web Scene and Save Web Link Chart update a share in place (share.saveWebMap, share.replaceWebLayer, share.saveWebScene, share.saveWebLinkChart). The item parameter chooses the share by ID or name; omitting it uses the latest of that kind. Upload File (share.upload) copies a file into a data store; it does not upload to a remote server.

After opening a project, register its data stores again before writing to them, and use Share As to choose each item's destination again before updating it. Saved share records do not grant permission to overwrite their paths. Undo changes the project record, not files already written.

items.title: Web Data
items.text:
Home › Add › Web Data gathers public web services and catalogs: the ones that cover the whole world in one alphabetical list, and those that cover one country in a submenu named after it. Each opens in the Web Data pane on the right, beside the map it searches. Unless a section says otherwise, the panes work in the web app too, provided the servers allow browser requests (CORS). The command-line examples below are for the desktop CLI; many network commands cannot fetch synchronously in the browser, where the panes fetch in the background instead. Commands that reach the network need the AI Assistant's approval when it runs them, and the network permission when a plugin does. ui.dialog opens a panel on a search with "search" ({"name": "nasaEarthdata", "search": "sea surface temperature"}).

Entry What it gives Section ArcGIS Portal… Public items on ArcGIS Online or another portal Web services Boundaries… A country's administrative boundaries (geoBoundaries) OpenStreetMap and administrative boundaries Dynamical… Weather and climate Zarr stores Web services Earthdata GIS… NASA's Earth science imagery, maps and features Web services Fields of the World… Agricultural field boundaries, worldwide Fields of the World GeoLens… A GeoLens server's vector datasets Web services Hugging Face… Geospatial files in Hugging Face datasets Web services NASA Earthaccess… NASA Earthdata granules (ICESat-2, GEDI, HLS…) NASA Earthaccess NASA Earthdata… NASA GIBS imagery, day by day NASA Earthdata Natural Earth… Natural Earth map data Natural Earth Ocean Data Platform… HUB Ocean's marine datasets Web services OpenAerialMap… Drone and aerial images Web services OpenStreetMap… OpenStreetMap features where the map is OpenStreetMap and administrative boundaries Overture Maps… Buildings, places, transportation and more Overture Maps Planet Open Data… Planet's disaster imagery Planet Open Data Portolan… Open data catalogs published with Portolan Portolan Satellite Embeddings… AlphaEarth, Earth Index and Tessera embeddings Satellite embeddings Search Open Data… data.gov, CKAN, Socrata and ArcGIS Hub datasets Open-data portals Sentinel-2 Explorer… Recent, clear Sentinel-2 scenes Sentinel-2 Explorer Source Cooperative… Files on Source Cooperative Source Cooperative STAC Search… Any STAC API or static catalog STAC catalogs Vantor… Vantor's (formerly Maxar's) disaster imagery Vantor France › IGN LiDAR HD… IGN's LiDAR HD point clouds Web services United States › … EnviroAtlas, FEMA NFHL, Tennessee GIS, The National Map, US Federal/State/Local GIS, USGS 3DEP DEM, USGS LiDAR, USGS NLDI United States

Data added by its address, from a web server or an S3 bucket, is described in Data and Files on the web.

items.title: STAC catalogs
items.text:
Home › Add › Web Data › STAC Search… searches a STAC API for imagery and other assets: by collection, dates, the most cloud cover and (by default) where the map is. The default API is Element 84's Earth Search; Microsoft's Planetary Computer is offered beside it, and other APIs with GET item search work. Collections lists what the API offers, and Find Items shows up to 50 items as cards (with "Showing 50 of 1234 items" when the API says how many match) and draws their footprints as a layer. Each card has the item's preview picture when it has one, its id, a collection · date · cloud cover line, and Zoom (to the item), the asset to add, Add and Details (the item's properties). The asset chosen at first is visual (true colour) when there is one, else the first GeoTIFF, else the first point cloud, else the first data asset, preferring HTTP(S) assets. Cloud-optimised GeoTIFF, GeoParquet and FlatGeobuf assets are read in place, and PMTiles a tile at a time; other assets download whole (see Files on the web).

The commands do the same: stac.collections ("url"), stac.search ("collections", "bbox" as [west, south, east, north] or "view", "datetime" such as 2024-06-01/2024-06-30, "limit" from 1 to 200, default 10, "maxCloud", "footprints", and "properties": true for the scalar item properties rather than just date and cloud cover), and stac.addAsset with an item returned by stac.search ("item") or an item's address ("url") and "asset". API searches return one page and a "next" address when there is another:

rustgis-cli run --cmd 'stac.search={"collections":"sentinel-2-c1-l2a","bbox":[7.4,46.9,7.5,47],"datetime":"2024-07-01/2024-07-31","maxCloud":20}' --cmd 'stac.addAsset={"url":"https://earth-search.aws.element84.com/v1/collections/sentinel-2-c1-l2a/items/S2B_T32TLS_20240727T103439_L2A","asset":"scl"}'

Assets can use HTTP(S) or s3:// addresses. S3 assets use the saved connection serving their bucket, or anonymous AWS access when none matches; see S3 buckets. An item on the web can't point into the local network. A Planetary Computer asset (in Azure Blob Storage) is signed first: RustGIS asks the Planetary Computer's token service for its storage container's token and reuses it for half an hour. The token is part of the layer's address, so a project saved with one reads it again only while the token lasts (about an hour): add the asset again after that. A ?stac= link opens the web app on an item or a collection (web app links). Searches reach the network, so the AI Assistant asks before it runs them, and plugins need the network permission.

items.title: Data cubes on the time slider
items.text:
When the items found span several dates, Add as Time Series (desktop; stac.addCube) adds a band of them as a data cube: a collection's cloud-optimised GeoTIFFs, with one file per tile, date and band, such as INPE's Brazil Data Cube or Sentinel-2 on Earth Search.

  • Search: the collection is searched over the area (the map's, or "bbox") and the period ("start", "end"), page after page, up to 2,000 items.
  • Grouping: items go by the grid tile they cover (grid:code, s2:mgrs_tile, Landsat's WRS path and row, the Brazil Data Cube's bdc:tiles, else their bounding box), and by day.
  • Layers: each tile becomes a tile layer read in place, a file per date. The time slider shows the last date in its window, and a tile with no date in it draws nothing. The slider turns on over the dates when it is off.
  • Range: a fixed "range" ([0, 0.9] for NDVI) is the same for every date and tile, so a grey means one value throughout. It is in the band's own units: its raster:bands (or eo:bands) scale and offset turn it into the files' stored values. Without one, each file is stretched on its own, between its 2nd and 98th percentiles.
  • Saved with the project: each tile's dates and addresses.
  • Files in public buckets: a collection whose items give their files as s3:// addresses (Digital Earth Australia, Digital Earth Africa, the Copernicus DEM on Earth Search) is read from AWS at the files' web addresses. Reads are anonymous unless an S3 connection explicitly names the bucket, in which case its credentials are used, as for other S3 reads. A bucket in a region AWS's global endpoint doesn't reach (Digital Earth Africa's, in Cape Town) is read at its own region's, found by reading one byte of its first file. Without a matching connection, a bucket that refuses anonymous reads (a private one, or one that charges the reader, as Landsat's does) is refused, naming it.
  • Web app: creating a cube with Add as Time Series is desktop-only. Saved cube tile layers can draw in the web app when their servers allow browser requests (CORS).
  • Its trend: the same search, given to Trend Analysis (cube.trend with collection, asset, bbox, start and end), reads the values over the area and works out each cell's trend: see Trend analysis.
rustgis-cli run --cmd 'stac.addCube={"url":"https://data.inpe.br/bdc/stac/v1","collection":"S2-16D-2","asset":"NDVI","bbox":[-55.9,-12.6,-55.5,-12.35],"start":"2024-08-01","end":"2025-06-30","range":[0,0.9]}' --cmd 'time.export={"path":"ndvi.gif"}'

items.title: A catalog of data cubes
items.text:
A data cube needs more than an API's address: the right collection and band, and often a range to show it with and a cell size to read it at. The catalog of data cubes lists cubes ready to open, each with those filled in, so none of them has to be looked up in a provider's catalog.

Home › Add › Web Data › Data Cubes lists them, filtered by theme, by words, and (ticked to begin with) to those with data where the map is. Each shows its provider, period, step, resolution, source and licence, with a link to the provider's page, and two buttons:

  • Add to Time Slider (desktop) adds it as cube.open does (below): a STAC cube where the map is, a Zarr cube whole. It is added over the period typed in From and To, or its last full calendar year when both are empty.
  • Trend Analysis… (desktop) opens Trend Analysis on it, with the period typed: a STAC cube is read where the map is, a Zarr cube whole, and Use layers instead goes back to the map's layers. A trend over a cube needs its period.

The list is kept up to date between releases with the app's other assets, so a cube can be added, or an address fixed, without a new version: the app reads it the first time the pane opens, and uses the copy built into it until then, offline, or when the list doesn't read whole. Commands, scripts and the assistant use the same list.

  • Finding a cube (cube.catalog): by "theme" (vegetation, land cover, water, climate, ocean, atmosphere or elevation), by area ("bbox", or "view": the entries with data there; with neither, anywhere) and by words in the name, provider or id ("query"). Each entry gives its provider, themes, area, period, step, resolution, source and licence, with a link to the provider's page.
  • Opening one (desktop; cube.open with the entry's "id"): a STAC entry is added as stac.addCube adds a cube, over the map's extent (or "bbox"), with the entry's collection, band, range and cloud cover cap ("range" and "maxCloud" override the last two). A Zarr entry is added as layer.addZarr adds a variable that follows the time slider; its variable is read whole, but an area given must meet the entry's. The period is "start" and "end", given together; with neither, it is the entry's last full calendar year (the year before this one while the cube is kept up to date). An end given as a day, a month or a year takes all of it, so an hourly variable's last day is read whole. An area the entry has no data in, or a period outside its dates, is refused, naming them. Undo takes the whole cube away.
  • Its trend or summary: Trend Analysis and the summary over time take an entry too (cube.trend or cube.reduce with "cube"), filling in the collection's API, band, cell size and cloud cap (a "cellSize" or "maxCloud" given is kept), or the Zarr store and variable. Data named alongside it (layer, url, collection…) is refused, since the entry would take its place.

The entries, all public and read in place:

Provider Cubes Brazil Data Cube (INPE) MODIS NDVI and EVI (MOD13Q1 v6.1, 232 m, from 2000); the 16-day NDVI cubes of Sentinel-2 (10 m, from 2017), Landsat (30 m) and CBERS-4 WFI (64 m, from 2016) Earth Search (Element 84) Sentinel-2 L2A Collection 1 scenes' red and near-infrared bands (10 m, from 2015), searched with at most 20% cloud cover; the Copernicus DEM GLO-30 (one date) Digital Earth Australia and Digital Earth Africa the yearly frequency of water seen by Landsat (30 m, from 1986 and 1984) ARCO-ERA5 (Google Cloud, ECMWF) hourly air temperature at 2 m, total precipitation and top-layer soil moisture (0.25°, from 1940), as a Zarr store the desktop reads

Only cubes RustGIS reads today are listed. Collections whose files sit behind signed addresses (Planetary Computer), need a sign-in (Copernicus Data Space, NASA Earthdata) or charge the reader (Landsat Collection 2 on Earth Search) are left out. Digital Earth Australia's catalog sits behind a firewall that may ask a program making many requests in a row for a browser check for a while; its searches then fail until it lets them through again.

An entry, as the list holds it (built in from crates/tiles/src/cubes.json, and kept with the app's assets); a cube is proposed by adding one:

{"id": "bdc-mod13q1-ndvi", "name": "MODIS NDVI, 16-day composites (MOD13Q1 v6.1)",
 "provider": "Brazil Data Cube (INPE)", "theme": ["vegetation"], "bbox": [-100, -60, -21.3, 20],
 "start": "2000-02-18", "end": null, "step": "16 days", "resolution": "232 m",
 "format": "stac", "url": "https://data.inpe.br/bdc/stac/v1/", "collection": "mod13q1-6.1",
 "asset": "NDVI", "range": [0, 0.9], "cellSize": 232,
 "license": "NASA LP DAAC: no restrictions on use", "about": "https://data.inpe.br/bdc/"}

A Zarr entry has "format": "zarr" and "variable" in place of "collection" and "asset", and no "range", "cellSize" or "maxCloud". "end" is null while a cube is kept up to date. Every address is a web address (https or http), the dates are YYYY-MM-DD, and each id is in the list once; the list is checked when it is read.

rustgis-cli run --cmd 'cube.catalog={"theme":"vegetation","bbox":[-43,-6,-42.5,-5.5]}' --cmd 'cube.open={"id":"bdc-mod13q1-ndvi","bbox":[-43,-6,-42.5,-5.5]}'

items.title: Saved connections
items.text: Once you have a STAC connection (Data Sources › Connections), its name appears in the API list at the top of STAC Search below the built-in APIs: picking it fills in the address and clears the collections and items of the previous one. Add From Service, Add From Database and S3 Buckets have the same Saved connection list for their kinds. An API you typed in by hand stays usable; once its collections are listed, Save as Connection keeps it under Data Sources › Connections (nothing is saved unless you click it, and never a password or key). Editing the address by hand drops the collections and items listed for the old one.

items.title: Static catalogs
items.text:
Many catalogs are plain files rather than an API: a catalog.json linking to child catalogs and collection.json files, which link to their items. Give STAC Search the address of one (or pick Planet Open Data, Portolan or Vantor Open Data from its list) and the Collection row becomes Catalog: its child catalogs and collections are listed, and picking one shows its own children (an ↑ entry goes back up; Browse reads the list again). Find Items walks the catalog from the one picked, several documents at a time, and keeps the items that match the dates, the most cloud cover and, with Only where the map is ticked, the map's extent. It lists the first 50 items it finds that match, sorted by date (the walk goes in the catalog's order, so in a large catalog these aren't the earliest or latest: pick a catalog further down for others). Undated items, and items without a footprint, are kept. A collection whose data are its own assets (as many Portolan collections' GeoParquet and PMTiles files are) is listed as an item of its own. A walk reads at most 400 documents and goes at most 8 catalogs deep; when it stops early, it says so: pick a catalog further down. Items are added as from an API: a cloud-optimised GeoTIFF is read in place, GeoParquet and FlatGeobuf by range, PMTiles a tile at a time.

stac.collections with a static catalog's "url" lists its children ("id" is each one's address), and stac.search walks one, with "phase" ("pre" or "post") for catalogs of events:

rustgis-cli run --cmd 'stac.search={"url":"https://vantor-opendata.s3.amazonaws.com/events/catalog.json","phase":"post"}'

The services below are STAC Search opened on one API or catalog, with the dialog titled after the service. Their commands (ui.stac.planet, ui.stac.portolan, ui.stac.sentinel2, ui.stac.vantor, ui.stac.usgsLidar) take "catalog" (a catalog's or collection's address to start from), "phase" and "search": true (find items at once).

items.title: Planet Open Data
items.text: Home › Add › Web Data › Planet Open Data… browses Planet's disaster data releases on Source Cooperative: imagery of earthquakes, floods, fires and storms from PlanetScope, SkySat and Pelican, before and after the event, licensed CC BY-NC 4.0. Pick an event (and, below it, its pre-event or post-event imagery or one collection), then Find Items; Add adds a scene's visual image.

items.title: Portolan
items.text: Home › Add › Web Data › Portolan… opens the Portolan registry, a catalog of the open data catalogs published with Portolan (cities, regions and agencies, most in Europe). Pick a publisher's catalog, then a theme or collection, then Find Items: each collection's files (GeoParquet, PMTiles and others) are listed, and Add adds the one chosen (visual first, often a PMTiles archive).

items.title: Sentinel-2 Explorer
items.text:
The Sentinel-2 Explorer: the clearest recent scenes where the map is, with their footprints.

Home › Add › Web Data › Sentinel-2 Explorer… searches Earth Search's Sentinel-2 Collection 1 Level-2A scenes (sentinel-2-c1-l2a) where the map is, over the last 90 days and with at most 20 % cloud cover, clearest first (sorted by cloud cover). Add adds the true colour image (visual); the asset list beside each scene offers its bands (red, nir, swir16, scl…), each a cloud-optimised GeoTIFF read in place. stac.search sorts with "sortby" ("eo:cloud_cover", "-datetime" for newest first) on APIs that sort.

items.title: Vantor
items.text: Home › Add › Web Data › Vantor… browses Vantor's open data (formerly Maxar's Open Data program): very high resolution imagery of disasters, one collection per event. Pick an event and a phase (before or after the event), then Find Items; Add adds a scene's visual cloud-optimised GeoTIFF.

items.title: USGS LiDAR
items.text: Home › Add › Web Data › United States › USGS LiDAR… searches the USGS 3D Elevation Program's LiDAR point clouds on the Planetary Computer (3dep-lidar-copc) where the map is: zoom to a town first. Each tile's data asset is a COPC file, signed with the Planetary Computer's token and added as a LiDAR point cloud (an evenly spread sample of its points, see Formats). A tile is downloaded whole, often tens of megabytes, so adding one takes a while.

items.title: Overture Maps
items.text:
Home › Add › Web Data › Overture Maps… adds Overture Maps' open data: buildings, places, transportation (segments and connectors), administrative divisions, base layers (land use, land, land cover, water, infrastructure, bathymetry) and addresses, from the latest release (or one named with "release"). Two ways:

  • The features where the map is. A theme's type is a few hundred GeoParquet files, each covering an area; Overture's STAC catalog gives every file's extent, so only the files that cover the map's view are read, in place by range like any GeoParquet by address (see Files on the web), and each becomes a layer read a view at a time. Zoom to a city or smaller: a view that takes more than six files is refused (a country takes dozens).
  • Map tiles of the whole world, from the theme's PMTiles archive, drawn a layer per type. Some themes' tiles hold their features only when zoomed in (places from zoom 14).

overture.add does the same ("theme", "type", "bbox" or the view, "tiles": true for the tiles):

rustgis-cli run --cmd 'map.zoomToExtent={"extent":[7.40,46.93,7.47,46.97]}' --cmd 'overture.add={"theme":"buildings"}' --cmd 'overture.add={"theme":"transportation"}' --cmd 'share.exportMap={"path":"bern.png"}'

The data's licences differ by theme (OpenStreetMap's ODbL for most, CDLA Permissive 2.0 for places); the layer says which.

items.title: Source Cooperative
items.text: Home › Add › Web Data › Source Cooperative… lists Source Cooperative's featured products (or an account's), browses a product's folders and adds a file by its address on the data proxy (https://data.source.coop/<account>/<product>/…): GeoParquet, FlatGeobuf, cloud-optimised GeoTIFFs and PMTiles are read in place, other files downloaded. sourcecoop.products ("account") and sourcecoop.list ("account", "product", "path", and "token" for the next page returned by a listing) list them; a listed file's "url" is added with layer.addUrl. These commands reach the network: the AI Assistant asks first and plugins need the network permission.

items.title: Natural Earth
items.text: Home › Add › Web Data › Natural Earth… is the Source Cooperative browser locked to Natural Earth's public domain map data as Source Cooperative holds it (opengeos/natural-earth): countries, states, coastlines, land, ocean, rivers, lakes, glaciers, urban areas, airports, railways and more. It opens on the pmtiles/ folder, whose archives are added as tile layers read in place; the geoparquet/, geojson/, gpkg/ and shapefiles/ folders hold the same themes as files, added as layers. With commands: sourcecoop.list ({"account": "opengeos", "product": "natural-earth", "path": "pmtiles/"}), then layer.addUrl with a file's "url".

items.title: Fields of the World
items.text:
Home › Add › Web Data › Fields of the World… adds the agricultural field boundaries the Fields of the World model found in Sentinel-2 imagery, worldwide, one year at a time (2017 to 2025; 2nd Edition, CC BY 4.0). Each year is a PMTiles archive on Source Cooperative read in place. Fields are drawn from zoom 9, filled and outlined by the model's score (0 to 100: red below 45, through orange and yellow, to green from 80); zoomed out, field density cells are drawn instead, coloured by the share of each cell covered by fields: Add field boundaries and Add field density add each. Score threshold hides the fields scoring below it. fieldsOfTheWorld.add does the same ("year", "draw": both, fields or density, "minScore"):

rustgis-cli run --cmd 'map.goToXY={"lon":-93.6,"lat":42.03,"scale":40000}' --cmd 'fieldsOfTheWorld.add={"year":2024,"minScore":40}' --cmd 'share.exportMap={"path":"fields.png"}'

The look is the tile layer's own style layers (map.addTiles takes MapLibre style layers as "styleLayers", drawing vector tiles in place of their default colours).

items.title: OpenStreetMap and administrative boundaries
items.text:
Home › Add › Web Data › OpenStreetMap… (osm.download) downloads OpenStreetMap data where the map is from an Overpass server: a preset (buildings, roads, railways, water, land use, parks, points of interest or administrative boundaries) or tag filters such as amenity=cafe, shop. The answer becomes up to three layers, points, lines and polygons: closed ways that are areas (buildings, land use and the like, as OSM reads their tags) are polygons, and multipolygon and boundary relations are assembled from their members. A layer's fields are its 25 most common tags, the rest in other_tags as GDAL writes them. The area can be up to 0.25 square degrees (about 50 × 50 km), and an answer up to 50,000 elements: the public servers are shared, so a larger area is better read from an extract (.osm.pbf). "url" names another Overpass server when the public one is busy.

Home › Add › Web Data › Boundaries… (boundaries.add) adds a country's administrative boundaries from geoBoundaries (CC BY 4.0): the country itself (ADM0), its states or provinces (ADM1) and finer divisions down to ADM5 where they exist, simplified for the map. boundaries.countries lists the countries.

rustgis-cli run --cmd 'osm.download={"bbox":[7.44,46.944,7.456,46.952],"preset":"buildings"}' --cmd 'boundaries.add={"country":"KEN","level":"ADM1"}'

Both reach the network: the AI Assistant asks before it runs them, and plugins need the network permission. OpenStreetMap data is © OpenStreetMap contributors (ODbL).

items.title: NASA
items.text: NASA's data comes two ways: NASA Earthdata… adds imagery that NASA serves as map tiles, and NASA Earthaccess… finds the data files themselves. Earthdata GIS… (see Web services) searches NASA's portal of map and feature services.

items.title: NASA Earthdata
items.text: Home › Add › Web Data › NASA Earthdata… lists the layers of NASA's Global Imagery Browse Services (GIBS) in Web Mercator: more than a thousand layers of satellite imagery and science data (MODIS, VIIRS, Landsat, sea surface temperature, aerosols, fires…), grouped by mission or instrument (the first part of their names) and searched by words. Most of them change day by day: they go on the time slider, as every layer with a time dimension does (see Layers that change with time).

items.title: NASA Earthaccess
items.text:
Home › Add › Web Data › NASA Earthaccess… searches NASA Earthdata as GeoLibre's Earthaccess panel does, through NASA's Common Metadata Repository (CMR):

  1. Dataset: pick one of the Popular datasets (ICESat-2 ATL03/ATL06/ATL08, GEDI L2A/L2B/L4A, HLS Landsat and Sentinel-2, NASADEM), or search by keyword (earthdata.collections), keeping to Earthdata Cloud only if you like, and pick one of the results. A popular dataset is its cloud-hosted, newest version.
  2. Granules: set the start and end dates (the last 30 days at first) and press Search this view (earthdata.granules): the granules where the map is, newest first, 25 at a time (Load more). Their footprints are drawn as a layer.
  3. Each granule is a card with its preview, date, size, cloud cover and number of files, and Add (its first GeoTIFF, desktop only, read in place when tiled), Download (a link to its first file), Zoom and Details (its page on Earthdata Search). Files lists every file, each GeoTIFF with its own desktop Add.

Searching needs no account, but NASA's data servers ask for an Earthdata Login token to read most files. Paste one in the pane's Earthdata Login section (or run earthdata.login). It is never put in the project, and is sent only over HTTPS to NASA's Earthdata data servers (*.earthdatacloud.nasa.gov and *.earthdata.nasa.gov), never to the login server itself; a redirect away from them (to the presigned address the file is served from) goes without it. A file the token doesn't open says so (an expired token, or a dataset whose EULA you haven't accepted on Earthdata Login).

The token is kept until RustGIS closes, unless you tick Remember on this computer (off by default; earthdata.login with "remember": true). The desktop app then keeps it in the system's credential store (macOS Keychain, Windows Credential Manager, or the Secret Service on Linux) and reads it back the next time it is needed: when the pane opens or a file is read from a data server. A token saved without the box ticked deletes the one remembered before. An expired token is forgotten, here and in the credential store, and the pane asks for a new one. earthdata.status reports whether a token is kept, its expiry, whether it is remembered and whether an expired one was forgotten; earthdata.logout (Remove token) forgets it and deletes the remembered one. The command line (--use-saved-secrets) and Python (use_saved_secrets=True) use the remembered token too; without them, and in the web app, a token lasts for the session.

In the web app, searching and footprints work, but NASA's data servers don't let web pages read their files (they send no CORS headers), so GeoTIFFs are added in the desktop app; Download still opens a file in a new tab, where Earthdata Login asks you to sign in.

rustgis-cli run --cmd 'earthdata.collections={"keyword":"GEDI biomass","cloudHosted":true}'
rustgis-cli run --sample --cmd 'earthdata.granules={"shortName":"HLSL30","bbox":[-90,42.5,-89,43.5],"start":"2024-06-01","end":"2024-06-30"}' --cmd 'share.exportMap={"path":"hls.png"}'
rustgis-cli run --sample --cmd 'earthdata.login={"token":"…"}' --cmd 'layer.addUrl={"url":"https://data.lpdaac.earthdatacloud.nasa.gov/lp-prod-protected/HLSL30.020/…/….B04.tif"}'
rustgis-cli run --sample --use-saved-secrets --cmd 'layer.addUrl={"url":"https://data.lpdaac.earthdatacloud.nasa.gov/lp-prod-protected/HLSL30.020/…/….B04.tif"}'

items.title: Open-data portals
items.text:
Home › Add › Web Data › Search Open Data… (portal.search) finds datasets by text in an open-data portal and lists, for each, the resources RustGIS can add, the best format first:

  • data.gov and CKAN catalogues: catalog.data.gov by default, using data.gov's own DCAT search, or a CKAN site by its address (https://open.canada.ca/data, https://data.gov.uk…). GeoJSON, FlatGeobuf, GeoParquet, GeoPackage, KML/KMZ, zipped Shapefiles, GeoTIFF, CSV, WMS, WFS and ArcGIS REST resources are offered; web pages, PDFs and the like are left out.
  • Socrata: every Socrata site through its discovery API, or one site such as data.cityofnewyork.us. Datasets with a location column are added as their GeoJSON export (up to 50,000 rows).
  • ArcGIS Hub: hub.arcgis.com or an organisation's Hub site; its feature services.

Only where the map is keeps to datasets covering the map's view. A file is added by its address (portal.add, read in place when it can be, as Add Data From URL… does); a service opens Add From Service… connected to it, to pick its layer (portal.add takes the first layer with features unless "layer" names one, or an ArcGIS map or image service's whole map). A search lists up to 50 datasets.

rustgis-cli run --cmd 'portal.search={"portal":"socrata","url":"data.cityofnewyork.us","query":"parks"}'
rustgis-cli run --sample --cmd 'portal.add={"url":"https://data.cityofnewyork.us/resource/enfh-gkve.geojson?$limit=50000","name":"Parks","portal":"https://api.us.socrata.com"}'

An address a portal lists is judged as one found in a document on the web: it may not point into the local network. Both commands reach the network, so the AI Assistant asks before it runs them, and plugins need the network permission. A dataset's licence is the portal's: its page (the Page link) says what it is.

items.title: Web services
items.text:
Several Home › Add › Web Data entries open the same search on one service, with its own choices (portal.search with the "portal" in brackets):

Entry What it finds Added as ArcGIS Portal… (arcgis-portal) Public items on ArcGIS Online, or on the portal whose address is given: feature, map, image and vector tile services, and GeoJSON files The service (Add From Service), or the file Dynamical… (dynamical) Weather and climate datasets from dynamical.org (NOAA GFS, GEFS and HRRR, ECMWF, DWD ICON…); Add opens the dataset's Zarr store in the pane to pick a variable and its time steps (a dataset published only as Icechunk says so) A Zarr variable's map Earthdata GIS… (earthdata-gis) NASA's Earthdata GIS portal: Earth science imagery, maps and features The service GeoLens… (geolens) A GeoLens server's vector datasets (https://datasets.geolibre.app by default) Features, the first 1,000 Hugging Face… (huggingface) Datasets on Hugging Face by name, or one by owner/name; Browse Files (portal.files) lists its GeoTIFFs, GeoParquet, GeoJSON, FlatGeobuf, GeoPackage, PMTiles, LiDAR and other files (public, not gated) The file Ocean Data Platform… (ocean-data) HUB Ocean's marine datasets, searched by words Features, up to 10,000 OpenAerialMap… (openaerialmap) Drone and aerial images on OpenAerialMap where the map is, newest first A COG, read in place France › IGN LiDAR HD… (ign-lidar) IGN's 1 km LiDAR HD tiles where the map is (a view of at most 2 square degrees) A COPC point cloud downloaded whole and sampled, like USGS LiDAR United States › Tennessee GIS… Tennessee's own portal, Tennessee GeoData: its public items, newest first, as it opens The service, or the file United States › US Federal GIS…, US State GIS…, US Local GIS… Curated public GIS portals of federal agencies (by department), states and the District of Columbia, and counties and cities (by state): pick a group and a portal; an ArcGIS organisation's public items (arcgis-portal with "org"), or a Socrata site The service, or the file United States › USGS 3DEP DEM… (usgs-dem) USGS elevation models from The National Map where the map is: 1 m, 1/9, 1/3 (the default) or 1 arc-second, or Alaska's 5 m ("dataset"), each tile's newest current edition A GeoTIFF, read in place

Results are cards, as in GeoLibre: a picture when the service has one, what the item is, who shared it and when, and Details (its description, id and extent), Portal (its page), Zoom (to its extent) and Add. A web map's Add lists its layers to add one by one. ArcGIS portals keep a search to All, Imagery, Maps, Features or Web maps, list their newest items when opened, and page with Load more.

The search by place (OpenAerialMap, LiDAR HD, 3DEP) is always where the map is, and its words, when given, keep to the images or tiles that have them: OpenAerialMap's to 200 images where the map is at a time (Load more looks at older ones), LiDAR HD's to the first 50 tiles. A Hugging Face dataset lists its first 1,000 files, and the Ocean Data Platform's catalogue is read whole (a few hundred datasets) and searched in RustGIS. In the web app, the Ocean Data Platform's features are read through GeoLibre's relay (tiles.geolibre.app), the platform answering only its own site, so those requests pass through it.

rustgis-cli run --cmd 'portal.search={"portal":"usgs-dem","bbox":[-122.25,46.15,-122.15,46.25]}'
rustgis-cli run --cmd 'portal.files={"dataset":"giswqs/geospatial"}'
rustgis-cli run --sample --cmd 'portal.add={"url":"https://data.geopf.fr/telechargement/download/LiDARHD-NUALID/NUALHD_1-0__LAZ_LAMB93_KE_2025-06-06/LHD_FXX_0652_6864_PTS_LAMB93_IGN69.copc.laz","name":"LiDAR HD 0652-6864"}'

items.title: Layers that change with time
items.text:
A WMS or WMTS layer with a time dimension, from any service, goes on the time slider by default: Follow the time slider, which the dialogs tick, and adding it from the Connections tree. Its requests then take the time of the slider's step, written as the layer writes its times (1995, 19951231, 2024-06-01, 2026-08-31T23:59:59Z), its GetFeatureInfo requests too, so identify answers for that time; time.export animates it.

  • A slider that is off is turned on with the layer's times: every step of a period it lists (2000-02-24/2026-10-28/P1D, a day at a time; when it lists only a period longer than the slider's 20,000 steps, every second, fourth… step), or the times it lists, at the layer's default (or its latest, when its default is no date). A slider already on keeps its steps; a service that lists other times may draw nothing at some of them, and a notice says so.
  • At one time instead: untick Follow the time slider. Date then takes one of the times the layer lists (hover over its "map by date" to see them, and its default), and empty adds it at the service's default. The same layer can be added at several times, each a layer named with its time.
  • A WMS layer (WMS 1.3.0 Annex C, 1.1.1) asks with TIME. Its default may be an interval; where the service lets a layer take several times at once (multipleValues), a list (1990,2000) or an interval (1990/2020, 1990/2020/P10Y) can be asked for too, otherwise one time.
  • One time only: a layer whose dimension lists a single time, a name (OGC's current, as most of swisstopo's WMTS layers list) or one date (1946), has no other to show: it is listed as a plain "map", without the dialogs' Follow the time slider, and added at its service's default (usually that time).
  • A time named, not dated: a layer whose times are only names (current, default), whose times are one period finer than the slider's hour (…/PT30M), or whose list of times would take more than the slider's 20,000 steps, isn't stepped through: it is added at its default.

With commands, service.add follows the slider when "time" is left out (or is "slider", or true); a time of the layer's draws it at that time, and "default" (or false) at the service's default. For example, a daily layer at one day, a yearly map on the slider exported as an animation, and a layer whose only time is current:

rustgis-cli run --cmd 'service.add={"url":"https://gibs.earthdata.nasa.gov/wmts/epsg3857/best/1.0.0/WMTSCapabilities.xml","layer":"MODIS_Terra_CorrectedReflectance_TrueColor","time":"2024-06-01"}' --cmd 'share.exportMap={"path":"gibs.png"}'
rustgis-cli run --cmd 'service.add={"url":"https://wms.geo.admin.ch/?SERVICE=WMS&REQUEST=GetCapabilities&VERSION=1.3.0","layer":"ch.swisstopo.pixelkarte-farbe-pk25.noscale"}' --cmd 'map.goToXY={"lon":7.4474,"lat":46.948,"scale":25000}' --cmd 'time.set={"interval":15}' --cmd 'time.export={"path":"bern.gif"}'
rustgis-cli run --cmd 'service.add={"url":"https://wmts.geo.admin.ch/EPSG/3857/1.0.0/WMTSCapabilities.xml","layer":"ch.swisstopo.pixelkarte-farbe"}' --cmd 'share.exportMap={"path":"map.png"}'

items.title: United States
items.text: Home › Add › Web Data › United States holds services covering the United States: the portals in the Web services table (Tennessee GIS, US Federal, State and Local GIS, USGS 3DEP DEM), USGS LiDAR, and the panels below.

items.title: EnviroAtlas, FEMA NFHL and The National Map
items.text:
EnviroAtlas… shows the US EPA's EnviroAtlas services (https://enviroatlas.epa.gov/arcgis/rest/services) as a tree: folders, their services (Add adds a service's whole map or image), and each service's layers, each with an Add of its own (drawn alone). A search looks through the services of every folder and of the folders in them, a few folders at a time. Add From Service also browses any ArcGIS services directory: its folders and the map, feature, image and vector tile services in them are listed with Open, which lists that folder or service (Back returns). A map service offers its whole map, each of its layers drawn alone (… (map)) and its layers' features. With commands, service.layers on a directory lists its folders and services, each with the url to list next.

FEMA NFHL… lists the layers of FEMA's National Flood Hazard Layer map service (https://hazards.fema.gov/arcgis/rest/services/public/NFHL/MapServer), searched by words: Add draws the whole map or one layer such as Flood Hazard Zones alone, and Features downloads a layer's features in the view (up to the server's limit). Its flood layers are drawn only from zoom 15 (closer than about 1:36,000), and FEMA's server can be slow to answer.

The National Map… lists 31 map services of the USGS The National Map and partners by category (basemaps, hydrography, elevation, imagery, cartography, hazards, other data, indexes), searched by words; Add adds one as a tile layer (the basemaps from their tile caches, the others as images the server draws). nationalMap.services lists them and nationalMap.add ("service": an id or title) adds one:

rustgis-cli run --cmd 'nationalMap.add={"service":"basemap/USGSTopo"}' --cmd 'nationalMap.add={"service":"hydro/wbd"}' --cmd 'map.goToXY={"lon":-105.27,"lat":40.0,"scale":300000}' --cmd 'share.exportMap={"path":"topo.png"}'

items.title: USGS NLDI
items.text:
Home › Add › Web Data › United States › USGS NLDI… uses the USGS Network-Linked Data Index on the NHDPlus river network, as GeoLibre's NLDI panel does. Each result is a layer:

  • Flowline: choose the whole flowline, or its part upstream or downstream of the point, and click the map (or type a longitude and latitude and press Trace, or Map centre). The flowline a raindrop falling there would reach is added, with the raindrop's path to it (nldi.flowline, the NLDI's flowtrace; when that fails, the nearest flowline and the way to it).
  • Basin from hydrolocation: the basin draining to the flowline (nldi.basin).
  • Navigation: pick upstream or downstream, main stem, tributaries or diversions, and a distance (1–9,999 km), and press Load sources & plot: the sources the navigation can list are loaded (nldi.sources) and the NHDPlus flowlines along it plotted (nldi.navigate). Pick another source (stream gages, water quality sites, wells, HUC12 pour points…) and press Plot another navigation layer to add it too.
  • Clear NLDI result removes the layers the pane added.

The NLDI's server is sometimes slow or fails for a point it hasn't seen before: try again a little later, or another point.

rustgis-cli run --sample --cmd 'nldi.flowline={"lon":-89.36083,"lat":43.08944}' --cmd 'nldi.basin={"comid":13293750}' --cmd 'nldi.navigate={"comid":13293750,"mode":"UM","distance":100}' --cmd 'nldi.navigate={"comid":13293750,"mode":"DM","distance":50,"source":"nwissite"}' --cmd 'share.exportMap={"path":"nldi.png"}'

items.title: Satellite embeddings
items.text:
Home › Add › Web Data › Satellite Embeddings… shows pre-computed satellite embeddings: vectors a geospatial foundation model made for every pixel or image patch, so that places alike have values alike. Pick a dataset (its provider, model, resolution, years, coverage, licence and links are shown), a year, and Search where the map is; the results are cards with Zoom and Add, their footprints drawn as a layer.

Dataset What RustGIS does with it AlphaEarth Foundations (Google's Satellite Embedding; 64 values a 10 m pixel, 2017–2025) Finds the year's UTM tiles where the map is in the dataset's GeoParquet index on Source Cooperative, read in place (its bounding boxes, then the rows that meet the map). Add shows a tile as a cloud-optimised GeoTIFF read in place: three bands (Bands, from 1; A01, A16 and A09 by default) as red, green and blue, dequantised (sign(v)·(v/127.5)²) and stretched over ±Stretch (0.3). Only the three bands shown are read, a band at a time. Apply to layers shows other bands or another stretch on the tiles already added. Earth Index (Earth Genome; 384 values every ~320 m, 2024) Names the Sentinel-2 (MGRS) tiles where the map is and keeps those with a file. Add points reads the file's points in the view in place (every point's position, then the vectors of those in view: zoom to a few kilometres) and colours them by their vectors' first three principal components (64 colours); Keep value keeps one of each vector's values as the points' value field. Tessera (Cambridge; 128 values a 10 m pixel, 2017–2025) Add view reads three bands (1, 2 and 3 by default) of the view from Tessera's Zarr store in place (the shard's index, then the chunks the view needs: at most about 6 km a side, its centre when the view is larger), as a 32-bit raster in UTM. Clay, Major TOM, Copernicus-Embed Listed with links to their data and papers; RustGIS doesn't read them.

AlphaEarth's tiles keep their look in their layer's address (#bands=2,17,10&range=-0.3,0.3&dequantize=aef), which map.setTiles changes for any cloud-optimised GeoTIFF read in place ("bands", "range", "dequantize"); GeoTIFFs with their bands stored apart (planar), signed bytes and bottom-up images are read in place too. The commands: embeddings.datasets, embeddings.search ("dataset", "year", "bbox" or the view, "footprints") and embeddings.add ("dataset", "url", "bands", "stretch", "dimension", "bbox", "year"):

rustgis-cli run --cmd 'map.zoomToExtent={"extent":[-122.55,37.7,-122.3,37.85]}' --cmd 'embeddings.search={"dataset":"alphaearth","year":2024}' --cmd 'embeddings.add={"dataset":"alphaearth","url":"https://data.source.coop/tge-labs/aef/v1/annual/2024/10N/xcyo46pot2fg6a61t-0000008192-0000000000.tiff"}' --cmd 'share.exportMap={"path":"aef.png"}'
rustgis-cli run --cmd 'map.zoomToExtent={"extent":[-83.96,35.94,-83.9,35.98]}' --cmd 'embeddings.add={"dataset":"tessera","year":2024}' --cmd 'share.exportMap={"path":"tessera.png"}'

These reach the network: the AI Assistant asks first and plugins need the network permission.

items.title: Workspace
items.text: Tools for working across maps and views, and for setting up the app the way you like it.

items.title: Projects
items.text:
Project › New, Open, Save and Save As manage .rgis project files; older .rgisx projects still open. A project keeps its maps, layers, styles, layouts, tables, tasks, models and other project items together. In-memory feature data is saved in the project; streamed layers reopen their sources, and file-backed rasters reopen their files. Keep those sources accessible when moving a project. See Project items for templates, packages and files for individual items.

Open also accepts a project package (.rgispkg), as do drag-and-drop and the desktop command line. A package opens as a new, unsaved project; Save writes a plain .rgis file. Opening or creating a project clears undo history; saving does not.

A • after the project's name in the title bar means it has unsaved changes. Undoing or redoing back to the state you last saved clears it. Before the desktop app discards unsaved changes, it asks Save changes to…? That happens when you quit or close the window, and when New, Open, the World Atlas sample, a template or a project dropped on the window would replace the project:

  • Save saves first and then goes on. A project that was never saved asks where to write it. If you cancel that, or the save fails, nothing is discarded.
  • Don't Save goes on without saving.
  • Cancel (or Escape) goes back to the project.

Commands don't ask: project.new, project.open and the rest replace the project as they always have when a script, a task, the AI Assistant, the command line or an attached agent runs them. The browser app doesn't ask yet; it warns before you leave a page with unsaved changes. On macOS, Quit RustGIS (⌘Q) and the Dock's Quit don't ask yet either. With autosave on (the default), RustGIS keeps your changes as a recovery copy and offers them back the next time it starts; with autosave off, they are lost, so save before you quit.

Saved layer addresses omit passwords, access keys, tokens and signatures. The open session keeps them, but after restarting RustGIS a protected source may need you to sign in to its connection again or add it again with credentials.

items.title: Autosave and recovery
items.text:
The desktop app keeps a recovery copy of unsaved work. While the project has changes that aren't saved, it writes a copy every few minutes (5 by default), and only when something changed since the last one. Choose how often, or turn it off, in Settings › Autosave (ui.autosave={"minutes": 10}; 0 is off). The copy is written in the background, so a large project doesn't hold up the app. It leaves out layer passwords, keys and tokens, as a saved project does. It is kept in the recovery folder of the app's data folder, not beside your project. Saving, opening or starting another project, and choosing Don't Save when you quit remove it.

If RustGIS crashes, is closed by the system or loses power, the next launch asks Recover unsaved work? and says how old the copy is.

  • Recover opens the work unsaved, under its file's name, so Save writes it back to that file. RustGIS warns you if the file was changed after the copy was made. A project that was never saved stays untitled, and Save asks where to write it.
  • Discard deletes the copy.
  • Later keeps the copy for the next launch.

If RustGIS crashes again before you decide, neither copy replaces the other. Up to five are kept and offered newest first, one per launch once you recover one. Recovering never replaces a project that has unsaved changes of its own: save it first.

The same choices are commands: ui.recover opens the copy, and ui.recover={"discard": true} deletes it. ui.autosave reports the interval and any copy waiting.

Quitting asks about unsaved changes first (see Projects). If RustGIS is quit without that answer (on macOS, Quit doesn't ask yet), it keeps a last copy of the work instead, and the next launch offers it back, saying RustGIS was quit without saving. With autosave off, nothing is kept. A second copy of RustGIS running alongside the first doesn't autosave, so it can't replace the first one's copy; it says so as it starts. Nor does RustGIS autosave when its settings folder can't lock files (some network or synced folders), where it can't tell a second copy apart. The browser app doesn't autosave yet; it warns before you leave a page with unsaved changes.

items.title: Session log
items.text:
RustGIS keeps a log of the commands run in the session: what was done, when, with what, and whether it worked. It is an audit trail of the session, for reviewing work or recalling what was run; it runs nothing again (History's Copy as code and recorded tasks do that). Every front end goes into it alike: the app, scripts, the AI Assistant, the command line, Python and MCP.

  • What goes in: each command that changes the project, and each that names a file, folder, address or connection, reads included (an export, a download, a save, opening a file), plus undo and redo, with the step they took back or brought back. Reading and looking around within the project (listing layers, describing a tool, reading features, moving the view) is left out. A command run by another (a script's lines, a model's steps) is inside its parent's entry. A plugin can't empty the log or turn it off, and reading it (project.log) takes the file permission, since it names the files and addresses the user's commands used.
  • Each entry: at (when it started, in milliseconds since 1970, UTC; for a plugin's command that waited for its downloads, when its last run started), command, params, ok, error when it failed, and millis, how long it took.
  • For the session only: the log is kept in memory, across the projects opened or made in the session, until RustGIS closes or the log is cleared. A saved project, its recovery copy, a package or a template carries none of it, so sharing a project shares no log. Reading, writing out, clearing or switching the log doesn't change the project and is no undo step; undoing a command doesn't take its entry back. Steps that undo takes back as one (a held arrow key nudging an element) are one entry, with the last one's parameters. Each copy of RustGIS (the desktop app, a browser tab, a Python program) keeps its own.
  • No secrets: the parameters lose passwords, keys and tokens as History's Copy as code does, and so does an error's text; a document given as text (a map, a project) or a file's contents in base64 (any text made only of base64's characters, so a long path with no dot too), past 200 characters, is kept as its size only (a shorter one is kept, its secrets taken out as any other text's), and an SQL CREATE SECRET's options as (…). A secret written as plain words, with no name or address form (a password typed into a note), isn't recognised: look at an exported log before sharing it. Each entry's parameters are clipped to about 4 KB of JSON (a long text is cut, a list keeps its first 100 items), its error to 500 characters and a …, and the log keeps its last 10,000 entries, the oldest dropped first. Plugins' commands take at most 1,000 of those places: past that, a plugin's new entry pushes out an older plugin entry, not one of the user's.

From scripts: project.log {"since"?, "until"?, "command"?, "failed"?, "limit"?} lists entries, newest last (command is an id, or the start of one ending in a dot, layer.; limit is a whole number, 100 by default and at most 1,000, with count saying how many match), and project.exportLog {"path": "log.csv"} writes it out as CSV (one row an entry, the parameters as a JSON column) or JSON Lines (.jsonl or .ndjson), as the path's extension says; any other extension (a .json, a project) is refused, whatever format is given. project.clearLog empties it (leaving its own entry) and project.logCommands {"on": false} stops it (what is there stays).

items.title: GeoLibre projects
items.text:
Open on desktop or Project › New › GeoLibre Project… opens a .geolibre or legacy .geolibre.json file as a new map in the current project. Existing maps stay in place. The same import is available to scripts:

project.importGeolibre={"path":"watershed.geolibre"}
project.importGeolibre={"url":"https://example.org/watershed.geolibre"}

The command also accepts JSON text, base64 data, and dir for moved local data files. An absolute data path is tried first, then its filename under dir (the project's folder by default). A desktop project may reference files outside that folder; import projects you trust to select those files. Browser imports can use inline GeoJSON and web addresses; local paths need desktop. A web app link such as ?project=https://example.org/watershed.geolibre imports the same map. This startup link takes precedence over other data/style links so download timing cannot change which map receives them.

The map keeps its view, bookmarks, background, layer visibility and opacity, and supported vector styles and field labels. The result includes map, layers and per-layer notes, distinguishing approximated presentation from skipped sources. Newer format versions are read as far as possible with a note. Unsupported layer kinds and project sections are reported rather than silently lost.

Colour classes and proportional sizes are supported separately. Combined colour-and-size styles keep colour and use a fixed size; graduated colour class boundaries are retained; proportional sizes use RustGIS's area scaling. Label halos use RustGIS defaults. Tile overlays draw above feature layers, and nested groups become flat folders with inherited visibility and opacity retained. Local data paths require a locally opened project or an explicit dir; URL and pasted-text imports cannot read local files without that folder. URL data downloaded in the browser fills its reserved layer position when it arrives; wait for those downloads before saving. Saving is refused while imported layers are still downloading. Recovery copies retain completed work and omit unfinished layers. A browser import can queue at most 16 whole-file downloads (fewer if other downloads are queued, active, or awaiting completion); a larger batch is refused before creating its map. Split that project into smaller imports or use the desktop app. Streaming tiles and COGs do not consume those download slots. Desktop GeoLibre URL imports wait for each download on the calling thread, which can pause the interface. Each request, including a remote MBTiles archive, has a 60-second timeout; download larger archives locally before importing. Zarr sources use their saved variable and dimension indices, or the first supported variable when those choices are absent. Imported Zarr stores are read one at a time with a 128 MiB download-buffer limit; larger slices must be reduced or opened through the desktop data workflow.

items.title: QGIS projects and styles
items.text:
A QGIS project (.qgs, or a .qgz archive) opens as a new map of the current project: Open on the desktop, or Project › New › QGIS Project… (project.importQgis={"path": "…/towns.qgs"}). The QGIS Project picker filters for .qgs and .qgz files on both desktop and web. Its layers come in the layer tree's order, each from its file (GeoPackage, Shapefile, GeoJSON, GeoTIFF and the other formats RustGIS reads), a CSV of points, XYZ tiles or a WMS layer, unchecked layers and groups hidden. The map takes the project's coordinate system and its saved view (or its layers' extent, when that view shows none of them), with no basemap and no graticule, as QGIS draws it. A project in degrees (EPSG:4326 and other supported longitude/latitude systems) opens in the Equirectangular projection, the plate carrée QGIS draws it in. The import is one undo step. Relative layer paths resolve from the project's folder on desktop. In the browser, relative file sources cannot be resolved and are listed in the import notes.

Each layer keeps its look:

  • Renderers: single symbol, categorized (as Unique Values, a category's merged values each a class, its "all other values" category the rest), graduated (as Graduated Colors), and rule-based where every rule picks values of one field (an else rule the rest); point cluster, displacement and other renderers that wrap one are drawn by the one inside.
  • Symbols: simple fills, lines and markers with their colours, widths in any unit, offsets, caps, joins, dashes and the symbol's opacity; a line's simple lines as stacked strokes, its rendering passes as their levels when the renderer draws in symbol levels; marker and hashed lines as strokes of markers or hash marks, at their places (intervals, vertices, the ends, the middle), turned with the line, their markers' offsets and angles kept; font markers as characters of their font, on points and along lines; a marker symbol of several layers, or one shifted, turned or anchored off its centre, as a point's marks; a marker angle taken from a field ("field" or - "field") as the layer's rotation field; a fill symbol of several layers as stacked fills, its brush patterns (horizontal, vertical, diagonal, cross) and line pattern fills as hatch lines, point pattern fills as markers on their grid, gradient and shapeburst fills with their colours or colour ramp, and the fills not drawn yet (dense brushes, SVG, raster and random fills as a tint of their colour).
  • Layer settings: opacity, blending, visibility range, filter (subset string), and the reference scale.
  • Rasters: singleband grey as a stretch from black to white, singleband pseudocolour as a stretch along its colour map (interpolated), as Classify (discrete) or as Unique Values (exact), paletted as Unique Values, multiband colour as RGB and hillshade as Shaded Relief; with the contrast enhancement's bounds as the stretch (following the view when QGIS works them out from the canvas), brightness, contrast and gamma, bilinear resampling, and the values its transparency, clipping and no-data settings hide as the raster's mask.
